title: Ala Wai Canal
theme: Once upon a time there were three streams

intro.text: Once upon a time there were 3 streams that flowed across the sands of
Waikīkī into the ocean!

To get away from the crowds, get some fresh air, yet still know that you are in Waikīkī, go for a leisurely walk or a gentle jog all around the Ala Wai Canal for a real surprise. And you will probably learn something new.
This walk is best taken in the cool of the early morning with water, a hat, and comfortable walking shoes.

The Ala Wai Canal can be circumnavigated beginning at any stop; however, from Waikīkī beach, this walk will begin at McCully Street and proceed in a clockwise direction all around the canal. In this way, the makai view of Waikīkī and the mountains from the mauka side of the Ala Wai Canal will be quite different.
This walk begins at the Ala Wai Canal and McCully Street. * Suggested reading on a bench

blocks.text: This street is named for Lawrence McCully, former owner of neighboring land and a Justice of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i Supreme Court during the reign of King Kalākaua. McCully Street Bridge crosses the Ala Wai Canal into the residential and commercial area of the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX.

From this vantage point, with your back to the beach, as you cross the bridge over the Ala Wai Canal is the Hawai‘i Convention Center on the ‘Ewa side, which opened in 1998. In 1931, this was the site of the Ala Wai Inn and the infamous Massie Case.
After the bridge, just before Kapi‘olani Boulevard, at the first opening in the lava stone wall, turn Diamond Head and walk into Ala Wai Community Park.

Bus routes and times www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator. 1.5 hour, 3 miles round trip, 6,000 steps PARKING: On-street parking can be found along Date Street on the mauka side of the canal. It’s free, except no parking 3:30 to 6:30 pm Mondays through Fridays. Parking garage across from the Hale Koa Hotel on Kālia Road. Parking lot on the corner of Kālia and Saratoga roads.
The Hau flower, which is related to the Hibiscus, lives for only one day, changing from yellow to reddish brown when it drops.
Kapi‘olani Boulevard is named for King Kalākaua’s wife, Queen Kapi‘olani. More about the Queen on the Kāneloa Walk VI.

Please take a moment to admire the different types of canoes, especially the outrigger canoes. In the afternoon, after school and work, men and women come to the canal to practice their strokes. Be sure to come back to watch them: it’s very picturesque! Perhaps you will be lucky to catch a practice.
Enjoy the shade of the trees:

• Milo, recognizable by its heart-shaped leaf; • Kou, identifiable by its small bright orange flower, easily strung into a lei; • Hau, related to the Hibiscus with a similar, but smaller flower and a large round leaf; • Monkey Pod, the large sprawling branches with a bristle-like pink flower.
• Palm trees also abound.
Continue walking Diamond Head toward the canoes along the mauka side of the canal.
*You might like to sit at the picnic table or on a bench and read about the history of the canal.

Present-day dredging of the canal is a relentless one since silt is a constant at the bottom. The first idea for a canal here was proposed as early as 1905, but actual construction began in 1921. By 1928, the Waikīkī Drainage Canal – the canal’s original name - was completed, thereby drastically altering not only the topography, lifestyle, and fate of the beach area known as Waikīkī, but also the lives of the Hawaiian people.
Ala Wai means ‘fresh waterway,’ referring to the freshwater streams that empty into it from the mountains and valleys.
The Ala Wai Canal, 9,700 feet long and 250 feet wide, varies in depth from 10 to 20 feet.

Today, due to lack of consistent dredging, the deepest point is only 6 feet. At some places, there are only a few inches of water, making it into a virtual mud pond, reminiscent of the earlier kalo (taro) fields and fish ponds in the area! The canal serves a watershed area of the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. The Ala Wai Canal is not lined with a cement floor; this is unlike many drainage canals and streams in Hawai‘i. The canal is carved out of natural solid coral.

Recently, the canal has been given some much-needed care and attention by having Genki Balls thrown into it! If you see a group of people throwing balls into the Ala Wai, that’s what is going on! These balls are made of mud and contain healthy microbial bacteria that digest and oxygenate the sludge at the bottom as well as destroy damaging bacteria. And it’s working – the canal is much cleaner and healthier than it has been in years past. Genki means ‘healthy’ in Japanese!

Original topography of the area included three streams running down from the mountains into the valleys and through Waikīkī, each emptying directly into the Pacific Ocean. Waikolu Way, a small street between Royal Hawaiian and Seaside avenues, is reminiscent of those three streams: Waikolu means ‘three waters.’
You will see these lovely green signs along the way. The intent is for people to walk from park to park around the island, like a lei. We will follow a Waikīkī lei of parks.
Those three rivers, beginning from the ‘Ewa side of Waikīkī and superimposed on the accompanying map are: Pi‘inaio Stream, ‘Āpuakehau Stream, and Kuekaunahi Stream.
• Pi‘inaio Stream exited ‘Ewa of Duke Kahanamoku Beach and Lagoon; • ‘Āpuakēhau Stream had its outlet near present-day Outrigger Hotel; • Kuekaunahi Stream met the ocean near Kapahulu Avenue.

These three streams once furnished Waikīkī with a natural freshwater irrigation system for all the fish ponds, taro fields, duck ponds, and rice fields in the area. These three streams, Makiki, Mānoa, and Pālolo streams, now supply the Ala Wai Canal with its water.

The entire region from the Ala Moana Shopping Center to Kapi‘olani Park was once replete with taro fields, fish ponds, and migrant ducks. After the arrival of the Chinese in the 19th century, rice fields and ponds for domesticated ducks were added.

By 1900, O‘ahu businessmen had recognized the fantastic development potential of the Waikīkī area. The waterfront had long been famous for its beauty and charm. But the neighboring ponds and fields came to be seen as obstacles to Waikīkī’s development. Soon, financial interests dictated that these fields and ponds be eliminated. Vast quantities of coral removed in the canal’s dredging were used as fill, thus raising Waikīkī to its average contemporary elevation of six feet above sea level.
Along with the disappearance of the taro and rice fields, fish and duck ponds, vanished a way of life for the Hawaiian people.
Soon after the canal was finished, local fishermen built chairs on stilts (called horses!) right into the water to fish – mainly mullet.
Originally, the canal was to empty into the Pacific Ocean at both ends. By the late 1920s, however, when the canal had reached its present configuration, funds for the project were exhausted.

Just past the second ballfield, at the opening in the chain-link fence, walk diagonally across toward the S-shaped blue and white building, the Marco-Polo, for a close-up view of the stream, a remnant of Fishermen on “horses” in the Ala Wai Canal (1930s) sitting on the makai side of the canal. Notice the Ko‘olau mountains in the background. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

‘Āpuakēhau Stream (Hawai‘i State Archives) an earlier stream that still flows from the Mānoa mountains and courses though the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili. This is most likely one of the branches of the historic ‘Āpuakēhau Stream (Stop 21 for more information). Notice the red JapaneseMonet-style bridge.
Alternatively, continue along the path, especially if the field is muddy.

After you cross the bridge walk diagonally makai across the next field to the Ala Wai Park and canoe hale ‘house,’ located on the Ala Wai Canal. Walk along the canal, stopping at a bench to read about the canal at Stop 8 .
Continue along to the Ala Wai Neighborhood Park and playground

Until recently, the Mālia, a sacred canoe, was housed at the Waikīkī Surf Club’s canoe hale. The Mālia, on the National Historic Register of Historic Places, was used as a model for today’s fiberglass canoes.
As its name implies, University Avenue mauka leads directly to the University of Hawai‘i. A bridge is planned to span the canal to Kālaimoku Street.
Looking mauka, with your back to the Ala Wai Canal, enjoy valley and mountain views.
The vegetables in the Ala Wai Community Garden are lovingly tended daily by residents from all around Honolulu. Please admire, but don’t take any produce – it’s private property.
Ala Wai Elementary School, a public school, is located behind the Community Garden.
You might see a lot of dogs here; they are probably being led to the Ala Wai Dog Parks where they can run around safely.
*There are many benches along the way where you can stop to rest and read about the next two places.
Wouldn’t it be lovely to learn how to paddle an outrigger canoe?
Enjoy walking in the shade of the Milo trees.

‘Iolani School, a private school, sits adjacent to Ala Wai Elementary. ‘Iolani, ‘heavenly hawk,’ is one of the largest private schools in the United States. ‘Iolani is affiliated with the Episcopal church and was founded as a mission school for boys, but today accepts students of all beliefs and backgrounds.
Dr. Sun Yat-Sen, the father of the Republic of China, was an 1882 graduate of ‘Iolani. A lovely statue of a young Sun Yat-Sen, usually graced with a lei, greets today’s students.
The gates on the Diamond Head side of ‘Iolani School are the original 1941 gates from its earlier location in Nu‘uanu.

After a while, the walkway veers off mauka. This is the mouth of the MānoaPālolo Drainage Canal. No, not a very poetic name… This “drainage canal” was originally two important streams, the Mānoa from Mānoa Valley, and the Pālolo from Pālolo Valley, which, before the canal came into existence in the 1920s, fed the lush aquaculture and agricultural ponds of Waikīkī. This canal is so-named because it drains water from both the Mānoa and Pālolo streams, each flowing out from its respective valley and joining together just mauka of the H-1 Freeway. The diversion and displacement of these streams came about with the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s.
Feel free to walk around the Ala Wai Garden, but please do not help yourself to any of the vegetation. Each garden is privately tended.

As you turn away from the Ala Wai Canal to walk mauka along the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal, you’ll be walking around the Ala Wai Golf Course to Date Street (then to Kapahulu Avenue, and back to the makai side of the canal and Waikīkī).
*This is a good vantage point for viewing the ridges and valleys of the Ko‘olau mountain range that provide an imposing backdrop for Waikīkī.
The valley directly ahead is Pālolo Valley. Its name refers to a type of clay.
Above Pālolo Valley on the Diamond Head side is Wilhelmina Rise, named for one of the Matson Navigation Company ships. ‘Ewa is Saint Louis Heights, named for a school located on its slopes.

Below St. Louis Heights, on the ‘Ewa side is Mānoa Valley, the largest valley on this side of O‘ahu. The main campus of the University of Hawai‘i is in this cool, lush valley. On a hot day, it’s a treat to hike back to Mānoa Waterfalls. (Please check to be sure it is open to visitors if you’d like to go.) Follow the Mānoa Walk X to access the waterfalls.

Between Mānoa Valley and the Ala Wai Canal is the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili, a residential and commercial district. Mō‘ili‘ili means ‘pebbled lizard’. Hawaiian mo‘olelo (legend) tells us that this name refers to a lizard destroyed by Hi‘iaka, sister of the volcano deity, Pele. If this intrigues you, there is a walk about the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili, Walk IX.

This location and anywhere along the canal are excellent viewing points for late afternoon double rainbows. Double rainbows, which are often seen in Hawai‘i after a rainfall, consist of a bright main rainbow below a fainter outer rainbow. The outside rainbow is always a mirror image of the main rainbow, and its colors are in reverse order. Perhaps you have noticed the two stylized rainbows on the side of the Hilton Hawaiian Village: that is not a double rainbow because it not a mirror image (refer to Kālia, Walk II).

This walk along the mauka side of the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal ends at Date Street, where you will turn Diamond Head to walk across the 1937 WPA bridge to Kapahulu Avenue. This is another great place to view the Ko‘olau mountain range.
This is the original confluence of the Mānoa and Pālolo streams. The joining of the two streams was moved mauka during the building of the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s.

Across Date Street are the sports fields of Kaimukī High School. This area was The tallest mountain in the Ko‘olau range is Konahuanui at just over 3,000 feet in Mānoa Valley. the original confluence of the Mānoa and Pālolo streams! When the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal was built, the convergence was moved about a ½ mile mauka of here (check your map to find it). The ditch at the edge of the golf course on the makai side of Date Street is a possible vestige of the original streams. A low lava stone wall on the mauka side of Date Street is across a ditch for the original stream.
WALKING BACK TO WAIKĪKĪ

stops.title: Ala Wai Golf Course and Club

blocks.text: The Ala Wai Golf Course, a 146-acre municipal course, located here on the mauka side of the canal, extends from the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal to Kapahulu Avenue. The golf course is laced with remnants of earlier streams.

The original nine-hole golf course opened on September 13, 1931, as the first municipal course in Hawai‘i. The course was built on the site of the Territorial Fairgrounds. The second nine holes opened on July 10, 1937, with one of the structures at the fair serving as its clubhouse. During World War II, the golf course was set up as an emergency landing air stip.
In 1948, a new clubhouse was built, named after Francis ‘Ī‘ī Brown, “the Father of Golf in Hawai‘i.” In 1989, a $5.8 million clubhouse was constructed.

Local lore relates that the origin of the golf course dates to the early 1920s when two local men sank a can where hole number 6 is now located for their on-thespot golf course! However, another story recounts that local caretakers of the Territorial Fairgrounds set up their own course, charging 25 cents a hole! At one time, this golf course was reputed to have been the busiest golf course in the United States!
Notice the incised WPA and 1937 on the bridge, a time when the federally-funded Works Progress Administration provided work and services.

Continue along Date Street with the golf course on the makai side, following the “Lei of Parks” walkway where you will notice the ponds and waterways on the course itself: remnants of ponds and streams of hundreds of years ago.

Along Date Street, on the mauka side, you will pass some unusual street names because even though they look Hawaiian, they are not. Frank L. James developed this area in 1926 and named these streets after people in his family. All except the first one are Hawaiianized English name:
• Olokele Avenue - ‘honeycreeper bird’

• Lukepane Avenue - ‘Lucy Frances,’ his wife • Ekela Avenue – ‘Ethel,’ family member • Makaleka Avenue - ‘Margaret,’ his daughter • Palani Avenue - ‘Frank,’ his son • Kamuela Avenue - ‘Samuel,’ family member • Date Street is the only extension of the plant and tree-named streets from Sheridan Tract and the McCully area.
Kiawe and Monkey Pod trees line the perimeter of the golf course with Palm trees scattered around the course.
Date Street ends at Kapahulu Avenue, where you will turn makai to continue around the makai side of the Ala Wai Canal.
Kapahulu means ‘the worn-out soil,’ from the overuse of the land for growing kalo (taro).

At this point if you need a break, cross Kapahulu Avenue to the eateries on Mo‘oheau (a former chief) Avenue, where you will find several eateries, including the local Kozo Sushi – stop in for hand rolled sushi (keeps the nori fresh)!
If you need a break from walking, there are several buses that run along Kapahulu Avenue back to Waikīkī.
Bus routes and time www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 – option 2 – for a live operator.

If you would like to continue on this adventure, follow the “Lei of Parks” asphalt walkway alongside the golf course. It is intended that this Lei of Parks will form a lei of walkways around the island.

The original intent of the configuration for the Ala Wai Canal was to have another exit to the ocean at this end, but (thankfully) the developers ran out of money; hence, the canal ends at ‘Āinakea Way.

Across Kapahulu Avenue is the Waikīkī Fire Station No. 7 with its dazzling yellow fire engines. Its sleek, clean lines make this building appear quite modern, but it was constructed 100 years ago, in 1927. The firehouse was designed by architects Davis and Fishbourne and is surely one of the loveliest firehouses, especially its Hawaiianstyle roof line, to be found anywhere.
As you turn the corner ‘Ewa you will go around the Waikīkī-Kapahulu Public Library.

The library is one of Waikīkī’s architectural gems. Its exterior walls are made of locally hewn sandstone blocks. The ceiling is of imported cedar wood; the interior doors, the reading bench, and children’s tables are of native koa wood. The cathedral windows provide natural reading light.
Walking on the makai side of the canal.

The first Waikīkī library was in a wooden cottage on the grounds of Thomas Jefferson School, across Ala Wai Boulevard. In 1952 this library, designed by Lemmon and Freeth, opened its doors to the public. In the entryway, view the wall sculpture of an outrigger canoe.
Behind Waikīkī-Kapahulu Library is another library – the Hawai‘i State Library for the Blind and the Physically Handicapped, which is why the walk signal across Kapahulu Avenue beeps.
The street mauka-‘Ewa of the libraries leads to the clubhouse of the Ala Wai Golf Course.
Thomas Jefferson Elementary School, like most local state schools, was originally an English standard school, converting to the state system in 1952.
Walking on the makai side of the canal This walk, which circumnavigates the Ala Wai Canal, continues along the makai side of the canal. Each street

name encountered will be described and its name translated. Some street names appear arbitrary; however, others are interrelated with neighboring streets, such as Paoakalani meaning ‘royal perfume’ and the three streets following it, all concern Queen Lili‘uokalani.
The view of the downtown skyscrapers downstream from the Diamond Head end is very impressive.

As you walk along this side of the canal you will notice small bridges, drainage holes, and drainage canals on the mauka side. Some of the streams still follow their earlier courses as shown on the accompanying map, but many have been diverted or altered. Both sides of the canal are lined with Palm trees and Hau trees, once abundant in Waikīkī. The trees with the large leaves are Hau.
‘Āinakea means ‘white land’. Its name refers to the appearance of a type of sugar cane grown in the islands.
*There are many benches along the way; please do stop, rest, and read in the shade as you go along. Also notice the bi-level Victorian lamp posts. And, as the signs state, do not eat the fish!

The water bubbling up and emptying into the canal across the way may be a remnant of Kuekaunahi Stream that once flowed into Waikīkī at this approximate area. The fresh waters flowed down from the mountains, through this section, and emptied into the Pacific Ocean near Kapahulu Avenue.

With the construction of the Ala Wai Canal, Kuekaunahi Stream was forever lost to history as it was diverted into the canal further upstream. The meaning and even the correct Hawaiian spelling of Kuekaunahi (Kukaunahi and Ku‘ekaunahi) have grown obscure with the passage of time. One possible meaning is ‘to remove scales from fish.’
The next four streets, which border on Ala Wai Boulevard, recall the reign of Hawai‘i’s last ruling monarch, Queen Lili‘uokalani. Notice that streets concerning the monarchy are “avenues.”

Queen Lili‘uokalani owned a large tract of land in this part of Waikīkī, known as Hamohamo, meaning ‘rub gently,’ referring perhaps to the action of the water on the sand. The Queen owned several homes in Waikīkī. The Queen lived from 1838 to 1917 but ruled slightly less than two years, from 1891 to 1893, when she was deposed by a small group of unscrupulous men.

Wai Nani means ‘beautiful water’ and most likely refers to the beautiful Kuekaunahi Stream that flowed through the Queen’s land. The Lili‘uokalani Garden Towers on the makai side of Ala Moana Boulevard are situated on or near her Paoakalani home.
Paoakalani, means the ‘royal perfume.’ This was the name of Queen Lili‘uokalani’s favorite Waikīkī home that was located between Paoakalani Avenue and Wai Nani Way.
‘Ōhua means ‘retainer’ or ‘servant,’ and refers to one of the residences of the retainers of Queen Lili‘uokalani. Kuekaunahi Stream may have coursed along here, through Hamohamo.
The building across the canal is the clubhouse of the Ala Wai Golf Course.

This street obviously commemorates Queen Lili‘uokalani, whose birth name, Lydia Lili‘u Loloku Walania Kamaka‘eha, literally means ‘smarting of the high born one.’ This Queen was so named, legend tells us, because on the day of her birth, her “Beautiful Water” meets Ala Wai Boulevard, the “way to the water” hanai (Hawaiian foster) mother’s aunt was suffering from eye pain.

The story of her life is put forth in her book, Hawai‘i’s Story by Hawai‘i’s Queen. This is a fascinating account of her life and those around her. It is illustrated and includes genealogies and appendices of major documents and events during her lifetime. The author is simply…Lili‘uokalani.

A graceful statue of Queen Lili‘uokalani is situated in downtown Honolulu, between ‘Iolani Palace (the only palace in the United States) and the State Capitol. Ironically, her back is to the palace where she was imprisoned after the overthrow.
‘Āpuakēhau Stream and the next street recall the life of Princess Ka‘iulani.

The small, bridged, palm-lined steam across the canal may be one of the branches of historic ‘Āpuakēhau Stream as it entered Waikīkī from Mānoa Valley. ‘Āpuakēhau means ‘basket of dew,’ but it also refers to a gentle rain. The royalty rinsed their bodies in this cool freshwater stream after swimming and surfing in the saltwater ocean.

The stream’s name may refer to the vast quantities of Hau trees, Palm trees, and Ti plants that lined its banks all the way to the ocean. ‘Āpuakēhau, the middle of Waikīkī’s three streams, flowed down from the mountains above Mānoa Valley, passed through the ‘Āinahau property where Princess Ka‘iulani lived, then emptied into the ocean ‘Ewa of the Moana Hotel. ‘Āpuakēhau was the best known of Waikīkī’s waterways because it flowed beside the royal residences and gave its name to the heiau near the ocean. A heiau is a Hawaiian open-air religious structure. (Follow the Helumoa Walk III for more information about that area.)
Enjoy the Plumeria grove.

There are two interesting historic plaques on the makai side of Ala Moana Boulevard: A Historic Residence plaque at 2457-2455 Ala Wai Boulevard dates the Mediterranean-Italianate Style Ala Wai Villas to 1936.
A plaque on the inside of a fence on the makai side of Ala Moana Boulevard states that this is the “site of the house on the ten-acre estate ‘Āinahau.”

Ka‘iulani means ‘the sacred height’ and is named in honor of Princess Ka‘iulani who lived near here with her parents who called this area ‘Āinahau, ‘land of the Hau tree.’ It is said that Princess Ka‘iulani traveled downstream on ‘Āpuakēhau Stream in a small boat to the ocean, possibly following the course of present-day meandering Ka‘iulani Avenue! For more information about Princess Ka‘iulani and her home in ‘Āinahau, stroll the streets on the ‘Āinahau-Hamohamo Walk III.
Across the plains to the Ko‘olau Mountains. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Kānekapōlei means ‘man of the thick flower lei.’ This street was named for Marion Kānekapōlei Guerrero Diamond, resident of this area in the 1930s, who was named for an uncle of a wife of King Kamehameha I.
Walina means ‘softness’. The bridged stream across the canal may be a small branch of ‘Āpuakehau Stream.
Nāhua means ‘the fruits.’ This street is named for Nāhua, a Hawaiian chiefess who owned property between the Royal Hawaiian and Halekūlani hotels.
Nohonani means ‘sit daintily.’ This is a poetic phrase often used in songs honoring royalty - here, Queen Lili‘uokalani..
This street is named for the Waikīkī Seaside Hotel, which preceded the Royal Hawaiian Hotel from 1894 to 1927.

The Mānoa-Pālolo Drainable Canal empties across the way. Ironically, the streets here are the only 3 with English names: Seaside, Royal Hawaiian (a block away), and Lewers. All the other street names along the canal are in ‘Ōlelo Hawai‘i (Hawaiian).
Follow the purple line to visit a few places of interest:
• Centennial Park: One block

makai on the corner of Aloha Drive is the newly created Centennial Park lovingly established by the Rotary Club. It is “an oasis of tropic beauty” that includes green and red Ti plants, Queen Emma spider lilies, and Pōhinahina, an indigenous ground cover.
• 413 Seaside Avenue: If you are
interested in pre-war architecture, continue makai, past Centennial Park to 413 Seaside Avenue, with the One of many streets along the Ala Wai named for associates and family of Kamehameha the Great.
Be sure to follow the Helumoa Walk (III) to visit with Gabby.
Moongate entryway. This 1938 Art Deco building, which is listed on the Historic Register, was built of concrete bricks and Philippine mahogany.
Waikolu Way: A few blocks makai of Aloha Drive is Waikolu Way, meaning ‘3 waters,’ waters that flowed though Waikīkī before the canal was built:

• Pi‘inaio Stream, ‘Ewa of here near today’s ‘Ilikai Hotel; • ‘Āpuakehau Stream, which exited near the Moana Hotel; and • Kuekaunahi Stream, at the Diamond Head of the canal, which flowed out near Kapahulu Avenue.

Originally Lewers Road, this is the longest north-south street in Waikīkī beach. At the turn of the 19th century, Robert Lewers (1836-1926), a New Yorker who became a local businessman and his family resided at the present site of the Halekūlani Hotel.

Lewers Street, aka Waikīkī Beach Walk, is a recently created walkway of stores and restaurants. However, it is also a tribute to Hawaiian music with the statue of Gabby Pahinui (1921-1980) at the makai end of “Beach Walk.” He played the slack key guitar and had a magnificent falsetto voice. He was instrumental in the Hawaiian Renaissance, which began in the 1970s.
Kai‘olu, ‘cool ocean,’ is a reference to a time when this street may have met the ocean, which it does not today.
Launiu refers to the ‘coconut leaf ’ of the ubiquitous Coconut (niu) trees.
The next five streets are named for persons associated with the first two Kamehameha kings, and their spouses.
King Kamehameha I (Kamehameha the Great), who lived from 1758 to 1819 and united the islands in 1810.
King Kamehameha II (Liholiho), who lived from 1797 to 1824 and reigned during his last five years.

Kālaimoku means ‘island manager’ or ‘island carver’. This street was named for a prime minister under King Kamehameha I and Queen Ka‘ahumanu. Also known as Kālanimoku, he died in 1827. Kālanimoku was victorious in the Battle at Kuamo‘o on Hawai‘i Island. (Continue reading at Kuamo‘o Street to learn more about the battle.) Kālanimoku State Office Building, in the downtown Civic Center, is named after him.
Looking directly across the canal from Kālaimoku Street is University Avenue, which leads into Mānoa Valley and the University of Hawai‘i.
John Young, advisor to Kamehameha the Great, is remembered in this street sign ‘Olohana.

‘Olohana was the Hawaiian name of John Young I, a castaway English sailor who was stranded in 1790 at Kealakekua, on Hawai‘i Island, where Captain Cook was killed. ‘Olohana became the principal advisor to Kamehameha the Great and helped the king invade and conquer Maui. ‘Olohana married Kuamo‘o, a niece of Kamehameha the Great. One of his grandchildren was Queen Emma, wife of Kamehameha IV. ‘Olohana died in 1835.

The name ‘Olohana is said to be a transliterated Hawaiian borrowing of the English phrase, ‘All hands!’ which Young reportedly shouted at his fellow sailors. Interestingly, the verb ‘olohani means ‘to strike’ or ‘to mutiny’.
Nāmāhana was mother to Queen Ka‘ahumanu, King Kamehameha I’s favorite wife. Ka‘ahumanu’s father was Ke‘eaumoku, as in the street name in Honolulu.
Nāmāhana means ‘the twins.’ Nāmāhana is one of many names for the twin constellation Castor and Pollux, Nānā Mua ‘look forward’ and Nānā Hope ‘look behind,’ respectively.

Kuamo‘o means ‘backbone of the lizard.’ This street is named for John Young I’s wife, Mary Kuamo‘o Ka‘o‘ana‘eha. John Young I, as in ‘Olohana Street, was advisor to Kamehameha I. Kuamo‘o was a niece of Kamehameha I. Kuamo‘o, in turn, had been named in honor of the place on Ala Wai Boulevard leaves Lē‘ahi behind but continues ‘Ewa around the canal to Ala Moana Boulevard.

Hawai‘i Island where her brother, Keauou Kekuaokalani, was killed in the failed December 1819 battle fought over maintaining the eating kapu (taboo), known as ‘ai kapu (eating taboo). At that time, women were forbidden to eat with men, and were allowed to eat only certain foods. For example, only certain types of bananas were permitted to be eaten by women; all other varieties were kapu. After Kamehameha I died in November 1819, his wives and son, Liholiho, who became Kamehameha II, overturned that kapu by eating together, thereafter known as ‘ai noa (eating free from taboo).

Kohala Kuamo‘o: Nae‘ole’s Race to Save a King (2011) is a bilingual (yes, HawaiianEnglish) oral tradition children’s book about a family name written by-then 12 year old Kekauleleanae‘ole Kawai‘ae‘a (Lele to his family and friends but notice Nae‘ole in his full Hawaiian name.). The story, about Kamehameha I and how Lele’s name is relevant, takes place not far from Kuamo‘o on Hawai‘i Island.
A stream that runs below the huge blue S-shaped condominium on the opposite side of the canal is a remnant of the stream from the Ko‘olau mountains.

Keoniana is a transliterated Hawaiian borrowing of the English name, John Young. The street is named for John Young II, son of ‘Olohana, who served as kahuna nui, ‘executive officer’ under Kamehameha II and as minister of foreign affairs under Kamehameha IV.
The author’s mother, who inspired the writing of this book, lived on this street in the 1970s.
Pa‘ū Street is named for the ‘ili, the sur-

rounding area and a nearby pond that was part of the Hawaiian agricultural and aquacultural system. The pond was first used for fish and kalo (taro) growing, and later, when the Chinese moved into the area, ducks and rice were introduced.
Pa‘ū Street today is a heavily traveled route connecting Ala Moana Boulevard with McCully Street.

This word, pa‘ū, shows the importance of marking long vowels and glottal stops in the Hawaiian spelling system: the long mark (kahakō) above the vowel to lengthen the vowel sound and the backwards apostrophe (‘okina) for the glottal consonant.
• pau without any diacritics means ‘finished.’
• pa‘u with an ‘okina between the vowels means ‘soot.’
• pa‘ū with a long u and an ‘okina between the vowels means ‘moist.’
• pā‘ū with a long a, long u, and an ‘okina between the vowels refers to ‘a woman’s skirt, a sarong’ or ‘a mat covering for a canoe’.
You can take your choice for the meaning of this street!
Niu is the Hawaiian word for coconut (recall Launiu Street), the most common Kahanamoku St.

Walk II Map Key

This walk covers part of a much larger district once known as Kālia, a vast area of ponds and fields on Kālia Bay where Hawaiians called home. Kālia of old extended as far as (present-day) Ala Moana Center.

Kālia was a subdivision, or ‘ili, of the ahupua‘a, ‘large land division’ of Waikīkī. The name Kālia is translated as ‘waited for.’ This name derives from a Hawaiian mo‘olelo (legend) based on the long wait undertaken by a young man whose beautiful wife had been wooed away by a rival Maui chieftain. We still don’t know whether his vigil was ever rewarded!
Kalia, without the kahakō, is a native tree. Note that neighboring ahupua’a, Honolulu, was originally known as Kou, also a tree; however, it is indigenous, not native.

In 1911, an enterprising American young man, Percy Martyn Pond (1870-1945), realized the potential of Kālia, buying up land in Kālia as well as land at the higher Diamond Head end of Waikīkī. He used that elevated land to fill in low-lying areas of Kālia where he built vacation cottages. He was also one of the first developers in Mānoa, starting up College Hill Tract (named after Punahou School, not the University of Hawai‘i. (Mānoa Walk X for more information.)
Kālia Road is mentioned in Earl Derr Biggers’ 1925 mystery novel, The House Without a Key, which took place at the site of the Halekūlani Hotel.

Up until the mid-1920s, Kālia was a very fertile area irrigated by Pi‘inaio Stream, one of three streams that flowed through Waikīkī before the Ala Wai Canal was built. Today, Pi‘inaio Stream is referred to as Makiki Stream.

Two of the largest lo‘i or kalo loko (taro ponds) in Kālia were Loko Pāweo (‘to turn away,’ as in, to avoid seeing someone) and Loko Ka‘ihikapu (interestingly translated as ‘the tabu sacredness’), each measuring more than 12 acres. These ponds were between two bodies of water: Pi‘inaio Stream on the ‘Ewa side and Kawehewehe near the Halekūlani Hotel on the Diamond Head side. It is believed that these complex agricultural and irrigation systems were first established in Waikīkī by the high chief

title: Kālia
theme: Early Hawaiian life: taro fields and fish ponds

intro.text: Kalamakuaakaipuholua (a.k.a. Kalamakua) in the 1400s.

There are many varieties of kalo, wet and dry. These lo‘i were planted with the wet variety. In the Hawaiian creation myth, kalo plays a pivotal role as Hāloa, the common ancestor of the Hawaiian people. Kalo was the kino lau, the body form of Kāne, the deity of creation and the ancestor of chiefs and commoners, alike. Poi, the staple of the native Hawaiian diet, is made from the root of the kalo (taro) plant. Hawaiians believe that the essence of Hāloa, their fabled ancestor, is among them when a container of poi is at the meal; consequently, all disagreements are put on hold.

Taro, or kalo in Hawaiian (The letter and sound “t” does not exist in standard Hawaiian.), is a starchy vegetable similar to the potato. Generally, all parts of this vital plant are eaten: the leaves are cooked as greens, similar to spinach; the fleshy stems and roots are eaten baked, boiled, or steamed with water to make poi. Parts of the kalo, however, if eaten raw can be a dangerous irritant or even toxic. It must be wellcooked before eating. My own grandson mistook the kalo stem for a green bean, and much to his dismay, he felt like something was stinging his mouth! The common garden or house plant, Elephant Ears with its huge leaf, is in the same plant family as the kalo.

Kawehewehe means ‘the removal.’ According to a mo‘olelo (legend), sick and injured people were brought to these waters for curative bathing treatments. Often, a seaweed lei was worn, to be removed and left behind as a symbolic request that a person’s sins, believed to be the cause of illness, be forgiven. Hawaiians today continue to use the ocean waters therapeutically. Kawehewehe can also mean ‘the opening in the reef,’ referring to the reef entrance, offshore channel, and a tide pool in this area.

These taro fields and fish ponds, and many other smaller ones, were located makai of today’s Kalākaua Avenue (then Waikīkī road). After the arrival of the Chinese in the 19th century, rice fields and ponds for domesticated ducks abounded alongside the Hawaiian taro fields and fish ponds. The Chinese also developed rice as a major export.

The fish ponds were linked to the sea by a canal controlled by a lock to retain the larger fish and to allow the small, undeveloped fish to go back out to sea. The lock, or stationary sluice, mākāhā in Hawaiian, has been used only in Hawai‘i and in the Gilbert Islands.

A mo‘olelo (legend) relates that the fish ponds were inhabited by mo‘o, 12 to 30foot black-bodied deities or water serpents. Waikīkī’s mo‘o was Kamō‘ili‘ili, ‘pebble lizard,’ whose name lives on in the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili. (Don’t worry -Kalo and Rice fields in 1890s Waikīkī (Hawai‘i State Archives) they all disappeared along with the ponds.) Stroll in Mō‘ili‘ili, Walk IX.

John Papa ‘Ī‘ī, one of Hawai‘i’s earliest historians, mentioned a large catch of fish from Kālia ponds given as a tribute to Kīna‘u, daughter of Kamehameha I and mother of Kamehameha IV and Kamehameha V. Another historian, Samuel Kamakau, told of a liquorselling establishment in a Kālia coconut grove.
Part of this land was deeded by King Kamehameha III to Ho‘olae Paoa, Duke Kahanamoku’s grandfather. You will read more about Duke Kahanamoku soon.

A revitalized 600 to 800-year-old large fish pond, He‘eia Fish Pond, has been tended near Kane‘ohe. The wall encircling the fish pond is over one mile long, possibly the largest fish pond in the islands today.
The walk begins at the makai-Diamond Head intersection of Ala Moana Boulevard and Kālia Road.

info: 2 - 2.5 hours; 2.5 - 3 miles; 7000-10,000 steps (The additional half-hour and half mile are for the optional time and distance walking around the Hilton Hawaiian Village) Parking: Parking lot on the corner of Saratoga and Kālia roads Bus routes and times www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator.

blocks.text: At the makai - Diamond Head intersection of Ala Moana Boulevard and Kālia (named for the district, or ‘ili, of Kālia) Road is a lovely bronze statue of hula dancers: Spirit of Hula and Land by Kim Duffett. The Hawaiian inscription, Kaha ka ‘Io me nā Makani translates as ‘The hawk soars with the winds.’ The figures are dancing hula kahiko, the old or ancient style.
Ala Moana means the ‘ocean road/way.’

Mauka and Diamond Head of the Ala Moana Boulevard-Kālia Road intersection is Fort DeRussy – an open grassy space which you will visit at the end of the walk, after you walk around the ‘ili (section) of Kālia.

Cross Ala Moana Boulevard at Kalia Road/‘Ena Road, then walk ‘Ewa along the mauka side to the Hobron Lane District. This is Waikīkī’s most densely populated residential area, consisting mainly of apartment buildings and condominiums.
On the makai side of Ala Moana Boulevard, you will go past the Hilton Hawaiian Village and the ‘Ilikai. The walk back from the Hobron Lane District will visit both hotels.
Do not cross the bridge over the canal; rather, walk on the Diamond Head side of the canal’s promenade. Take the ramp down to the canal.
Promenades from Ala Moana Boulevard to Kalākaua Avenue line both sides of the Ala Wai Canal.
Duck ponds behind Waikīkī 1908 photo (Hawai‘i State Archives)
Sculpture of male hula dancer - Kaha ka ‘Io me nā makani
The Hawai‘i Convention Center is located on the ‘Ewa side of the canal, near the bridge on Kalākaua Avenue (and Kapi‘olani Boulevard). The convention center, which was built in 1998, is on 10 acres.
This is all part of the ‘ili of Kālia.

The grand stairway of the convention center is best viewed from this side of the canal. Known as “Alapi‘i Lani, Royal Stairway,” the plaque states that this is the “center’s open gateway to Waikīkī.” It is aptly named because for hundreds of years, Waikīkī was the royal capital of the Kingdom of O‘ahu.
On another day, you might want to walk around inside the convention center, marveling in its Hawaiian artworks and motifs.

Diagonally across from the corner where the canal meets Kalākaua Avenue look for a pedestrian bridge over the small stream that empties into the canal. This is the newest (2000) bridge crossing the canal.

The stream emptying into the canal is a remanant of Pi‘inaio Stream. Although the exact menaing of Pi‘inaio has been lost, two meanings are possible: pi‘i (going inland or climbing) and nā io (the Hawks) or Naio, a type of native tree (false Sandalewood. The stream is now referred to as Makiki Sream since it flows though the neighborhood of Makiki.

From the Tantalus mountains above the neighborhood of Makiki two streams meet in the plains of Makiki. Makiki (a type of stone weight) Stream and Kanahā (‘the cracked; to split’) Stream continue as Makiki Stream into the ocean.

Until the construction of the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s, Pi‘inaio Stream ran through this area, met the western branch of Mānoa-Pālolo Stream, and emptied as a delta into the ocean between the Duke Kahanamoku Lagoon and the ‘Ilikai Hotel (which we will visit on this walk). Pi‘inaio Sculpture of female hula dancer - Kaha ka ‘Io me nā makani Stream was one of the three major streams that fed Waikīkī’s intricate irrigation system, which gave rise to the ubiquitous fishponds in the area.

Pi‘inaio Stream ended inland from the ocean where it became a rich muddy delta. For the Hawaiians, this delta provided a perfect area for fish ponds and taro fields, and later at the end of the 19th century, for the Chinese, duck ponds and rice fields.
When the Ala Wai Canal was built to intentionally divert those rivers, Waikīkī’s ponds and fields dried up, and, with them, vanished the traditional Hawaiian way of life in Waikīkī.
On your walk back to the Hobron Lane District, notice the date on the Kalākaua Avenue bridge, 1929. The bridge was one of the first overpasses built after the Ala Wai Canal was completed.
Walk Diamond Head along Kalākaua Avenue, admiring the over 100-year-old stately Mahogany trees in the median, to ‘Ena Road.
Turn makai at the first street, ‘Ena Road,

which is named for the son of John ‘Ena, a Chinese merchant and the Hawaiian Chiefess Kaikilani. The son, John Kauluhinano ‘Ena (1845-1906), was advisor to both King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani. He was also a co-founder of the Inter-Island Steamship Company. The ‘Ena family owned land in this area.
In the early 20th century, at the intersection of Hobron Lane and ‘Ena Road stood a poi factory! Poi is the staple of the native Hawaiian diet, made from the of the kalo (taro) plant.
Turn ‘Ewa onto Hobron Lane, which is Lshaped, then makai and relax on the benches in the mini park on the corner of Hobron Lane and Līpe‘epe‘e Street.

Tiny Līpe‘epe‘e Street is best known for its unusual name. Līpe‘epe‘e is a type of seaweed, limu (here contacted to lī), which was kapu (taboo) to students of the hula because the deities were believed to hide, pe‘e, the secrets of the hula from anyone who ate this seaweed.
Eaton Square and Condominium with its blue tiled roof was built by Bob Magoon, who named the development after his father.
Hobron Lane is named for the Hobron brothers, Captain Coit Hobron and Thomas H. Hobron, who lived in Hawai‘i during the days of the monarchy and owned property near here.
In the 1920s and 1930s, this district was a place of great fun: Aloha Amusement Park, and later Waikīkī Park. The entry arcade was based on the entrance to San Francisco’s Palace of Fine Arts.

Continue makai-Diamond Head along Hobron Lane toward Ala Moana Boulevard, crossing Kaio‘o ‘strong sea’ Drive, which loops around. In case you were wondering, kai refers specifically to open water, sea water; whereas, wai, as in Waikīkī, refers to any other water, including streams and fresh waterways, other than kai.
Stay on Hobron lane, makai to the corner at Ala Moana Boulevard.
The hidden meaning of this street name is special to hula.

stops.title: Koa wood in McDonald’s at Discovery Bay

blocks.text: Discovery Bay, the twin-tower condominium on the mauka-Diamond Head corner of Hobron Lane and Ala Moana Boulevard, houses McDonald’s on the ground floor. Go inside to appreciate the dazzling use of Hawai‘i’s native koa wood in the spectacular koa-paneled walls and ceiling. Koa is a medium hardwood tree unique to Hawai‘i that is also used in artistic carvings; it is the largest of the native trees.

From Hobron Lane, cross Ala Moana Boulevard to the ‘Ilikai Hotel, one of the early high-rise modern hotels in Waikīkī. Walk up the ramp to the front steps, through the lobby to the lānai overlooking the harbor.

stops.title: ‘Ilikai Hotel
stops.subtitle: The Chinn Ho Tree on the Lānai of the ‘Ilikai

blocks.text: A Japanese nightclub and teahouse, the Ikesu, preceded the ‘Ilikai on this site. The Japanese word Ikesu means ‘holding pond for fish,’ perhaps so named because of the large Hawaiian fish ponds in this area.
A 1923 ad in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin ran:
“One Delightful Hour at Ikesu’s Is Worth a Year of Loneliness”
And “No Trip to Hawai‘i is Complete Without a Trip to Ikesu’s.”

The ‘Ilikai, ‘surface of the sea,’ which was originally conceived as a huge apartment building in the early 60s, under the magic hands of businessman Chinn Ho (19041987) morphed into a hotel and apartment complex.

When the ‘Ilikai was opened in 1964 it was touted as the largest condominium in the world. Interesting fact. But more interestingly, it was built by Chinn Ho, whose parents, as Chinese immigrants had rice fields and duck ponds nearby. Furthermore, this son of immigrants was once the publisher of the Honolulu StarBulletin, now the Honolulu Star Advertiser.
The architect, John Graham Jr, also designed the Seattle Space Needle.

The building is famously featured in the balcony scene in the opening credits of the TV show Hawai‘i Five-O; one of the fictional detectives in the series was named Chin Ho Kelly. Chinn Ho was also widely believed to be the inspiration for the fictional character of Hong Kong Kee, a Chinese man who outwitted the white gentry in James Michener’s novel Hawai‘i.

The Monkey Pod tree in the center of the courtyard overlooking the water was planted at the time of the groundbreaking ceremony by Chinn Ho and world-famous Hawaiian surfer Duke Kahanamoku. Kahanamoku and Ho were McKinley High School classmates and lifelong friends. (More about Duke Kahanamoku soon.)
Be sure to enjoy the overlook at the Ala Wai Harbor, especially late afternoon when the sun drops into the ocean leaving behind the legendary Green Flash:
 The plaque reads:
“This monkeypod tree was planted by Chinn Ho, founder and original owner of the ‘Ilikai.
The Chinn Ho tree was rededicated in 1994 in celebration of the 30th anniversary of the‘Ilikai.” a momentary burst of bright green light, the result of the after-effect of the image of the sun.
I hope you find eternal happiness!
Walk out across the ‘Ilikai lānai toward the ocean and look across the Ala Wai Harbor.
The marina was constructed following the dredging of the Ala Wai Canal in the late 1920s, but this area had been used by fisherman long before.

The Ala Wai Harbor is home to the Hawai‘i Yacht Club and Waikīkī Yacht Club. With 700 slips, only 15% of the boats are permitted to be lived in. The Hawai‘i Yacht Club was chartered in 1901 by the 2 royal brothers, Kūhiō Kalaniana‘ole and David Kawānanakoa. Hawai‘i Yacht Club is located across the mouth of the canal near Ala Moana Beach Park. Waikīkī Yacht Club, replete with pool, restaurant, and bar is the larger of the two. There is a long wait for a slip in the marina!
Come back in the evening to walk around the docks to watch the brilliant sunset.
The majestic Wai‘anae mountain range stretches ‘Ewa.
Ala Wai Harbor at sunrise  ‘Ena Rd.
Jules Verne, of science fiction fame, described the green flash:

“It will be a green ray of such a fabulous beauty that no painter could produce it upon his palate, a green that nature with all her varied vegetation and all her colored waters, no matter how limpid, has ever equaled. If there is a color called green in paradise, it is perhaps this green, which is without doubt, the true green of hope. Legend declares that happiness will be the portion of those who behold this spectacle. Those who do not know what happiness is should search after the green ray.”
From the Duke Kahanamoku Lagoon there is a view of Lē‘ahi and the buildings at the ocean’s edge.
Walk down the curved walkway of the ‘Ilikai on the makai-Diamond Head side of the hotel to Kahanamoku Street.

As you walk down the ramp, you will see a lagoon near the Hilton Hawaiian Village. This 5-acre saltwater lagoon is named in honor and memory of Hawai‘i’s favorite sportsman, Duke Paoa Kahanamoku, affectionately known as “The Duke.” Anyone can swim in this lagoon, not just guests at the Hilton Hawaiian Village since the Hilton does not own it. All beaches are free and open to the public in Hawai‘i. The lagoon is not very deep with no waves – perfect for keiki (children).

At the bottom of the ramp, make a U-turn and walk mauka on Kahanamoku Street, passing recreated “lava” walls, pools, and waterfalls, reminiscent of the ponds and streams that once flourished in this area. Walk past the faux lava formations and the ramp up to the hotel, where you will see an opening/underpass toward the Hilton. In this passageway is an interesting display of memorabilia about Duke Kahanamoku.

Follow the purple line if the ocean and beach beckon you. The fence will take you to an opening to the lagoon. Notice the stately Palm trees, Kou trees with lei flowers, and the lovely half flower on the Naupaka bushes.
Kahanamoku Street separates the ‘Ilikai Hotel from the Hilton Hawaiian Village.

The Duke won several Olympic medals for swimming: In 1912 he won gold for 100-meter freestyle and silver for free relay; in 1920, two golds: one in freestyle and one in free relay; and in 1924, silver in free relay. In 1966, he was the first person to be inducted into the Surfing Hall of Fame. The International Surfing Championship continues to be held in his honor and memory.

The Duke and his eight brothers were raised near here on his mother’s family property. Duke Kahanamoku, native-born Hawaiian, was named for his father, who in turn had been named by Princess Pauahi Bishop in commemoration of the 1869 visit to Hawai‘i of Alfred Ernest Albert, Duke of Edinburgh. Paoa, his mother’s family name, means ‘fragrant.’ Kahanamoku translates as ‘island work.’ Duke was born in what is now the business district of downtown Honolulu.

Duke was not only a world-renowned swimmer, but also movie actor, sheriff of Honolulu, and true hero: in 1925 he saved 8 people with his surfboard when their boat capsized in the Pacific Ocean off California.
Duke Kahanamoku Park, just past the Hilton Hawaiian Village, is also named in his memory.

The Duke passed away on January 22, 1968. On August 24, 2002, the 112th anniversary of his birth, the U.S. Postal Service, unveiled a stamp to commemorate his life. A larger-than-life bronze statue of Duke Kahanamoku with a surfboard strategically placed behind him can be found on Kalākaua Avenue just ‘Ewa of Uluniu Street, at Kūhiō Beach. Ironically, his back is to the ocean, contrary to Hawaiian custom and, as a surfer, he never would have done!
Local lore has it that The Duke rode the longest wave ever: a mile and a quarter on a 35-foot wave!

The Hilton Hawaiian Village sits on most of the property that the Paoa family once owned. The land was deeded to Duke’s ancestors during the Mahele of 1848, the division of Hawaiian land among the rulers and commoners.
After you walk through the passageway, enjoying the photos and life of The Duke, be sure to visit Lappert’s Hawai‘i, a Kaua‘i ice cream store, around the corner.

stops.title: Walk along the beach toward Lē‘ahi, reading the history of the Hilton Hawaiian Village

blocks.text: If you would rather walk around the grounds of the Hilton Hawaiian Village, follow the hotel buildings around from the makai-‘Ewa side, then toward Kālia Road, then back on the Diamond Head side to the beach, stops 13 A, B, C and D.
Or follow the purple line to visit a few places of interest at the Hilton.

If you would like to walk along the beach, find a comfortable place to read about the Hilton Hawaiian Village, then walk to Stop 14 at Paoa Place and Duke Kahanamoku Park, located between the Hilton and the Hale Koa hotels.

Before the parade of hotels began on this property, the area was replete with ponds. Māmala (the name of a shark woman) Bay supported the life cycles not only of fish, but also of lobsters, crabs, and octopodes. Several bathhouses and boarding houses in Waikīkī were first established as annexes for downtown Honolulu Hotel.

In the early 1890s, the earliest commercial structure on this beach was a bathhouseboarding house called Old Waikīkī. By the early 1900s, it had become more of a boarding house, first under the ownership of John and Eliza Cassidy who called their hotel Cassidy’s At-the-Beach, and later as the Pierpont Hotel. In the mid-1920s, this property and several other boarding houses in the immediate area were bought up by Afong Heen, a local Chinese merchant and architect. Heen renovated, enlarged, and turned these structures into the Niumalu Hotel, ‘shade of the coconut tree.’
The Hawai‘i Kai Beach Club Hotel, built by Henry Kaiser (as in Kaiser Permanente Medical Care Program/Hospital and Kaiser Aluminum) in 1951 was the next hotel in this area.
Sunbathing on the beach in front of the Hilton in the shade of Palm trees and the beauty of the distant Wai‘anae Range.
In 1956 the Hawai‘i Kai Hotel was purchased by Conrad Hilton, and expansion to the present-day Hilton Hawaiian Village was begun.
13A Stylized Rainbow Mural on the Hilton Rainbow Tower

The Hilton Rainbow Tower is known for its two 286-foot ceramic tile murals, one on the mauka (mountain) side of the building, the other on the makai (ocean) side. When these murals were created in 1968 by the artist Millard Sheets (1907 - 1990), it was claimed that they were the tallest murals in the world. More than 8,000 ceramic tiles were used in each mural.

This mural portrays two separate stylized rainbows rather than the double rainbow often seen in Hawai‘i after a rainfall. Double rainbows consist of a bright main rainbow below a fainter outer rainbow. The outer rainbow is always a mirror image of the main rainbow, and its colors are in reverse order. Notice that in this mural the colors of both rainbows are in the same order. Perhaps Mr. Sheets didn’t spend enough time in Hawai‘i or perhaps he didn’t walk into Mānoa Valley where double rainbows appear daily.
Rainbows are often visible from Waikīkī looking mauka (toward the mountains) in the afternoons. Look carefully at the next rainbow you see – it may well be a double rainbow!
The inscription beneath the mauka rainbow: Ua ao mālamalama ‘o Waikīkī i ka nani ‘ōlino o ke ‘ānuenue “Waikīkī is enlightened with the beauty of a rainbow.”
If you love rainbows, be sure to read The Rainbow Goblins by Ul de Rico. Or follow a walk into Mānoa Valley Walk X, after you finish the Waikīkī Beach Walks.
13B Kālia Tower
The building on Kālia Road is the Kālia Tower, named for the local area, Kālia. The lobby is splendid with a carpet of flowers and murals of Hawaiian women by island artist Yvonne Cheng.

If you have visited Waikīkī before, between the 60s and 80s, you may be looking for the Buckminster Fuller Dome, built in 1957 of Kaiser Aluminum and the 1980s home of Don Ho. Demolished in 1999, The Dome was replaced by the Kālia Tower. It was at the Buckminster Fuller Dome where Hawai‘i saw its first color TV program on May 5, 1957.
13C Tapa Tower
Walk through the lobby of the Tapa Tower on the Diamond Head side of the Hilton Hawaiian Village, stopping to learn about tapa.

Here tapa refers to the pattern carved on the building. Tapa is the Anglicized version of the Hawaiian word, kapa: there’s no “t” letter or sound in standard Hawaiian. (Compare English “taboo” and Hawaiian kapu, the original word.) Kapa is the Hawaiian fabric made from the bark of the Wauke, paper mulberry trees. Kapa has been used for clothing and bedding. The term also refers to the geometric patterns made by wooden beaters applied to the cloth. To see actual fabric and the beaters, visit the Bishop Museum.

A bronze sculpture and accompanying wall text describe the process of tapa making. In the 1970s Puanani Van Dorpe (1933-2014) revived the ancient art of kapa making. She was considered to be a Living Treasure of Hawai‘i.

Nearby are two bronze statues of Hawaiian performers. One is of Alfred Apaka (1919-1960), singer and ‘ukulele player who was greatly loved at the Hilton Hawaiian Village. The other statue is of ‘Iolani Luahine (1915-1978), one of Hawai‘i’s greatest hula dancers who performed here in the 1950s. Both statues are by local artist, Kim Duffett.
13D Ali‘i Tower
Ali‘i means royalty.

One plant, in particular, the ‘akia, a small leaf ground cover with tiny yellow flowers and reddish fruits is growing beautifully on the corner of the Ali‘i Tower, as well as on Kālia Avenue. The ‘akia plant is unique to Hawai‘i. The root and bark can be used to stun fish, temporarily, long enough to capture a net-full of fish!

Walk around the gardens of the Hilton, reading the plaques to learn about the local plants, some unique to Hawai‘i and nowhere else in the world; others, indigenous plants are native to Hawai‘i and elsewhere in the Pacific. A Loulu Palm tree, unique to Hawai‘i, is located makai of Tapa Tower, in the open courtyard.
The Hau Tree Bar is cover with hau, from the stalwart Hau tree.

The street is named for the Paoa family, Duke Kahanamoku’s mother’s family, who owned property near here. The land was deeded to Duke’s ancestors during the Mahele of 1848, the division of Hawaiian land among the rulers and the commoners. The family farmed taro and sweet potatoes here and partook of the bounties of the sea.

The open grassy area is a lovely place to sit and rest under the Monkey Pod trees. The large lava boulders scattered around the open park-like area most likely originated at the Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry at the entrance to Mānoa Valley. (Follow the Lower Campus Walk XII for more information)
Continue along the walkway bordering the beach.

The beach along here was developed with imported sand, resulting in one of the widest beaches along the Waikīkī waterfront. Up to 60 years ago, there was simply a seawall between the land and the ocean. In the 1970s, this wide beach was created from crushed coral for your enjoyment.

As mentioned in the introduction to this walk, in the years before the Ala Wai Canal, this area was covered with fishponds, in particular, Loko (pond, lake) Pāweo and Loko Ka‘ihikapu, which were over 12 acres each.

Can you imagine this area like that? No buildings. Just wide open fish ponds, taro fields, and coconut trees. Notice the stately Palm trees on the beach. If you can find some shade, be aware that it “moves around,” following the sun! Unfortunately, many of the trees have recently succumbed to the chopping block. Most likely, these trees are descendants of the 10,000 trees from the time of the Hawaiian monarchy.
The view from the Hale Koa beach presents the grandeur of Lē‘ahi and condominium row.

The hotel is spread out over 72 acres of oceanfront splendor, including two hotel buildings, restaurants, gardens, pools, a post exchange, and a lū‘au setting. By the way, a more appropriate Hawaiian term for lū‘au is pā‘ina or ‘aha‘aina, ‘feast.’

Hale Koa can mean “House of Koa Wood,” “House of the Brave,” and “House of the Warrior.” House of the Warrior or Brave is apt considering this hotel is for use by military, or “brave warriors.” However, koa is also a beautiful, strong hardwood found only in the native forests of Hawai‘i.

The Hale Koa Hotel, as the ‘Ilima (a native yellow-orange flower) was first known, was completed in 1975 to accommodate the many soldiers and families getting together for some R & R. The newer building, Maile (a fragrant vine that grows in the forests) opened in 1995. Every year, over one million military and their dependents get a chance to rest in this hotel on the beach! The Hale Koa boasts that the hotel is completely self-sufficient and that “not one taxpayer dollar supports the upkeep or operation.”
If the pathway between the two Hale Koa buildings is open, walk around enjoying the excellent landscaping, and then come back to the beach to walk to the Army Museum.

To reach the U.S. Army Museum, walk diagonally just past the Hale Koa grounds, across the park toward Kālia Road. The museum building, former Battery Randolph, will be on the makai side of the pathway.
This beach, like all beaches in Hawai‘i, is public property; although, it serves mainly the military and their families staying at the Hale Koa Hotel.

In the late 1880s, one of the first bath houses in Waikīkī, the Saratoga Baths, prospered in this area. The bath house was named for Saratoga Springs in upstate New York, a fashionable hot spring resort at that time.
The green building behind the terrace is Battery Randolph, once a coastal auxiliary and now The United States Army Museum of Hawai‘i.

Along the beach and on the way to the Army Museum are groves of Naupaka, a native beach plant, found on other Pacific islands, as well. Look closely for its small white flower: you will see a “half flower.” There are many mo‘olelo (legend) concerning this half blossom. One mo‘olelo involves a maiden who became suspicious of her lover’s faithfulness. As a test, she tore the flower in two and gave him one half, telling him to bring back a complete flower as proof of his love. Her lover was unsuccessful.

Another mo‘olelo involves a related mountain plant that bears an identical flower but has significantly different leaves. In this legend, a Hawaiian Romeo and Juliet, 1901 Photo of the Chung Afong Villa. The villa and property were sold in 1904. Battery Randolph was built in its place in 1911. forbidden to marry because of their different backgrounds and social class, decide to die together. The Hawaiian deities turned the woman into the Naupaka Kahakai (‘by the sea’) and the man into the Naupaka Kuahiwi (‘mountain’), joining their love in spirit.
At one time there were diving platforms floating offshore, which were fun to swim to, climb on, rest a while, and then dive off!

In the late-1800s, the home of Chun Afong (1825-1906), the first Chinese millionaire in Hawai‘i, occupied three acres along the waterfront. This was a home of opulent parties for local and foreign dignitaries. Chun Afong was known as “the merchant prince of the Sandalwood Mountains.” Because of the great deal of Sandalwood trees and the Chinese love for Sandalwood, Hawai‘i was referred to as the “Sandalwood Mountains.” Unfortunately, these trees are endangered, if not for all practical purposes, extinct. Chun Afong was a shrewd businessman: He had his hand in real estate, rice, sugar, and even opium! However, he was also a keen politician under King Kalākaua, having married Julia Fayerweather, of the Hawaiian monarchy. The Afong family served as character models in Jack London’s short story Chun Ah Chun. A book recounting the life of Chun Afong is revealed in Bob Dye’s, Merchant Prince of the Sandalwood Mountains: Afong and the Chinese in Hawai‘i.

An early building in this area was the large home of Alexander Joy Cartwright Jr., a merchant who settled in Honolulu in 1849 and died in 1893. Alexander Cartwright, who was born in New York, is best known as the “Father of Modern Baseball” and was inducted into Cooperstown’s Baseball Hall of Fame in 1934. Cartwright established baseball’s first organized association, the New York Knickerbocker Base Ball Club and created the rules and regulations of nine players and nine innings. Cartwright Field, in Makiki, ‘Ewa-mauka of Waikīkī, is a baseball field named in his memory. Cartwright Road, in the Diamond Head end of Waikīkī, is also named after him. His son, Bruce Cartwright Sr., was one of the subdividers of Waikīkī.
Fort DeRussy in 1949 (Hawai‘i State Archives)

The Man Who Invented Baseball by Harold Peterson tells the complete story of Alexander Joy Cartwright Jr.’s life. Cartwright’s grave in Nu‘uanu Memorial Park (cemetery) has been visited by many baseball greats, including the famous Babe Ruth!

The terrace along the beach is covered with Hau trees. Hau belongs to the Malvaeceae (Mallow) family, which includes the Hibiscus. In the course of its life (one day!), the Hau blossom displays three different colors: yellow upon opening, then bright orange, and finally red-brown when it drops. The Hau tree has many traditional uses: its rough but lightweight wood is used for making canoe outriggers, its fiber is made into rope, and its sap and flowers are used medicinally.
Enjoy the view of Lē‘ahi straight ahead and the Wai‘anae range in the west as you walk along the beach.

stops.title: Fort DeRussy and Battery
stops.subtitle: Randolph U.S. Army Museum of Hawai‘i Saratoga Road

blocks.text: Don’t look for the physical structure of a fort: there isn’t one and there never was one. “Fort” simply denotes a permanent military installation of any type - here, specifically the army.

This region is all part of Fort DeRussy: both makai and mauka of Kālia Road. The US Army Museum of Hawai‘i, Hale Koa Hotel, Kuroda Field (Stop 18 ), and Fort DeRussy Beach make up the greater Fort DeRussy Armed Forces Recreation Center. This entire area was once home to vast taro and fish ponds, the walls of which remain below your feet.

In 1904 the area began to be acquired by the United States government through the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. By 1915, and after 12 different land purchases, the government accumulated 72 acres. Chung Afong aside, the homes were owned mainly by European-sounding names: Hobron, Waterhouse, Shaefer, McCandless, and Carter.

The first military installation here was known as the Waikīkī Military Reservation, then as the Kālia Military Reservation. In 1909 it was renamed Fort DeRussy in honor of Brevet Brigadier General René Edward DeRussy (1789– 1865).

General DeRussy not only fought in the Civil War, but also designed fortifications in New York and in San Francisco Harbors. Furthermore, he invented the Barbette Depressing Gun Carriage, precursor for the big disappearing guns. Other Forts DeRussy exist in America, named in his honor or his brother, Lewis.

Fort DeRussy was originally established not as a recreation area, which is what it is today, but rather as a defense for Honolulu Harbor and Pearl Harbor. Most important was Battery Randolph, the building that now houses the U.S. Army Museum of Hawai‘i. Completed in 1911, this coastal auxiliary was named after Major Benjamin Harrison Randolph, who helped subdue the Philippine Insurrection of 1898-1901.

In 1969 the army endeavored to knock down the walls of Battery Randolph. However, its 12-foot steel reinforced cement walls and 22-foot cement gun platform proved impervious to the army’s efforts and the structure is still standing. Notice the massive gun emplacements.

The U.S. Army Museum of Hawai‘i houses many exhibits, including pre-contact Hawai‘i, especially that of early native Hawaiian weapons, and the history of conflicts and wars in the Pacific arena. Be sure to notice the use of native Koa wood in the reception area and the frames throughout the museum. The paint in the hallway is of interest: the light grey paint covers the walls of the original 1911 structure; furthermore, the barred windows, as well as the hallway metal doors (which were once exterior doors), are original.

The 5 large carved varying images of Kū form a kukalepa, a memorial that commemorates fallen Hawaiian warriors. The Kū images were carved from ‘Ohia wood by Rocky Ka‘iouliokahihikolo ‘Ehu Jensen in 1999. Kū was one of 4 major akua (deity); Kū was the deity of war, politics, farming, and fishing. These statues, titled Nā Lehua Helele‘i, ‘The Scattered Lehua Blossoms,’ memorialize the “fallen Maoli (Maoli means ‘native’) Warriors of Native Hawaiian Conflicts.” The Lehua blossom grows on the native Hawaiian ‘Ōhi‘a tree. Jensen intended for these images to transmit a feeling of power: the statues rest on a platform, representing the heiau, a religious structure.
The museum also houses the best kept military secret: a reference library open to the public with thousands of pictures and documents relating to the wars in the Pacific dating to 1898.
Saratoga Road, which terminates at the US Army Museum of Hawai‘i, is named for an 1880s bath house that operated on the beachfront.

Walk ‘Ewa on Kālia Road to the intersection at the Hale Koa Hotel at Maluhia Road. Kuroda Field is located on the mauka side of Kālia Road. The two 12 to13 acre loko of kalo and fish and, later, of rice and ducks would have been located mauka of the road.
Maluhia ‘peaceful or solemn stillness’ Road dead ends in a lovely garden.
Notice our native White Terns flying around (in 2s or 3s) or nesting in the trees with the blue ribbon around the trunks.

Kuroda Field is named in memory and honor of the patriotism of Staff Sergeant Robert T. Kuroda who was awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions on October 20, 1944, as part of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The Medal of Honor was awarded posthumously by President Clinton in 2000. Staff Sergeant Kuroda is buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Punchbowl. He was felled by a sniper near Bruyères, France after killing enemy soldiers.
Nā Lehua Helele‘i – The Kū images honor fallen Hawaiian warriors.
Some interesting facts about the 100th and 442nd regiments include:

• In 1944 the 442nd merged with the 100th Battalion. The 100th Infantry was the first all-Japanese-American combat unit; • “Go For Broke!” the 442nd Infantry’s motto for “Shoot the Works,” underscored its deserved reputation: for its size and duration of service, it was the most highly decorated unit in military history; • The 100th and 442nd fought 8 campaigns in Germany, Italy, and France.
The plaque on the field states “Fort DeRussy was the home of the 100th Infantry Battalion, 442nd Infantry Regiment.” Kuroda Field honors the memory of those brave soldiers.
A memorial to these soldiers, “Brothers in Valor,” is located at Kalākaua Avenue. A tour of that memorial is on the Kalākaua Avenue Walk IV.
Continue mauka along Maluhia Road.
On the Diamond Head side of Maluhia Road and on the cul-de-sac is the Fort DeRussy Army Chapel - a low, Hawaiianstyle, white building. Notice the inscriptions on the welcome mat:
Ft. DeRussy Chapel, 1775, and Pro Deo et Patria (Latin: ‘For God and Country’)

On the ‘Ewa side of Maluhia Road is the green copper roofed Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies. Daniel Inouye was not only a World War II hero, but also served as the Hawaiian representative in the US Senate from 1963 until his death in 2012.

On the grassy area at the mauka-‘Ewa end of Maluhia Road, stood the Maluhia Club (mid-1940s to mid-1970s), an entertainment-dance facility opened during World War II. This club, which accommodated 1,200 people, marked the beginning of Fort DeRussy’s transition from military installation to recreation center.

Follow the walkway into the open grass area behind the Inouye Center to the areas of thoughtfully labeled native plants. The signs in the garden tell you not only the Hawaiian and English names, but also educate you with the Ethno-Botanical uses!
You are not far from your starting point at Kālia Road and Ala Moana Boulevard.
Or walk up to Kalākaua Avenue for the Kalākaua Avenue Walk IV. Bus routes and
times www.thebus.org or
call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for live operator.
Kalo loko in Waikīkī. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
