title: Helumoa
theme: Residence and recreation of the early royals

intro.text: Central Waikīkī along the beach.

This walk compresses hundreds of years of Hawaiian history into a half-hour walk. You will need to use your imagination to contemplate what might have been, for nothing remains from the years before western contact except for the reminders contained in two street names: Helumoa Road and Uluniu Street.
As part of the ahupua’a of Waikīkī, Helumoa - the seat of royalty - was the best known of the many ‘ili (smaller districts) in this area.

At around the year 1400, O‘ahu King Mā‘ilikūkahi moved his capital from ‘Ewa to Waikīkī. Waikiki reigned supreme for almost 400 years. King Mā‘ilikūkahi also initiated not only the land divisions (moku - major area and ahupua‘a - smaller unit) that continue to exist today, but also established nonsacrificial heiau (open-air religious structure).

Kākuhihewa, his successor and equally benevolent, was concerned with uniting the island. A succession of chiefs ruled over O‘ahu until January 1783 when Kahekili, the king of Maui invaded Waikīkī, taking over the entire island.

Kamehameha the Great moved his court, including his favorite wife, Ka‘ahumanu, and his sacred wife, Keōpūolani, from Hawai‘i Island here in 1795 soon after Kahekili died at Ulukou in Waikīkī (Stop 10 ). With Waikīkī as the capital of O‘ahu, he remained here off and on until 1809, a year before he unified the islands.
This walk begins at the corner of Helumoa Road and Lewers Street.

info: From Lewers Street & Road to Uluniu Avenue & Kalākaua Avenue 0.5 to 2 hours, depending upon your imagination; 1 mile; 2,000-4,000 steps Parking lot: corner of Saratoga and Kālia roads

blocks.text: The street is named for Robert Lewers (1836 – 1926), a local businessman from New York who resided at the present site of the Halekūlani Hotel.

The walk proceeds to the beachfront, but not before paying homage to Gabby Pahinui, one of Hawai‘i’s greatest musicians. Appreciate the statue of Gabby Pahinui - labeled “Kanikapila (let’s make music)” in his overalls - at the end of “Beach Walk” on Lewers Street. How we wish we could enjoy a concert by Gabby!
Helumoa
Helumoa Road runs parallel to the beach between Kālia Road and Kalākaua Avenue, one block mauka of the Halekulani Hotel.

Helumoa Road, ‘chicken scratch,’ is our only reminder of an important place in ancient Hawaiian times. Helumoa, where Hawaiian royalty lived, was an ‘ili and beach area located from here to the beach and is thought to have extended from the Royal Hawaiian Hotel to the Outrigger Hotel, the former site of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream.

The earliest features in Helumoa were the homes of the local chiefs, followed by the royal residences of most of the Hawaiian monarchy from Kamehameha on. Other structures at Helumoa included a heiau (religious structure) and an athletic field both based on artifacts found in the area.

There are several stories about Helumoa. According to one mo‘olelo (legend), a chief was playing Hawaiian games in this area one day when a legendary phantom rooster, Ka‘auhelemoa, suddenly landed in front of him and began to scratch the earth. Just as suddenly, the rooster disappeared. The chief directed his men to plant a coconut in the exact spot where Ka‘auhelemoa had scratched. This coconut came to be known as Helumoa and, in turn, supported a grove of several thousand coconut trees. Helumoa was always the tallest and strongest.
Another mo‘olelo tells of chickens scratching the ground for maggots in the shallow graves of sacrificial victims from the nearby ‘Āpuakēhau Heiau.

Walk makai on Lewers Street to Kālia Road. The tour continues Diamond Head onto the beach, but before turning Diamond Head, walk one block the opposite way to the ocean-side corner of Kālia and Saratoga roads: Something very interesting happens at the street grate on
this corner. At high tide you can see (and hear!) the ocean water rushing inland meeting Kawehewehe, the former reef entrance and channel (Stop 3 ). Careful you might get splashed!
After getting splashed, turn around to walk Diamond Head along Kālia Road to a right-of-way to the beach.

You will pass the Outrigger East/ Reef Hotel that has a lively Kani Ka Pila Grille open-air restaurant. Stop in at night for authentic Hawaiian music. While you are there, feast your eyes on the Waikīkī mural ‘I Ka Wā Ma Mua, Ka Wā Ma Hope’ (‘Through the Past is the Future’) by local artist Kamea Hadar. The little girl playing the ‘ukulele is Israel ‘Iz’
Kamakawiwo‘ole’s niece.
Oh, the music Gabby would make! - Kanikapila!
Helumoa – “chicken scratch” –where the monarchy lived.
Walk toward the ocean between the Halekūlani Hotel (on the ‘Ewa side) and the Sheraton Hotel (on the Diamond Head side).

As you walk toward the beach notice the local, but not unique to Hawai‘i, plants: Bamboo, Palm trees, and groves of Naupaka, a native beach plant, found on other Pacific islands, as well. Look closely for its small white flower: you will see a “half flower.” There are many mo‘olelo concerning this half blossom. One mo‘olelo involves a maiden who became suspicious of her lover’s faithfulness. As a test, she tore the flower in two and gave him one half, telling him to bring back a complete flower as proof of his love. Her lover was unsuccessful.

Another mo‘olelo involves a related mountain plant that bears an identical flower but has drastically different leaves. In this mo‘olelo, a Hawaiian Romeo and Juliet, forbidden to marry because of their different backgrounds and social class, decide to die together. The Hawaiian deities turned the woman into the naupaka kahakai (by the sea) and the man into the naupaka kuahiwi (mountain), joining their love in spirit.

Notice the solitary Hau tree on the beach: beachgoers favorite spot in the shade. Grab the shade whenever you can! Hau belongs to the Malvaeceae (Mallow) family, which includes the Hibiscus. In the course of its life (one day!), the Hau blossom displays three different colors: yellow upon opening, then bright orange, and finally red-brown when it drops. The Hau tree has many traditional uses: its rough but lightweight wood is used for making canoe outriggers, its fiber is made into rope, and its sap and flowers are used medicinally.

The beach and waters on the ‘Ewa side of this beach right-of way were called Kawehewehe, ‘the removal,’ by Hawaiians. According to mo‘olelo, sick and injured people were brought here for curative bathing treatments. Often, a seaweed lei was worn, to be removed and left behind as a This Hau tree provides the only shade on the beach. Walking Diamond Head, the beach ends here but resumes at the Royal Hawaiian Hotel. symbolic request that a person’s sins, believed to be the cause of illness, be forgiven. Traditional Native Hawaiians today continue to use the ocean waters therapeutically for healing and purification rites.
Kawehewehe also means ‘the opening in the reef,’ referring to the reef entrance, offshore channel, and a tide pool in this area.
Walk Diamond Head toward the Sheraton Hotel, where – unfortunately - you cannot walk on the beach side. The concrete walkway is closed as it is deemed too dangerous to walk on.
(The Halekulani also has a raised concrete walkway that is open but is sometimes difficult to walk on when the waves are wild, especially at high tide. If so, please do not attempt it.)
Walk toward the lobby of the Sheraton Hotel, around the pool, then back to the beach to the very pink Royal Hawaiian Hotel.
Kahāloa

In earlier times, the beach was also known as the ‘ili of Kahāloa, ‘long or eternal breath,’ named for one of the 4 kāhuna who came to Hawai‘i from Tahiti in ancient times (Stop 11 ). However, Hāloa, was the first Hawaiian man who, because of his birth, was responsible for the kalo (‘taro’) plant. At one time, kalo grew abundantly here.

The Royal Hawaiian Hotel opened its doors in Waikīkī on February 1, 1927. The Spanish-Baroque-Moorish style (yes, that’s its classification!) hotel was designed by architects Warren and Westmore, who also designed New York’s Grand Central Station and Washington, D.C.’s Mayflower Hotel. The Royal Hawaiian Hotel was built by Matson Navigation and Territorial Hotel Co. However, this was not the first Royal Hawaiian Hotel: the original Royal Hawaiian Hotel was opened in 1872 in downtown Honolulu on the corner of Hotel and Richards streets and was demolished in the 1920s.

The Royal Hawaiian Hotel was originally set in a huge expanse of tropical gardens incorporating the coconut grove of the early monarchs. At that time, the gardens extended up to Kalākaua Avenue. Part of that garden is still in evidence today. Perhaps you can envision some of the lava rocks strewn around the Royal Hawaiian Garden as having been part of the heiau alongside the stream.

Hotel facilities of the Royal Hawaiian included tennis courts and a dance floor on the beach terrace. Understandably, the hotel immediately became known as “The Pink Palace.” The importance of the opening was celebrated in the song “Royal Hawaiian Hotel” by Mary Pula‘a Robins.

During World War II with the beach lined with barbed wire, The Pink Palace housed A glimpse of the stunning architecture of the Royal Hawaiian Hotel Navy personnel. After the war, extensive renovations and remodeling were completed.

In the 1980s the Royal Hawaiian Hotel was threatened with demolition and replacement with a modern high-rise structure. Now in these times of appreciating our history and historic structures, this is unthinkable!
The grand entrance, with a porte cochère, is on the ‘Ewa side of the building. The plants are surely descendants of the original 1927 garden.
Objects of Hawaiian interest are on display throughout the hotel, even in the restrooms.
One of the most interesting, and relevant to this walk, is a painting of Hawaiian war canoes, by Herb Kane (his last painting) located in the makai-‘Ewa lobby.
Walk ‘Ewa around the pool along the path to the garden of the Royal Hawaiian Hotel.
Continue Diamond Head along the water’s edge fronting the Outrigger Hotel.
Try to imagine no hotels, except, perhaps, the Moana, which went up in 1901. But before that only small structures, including homes for the monarchy; a heiau; canoes; and an athletic field.
Take your shoes off to walk in the sand as you read (and imagine) what this magnificent place once looked like.
‘Āpuakēhau Stream, a wide freshwater

stream, flowed on the Diamond Head side of the sports field until the 1920s, when this river was diverted by the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal to create the Ala Wai Canal. The Mānoa and Pālolo streams came down from the Ko‘olau mountain range, flowed into this area, then out to the ocean. ‘Āpuakēhau Stream was the middle of three rivers that flowed through Waikīkī. The other two were Pi‘inaio Stream near today’s ‘Ilikai Hotel at the ‘Ewa end of Waikīkī and Kuekaunahi Stream near the Diamond Head end of the Ala Wai Canal.
The royalty rinsed their bodies in this cool The Royal Hawaiian Hotel on the ocean. (Hawai‘i State Archives) freshwater stream after swimming and surfing in the salt water ocean.

If you need proof that there was once a fresh water stream here, just wade into the water in front of the Outrigger Hotel and wait for a rush of cold water to hit your toes: the fresh water of the wai (as in Waikīkī) of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream! It still lives!

The name for this stream ‘Āpuakēhau, ‘basket of dew,’ may derive from the vast quantities of Ti, Hau, and Palm plants that lined its banks. There are still many areas of Hau along the beach, today. Just look for a Hibiscus-like flower

Kahuamokomoko, (sports field for boxing) was located ‘Ewa of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream, on the site of the Royal Hawaiian Hotel since game stones, ‘ulu maika (stone disks used in a game similar to bowling) have been unearthed there. The historian George Kanahele relates a description from a visitor in 1813-15: “a course 500 to 600 feet long and ‘ulu maika discs weighing two to three pounds… The course was… in a grove of coconut trees planted along the beach in three parallel rows nearly a quarter of a mile.”
Another game still played today is konane, similar to checkers, with small black lava stones and small coral pieces. Boxing and a form of bowling were also popular sports among Hawaiians.

If you would like to participate in authentic Hawaiian games, visit Bishop Museum, mauka of downtown Honolulu, as well as Waimea Valley, on the north shore of O‘ahu. Waimea Valley Park has set up an area for traditional Hawaiian games. There you, too, can play ‘ulu maika! Visit
their website at www.waimeavalley.net for
events and admission information.

Standing on the beach in front of the Outrigger Hotel, try to imagine this area 200 years ago: a stream surrounded by kings’ homes on both sides of the stream, an open religious structure (heiau), and a sports field. As a royal residence, the area was kapu, ‘taboo,’ to commoners (yes, you and me!). Whatever the actual layout of those ancient sites may have been, the area, no doubt, presented a striking panorama from the ocean.
Depending on where the glottal stop (the sound between the two vowel sounds in 1880s photo - ‘Āpuakēhau Stream and Kamehameha V’s grass house. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

“oh oh”) is placed, there can be two entirely different meanings for this place name: pua ali‘il‘ii means ‘flower of the exalted royalty,’ but pua‘a li‘ili‘i means ‘little pig’! (Kanahele). The most likely meaning of the area is preserved in the first sense, since this seems more appropriate for a royal residence. However, the pig was formerly held sacred, coming down through history in mo‘olelo. This double meaning may be deliberate, based on the kaona, double or hidden meaning, in Hawaiian.

The archeologist, J. Gilbert McAllister, who wrote the definitive Archeology of O‘ahu in 1933, describes the area: “The village of Waikīkī probably centered around the mouth of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream, near the present Moana Hotel. The region is rich in traditional lore, but the exact location of former sites is difficult to determine. There was a heiau in the village that the present Hawaiians say was called ‘Āpuakēhau on the land known as Helumoa.”

McAllister continues,“The present Hawaiians believe that this heiau was located nearer the Moana Hotel and that the Royal Hawaiian Hotel is the site of the former athletic field of the ali’i, called Kahuamokomoko. When the excavation for the hotel was made, many game stones (‘ulu maika) were found.”
Royal homes were located in on both sides of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream, including the land where the Royal Hawaiian Hotel is located today.
• King Kamehameha the Great’s
stone house. He called his home here Kūihelani, ‘heavenly spear of Kū – the war deity.’ He lived here intermittently from 1795 to 1809, the year before he unified the islands.

The historian, George Kanahele, writes that Kamehameha’s kauhale (residence) was situated between ‘Āpuakēhau Stream and Helumoa, next to the footpath that came from Pu‘uwaina (Punchbowl). Kamehameha had a Western influenced fence-enclosed stone house.

Furthermore, two of his wives, his favorite, Ka‘ahumanu, and his most sacred, Keōpūolani, and their retainers lived nearby. Ka‘ahumanu’s home, Hale‘ope‘ope (‘house where folded clothes are kept’) was closer to where the Royal Hawaiian Hotel is situated.

‘Āpuakēhau Stream flowed from the Ko‘olau Mountains through Helumoa providing fresh water for both the lo‘i in the plains and for the bathers in the ocean. The triple row of Palm trees shield the Athletic Field from the strong rays of the sun. ‘Āpuakēhau Heiau, next to the stream, stands ready for ceremonial purposes.
Kamehameha the Great also provided housing for his other wives, his children, more retainers, more servants, more attendants, possibly hundreds in all.

Kamehameha the Great moved his Royal Residence to downtown Honolulu at today’s junction of Queen Street and Nimitz Highway. In 1812 he returned to his home in Kona on Hawai‘i Island where he remained until his death in 1819. Since Kamehameha’s descendants continued living on this beach, the area came to be known, not surprisingly, as the King’s Park and Grove.
• King Kamehameha III’s home was here
in the 1830s. This was also a Western-style, but a smaller, one-bedroom house.

• Kamehameha IV was well-known for working in the lo‘i (kalo fields), emphasizing the importance of kalo (taro) on many levels: economic, cultural, and spiritual connections for the Hawaiian people, after all, kalo was the Hawaiians’ lifeline. Kalo was the kino lau, the body form of Kāne; the deity of creation and the ancestor of chiefs and commoners, alike.

• Kamehameha V lived here for part of the time during his reign from 1863 to 1872. His thatch-roofed lava stone house was referred to as Hale Lama because of its native lama wood (a type of ebony found only in Hawai‘i). It was around this time, that the kalo production diminished, and, due to the influx of Chinese immigrants, rice became a popular staple. According to Kanahele, “although the king [Kamehameha V] was a powerful advocate of preserving culture [growing kalo], clearly in this instance, economics was allowed to triumph over tradition.”

There would have been several reasons making this site ideal for a royal home: the freshwater stream; the area’s elevation and natural irrigation system; Waikīkī ’s suitability as a safe harbor for war canoes; immediate availability of food staples, such as fish and fowl, and the plants of Kalo, Coconut, Ki; as well as the beauty of the beach and its surroundings.

Kamehameha V passed the land to his half-sister, Ruth Ke‘elikōlani, who in turn passed it on to Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop. Today, Kamehameha Schools educates Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian children and is the sole owner.
Subsequent rulers set up their Waikīkī residences Diamond Head and mauka of Pua‘ali‘ili‘i. (‘Āinahau-Hamohamo Walk V for more information.)
View of Waikīkī with Hale Lama, Kamehameha V’s home – where the Royal Hawai‘i Hotel now stands. 1880 photo (Hawai‘i State Archives)
1878 photo of Hale Lama, Kamehameha V’s house
at Helumoa on ‘Āpuakēhau Stream.
(Hawai‘i State Archives)
‘Āpuakēhau Heiau, a religious structure, was located near the present-day site of the Royal Hawaiian Hotel. The name is taken from ‘Āpuakēhau Stream.
This heiau was rectangular and exceptionally large, approximately 130 feet by 70 feet, with 4 to 8foot walls on three sides, the open side parallel with the shoreline.

A heiau is a sacred stone structure to which access for commoners was strictly limited. There were several types of heiau, but mainly agricultural and sacrificial. The agricultural heiau was used for economic needs or husbandry, to ensure the livelihood of the people; the sacrificial heiau was a war structure. Most heiau were damaged in 1819 or soon after when the Hawaiian religion and kapu ‘taboo,’ systems were challenged by Kamehameha II.

Shortly after the death of Kamehameha I in 1819, his wives and son, Kamehameha II, set about to abolish the ways of their traditional religion. This did not come about overnight: Ka‘ahumanu, Kamehameha I’s favorite wife, and Keōpūolani, his sacred wife, had already challenged and, thereby, had broken the kapu not only of eating with men, but also eating food including a certain type of banana, lele, which was forbidden to women since it was used for “love magic” – its lifeforce was thought to soar (lele) to the deities. This change opened the way for the Christian religion that was brought to Hawai‘i by the missionaries the following year, 1820.

Yes, there were human sacrifices in Hawai‘i. One of the most famous people to have been sacrificed here was Kauhiakama, the high chief of Maui, in 1610. His death was avenged 170 years later by Kahekili of Maui with another sacrifice at Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau on the slope of Lē‘ahi.

The first non-royal structure on this former sacred land, and perhaps the first formal hotel-type structure in Waikīkī , was Dodd’s Long Branch Bathhouse in 1881. Dodd named it for Long Branch, New Jersey, a then-fashionable resort, even for presidents. A later owner, Jim Sherwood in 1889, added not only more room, but also a 200-foot-long toboggan, offering a slide into the ocean 100 feet off-shore!
The Moana Hotel on the bank of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream (Hawai‘i State Archives)

The colonial-style Moana ‘ocean’ Hotel, loving referred to as “The First Lady of Waikīkī” as Waikīkī ’s oldest surviving hotel, opened on March 11, 1901 to serve the classy “steamboat set” from the United States Mainland. Contrary to its publicity, the Moana is not Waikīkī’s first hotel: there were many hotels before the Moana.

The family residence of Walter Chamberlain Peacock, an English businessman, was located here in the 1890s. Mr. Peacock invested $150,000 in the building of the Moana Hotel, ensuring that he had an office on the top, overlooking the mighty Pacific Ocean. When Hawai‘i was still an independent republic, a large new hotel in the middle of Waikīkī was proposed. The idea materialized as the present structure, minus the side wings and two upper floors, which were added in 1918. By that time, Hawai‘i had been annexed and had become a United States territory. The hotel building was designed by Minnesota architect Oliver G. Traphagen, who also planned the Archives building in downtown Honolulu, the magnificent (demolished in 1959) Castle Home at the Diamond End of Waikīkī, the fire station in Pālama on O‘ahu, and homes in Honolulu.

The original 1901 Moana, an eclectic style of Colonial and Queen Anne, was four stories tall and contained 75 rooms. The building’s interior is of oak and pine, with each floor in different wood decoration: The first floor with oak; second, mahogany; third floor, maple; fourth floor, koa; and fifth, cherry. On the rooftop was an observation tower, which housed Walter Peacock’s office. The Banyan Wing is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and boasts the islands’ first electric elevator.
The hotel dining room included a dance floor that extended out over the ocean. Alongside the dining room was a 300-foot pier where locals and tourists walked at night.

On July 3, 1935, the popular Hawai‘i Calls radio program was first broadcast from the Banyan Court of the Moana Hotel. Webley Edwards and Harry Owens were the originators and producers of the show. Broadcast audiences in the courtyard often numbered 2000 people. For years there was a plaque on the almost 100-year-old Banyan tree that stated that Robert Louis Stevenson did much of his writing there, under the tree. However, this tree and Stevenson never met: the tree was planted in 1904 and Stevenson died in Samoa in 1894! So much for historical authenticity! This Banyan tree, 75 feet tall and 150 feet across, is listed on Hawai‘i’s Rare and Exceptional Tree list, giving it protection under state law.
During World War II, while the Royal Hawaiian Hotel was leased to the Navy and barbed wire lined Waikīkī Beach, the Moana Hotel continued to provide its guests with its accustomed elegance.

Do spend some time at the Moana’s Historical Room on the second floor: replete with an old video, photos, artifacts, and facts. Historic tours are offered throughout the week: check on dates and times in the main lobby.
Ulukou surrounded the royal residences that were located near ‘Āpuakēhau Stream. Ulukou was an exclusive place for the chiefs, rendering it kapu, ‘taboo,’ to commoners.

Ulukou, ‘Kou tree grove,’ refers to the Kou tree, found in the Pacific Islands and is the authentic name for the ‘ahupua‘a of Honolulu. Kou wood is most useful, often carved into bowls, cups, and dishes. Ulukou has seen many residents, but the most intriguing are the kāhuna as told in the story of the Kāhuna Stones located on the grass just before Uluniu Avenue.
Many O‘ahu chiefs made their home in the ‘ili of Ulukou, making Waikīkī the capital of O‘ahu for over 400 years!
Some of these chiefs were: • ‘Aikanaka ‘man eater,’ a ruling chief.
• Kahekili, a conquering chief from Maui, who invaded Waikīkī and spent his final days here at the end of the 18th century.
• Kalanikūpule, Kahekili’s son, who lived here until being conquered by Kamehameha I in 1795.

Continue along the beach and walk up to the grassy area close to the sidewalk at Kalākaua Avenue. In front of you are the gems of Waikīkī ! These stones are located on the sand near the Waikīkī Beach Center pavilion and are surrounded by native Naupaka plants.
Kapuni The Stones of Life
You may have seen (or heard of) the animated movie, Kapaemāhū. Well, these magnificent stones before you are the real thing! Read on for the history of these precious stones.
The Kāhuna stones, sometimes referred to as the Wizard Stones and the Healing Stones, are the most sacred remaining vestige of old Waikīkī . Please afford them the respect they deserve.

These four revered stones were enclosed in 1997 with a sacred ahu in front. The beautiful renovation was done by Billy Fields of Hawai‘i Island. Notice that the lava stones at the base of the platform are not held together by mortar. This ancient Hawaiian method is called dry stack rock construction. The rocks are carefully placed so that they fit and “lock” in place.

The stones commemorate four legendary professional men (kāhuna) who were specialists in medicine, religion, and education. They were Kapaemāhū, Kīnohi, Kapuni, and Kahaloa, all mahu, or hermaphrodites, or perhaps, today’s term, transgender. After arriving from Tahiti, most likely in the 14th century, they settled in Ulukou and proceeded to exercise their enormous healing powers. Hawaiians came from afar to be cured.
Information plaque of Nā Pōhaku Ola Kapaemāhū ā Kapuni in Hawaiian (‘Ōlelo Hawai‘i).

Upon the departure of the four kāhuna from Hawai‘i, four large commemorative boulders were brought in from Kaimukī. The stones were originally set in different locations: Kapuni’s stone was placed where the surf meets the beach, the name of a surfing area; the stones of Kapaemāhū and Kīnohi were set above the shoreline at Ulukou where the four kāhuna lived; and the stone of Kahaloa was placed near ‘Āpuakehau Stream. After a ceremony transferring their power to those rocks, the four kāhuna departed.
Over time, these sacred stones were scattered around Waikīkī, only to have been rediscovered at various places, including ‘Āinahau and under the former Waikīkī Bowling Alley!
The small upright stone is Ta‘ahu Ea, which was brought from Ra‘iātea in 1997.
These ancient stones are part of the spiritual history of Waikīkī and the native Hawaiian people. They remind us of the need to preserve and honor Hawai‘i’s unique heritage for generations to come.

McAllister in his Archeology of O‘ahu writes that the stones are “said to be memorials to four men, Kapaemāhū, Kahaloa, Kapuni, and Kīnohi, who came to O‘ahu many years ago and lived with the Hawaiians. They proved to be adept in the science of healing.”
If this Hawaiian history interests you, be sure to read The Kāhuna: Versatile Masters of Old Hawai‘i by Likeke R. McBride, lovingly edited by his son, Andrew S. McBride.

The area between ‘Āpuakēhau and Kuekaunahi streams (at the Diamond Head end of Waikīkī ) was known as the ‘ili of Hamohamo ‘soothing or rub gently.’ Its name may have referred to the water lapping at the shoreline. This area was the home of Hawai‘i’s last reigning monarch, Queen Lili‘uokalani, who named her residences Paoakalani (‘royal perfume’) and Kealohilani (‘the royal brightness’) - both names are preserved as street names at this end of Waikīkī beach. (For more detail about Hamohamo, refer to ‘Āinahau and Hamohamo Walk V.)
Hawaiians, especially the royalty of old, traditionally enjoyed the fine surf of Waikīkī. Kalehuawehe, ‘the removed or untied lehua lei,’ was a surfing area.
There are two mo‘olelo ( legend) associated with the name Kalehuawehe:

According to one mo‘olelo, the name originated when a young chief from Mānoa removed his lei lehua and gave it to the daughter of Chief Kākuhihewa. Until then, only the princess has been permitted to surf there, but she broke the kapu (taboo) by accepting the lei.

The other mo‘olelo tells of a Hawaiian Robin Hood type fellow, Pīkoi, who went to Waikīkī wearing a lei lehua. He asked a surfing princess if he could borrow her surfboard, which, of course, she refused, ‘Ena Rd.
The plaque reads:

In 1997, the stones were raised onto a paepae (stone platform), and an ahu (altar) and fence were built to honor and protect them. The largest stone was estimated to weigh 7.5 tons. As part of the project ceremonies, Tahitians from Ra‘iatea presented a stone from the healers’ homeland which they named Ta‘ahu Ea (the life). as the board was kapu. The mo‘olelo does a flip-flop, however, and they surfed anyway after Pīkoi gave the princess his lei!
Uluniu
King’s Coconut Grove

Uluniu, ‘coconut grove,’ referred to a grove of several thousand coconut trees that surrounded both King Kalākaua’s and Queen Lili‘uokalani’s beach residences here. Their primary royal residence, however, was ‘Iolani Palace in downtown Honolulu. Be sure to visit the only palace in the United States of America!

The coconut trees along the beach today are descendants of trees from the time of the early Hawaiian monarchs. During his visit in 1866, Mark Twain referred to the coconut trees as “The King’s Coconut Grove.”
Uluniu Street, at the Exceptional Banyan Tree, is the only reminder today of the King’s Royal Grove, unless you consider a hotel by that name on Uluniu Street also a remembrance.

King Kalākaua’s land and home were left to Prince Kūhiō. Prince Kūhiō, the last royal to live here until his death in 1922, called his home Pualeilani ‘Heavenly flower lei.’ In turn, the land was left to Kapi‘olani Medical Center for Women and Children, named in memory and in honor of Queen Kapi‘olani.

The Hyatt Regency Hotel calls its atrium, the Pualeilani Lobby, which is particularly restful with its massive waterfalls, birds, and plants. If you have time to spare (if not, please do come back), visit the Ho‘okela Hawaiian Heritage and Culture Center on the 2nd Floor, Diamond Head Tower (Ho‘okela means ‘excellence’.) Monday through Friday 8 to 3. This the place where you will experience true Hawaiian culture.
The walk ends here, near the end of Waikīkī beach proper and the Duke Kahanamoku statue.
Another Walk VII, Kapua, overlaps with this walk, which starts on Kalākaua Avenue.
Waikīkī Coconut Grove (Hawai‘i State Archives)

title: Kalākaua Avenue
theme: King Kalākaua welcomes you to his “Great Street”

intro.text: This walk begins at the intersection of Kūhiō and Kalākaua avenues and proceeds Diamond Head along Kalākaua Avenue.
In 2013, Kalākaua Avenue was named a “Great Street.” The plaque proclaiming this honor is embedded in a lava rock at the Diamond Head end of King Kalākaua Park.
Please try to walk in the shade: mauka side in the morning; makai side in the afternoon.

blocks.text: Waikīkī Gateway Park Kalākaua Avenue Kūhiō Avenue King Kalākaua welcomes you to Waikīkī!
King David Kalākaua’s bronze statue at Waikīkī Gateway Park - the intersection of Kalākaua Avenue, Kūhiō Avenue, and Nāmāhana Street – stands tall and proud.

The park and the main avenue through Waikīkī are named after one of the last rulers of Hawai‘i: King David La‘amea Kalākaua. Waikīkī Gateway Park, also known as King Kalākaua Park, marks the entrance to Waikīkī.

The makai street is named in his honor and memory; the mauka street, Kūhiō Avenue, is named for the royal Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalaniana‘ole, who lived from 1871 to 1922 and served as a delegate to the United States Congress (More about Prince Kūhiō later when we reach his statue at Kūhiō Beach Park – Stop 28 ).
In the late-1990s/early-2000s, the sidewalks of Kalākaua and Kūhiō avenues were widened adding not only more pedestrian space, but also trees and shrubs. Enjoy your walk!

As you continue to walk along Kalākaua Avenue, appreciate the stone pavers with carved Hawaiian words beginning on the mauka side at Beachwalk (street) and on the makai side at the Saratoga Road triangle.

Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator. Buses 2,8,13,20,23,42 run along Kūhiō Avenue Parking Parking lot at the corner of Saratoga Avenue and Kālia Road Parking garage across from the Hale Koa Hotel on Kālia Road Walking times: 2 miles; 45 minutes to 1 hour; 6,000 steps

Kalākaua Avenue has been the main entryway into Waikīkī since the 1800s. Known as Waikīkī Road until 1908, the roadway was unpaved and later filled in with lava stones from the mountains. Streetcars in Waikīkī began with mules and horse-drawn carriages, followed by trolley cars, and in 1901 electric trolleys.
Kalākaua Avenue begins mauka of here, at S. Beretania Street and ends at the foot of Lē‘ahi.

King Kalākaua, affectionately known as The Merrie Monarch, was a popular and fun-loving king who ruled in a period of great turmoil for the monarchy. He lived from 1836 to 1891 and reigned from 1874 until his death in 1891. He was followed by Queen Lili‘uokalani who ruled only two years, when the “Provisional Government” took over. King Kalākaua’s Hawaiian names are very significant: La‘amea means ‘sacred one’ and Kalākaua means ‘the day of battle.’ It was during Kalākaua’s reign that business and money interests, unfortunately, succeeded in usurping many powers that had traditionally belonged to the throne.

King Kalākaua, a Mason, is fondly remembered for his love of the Hawaiian people and their culture and is considered the driving force behind the renaissance of Hawaiian culture in the 19th century. His motto was: Ho‘oūlu lāhui, ‘Let the Hawaiian race flourish.’
Some of the ways he left his mark include: • the first monarch – anywhere - to travel around the world (1881)

• reintroducing the hula, which had been banned by the missionaries in 1820; • building beautiful ‘Iolani Palace, the only palace in the United States; • establishing Kapi‘olani Park, the first major park in the islands; and • music: he wrote Hawai‘i Pono‘ī, official anthem of the State of Hawai‘i, meaning ‘Hawai‘i’s own (people).’

The statue of King Kalākaua commemorates the 100th anniversary of the arrival of Japanese sugar plantation workers in Hawai‘ithe reason that the inscription is in both English and Japanese. When King Kalākaua visited Japan in 1881 as part of his world tour, he signed an agreement to bring Japanese contract laborers to Hawai‘i to work on the sugar plantations. Between 1885, when the 994 Japanese government contract immigrants (Imin) began to arrive, until 1924, 220,000 Japanese came. The statue was designed by musician Palani Vaughan, architect Leland Onekea, and Native Hawaiian artist Sean Kekamakūpa’aikapono Ka‘ōnohiokalani Lee Loy Browne (Sean K. L. Browne, as carved on the statue, doesn’t sound very Hawaiian, does it?) He is also the artist for the Bernice Pauahi Bishop statue at the Royal Hawaiian Center.
Kalākaua Avenue was first known as Waikīkī Road. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

King Kalākaua and Robert Louis Stevenson, the famous author who was enamored with Hawai‘i, were often seen together. Stevenson considered King Kalākaua a “cultured intellectual of unusual mental powers.” King Kalākaua was related to King Kamehameha I through a common ancestor. The ruling line shifted over to the Kalākaua lineage when the Kamehameha line failed to produce an heir to the throne, and Kalākaua was elected monarch.

stops.title: Kalakaua Avenue – one of America’s Great Streets

blocks.text: The 2013 plaque recognizing Kalākaua Avenue as one of America’s “Great Streets” by the American Planning Association is embedded in a lava rock at the end of the park. The APA was founded in 1978 to represent the field of urban planning in the United States.

As you walk along Kalākaua Avenue, notice the elegant Victorian street lamps and splendid Rainbow Shower trees. The Rainbow Shower tree, the official tree of Honolulu and conceived in Hawai‘i, is a cross between the Golden Shower tree from India and the Pink and White Shower tree from Indonesia.

Look up and revel in Honolulu’s official bird, the White Tern, flitting around in the trees overhead. If you see a blue ribbon around the trunk of a tree, that could mean that the Terns are nesting. However, they do not make nests; rather, they lay the egg on the Y of a tree branch!
Nāmāhana was the mother of Queen Ka‘ahumanu (Ka‘ahumanu was King Kamehameha I’s favorite wife). Ka‘ahumanu’s father was Ke‘eaumoku, as in the street name in Honolulu.
Nāmāhana means ‘the twins.’ Nāmāhana is one of many names for the twin constellation Castor and Pollux, Nānā Mua ‘look forward’ and Nānā Hope ‘look behind,’ respectively.
Continue walking Diamond Head. Cross Kalākaua Avenue makai at ‘Olohana Street to visit the Brothers in Valor Memorial Park.
‘Olohana was part of Kamehameha the Great’s entourage.
Streetcar on Waikīkī Road, today’s Kalākaua Avenue. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

‘Olohana was the Hawaiian name of John Young I, a castaway English sailor who was stranded in 1790 at Kealakekua, Hawai‘i Island, where Captain Cook was killed. ‘Olohana became the principal advisor to Kamehameha I and helped the king invade and conquer Maui. ‘Olohana married Kuamo‘o, a niece of Kamehameha I. One of his grandchildren was Queen Emma, wife of Kamehameha IV. ‘Olohana died in 1835.

The name ‘Olohana is said to be a transliterated Hawaiian borrowing of the English phrase, “All hands!” which Young reportedly shouted at his fellow sailors. Interestingly, the verb ‘olohani means ‘to strike’ or ‘to mutiny’.

This very moving sculpture by Honolulu artist Bumpei Akaji, a 442nd Infantry veteran, honors World War II veterans. Akaji, who was born on Kaua‘i, has sculptures across Hawai‘i, notably “The Eternal Flame” at the state capitol.
The monument includes a time capsule with the names of soldiers killed in action. Walk around, sit for a while, and contemplate the power of these soldiers who fought for our freedom.

The concept for this memorial originated with Judy M. Weightman (1941-1998), a University of Hawai‘i law professor. She interviewed Japanese soldiers who helped liberate Dachau Concentration Camp. A plaque in her memory is located next to the main plaque.
This memorial is aptly situated here: This is Fort De Russy land. The U.S. Army Museum of Hawai‘i is located makai and is open to the public. (The Kālia Walk II visits these places.)
On the mauka corner of Kalākaua Avenue and Kālaimoku Street is a sculpture of a Hawaiian lady as “Storyteller,” a bronze statue by local artist, Shige Yamada.

Kālaimoku means ‘island manager’ or ‘island carver’. This street was named for a prime minister under King Kamehameha I and Queen Ka‘ahumanu. Kālaimoku, also known as Kālanimoku, died in 1827. (Saratoga Road is a makai extension of Kālaimoku Street.)
As you walk along Kalākaua Avenue, notice the newspaper stands with the palm leaf motif.

The stone pavers on the sidewalk corners have Hawaiian words carved into the tile. The words begin at Beachwalk (street) on the mauka side and Saratoga Road on the Memorial to Hawaiian Brothers in Valor makai side. See how many you can find; most are on the mauka side of Kalākaua Avenue. (A list and their meanings can be found at the end of this walk.)

A block further - at 2138 Kalākaua Avenue at the ABC store - is a plaque honoring the founding parents of the ABC stores, Sidney and Minnie Kosasa. The 50 years mentioned on the plaque, back to 1949, refer to their first store in Kaimukī (mauka of Waikīkī).
1908 photo - looking mauka along (what will become) Kālaimoku Street (Hawai‘i State Archives)
‘Ōpala means ‘trash’ in Hawaiian.

The white building with the stunning and glistening, blue-tiled roof diagonally across on the mauka-Diamond Head corner of Lewers Street and Kalākaua Avenue housed one of Waikīkī’s earliest retail stores. Though rarely noticed, it remains the most beautiful building in Waikīkī. This stately and elegant structure by the local architect, Hart Wood, dates to 1929 when it first opened its doors as a branch of the San Francisco art dealer S. & G. Gump, a firm itself dating to 1861. Today this spectacular building houses a popular retail store.

Notice the fine building features: imperial, blue-tiled roof, dark-stained imported teak wood exterior, antique copper gutters and window frames, and iron railing. When Gump’s opened to its “steamboat set” clientele in the late 1920s, the interior walls were carpeted.

Makai of Kalākaua Avenue is newly named “Waikīkī Beach Walk” – not to be confused with the street Beachwalk, which you just crossed ‘Ewa of here. This is actually Lewers Street –the longest north-south street in Waikīkī. At the turn of the 19th century, Robert Lewers (1836-1926), a New Yorker who became a local businessman, and his family, resided at the present site of the Halekūlani Hotel.

The main attraction on “Waikīkī Beach Walk” is the statue at the end of the “walk,” that of Gabby “Pops” Pahinui, labeled Kanikapila, ‘let’s play music’ by Kim Duffett. Pahinui (1921-1980) was one of Hawai‘i’s greatest musicians. Duffett also created the beautiful hula sculptures at the Hilton Hawaiian Village.
Elegant roofline on the Gump Building The fine details on this almost 100-year-old building should not be overlooked! Intricate metal work on the side staircase at the Gump Building

This area was known as Helumoa, with the only trace as Helumoa Road near Gabby Pahinui’s statue. Helumoa Road, ‘chicken scratch,’ is our only reminder of this important place in ancient Hawaiian times. Helumoa, where Hawaiian royalty lived, was a beach area located from here to ‘Āpuakēhau Stream at the Moana hotel.

There are several mo‘olelo (legend) about this place, Helumoa. According to one story, a chief of O‘ahu in the 16th century, was playing Hawaiian games in this area one day when a legendary phantom rooster, Ka‘auhelemoa, suddenly landed in front of him and began to scratch the earth. Just as suddenly, the rooster disappeared. The chief directed his men to plant a coconut in the exact spot where Ka‘auhelemoa had scratched. This coconut came to be known as Helumoa and, in turn, supported a grove of several thousand coconut trees. Helumoa was always the tallest and strongest.

Another mo‘olelo tells of chickens scratching the ground for maggots in the shallow graves of sacrificial victims from the nearby ‘Āpuakēhau Heiau. A heiau was a religious structure – more about the heiau on the Helumoa Urban Walk III.
Royal Hawaiian Avenue leads to the Royal Hawaiian Hotel, as well as a pathway out back.
Continuing along the makai side of Kalākaua Avenue, cross at Lewers Street to access the 3-block long stretch of the Royal Hawaiian Center. A plaque in the center refers to the place name Helumoa.

The Royal Hawaiian Center is a threeblock long mall with over 100 shops. However, there is a right-of-way to the beach at the ‘Ewa end of the center. The land is owned by the Kamehameha Schools for Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian children. The building material is an aggregate of cement, local volcanic cinder, local coral, and vulcanite. The Royal Hawaiian Center offers much more than conventional shopping and eating. Activities include lei ‘Āpuakēhau Stream, from the Ko‘olau mountains, emptied into the ocean next to the Moana Hotel. It was diverted into the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s (Hawai‘i State Archives) making, hula lessons, and torch lighting. As you meander around, do notice all the Hawaiian elements in this shopping center: the ferns, flowers, lava walls, torches.
The Royal Hawaiian Center is organized into 3 buildings:

• Building A has the courtyard leading out to the Royal Hawaiian Hotel • Building B houses the Heritage welcome room, Helumoa Hale • Building C has a ramp out back to the Royal Hawaiian gardens with the flowering Monkey Pod trees.
• Seaside Avenue leads to a lovely outdoor space with a facsimile of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream with kalo (taro) plants.

Look for the bronze statue by Sean Kekamakūpa’aikapono Ka‘ōnohiokalani Lee Loy Browne that depicts Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop reading to a little girl. He is also the artist for the King David Kalākaua statue.

This land, which was once the home and estate of Princess Bernice, passed on to the Kamehameha Schools for Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian students. Princess Bernice was the great-granddaughter of Kamehameha I.
PĀ KA MAKANI Blows –the wind NAUE KA LAU O KA NIU Sway –the leaves of the coconut tree HA‘A KA PUA KOALI I KE KULA Dance – the Koali flower on the plain
‘Āpuakēhau Stream

Until the 1920s, rivers from the Ko‘olau mountains, ran through Mānoa and Pālolo valleys, then flowed into this area and out to the ocean. ‘Āpuakēhau Stream was the middle of three rivers (Waikolu ‘3 waters’ Way, a small street mauka of here linking Royal Hawaiian and Seaside avenues, carries the name), which flowed through Waikīkī .
‘Āpuakēhau means ‘basket of dew.’ The name for this stream may derive from the vast quantities of Ti, Hau, and Palm plants that lined its banks.
Hau belongs to the Malvaeceae Mallow family, which includes the Hibiscus. In the course of its life (one day!), the Hau The opening lines of a dance chant –mele hula –is written on the ‘Ewa pillar.

1880 Waikīkī residence of Charles Reed Bishop and Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop on ‘Āpuakēhau Stream. Kamehameha V’s former residence is visible on the left. (Hawai‘i State Archives) blossom displays three different colors: yellow upon opening, then bright orange, finally red-brown when it drops. The Hau tree had many traditional uses: its rough but lightweight wood was used for making canoe outriggers, its fibers were made into rope, and its sap and flowers were used medicinally. There are still many areas of Hau along the beach today. Just look for a Hibiscus-like flower.

Until it was diverted by the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal in the late 1920s to create the Ala Wai Canal, ‘Āpuakēhau Stream flowed down from the mountains and emptied near the Moana Hotel. The Royalty rinsed their bodies in this cool freshwater stream after swimming and surfing in the ocean. The other two streams were Pi‘inaio, near the ‘Ilikai Hotel; the other Kuekaunahi, at Kapahulu Avenue.
Three smaller shopping areas are located across from this stretch of the Royal Hawaiian Shopping Center:
• Waikīkī Galleria Tower • Waikīkī Shopping Plaza, which has multi-level stores and restaurants • Waikīkī Business Plaza, which houses Top of Waikīkī, a revolving restaurant, on its 21st floor.

As you cross Kalākaua Avenue at Seaside Avenue, enjoy the Barnes dance diagonal crossing. Henry Barnes popularized the “pedestrian scramble” in the 1950s in Denver, Colorado. According to a Denver reporter, the crossings “made the people so happy they’re dancing in the streets.”
Cross Kalākaua Avenue mauka at Seaside Avenue, named for the Waikīkī Seaside Hotel that stood on the site of the Royal Hawaiian Hotel from 1894 to 1927.
As you walk, admire the stylized crosswalk (chicken scratches). This design is based on the Mo‘olelo Kaha (‘story about the scratches’). Refer to Stop 11 to read the mo‘olelo.
Once you cross over diagonally at Seaside Avenue with the lovely crosswalk markings, look up at the overhangs with the Hawaiian design cutouts on Seaside Avenue.

Follow the purple line if you are interested in pre-war architecture. Continue mauka past Kūhiō Avenue to 413 Seaside Avenue, with the Moongate entryway. This 1938 Art Deco building, which is listed on the Historic Register, was built of concrete bricks and Philippine mahogany.

Along the way, you will pass Lau‘ula ‘red leaf ’ Street and Waikolu ‘3 waterways’ Way. Waikolu Way commemorate the 3 rivers that historically entered Waikīkī Beach but were lost to history when the Ala Wai Canal was built in the 1920s.
Return to walk Diamond Head along the mauka side of Kalākaua Avenue.

The Art Deco movie theater was designed by Charles W. Dickey of Halekūlani fame in 1936, closed in 2002, and was demolished in 2005. In 1937, Waikīkī This crosswalk design is based on the Mo‘olelo Kaha (‘story about the scratches’).

Theater held the world premiere of Bing Crosby’s “Waikīkī Wedding” in which he sang “Sweet Leilani” and “Blue Hawai‘i.” Along the walls of the present stairwell, is a poster of “Waikīkī Wedding,” as well as posters of other old-time movies. The two mural-size photographs at the top of the stairs are of the original theater, which was known for its unusual interior: a ceiling with moving clouds and full-scale reproductions of Banana and Palm trees along the walls.
Continue along Kalākaua Avenue, passing Duke’s Lane -- so narrow that it’s easy to miss.

Duke’s Lane, just after the Waikīkī “theater,” is named for Duke Kahanamoku, Hawai‘i’s most famous sportsman and swimmer who won Olympic gold and silver medals. Duke Paoa Kahanamoku (18901968) was a full-blooded Hawaiian, born and raised in Waikīkī, He was well-loved in Hawai‘i not only for winning Olympic silver and gold medals in swimming, but also as a hero, movie actor, and Honolulu sheriff.

Duke Kahanamoku was employed at the Outrigger Canoe Club that was located across Kalākaua Avenue on the site of the present-day Outrigger Hotel. The Outrigger Hotel houses Duke’s Restaurant. In 1964 the Outrigger Canoe Club moved to its present location at the foot of Lē‘ahi (Walk VII – Kapua).
If you would like to spend a few minutes walking around the 100 or so bargain souvenir kiosks, you’ll probably find something to buy.
Former Liberty House

Look up! The overhang of this Macy’s department store has several puka (‘hole’) for its Palm trees. Look up even higher to admire the palm leaf motif on the copper grillwork on the eaves. Enjoy the graceful Plumeria trees in front of the department store.

Federated Department Stores, which own Macy’s and Bloomingdale’s, took over the Liberty House chain of Department Stores in 2001. This department store has The garden courtyard of the Waikīkī Theater was decorated with The Fountain of Stars and 150 actors’ autographs engraved on plaques. (Lowell Angell Collection) another interesting bit of history to its name change. It was founded in downtown Honolulu as Hackfeld’s Dry Goods in 1849; however, in 1918, during World War I, its Germanic name underwent a change to the patriotic sounding Liberty House. Heinrich Hackfeld was a German sea captain who settled in Hawai‘i. Hackfeld was one of the founding partners of American Factors, today known as Amfac, Inc., the Biggest of Hawai‘i’s “Big Five” companies.
Kaluaokau
The land of the International Market Place was once a summer retreat for Hawaiian royalty.

Kaluaokau, ‘the place of the pit,’ was the summer residence, Marine Residence, of the first elected Hawaiian monarch, King William Charles Lunalilo (1835-1874), who reigned for a little over one year until his death from tuberculosis. He left his estate to the wife of King Kamehameha IV, Queen Emma who also lived here. King Lunalilo founded Lunalilo Home for the Elderly; she, in turn, founded and supported Queen’s Hospital, now Queen’s Medical Center.

The 2016 International Market Place has thoughtfully integrated informational signage about Kaluaokau, complete with a simulated ‘Āpuakēhau Stream running through to Kūhiō Avenue! Recall the re-created water for ‘Āpuakēhau Stream across the way at the Royal Hawaiian Center.
Now try to picture ‘Āpuakēhau Stream without hotels and shops.

Admire the Celestial Pool in the center, featuring the Hawaiian names for Orion Ka Heihei o Nā Keiki –‘ the race of the children’ and the Pleiades Makali’i – ‘very small’ also, a chief of Waimea, Kauai. He was considered to be a navigator.

The original International Market Place, designed by Wimberly and Associates, opened in 1957 with 50 shops, a large assortment of shops for the time. A structure in the Banyan tree, now long gone, was the first home of KCCN Radio, all-Hawaiian music station. The Banyan tree is labeled “Exceptional tree,” which as you can see by its size, is quite exceptional; however, the exceptional feature refers to its local cultural value.
19 Next to the International Marketplace are the Princess Ka‘iulani Shops and the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel, which are visited on the ‘Āinahau-Hamohamo Walk V.

The first public school and first church in Waikīkī were established on the mauka- ‘Ewa corner of Kalākaua Avenue and Ka‘iulani Street, as located on 1874 and 1897 maps. The church was a ‘apana, ‘branch,’ of Kawaiaha‘o Church downtown. The church and school were razed to make way for the additional small Moana Hotel buildings. In the 1950s the cottage and nursery that were part of the Moana Hotel across the street were, in turn, razed to make way for the Princess Ka‘iulani Shops. The shops, as well as the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel, were designed by architect Gardner Dailey of San Francisco, who employed a “Hawaiian Dickey-style” roof that flares out to block the harsh rays of the sun. Dailey also designed a building on the Berkeley campus of the University of California. (For more information about Princess Ka‘iulani follow the ‘ĀinahauHamohamo Walk V)
The Outrigger Hotel - directly across Kalākaua Avenue - built in 1967, is located on the former ‘Āpuakēhau Stream.

In 1908, the Outrigger Canoe Club leased 1.5 acres of beach from the Queen Emma Estate for surfing and canoe paddling. Queen Emma Estate continues to own the land occupied by the Outrigger, Surfrider, and Moana Hotels. The beneficiary of the Queen Emma Estate is Queen’s Medical Center in downtown Honolulu. Beachfront land further ‘Ewa is owned by the Kamehameha Schools for Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian children.

The Outrigger Canoe Club, organized by Alexander Hume Ford with 150 male members, was founded in order to revive the ancient Hawaiian sport of surfing. Within a year, a women’s counterpart was formed, the Uluniu Swim Club, named for the King’s Coconut Grove. In 1916, the first official lifesaving course in the United States was taught at the Outrigger Canoe Club. The club relocated in 1963 to the foot of Lē‘ahi (Kapua, Walk VII)
This present structure, the Outrigger Hotel is graced with lovely taro leaf imprints on the exterior of the hotel.

If you have time, go to the upper lobby to see an authentic Outrigger canoe from the late 1880s and restored in 1996. Made of local koa wood, it is named Kaukahi, ‘singleness of purpose.’ Also, view the mural of an Outrigger canoe on the wall behind the reception desk, as well as the makai wall about Duke Kahanamoku and the Beachboys.

Duke’s Restaurant, named for Duke Kahanamoku, Hawai‘i’s famed sportsman, is where Don Ho first made a name for himself. Do walk around the restaurant if you don’t have time for a snack or a drink and view the fabulous photos of old. The lobby of the restaurant has a comprehensive history and photos of the Duke and of surfing.
Enjoy the old-fashioned rocking chairs on the lānai under the port cochère.

The colonial-style Moana ‘ocean’ Hotel, loving referred to as “The First Lady of Waikīkī,” is Waikīkī’s oldest surviving hotel, opened on March 11, 1901, to serve the classy “steamboat set” from the United States Mainland. This central building is referred to as the Banyan Wing. The two wings were added in 1918.
Contrary to the sign, the Moana Hotel is not “Waikīkī’s first hotel;” there were many hotels before the Moana.

The original Surfrider Hotel opened in 1952 as Waikīkī’s first post-Moana high-rise hotel. Before this hotel went up there was a string of homes including the homes of Judge Steiner, Frank Hustace, and Emmanuel S. Cunha and small, but very popular, businesses, some of which remained until the 1970s. The businesses included the Waikīkī Tavern built in 1884, later known as the Waikīkī Inn and Tavern, with the Waikīkī Surf Club housed in the lower level; the all-you-can-eat buffet for 75¢ at the Waikīkī Sands Restaurant; the Merry-go-Round Bar; The Huddles Restaurant; Heine’s, a popular drinking establishment; and Waikīkī Bowling.
Today, the former Surfrider Hotel comprises the Diamond Wing of the Moana Hotel on the Diamond Head side of the Historic Banyan Wing.
The architectural details of the 1901 Moana Hotel are often overlooked, especially when you’re carrying a surfboard!

In 1969, the next Surfrider Hotel - ‘Ewa of the historic Banyan Wing - was built on a portion of the filled-in stream bed of ‘Āpuakēhau Stream. The lobby of this 21-story Tower Wing of the Moana Hotel has an interesting display of surfboards and their history.

The family residence of Walter C. Peacock, an English businessman, was located here in the 1890s. Mr. Peacock invested $150,000 in the building of the Moana Hotel, ensuring that he had an office on the top, overlooking the mighty Pacific Ocean. When Hawai‘i was still an independent republic, a large new hotel in the middle of Waikīkī was proposed. The idea materialized as the present structure, minus the side wings and two upper floors. By that time, Hawai‘i had been annexed and had become a United States territory. The hotel building was designed by Minnesota architect Oliver G. Traphagen (1854 – 1932), who also planned the Archives building in downtown Honolulu, the Castle home in Waikīkī, the fire station in Pālama on O‘ahu, and houses in Honolulu.

The main Moana building, an eclectic style of Colonial and Queen Anne - sometimes called Beaux-Arts style, was four stories tall and contained 75 rooms. The building’s interior is of oak and pine, with each floor in different wood decoration: The first floor, oak; second, mahogany; third floor, maple; fourth floor, koa; and fifth, cherry. On the rooftop was an observation tower, which housed Walter Peacock’s office. The Banyan Wing, the main and central building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and boasts the islands’ first electric elevator.
The hotel dining room included a dance floor that extended out over the ocean. Alongside the dining room was a 300-foot pier where locals and tourists walked at night, which was removed in 1930.

On July 3, 1935, the popular Hawai‘i Calls radio program was first broadcast from the Banyan Court of the Moana Hotel. Webley Edwards and Harry Owens were the originators and producers of the show, which ended in 1975. Broadcast audiences in the courtyard often numbered 2000 people.

For years, there was a plaque on the almost 100-year-old Indian Banyan tree that stated that Robert Louis Stevenson did much of his writing there, under the tree. However, this tree and Stevenson never met: the tree was planted in 1904 and Stevenson died in Samoa in 1894! This Banyan tree, over 75 feet tall and 150 feet across, is listed on Hawai‘i‘s Rare and Exceptional Tree list, giving it protection under state law.
Peacock Residence
The Walter Peacock home was moved to this site from across the street to make way for the construction of the Moana Hotel wings in 1918.
Eventually the Peacock home was razed to be replaced by the Waikīkī Biltmore, which after a 20-year life, was imploded to make way for the 1976 appearance of this 40-story twin tower hotel.

Pualeilani (heavenly flower lei) Atrium of the Hyatt Regency was the royal name for the monarchial residences in Waikīkī. Queen Kapi‘olani retreated to Pualeilani after her husband, King Kalākaua, died in 1891; she died at her home in Pualeilani in 1899, less than 3 months after Princess Ka‘iulani’s death in nearby ‘Āinahau!
The Pualeilani lobby atrium is particularly restful with its massive waterfalls and plants.

A plaque behind one of the columns in the atrium recalls James Steiner (18601939), who had a home and property near here on the makai side of Kalākaua Avenue. The hotel lobby and second floor complete the Hawaiian connection with fascinating old photos. Be sure to visit the Ho‘okela Hawaiian Heritage and Culture Center on the 2nd Floor, Diamond Head Tower (Ho‘okela means ‘excellence’). Monday through Friday 8 to 3. This the place where you will experience true Hawaiian culture.
Cross Uluniu ‘coconut grove’ Avenue.

The area between the police station and the main Moana building was land once owned by King Kamehameha IV, who deeded the land to a missionary physician, who in turn, leased the land to various homeowners and businesses. The royal home, Pualeilani, was located nearby.
Uluniu
The gems of Waikīkī ! These stones are located on the sand near the Waikīkī Beach Center pavilion and are surrounded by native Naupaka plants (notice the half-flower).
You may have seen (or heard of) the animated movie, Kapaemāhū. Well, these magnificent stones before you are the real thing! Read on for the history of the stones.

These Kāhuna stones, which, in the past, have been referred to as the Wizard Stones and the Healing Stones, are the most sacred remaining vestige of old Waikīkī. Please afford them the respect they deserve.
These four revered stones were enclosed in 1997 by Billy Fields of Hawai‘i Island.

Notice that the lava stones at the base of the platform are not held together by mortar. This ancient Hawaiian method is called dry stack rock construction. The rocks are carefully placed so that they fit and “lock” in place.

The stones commemorate four legendary professional men (kāhuna) who were specialists in medicine, religion, and education. They were Kapaemāhū, Kīnohi, Kapuni, and Kahaloa, all mahu, or hermaphrodites. After arriving from Tahiti, most likely in the 14th century, they settled in Ulukou and proceeded to exercise their enormous healing powers. Hawaiians came from afar to be cured.

Upon the departure of the four Kāhuna from Hawai‘i, four large commemorative boulders were brought in from the Bell Stone in Kaimukī. The stones were originally set in different locations: Kapuni’s stone was placed where the surf meets the beach, the name of a surfing area; the stones of Kapaemāhū and Kīnohi were set above the shoreline at Ulukou where the four kāhuna lived; and the stone of Kahaloa was placed on the ‘Ewa bank of ‘Āpuakehau Stream, lending that name to the beach. After a ceremony transferring The small upright stone is Ta‘ahu Ea, which was brought from Ra‘iātea in 1997. their power to those rocks, the four kāhuna departed.
Over time, these sacred stones were scattered around Waikīkī, only to have been rediscovered at various places, including ‘Āinahau and under the former Waikīkī Bowling Alley!
These ancient stones are part of the spiritual history of Waikīkī and the native Hawaiian people. They remind us of the need to preserve and honor Hawai‘i’s unique heritage for generations to come.
Pīpī Holo Ka‘ao ‘Sprinkled, the tale runs’
If this interests you, be sure to read The Kāhuna: Versatile Masters of Old Hawai‘i by Likeke R. McBride, lovingly edited by his son, Andrew S. McBride.

Uluniu Avenue is the street that runs mauka; named in honor of the royalty who once lived here. Uluniu, ‘coconut grove,’ referred to a grove of several thousand coconut trees that surrounded the royal residences here. Many of the coconut trees in Waikīkī today are descendants of trees from the time of the early Hawaiians.

Duke Paoa Kahanamoku (1890-1968) appears bigger than life in this beautifully crafted bronze statue. Full-blooded Hawaiian, born and raised in Waikīkī, he was well loved in Hawai‘i, not only for winning Olympic silver and gold medals in swimming, but also as a hero, movie actor, and Honolulu sheriff.
Local lore relates that in 1917 the Duke rode the longest wave ever: a mile and a quarter on a 35 foot wave!
Kūhiō Beach stretches from Waikīkī Beach Center to the grassy area on the beach.
Notice the magnificent Banyan tree – so magnificent that it is labeled an “Exceptional Tree,” a tree with historic or cultural value.
The four streets in this area recall the reign of Hawai‘i’s last ruling monarch, Queen Lili‘uokalani. Notice that these streets are “avenue.”
The Queen lived from 1838 to 1917 but ruled slightly less than two years, from 1891 to 1893. Queen Lili‘uokalani had several houses in this area on a large tract of land in this part of Waikīkī.
Lili‘uokalani Avenue obviously

commemorates Queen Lili‘uokalani, whose birth name Lydia Lili‘u Loloku Walania Kamaka‘eha, literally means ‘smarting of the high born one.’ This queen was so named because on the day of her birth, her hanai (foster) mother’s aunt was suffering from eye pain. The story of her life is put forth in her book, Hawai‘i’s Story by Hawai‘i’s Queen. This is a fascinating account of her life and those around her. It is illustrated and includes genealogies and appendices of major documents and events during her  Ena Rd.
The plaque reads:

In 1997, the stones were raised onto a paepae (stone platform), and an ahu (altar) and fence were built to honor and protect them. The largest stone was estimated to weigh 7.5 tons. As part of the project ceremonies, Tahitians from Ra‘iatea presented a stone from the healers’ homeland which they named Ta‘ahu Ea (the life). lifetime. The author is simply Lili‘uokalani. traditional Hawaiian name from early times meaning ‘the royal brightness’ or ‘the glitter of heaven.’ Kealohilani was a cottage owned by Queen Lili‘uokalani. After her death in 1917, Prince Kūhiō and his wife lived there.
The next 2 streets have views of the Ko‘olau mountains in Mānoa Valley.

‘Ōhua Avenue -‘Ōhua means ‘retainer’ or ‘servant’ and refers to a residence of the retainers of King Kalākaua and of Queen Lili‘uokalani. Kuekaunahi Stream may have coursed along here, through Hamohamo.
Paoakalani Avenue - Paoakalani, means

the ‘royal perfume.’ This was the name of the main house where Queen Lili‘uokalani lived in Waikīkī, which was located between Paoakalani Avenue and Wai Nani way, mauka of the main beach area. (None of those streets was in existence at the time).
Pualeilani
Kūhiō Beach Park is named

for Prince Kūhiō Kalaniana‘ole Pi‘ikoi (1871-1922) whose home, Pualeilani, was nearby. The statue is by Sean Kekamakūpa’aikapono Ka‘ōnohiokalani Lee Loy Browne (sound familiar?). Prince Kūhiō’s mother was sister to Queen Kapi‘olani; his father was heir to the last ruling chief of Kaua‘i. When Kūhiō’s mother died shortly after his birth in 1871, he and his brothers were hanai (adopted) by their aunt, Queen Kapi‘olani. When Kalākaua became king in 1874, he gave royal titles to his sisters, Lili‘uokalani and Miriam Likelike, and to his hanai (foster) child, Kūhiō.

Prince Kūhiō served as a Delegate to the United States Congress from 1902 until his death in 1922 at the age of 50. He was instrumental in enacting the 1920 Hawaiian Homes Commission Act, which granted 200,000 acres of land to Native Hawaiians.

Prince Kūhiō’s death marked the end of an era: the royal realm at Waikīkī would be no longer. This beach was dedicated to him in 1940. He was fondly referred to by many nicknames, including Prince Cupid, The Chief of the People, and The Citizen’s Prince. Prince Kūhiō Day is celebrated on March 26, an official state holiday.
The road to Hanauma Bay along the coast is also named after him:
Kalaniana‘ole Highway.
Queen Lili‘uokalani’s land, mauka and Diamond Head, was known as Hamohamo, ‘rub gently,’ referring to the Prince Kūhiō in Waikīkī (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Always elegant. This statue is a true representation of the greatness of Prince Kūhiō Kalaniana‘ole Pi‘ikoi ocean lapping at the shore. She gave a portion of her estate to Prince Kūhiō. Hamohamo, bordered by ‘Āpuakēhau Stream on the ‘Ewa side and Kuekaunahi on the Diamond Head Side, extended back past present-day Ala Wai Canal (Walk V).
Uluniu was the summer residence of King Kalākaua and Queen Kapi‘olani; in fact, the Queen died here at her Waikīkī home, Pualeilani, in the summer of 1899.
Across Kalākaua Avenue, behind the store fronts, sits St. Augustine Church and a related museum.

stops.title: St. Augustine Catholic Church
stops.subtitle: The Damien and Marianne of Moloka‘i Education Center

blocks.text: Saint Damien, who was born Joseph De Veuster in Belgium in 1840, served as minister in Hawai‘i from 1864 until his death in 1889. He cared for Hawaiians afflicted with leprosy, known as Hansen’s disease, on the island of Moloka‘i until he succumbed to leprosy himself in 1884. A stylized bronze statue of Father Damien stands in front of the Hawai‘i State Capitol on S. Beretania Street. This statue, by Marisol Escobar, is one of two Hawai‘i statues in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. ; the other statue is of King Kamehameha the Great. The statue of Father Damien presents him as human – a great human replete with the scars from leprosy on his face and his arm in a sling holding a cane.
Pualeilani’s luxurious grounds rivaled that of ‘Āinahau (Walk V)
King Kalākaua and Queen Kapi‘olani, as well as Prince Kūhiō, lived at Pualeilani. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Mother Marianne, known as the Heroine of Moloka‘i, was born Barbara Koob in 1838 in Germany, and arrived in Hawai‘i in 1883 to work at a leprosy hospital in Kaka‘ako on O‘ahu, where she is memorialized in a statue at Kewalo Basin Beach Park, at the ‘Ewa end of Ala Moana Beach Park. In 1888, she arrived in Kalaupapa on Moloka‘i several months before Father Damien’s death and took on his duties. She died of natural causes in 1918.
St. Augustine by the Sea Catholic Church

The original St. Augustine by the Sea Catholic Church was established in 1854 for local Catholics. In the summer of 1898, during the Spanish-American War, soldiers camped at nearby Kapi‘olani Park were among its congregants. That first Hawaiian-style, open latticework church was built by the priest himself. By the early 1960s the building had been so seriously termite damaged that it was replaced by the present French-Gothic style church, designed by local architect George McLaughlin.

The interior is highlighted by the stainedglass windows made in Innsbruck, Austria. The koa baptismal font was presented to the church in 1903 at the baptism of the daughter of Prince and Princess David Kawānanakoa.

St. Augustine-by-the Sea is so named because it was once completely visible from ships at sea. Today it is obstructed by the museum and stores fronting it on Kalākaua Avenue. However, its copper roof is quite striking when viewed from the ocean or air.
St. Augustine and its elementary school were located mauka, on Paoakalani Street, hence the crosses on the perimeter walls.
Today that building houses the Waikīkī Community Center.
This walk overlaps with the Kapua Walk VII if you would like to continue walking.
Or continue on Kalākaua Avenue to Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park and the area once known as Kāneloa, Walk VI.

Last Days of the Monarchy: Princess Ka‘iulani and Queen Lili‘uokalani
‘Au‘aukai, ‘bathing in the sea’
From ‘Āinahau, ‘Hau tree land’ to Hamohamo, ‘rub gently’ (as in the sea at the beach)
You will cross 2 former streams: ‘Āpuakēhau Stream in the center of Waikīkī beach and Kuekaunahi Stream at the Diamond Head end of the Ala Wai Canal.
‘Au‘aukai
Hawaiians called this area ‘Au‘aukai, ‘Au‘aukai, meaning ‘to bathe in the sea,’ in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī.

On January 17, 1893, Queen Lili‘uokalani, after a 2-year reign, was overthrown by foreign businessmen, some of whom were sons of missionaries and made Hawai‘i their home. It is on that date that the Hawaiian monarchy officially ended. This walk focuses on the lives of Hawai‘i’s last monarch, Queen Lili‘uokalani; her heir apparent, Princess Ka‘iulani and her parents; and her nephew, Prince Kūhiō. The royal personages mentioned here are:

title: ‘Āinahau and Hamohamo
theme: Princess Ka‘iulani welcomes you to her ‘āina
