King Kalākaua, Queen Lili‘uokalani, and Princess Likelike were siblings and very musical; Princess Ka‘iulani was the daughter of Princess Likelike and was heir apparent; Prince Kūhiō was nephew and was hanai to Queen Kapi‘olani. He was heir apparent.

The Kalākaua lineage was related to Kamehameha the Great through a common ancestor. When the Kamehameha line failed to produce an heir to the throne, Lunalilo, grandson of a half-brother to Kamehameha I, was elected by the Hawai‘i Legislative Assembly. When he died a year later, David La‘amea Kalākaua was elected in 1874.

Upon King Kalākaua’s death in San Francisco in 1891, his sister Lili‘uokalani ascended to the throne. Queen Lili‘uokalani reigned for only two years until the Hawaiian monarchy was overthrown, and she was deposed.

This walk passes through the areas of two royal residences: ‘Āinahau and Hamohamo. The only reminder of ‘Āinahau is the ‘Āinahau Triangle Park with the statue of Princess Ka‘iulani. Nothing remains of the name Hamohamo. Even Hamohamo Street, which once ran off Kāneloa Road, no longer exists.
‘ĀINAHAU AND PRINCESS KA‘IULANI Princess Ka‘iulani welcomes you to
‘Āinahau.

‘Āinahau was the area in Waikīkī that Princess Victoria Kawēkiu I Lunalilo Kalaninuiahilapalapa Ka‘iulani Cleghorn (Princess Ka‘iulani, as she is popularly known) (1875-1899) called home. Ka‘iulani means ‘the royal sacred heights.’

Around the end of the nineteenth century, when the Cleghorns (Princess Ka‘iulani’s family) lived here, they called their land ‘Āinahau, meaning ‘land of the Hau tree.’ The Hau tree is related to the HiQueen Lili‘uokalani (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Princess Ka‘iulani (Hawai‘i State Archives) biscus plant and was common here until ‘Āpuakehau Stream was diverted from Waikīkī during the building of the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s. Today, few Hau trees are found here, but they still abound along the Ala Wai Canal and on the beaches. ‘Āinahau was abundant with flora and fauna, especially peacocks, Ka‘iulani’s favorite bird.

A ten-acre plot of land was given to the princess as a christening gift on December 25, 1875, by her aunt, Princess Ruth Ke‘elikōlani. Princess Ruth (18261883) had inherited the land from her father, who was a governor of O‘ahu and husband of Kamehameha I’s granddaughter, Pauahi. Princess Ka‘iulani called her aunt, Mama Nui, ‘Big Mama’! Princess Ka‘iulani’s mother, Princess Likelike, died at ‘Āinahau in 1887 at the age of 36, when Ka‘iulani was only 12.

This walk starts at the Princess Ka‘iulani Shops on Kalākaua Avenue; although, the entry to the lobby of the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel is on Ka‘iulani Avenue. The walk meanders along several streets in this area.

info: 2 miles; 1 hour; 6,000 steps Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator. Parking: Honolulu Zoo parking lot Corner of Monsarrat and Paki avenues

blocks.text: In the 1950s, the cottage and nursery that were part of the Moana Hotel were razed to make way for the Princess Ka‘iulani Shops. The shops were designed by architect Gardner Dailey of San Francisco in the Hawaiian style of sloped roofs. Dailey also remodeled the Royal Hawaiian Hotel in 1947.
Turn mauka at Ka‘iulaniAvenue to the entrance of the hotel.

The Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel, one of Waikīkī’s earliest high-rises, was constructed in 1954 by Matson Navigation, a local transportation company established in 1880. The hotel officially opened on Kamehameha Day, June 11 in 1955. Matson had also built several other hotels including the Moana and the Royal Hawaiian. The entryway at the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel is particularly attractive: waterfalls over lava with graceful koi (a type of goldfish) swimming in the pool below.

The architect for the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel was Gardner Dailey, who also designed the Princess Ka‘iulani Shops on Kalākaua Avenue. In the lobby is a striking portrait of Princess Ka‘iulani with a koa wood display case about the princess. The lobby is replete with photographs of the princess and her family in ‘Āinahau. Local lore relates that the hotel is haunted with the spirit of Princess Ka‘iulani since it is built near the site of her former home.

The plants surrounding the pool are particularly attractive: flowering Plumeria trees (the most popular flower for lei); Ficus trees with their large, round leaves; Coconut Palm trees, and Money Plants with long leaves - all exotics or non-native plants that grow beautifully in the Hawaiian climate. Notice the lava stone bench, which was once in front of a Banyan tree at ‘Āinahau, is now poolside at the Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel.
Look up into the trees to see if you can spot the carved peacock. It is carved into an old coconut tree! What a great recycling concept!

As you walk mauka to Kūhiō Avenue to greet the statue of Princess Ka‘iulani, notice the names of the streets across Ka‘iulani Avenue. The two streets are named for Prince Kūhiō’s brothers. The brothers were adopted by King Kalākaua and Queen Kapi‘olani who had no children of their own.

Koa, a native Hawaiian hardwood, means ‘brave’ or ‘soldier,’ and refers here to Prince David Kawānanakoa, a brother of Prince Kūhiō, who lived near here from 1868 to 1908. More about Prince Kūhiō at the end of the walk.
Prince Kawānanakoa, ‘brave or fearless prophecy,’ was named for a battle in Nu‘uanu, a valley mauka of downtown Honolulu.
This street was named for Prince Edward Keli‘iahonui, another brother of Prince Kūhiō, who lived here from 1869 to 1887. Keli‘iahonui means ‘the long suffering,
Walk mauka to the grassy triangle park on Ka‘iulani Avenue.
‘Āpuakēhau Stream

‘Āinahau, ‘land of the Hau tree,’ as this entire district was known 100 years ago, survives today in the name of this small grassy area. Most likely, this park would have been along the Palm tree-lined driveway into the ‘Āinahau manor, which stood mauka of this point. ‘Āinahau was developed by Princess Ka‘iulani’s father, Archibald Cleghorn, a Scottish businessman.
This lovely statue of Princess Victoria Kawēkiu I Lunalilo Kalaninuiahilapalapa Ka‘iulani Cleghorn (There are multiple variation on the order of her name.) stands atop a half Doric-style column.

The princess has a delicate pīkake lei necklace draped around her neck. Pīkake, which is Hawaiian for Jasmine, was her favorite flower. Notice the peacock (her favorite bird), also pīkake in Hawaiian, at her feet. The inscription reveals her full Hawaiian name, her royal lineage, and various aspects of her life. The statue was commisPrince Koa (David Kawānanakoa) and Princess Ka‘iulani were cousins. It was rumored that they would marry.
The beauty of Princess Ka‘iulani is evident even in this statue. Princess Ka‘iulani welcomes you to her home at ‘Āinahau.

A bench that now encircles an ‘Ōhi‘a tree at Kawaiaha‘o Church downtown was once on the sioned by the Outrigger Hotel chain and was created by Jan Gordon Fisher, who also fashioned the statue of Duke Kahanamoku at Kūhiō Beach. When Princess Ka‘iulani’s statue was dedicated on the 124th anniversary of her birth, October 16, 1999, it was surrounded by 23 Coconut trees, one for each year of her life.
Princess Ka‘iulani’s birthplace is marked by a medallion and plaque at the Pacific Club in Nu‘uanu.

Princess Ka‘iulani died at ‘Āinahau in 1899, not long after returning from Washington, D.C. where she met with President McKinley in the hope of restoring the monarchy. Following the trip to the mainland, she went to Hawai‘i Island where she fell ill while riding a horse in the rain. She died, probably from pneumonia on March 6, at the age of 23.
Cross Kūhiō Avenue at Kānekapōlei Street, walking mauka, to view one of the legendary banyan trees in Waikīkī, a tree with 9 lives.

‘Āpuakēhau Stream was the middle of 3 streams that entered the ocean at Waikīkī, hence the street name, Waikolu ‘3 waters’ Way, between Seaside and Royal Hawaiian avenues (several blocks ‘Ewa of here).
‘Āpuakēhau means ‘basket of dew.’ The royalty rinsed their bodies in this cool freshwater stream after swimming and surfing in the saltwater ocean.
It is said that Princess Ka‘iulani traveled downstream in a small boat to the ocean, possibly paralleling the course of present-day meandering Ka‘iulani Avenue!

The stream’s name may refer to the vast quantities of Hau trees, Palm trees, and Ti plants that lined its banks all the way to the ocean. ‘Āpuakehau stream, which originated as Mānoa-Pālolo Stream in the Ko‘olau from the mountains above Mānoa and Pālolo valleys, passed through the ‘Āinahau property where Princess Ka‘iulani lived. It emptied into the ocean ‘Ewa of the Moana Hotel. ‘Āpuakehau was the best The elegant Princess Ka‘iulani with her favorite peacocks. (Hawai‘i State Archives) known of Waikīkī’s 3 waterways because it flowed beside the royal residences and gave its name to the heiau, a Hawaiian open-air religious structure, near the ocean.
Kalākaua Avenue Walk IV and Helumoa (playground of the royalty) Walk III discuss the heiau in more detail. (A restored heiau can be visited on the Mānoa Walk X.)

Kānekapōlei Street is named for Marion Kānekapōlei Guerrero Diamond, a resident of this area in the 1930s, who was named for an uncle of a wife of King Kamehameha I. Kānekapōlei was also the name of a deity of flowers.

Behind the fence of Līlia (‘lily’) Waikīkī is a magnificent Banyan tree that has stood the test of time. This tree has been saved twice: once in 1978 when the property owners proposed removing the tree in order to enlarge the parking lot; then in 2019 when the small structures on Kūhiō Avenue were demolished to make way for a new building, Līlia. Again, the executioner’s hand was stayed!

The Banyan tree is the type of tree around which legends of Robert Lewis Stevenson’s reading to Princes Ka‘iulani flourished. Perhaps this legendary Banyan tree is the progenitor of all the Banyan trees, not only in Waikīkī, but also in Honolulu, even the Banyan tree at ‘Iolani Palace! Archibald Cleghorn, Princess Ka‘iulani’s father brought in the first Banyan tree.
Continue mauka on Kānekapōlei Street, then Diamond Head on Ala Wai Boulevard back makai on Ka‘iulani Avenue, as you enjoy the fantastic mountain views.
‘Āpuakēhau Stream ran through the Cleghorn property. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
At the first street, Tusitala Street, turn Diamond Head.

The Cleghorn home would have been in this vicinity. Princess Ka‘iulani spent almost 10 years as a student in England and traveling in Europe. While she was away at school, her father, O‘ahu Governor Archibald Cleghorn, built a two-story Victorian house with a tower. It was located Diamond Head and mauka of the present-day Princess Ka‘iulani Hotel. The architect of the Cleghorn home was Clinton Briggs Ripley who, with C.W. Dickey, another local architect, designed buildings in downtown Honolulu in the distinct Richardsonian Romanesque style, architecture inspired by ancient Roman structures.

In 1910, Cleghorn opened ‘Āinahau to the public (for a small fee, of course); unfortunately, a few months later, he passed away. In 1915, ‘Āinahau became ‘Āinahau Hotel! In 1921, the house was wiped out by fire. By 1925, along with the filling in of nearby Āpuakēhau Stream and the building of the Ala Wai Canal, ‘Āinahau was subdivided into the small lots you see around you today.

A plaque behind a fence at the ‘Āinahau Vista apartments on the makai side of Ala Wai Boulevard attests to the area once known as ‘Āinahau; unfortunately, at last viewing the plaque was so badly weathered as to render it unreadable.

This area was once affectionately called “The Jungle” because of the lush, overgrown gardens interspersed with small Governor Cleghorn built this house at ‘Āinahau especially for Ka‘iulani when she returned from Europe in 1897. The peacocks at the zoo are probably the great-great-great grandchicks of these peacocks. (Hawai‘i State Archives) wooden houses. Although high-rise condominiums and hotels have encroached on “The Jungle,” it still contains many interesting small frame houses. Walk leisurely along this street, appreciating the intimacy of the neighborhood and visualizing ‘Āinahau as it once was. The entire area, all around was ‘Āinahau.
Tusitala was Robert Louis Stevenson’s Samoan name, meaning ‘teller of tales.’ Samoan and Hawaiian are related languages, both belong to the Polynesian language family.

Poet and author, Robert Louis Stevenson, who was a close friend of Ka‘iulani’s family, often read to the princess during his stays in Hawai‘i. It is said that he read to her beneath one of the many Banyan trees, perhaps similar to the huge one near Kānekapōlei Street. The Banyan tree at ‘Āinahau was cut down due to decay, but cuttings were taken. The Banyan, a Ficus, can reach 100 feet in height. It is supported by its aerial roots, which hang down and become embedded in the soil, becoming secondary trunks.

Stevenson stayed in Hawai‘i for five months in 1889 and made a shorter visit again in 1893, staying at Sans Souci Beach. Stevenson, who was born in Scotland, became a close friend of his compatriot, Governor Cleghorn. Stevenson wrote to Princess Ka‘iulani during his second visit to Hawai‘i, while she was away, studying in England. Stevenson continued on to Samoa where he died, never to see the princess again.
John Cummins Mebane in his novel, The April of Her Age (1994), sets forth a different interpretation of the relationship between Princess Ka‘iulani and Stevenson, referred to as Victoria and Louis.
A feast in 1889 with Robert Lewis Stevenson, the future Queen Lili‘uokalani, and King Kalākaua (Hawai‘i State Archives)
A children’s book, His Majesty’s Goldfish (2015), by Leslie Hayashi is the retelling of a true story between Stevenson’s step-grandson and King Kalākaua.

A plaque engraved with a verse by Stevenson was attached to a large Banyan tree that stood along this street until the tree was removed in 1949 due to decay. Fortunately, a cutting of the tree was planted at the Princess Ka‘iulani Elementary School in Honolulu.
From the school’s website:
This cutting is the only documented descendant of the tree, but it is assumed that all Banyan trees in Waikīkī originated from that one first tree.
Cross Kapili Street, which connects Tusitala and Cleghorn streets at the Diamond Head end.

Kapili is the signature name that Princess Miriam Kapili Likelike (1851-1887) used for her musical compositions. She was sister to King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani, who were also very musical, and mother of Princess Ka‘iulani. Highway 63, known locally as Likelike Highway and connects this side of O‘ahu with the windward side of the island, is named for her.
The four siblings who were known as Nā Lani ‘Ehā, ‘The Heavenly Four,’ also included Prince William Pitt Leleiohoku II (1854–1877).
Follow the purple line to a secret stone path. Walk around the stone garden admiring the garden of Papyrus plants, Palm trees, Ti plants, and Plumeria.
Return to Kapili Street, walk makai to Cleghorn Street, then Diamond Head to Lili‘uokalani Avenue.

Archibald Scott Cleghorn was born in Scotland, and in 1851 at the age of 16, he immigrated to Hawai‘i with his parents. In Honolulu, Cleghorn met and married Princess Miriam Likelike Kekāuluohi Keahelapalapa Kapili in 1870, who bore their only child, Princess Ka‘iulani, five years later.
Cleghorn was named governor of O‘ahu in 1891 after the death of John Owen Dominis, governor of O‘ahu and husband of Queen Lili‘uokalani.

Cleghorn was the first president of Queen’s Hospital, a major medical facility in Hawai‘i, known today as Queen’s Medical Center. Cleghorn also owned an import and dry goods store on Nu‘uanu Street in downtown Honolulu.
As the first Commissioner of Parks, he is remembered as the “Father of Honolulu’s Park System.” As vice-president of the  ‘Ena Rd.

We are named after Hawai‘i’s heir apparent, Princess Victoria Ka‘iulani Kalaninuiahilapalapa Kawēkiu i Lunalilo Cleghorn. In the year of her untimely death in 1899, Princess Victoria Ka‘iulani Elementary School opened its doors. A clipping of her banyan tree from her home, ‘Āinahau was given to the school. Today our banyan tree continues to flourish on the makai side of our campus.

Kapi‘olani Park Association in the 1870s, he was instrumental in designing Queen Kapi‘olani Park, especially landscaping the trees. Always interested in plants, Cleghorn also developed a beautiful garden around his home in ‘Āinahau.

In 1910, he passed away at ‘Āinahau. Since he had no heirs, he willed the family lands to the Hawaiian government with the hope that ‘Āinahau would be used to augment Kapi‘olani Park. The government accepted the land, but with the overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy, the area was subdivided, depriving Kapi‘olani Park of this lovely addition. Only the ‘Āinahau peacock flock became part of the park: the peacocks in the Honolulu Zoo may well be descendants of Ka‘iulani’s favorite birds. The elegant home that Archibald Cleghorn lovingly built was destroyed by fire in the 1920s.

Upon subdivision of the ‘Āinahau land, the grass thatched houses on the property were to be destroyed. Fortunately, Rachel Payne of the Salvation Army noticed a newspaper advertisement offering the grass houses located on the property for sale. One of the grass houses was purchased by James Bergstrom who donated it to the Salvation Army, and had it moved to the Wai‘oli ‘joyful water’ Tea Room in Mānoa Valley where it stands to this day. That grass shack is said to be the “Little Grass Shack” where Stevenson lived, wrote, and worked, and, perhaps, even read to Princess Ka‘iulani. At least, an authentic grass shack has been preserved! The interior posts of the hut are made of ‘Ōhi‘a wood, a unique tree, found only in Hawai‘i and nowhere else. The thatch was originally of native pili grasses but has been replaced by the more available exotic (non-native) broom grass. (If this interests you, be sure to walk in Mānoa Valley, Walk X.)
Walk Diamond Head on Cleghorn Street, passing Kapuni ‘the surrounding’ Street, then mauka on Lili‘uokalani Avenue.
Queen Lili‘uokalani’s Waikīkī residence, Paoakalani (‘the royal perfume’)
Hamohamo

This street is clearly named for Queen Lili‘uokalani, who lived from 1838 to 1917 and reigned from 1891 to 1893. Her birth name is Lili‘u Loloku Walania Wewehi Kamaka‘eha, ‘smarting of the high born one.’ This queen was so named, legend tells us, because on the day of her birth, her hanai (foster) mother’s aunt was suffering from eye pain. Her baptismal name was Lydia. Her brother, Kalākaua, granted her the name Lili‘uokalani “heavenly” when he became king.

This street and the next 3 recall Queen Lili‘uokalani’s reign. Notice that they are all “avenues.” The queen owned several houses in this part of Waikīkī, known as Hamohamo, meaning ‘rub gently,’ referring to the ocean lapping at the shore, perhaps to the action of the water on the sand.
Hamohamo Road was absorbed into Kūhiō Avenue when Kūhiō Avenue was extended to Kapahulu Avenue.

One of Queen Lili‘uokalani’s houses, Paoakalani (‘the royal perfume’), was most likely located near here, between Paoakalani Street and Wai Nani (‘beautiful water’) Way. The Queen owned a large tract of land extending from just mauka of today’s Ala Wai Canal to the beachfront (today’s Kūhiō Beach), the location of her second home, Kealohilani (the royal brightness). Queen Lili‘uokalani gave a portion of her estate to Prince Kūhiō – more about him, later.

A regal statue of Queen Lili‘uokalani is located in downtown Honolulu between the State Capitol and ‘Iolani Palace. In an ironic twist, her back is to the palace where she once lived and ruled, but more poignant, where she was imprisoned after the overthrow of the Hawaiian Monarchy in 1893.
Walk mauka along Lili‘uokalani Avenue to Ala Wai Boulevard, continue Diamond Head, where you will pass street names relating to Queen Lili‘uokalani, turning makai at Wai Nani Way.
Kuekaunahi Stream
‘Ōhua means ‘retainer’ or ‘servant’ and refers to the retainers of Queen Lili‘uokalani who were housed along this street.

Kuekaunahi Stream, the eastern branch of the 3 streams that came off Mānoa-Palolo Stream just mauka of the Cleghorn property, turned Diamond Head to flow through Hamohamo to the Pacific Ocean near today’s Kapahulu Avenue. A probable meaning for Kuekaunahi is ‘to remove scales from fish.’ All the streams were diverted to the Ala Wai Canal in the 1920s.
Paoakalani and ‘Ōhua have unobstructed mountain views.
Paoakalani, ‘royal perfume,’ was the name of Queen Lili‘uokalani’s principal home, which she referred to as her “pretty seaside cottage.”

Paoakalani is memorialized in two songs written by the Queen. “Ku‘u Pua I Paoakalani” recalls the wistful days when the flowers bloomed at her home; “Paoakalani” tends to express her anguish of love for her former home.
One of the towers at the Waikīkī Beach Marriot Hotel (Stop 16 ) incorporates Paoakalani as the name of one of Queen Lili‘uokani’s homes.

After crossing Paoakalani Avenue, look back on the ‘Ewa side to see cutout crosses on the sides of a small building: this was once the elementary school and convent for St. Augustine Church. The church is now located on Kalākaua and ‘Ōhua avenues. The Waikīkī Community Center is located on this street.
Turn makai on Wai Nani Way to the entrance of Lili‘uokalani Gardens.
Wai Nani means ‘beautiful water’ and most likely refers to the beautiful Kuekaunahi Stream that flowed through the Queen’s land.

Queen Lili‘uokalani’s primary home, Paoakalani, may have been located where the Lili‘uokalani Gardens towers are today. Built in 1983, this complex - King Tower on the mauka side and Queen Tower on the makai side – later replaced small homes similar to those on the surrounding streets. The Queen’s home was most likely located at or near the King Tower -- yes, it should have been Queen Tower! The towers are in the shape of the royal standard, the kāhili - tall poles with feathers at the top; the kāhili stood at the sides of the monarch.

Walk into the driveway area to admire the lovely gardens and ponds. Notice the interesting crest of flowers in the center of the driveway and the crown-like lattice work above the walkway. A recreation of Kuekaunahi Stream, in the midst of an explosive garden, runs between the 2 kāhili-shaped towers.

Enjoy walking makai in the cool of the shade of the trees along Wai Nani Way, crossing Pualani Way, which means ‘flower of heaven,’ and may refer, figuratively, to the royalty who once lived here. Turn ‘Ewa on Kāneloa Road to Paoakalani Avenue.
Kāneloa means ‘long or tall man,’ but Kāne is also the name of an important Hawaiian deity. Kāneloa Road is named for a tract of land which extended from this area up through Kapi‘olani Park.
The Towers of Lili‘uokalani Gardens are modeled after the royal kāhili. These kāhili are on display at Ho‘okela at the Hyatt Regency (stop 13). The photo is of Princess Bernice Bishop Pauahi.
The name and crown in Lili‘uokalani Gardens are reminders of the days when Queen Lili‘uokalani lived in Waikīkī.
(The Kapi‘olani Park - Zoo Walk, Kāneloa Walk VI, takes you through that area.)

You are passing Thomas Jefferson Elementary School on the Diamond Head side of the road. Thomas Jefferson is one of two elementary schools in Waikīkī; the other is Waikīkī Elementary, Diamond Head of Kapi‘olani Park.
Come back to Paoakalani Avenue to the restful bus stop and the lovely plantings at the mauka-Diamond Head corner at Kūhiō Avenue. Many of the bus stops along Kūhiō Avenue are artfully landscaped.
Continue ‘Ewa along Kūhiō Avenue, passing two hotels:
First, Waikīkī Beach Marriot Hotel across the way, then Prince Kūhiō (Hilton) Hotel at the corner of Lili‘uokalani Avenue.
Lalani Village, which was located at the makai -‘Ewa corner of Kalākaua and Paoakalani avenues from 1932 to 1955, was the first Hawaiian-Polynesian cultural center.

James Kapihe Palea, known as Kuluwaimaka, “Tear Drop,” for the tears of emotion brought to the eyes of his audience, was the Hawaiian chanter at the Village. Earlier in his career, he was chief chanter under King Kalākaua.

Today, the Waikīkī Beach Marriot Hotel is located on that site. Before the 1920s, Kuekaunahi Stream once flowed nearby. The two towers are named after Queen Lili‘uokalani’s homes: the mauka tower, Paoakalani; the makai tower, Kealohilani.
Kealohilani Avenue, which connects Kūhiō and Kalākaua avenues, is a traditional Hawaiian name from early times meaning ‘the royal brightness’ or ‘the glitter of heaven.’

This street was named for one of the residences of Queen Lili‘uokalani. The name had also been used earlier by Kamehameha V for his beach home at Helumoa (Helumoa, Walk III, is about the earlier Royal Residences.)

Kealohilani was the name of members of the royal family as well as the name of a star that rises in the night of Mauli, during the month of Welo (a spring month) and sets in the night of Muku in the month of Māhoe-mua (a summer month). A ring around this star is said to portend revolution, and indeed a ring did appear around the star Kealohilani before the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.
The hotel on the corner of Kūhiō and Lili‘uokalani avenues houses interesting Hawaiian artifacts and photos of Prince Kūhiō in the display cases.
Kealohilani – the royal brightness – Avenue refers to one of the houses owned by Queen Lili‘uokanlani.
Walk back to Kealohilani Avenue , turning makai to where Kūhiō Beach Park begins. Continuing along the beach side to the statue of Prince Kūhiō.
Pualeilani
Kūhiō Beach stretches from Waikīkī Beach Center to somewhere along the grassy area on the beach.

The statue of Prince Kūhiō is located at Kūhiō Beach between ‘Ōhua and Kealohilani avenues. Kūhiō Beach Park is named for Prince Kūhiō Kalaniana‘ole, whose home, Pualeilani ‘heavenly flower lei,’ was nearby. Prince Kūhiō demolished Queen Lili‘uokani’s Kealohilani and replaced it with Pualeilani, the name borrowed from Queen Kapi‘olani’s home.

The Pualeilani (‘heavenly flower lei’) Atrium of the Hyatt Regency is particularly restful with its massive waterfalls and plants. If you have time to spare (if not, please do come back), visit the Ho‘okela Hawaiian Heritage and Culture Center on the 2nd Floor, Diamond Head Tower (Ho‘okela means ‘excellence’.) Monday through Friday 8 to 3. This the place where you will experience true Hawaiian culture.

Prince Kūhiō (1871-1922) served as a delegate to the United States Congress from 1902 until his death in 1922. He was instrumental in enacting the Homes Commission Act, which granted 200,000 acres of land to Native Hawaiians. Kūhiō’s death marked the end of an era: the royal realm at Waikīkī would be no longer; although, the beach was dedicated in his honor in 1940.

After Kūhiō’s mother died, he and his brothers were hanai (adopted) by their aunt, Queen Kapi‘olani. When Kalākaua became king in 1874, he gave royal titles to his sisters, Lili‘uokalani and Miriam Likelike, and to his foster child, Kūhiō. Queen Lili‘uokalani later gave a portion of her Hamohamo estate to Kūhiō.
Walk one block ‘Ewa of Lili‘uokalani Avenue to Uluniu Avenue
Uluniu Līloa (Ka Paepae Kapu a Līloa)

Uluniu, ‘coconut grove,’ refers to a grove of thousands of coconut trees that once presided here along with the monarchy and surrounded the royal residences from this area to the ocean. The coconut trees along the beach today are descendants of trees from the time of the Hawaiian monarchs.
Uluniu, later known as Pualeilani was the summer residence of King Kalākaua and Prince Kūhiō Day is celebrated on March 26, a state holiday.
Queen Kapi‘olani; in fact, the Queen died here at Pualeilani, her Waikīkī home, in the summer of 1899.
Ka Paepae Kapu a Līloa is the sacred/

forbidden threshold that King Kalākaua brought to his home, Pualeilani. The ‘Sacred Stone of Līloa’ now resides at the Hawai‘i State Archives near ‘Iolani Palace. The stone and legend are from Waipi‘o (‘curved water’) Valley on the north part of Hawai‘i Island. Waipi‘o was home to the rulers of Hawai‘i Island, including Chief Līloa, before Kamehameha the Great.
You can continue walking on the Kāneloa Walk VI, which encompasses Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park and the Honolulu Zoo.
Pualeilani, King Kalākaua and Queen Kapi‘olani’s residence, is in the background. Notice all the coconut trees in Uluniu. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park and Honolulu Zoo
There is no estimated time or mileage for this walk since you are encouraged to wander around and explore as you follow the designated stops.
The district where the park and zoo are now located was known as Kāneloa, meaning ‘tall man.’ Kāne was also the name of one of the most important Hawaiian deities.

Kāneloa Road is named for a tract of land that extended from this area up through Kapi‘olani Park between the Ala Wai Canal and Kūhiō Avenue. The truncated street is the only reminder of an important place in Hawaiian history.
The area directly makai of Kāneloa was known as Kekio, ‘the protuberance.’

On this walk you can meander around Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park, ending at the Honolulu Zoo, stopping occasionally to contemplate historic sites, such as a statue of Queen Kapi‘olani, a statue of Gandhi, replica of a trolley stop, and a racetrack long-gone.
This walk begins on the corner of Kapahulu and Monsarrat avenues at the unusual lava stone structure.

Parking: Honolulu zoo parking lot Corner of Monsarrat and Paki avenues

blocks.text: Hawaiians of old who lived and died in Waikīkī. There are approximately 200 sets of Hawaiian remains.

The architectural design is quite intriguing: older lava stones at the bottom of the wall and newer lava above, topped by a torch, which is lit whenever another body is interred. Benches are strategically placed inside the memorial for rest and contemplation for the lineal descendants. The green and red Ti plants have been planted as good luck and to keep evil away.

As was stated in the mayor’s office news release, “The Memorial is the first of its kind to offer permanent and dignified protection to generations of Hawaiian ancestral remains unearthed and/or repatriated from museum collections across the nation.”
The bronze plaque is a message to us from the lineal descendants.
The Banyan trees shade a statue of Indian nationalist and spiritual leader Mahatma (“great soul”) Gandhi. As a continuing gesture of harmony, this statue and these words of Gandhi welcome visitors:
It is Possible to Live in Peace.
Gandhi, who preached non-violence protest, lived from 1869 to 1948. He was killed on his way to evening prayers in Delhi by an assassin’s bullet.

There are 3 plaques that describe Gandhi’s life, his struggles for India’s freedom for which he is known as “The Father of India,” and the relationship of this teaching to Hawaiian values as “The Gentle Messenger.” The This memorial is a final and respectful place for the iwi (bones) of the Hawaiians who once lived in this area.
“A Fistful of Salt” is a poignant tale. plaque titled “A Fistful of Salt” is particularly moving.

The plaque at the bronze statue of Queen Kapi‘olani is inscribed with her legacy: Kūlia I Ka Nu‘u, ‘Strive for the Highest.’ In 1890, the queen left a bequest to Kapi‘olani Maternity Home, now known as Kapi‘olani Medical Center for Women and Children, where President Barack Obama was born.
Walk behind the statue toward the ponds and bandstand.

Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park, a 100acre recreation area, is named for Queen Kapi‘olani, ‘the arch (of a rainbow) of heaven,’ who lived from 1834 to 1899. She and her husband, King David Kalākaua, reigned from 1874 to 1891.

King Kalākaua presented the park as a gift to the people of his kingdom in 1877, and it was officially named and dedicated to his wife, Queen Kapi‘olani on Kamehameha Day, June 11, of that year. It was the first major public park in the kingdom. The oldest park in Hawai‘i, Thomas Square downtown, was dedicated in 1843.
Kamehameha V proclaimed Kamehameha Day on June 11, 1871, in honor of Kamehameha I; June 11 is the attributed date of Kamehameha I’s birth.

The holiday is celebrated with festivities in Kapi‘olani Park and an elaborate parade through Honolulu. Kamehameha Day is even celebrated in our nation’s capital, in Washington D.C. in the U.S. Capitol: A bronze statue of Kamehameha I is festooned with lei accompanied by Hawaiian chanting and dancing!

Kapi‘olani Park is the place to be on May 1st : May Day is Lei Day. The area near Kapi‘olani Bandstand (Stop 7 ) is festooned with hundreds of unique handmade lei with prizes for the best in several categories. The first Lei Day was celebrated in 1928 in downtown Honolulu, moving to Waikīkī in the 1970s.
In 1898, soldiers at Camp McKinley called Kapi‘olani Park home.(Hawai‘i State Archives)
Queen Kapi‘olani welcomes you to her park!
Archibald Cleghorn, Princess Ka‘iulani’s father, helped design Kapi‘olani Park, including the trees. Greater Kapi‘olani Park includes Kapi‘olani Park Beach and Queen’s Surf Beach.

The parklands were created by the Kapi‘olani Park Association, a collaboration of royal grants from the crown and 200 private members. The park originally included the land ‘Ewa of this point, now occupied by the Honolulu Zoo.

In its early days, the park contained numerous lily and goldfish ponds, dotted by islands planted with Palm trees, Hibiscus, and Crotons. The Royal Hawaiian Band, the oldest municipal band in the country, performed atop one of the islands, much to the delight of picnickers. Check the website, www.rhb-music.com for their schedule.

During the Spanish-American War (April to August 1898), the first military camps in Hawai‘i were established in Kapi‘olani Park, where they remained until 1907. The military troops marched from Honolulu Harbor to Kapi‘olani Park! Camp McKinley opened in 1898 and Camp Otis soon followed. Today, nothing remains of those temporary military sites. The military moved to Fort De Russy, on the ‘Ewa side of Waikīkī.
Kapi‘olani Park also boasts accommodating one of the first airfields in Hawai‘i, including a balloon ascent in 1889.

In the 1920s the park’s ponds were filled with dredgings from the Ala Wai Canal project. It was claimed, at the time, that the park was falling into disrepair due to poor maintenance by the territorial government that took control of Hawai‘i.
Makee Island in 1900 – lagoons, bridges, Ironwood and Kiawe trees – a lover’s paradise. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Kapi‘olani Park is very popular today for picnicking and sports: baseball, football, soccer, rugby, and other more exotic games. More impressively, the park is Honolulu’s favorite jogging route, measuring 1.8 miles, adding the zoo for 2.2 miles. There are also exercise stations and a jogger’s course along the way.
Along Paki Avenue, mauka of here, are tennis courts, as well as a lifeguard station, which was moved there in 1976 when the Natatorium was condemned.

Come December, the Honolulu Marathon transforms this peaceful setting into a wild party! The original marathon distance 26.2 miles was based on the distance from Athens to Marathon, a city northeast of Athens. The marathon is founded on the legend that Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory of Athens over the Persians in 490 BCE. The first Honolulu Marathon was held on Sunday, December 16, 1973.
There are 2 huge Banyan trees on the Diamond Head side of Kapi‘olani Park. Can you find the main/original trunk for each Banyan tree?

Before the zoo was established, a large man-made island, Makee Island, was located here, covering most of the present-day zoo. Captain James Makee, a Scotsman of many resources and talents, was captain of whaling ships, a rancher, and a commercial developer. In the 1860s he established Rose Ranch on the slopes of Haleakalā on Maui, developing it into a cattle ranch estate where the Hawaiian monarchy enjoyed being wined and dined. He also owned a sugar company with King Kalākaua.

In 1876, Makee was one of the organizers of Kapi‘olani Park Association and one of the developers of the long-gone racetrack in Kapi‘olani Park. Makee Road, a short diagonal road ‘Ewa of the Zoo, off Kapahulu Avenue is named for him. Makee Road was almost completely absorbed by Kapahulu Avenue when Kapahulu Avenue was extended makai.

The area around the bandstand has been landscaped with ponds and lakes to reflect Makee Island and earlier days of Kapi‘olani Park before the Ala Wai Canal. Enjoy walking around the recreated ponds, especially the sculptures, the Joy of Music and Pinao, ‘dragonfly.’
Racetrack
The double row of Ironwood trees lines the carriageway that led to the racetrack viewing stand. The Ironwood trees are registered as Exception Trees, meaning that they have cultural significance.
Can you find the various poses of the hula dancers etched on the columns of Kapi‘olani Bandstand?

A curved row of Date Palm trees lined the far end of the Kapi‘olani Park Racetrack. A few stately Date Palms continue to outline the Diamond Head end of the racetrack. Designed by Captain Makee, the racetrack was complete with a truly grand Grandstand.

Horse racing was extremely popular in the late 1890s, especially the Rosita Cup, an annual event on Kamehameha Day, June 11. Due to excessive betting, the park commissioner banned horse racing, demolishing both the racetrack and grandstand in the 1920s. Horse racing was soon replaced with polo games and a polo field. Today, you are more likely to see pick-up soccer and volleyball games.
Walk along Kalākaua Avenue, toward Lē‘ahi. First you will come to the bandstand. A little further down Kalākaua Avenue is a reproduction of a trolley shelter.

The beautiful Victorian-style gazebo was designed by David Ayer. The bandstand, dedicated on Independence Day in 2000, is a 15-sided polygon with a sloped copper roof topped with circular glass skylights and a copper cupola (and often with a bird perched on top!). Notice the lovely etched hula poses at the top of the columns. The roof is installed with roll-down walls for night security and sound control.

An earlier bandstand was designed by Hart Wood in 1926 who was the architect for many buildings in and around Hawai‘i, including the Gump building in Waikīkī, the Chinese Christian Church in Honolulu, and the Board of Water Supply administrative building.

The Royal Hawaiian Band, established in 1836 by Kamehameha III, sometimes holds its Sunday afternoon concerts here. Its office is in the back of the Waikīkī Shell Amphitheater. Check their website, rhb-music.com for their up-to-date schedule.
Sit for a while and relax in the shade of the Monkey Pod trees (but watch out for the sprinklers).
Be sure to come back on May first for Lei Day (Stop 5 ).

Diamond Head-makai of the bandstand is a small odd-shaped lava stone formation. It contains a time capsule that celebrated the 100th anniversary of Kapi‘olani Park. The time capsule is to be opened on June 11, 2077. It is hard to imagine what Waikīkī was like in 1877, but it’s impossible to imagine what Waikīkī will look like in 2077!
Continue along the sidewalk on Kalākaua Avenue.
Lē‘ahi is a Registered National Natural Landmark

The quaint looking structure on Kalākaua Avenue is a replica of a trolley stop. Today it is a jogger’s rest stop. Kapi‘olani Park offers a long course and short course with exercise stations along the way.

At the end of the 19th century/beginning of the 20th century, two local transportation systems co-existed: The Hawaiian Tramways Company, a horse-tram system, and the Honolulu Rapid Transit Company, which provided an electric trolley.

A similar Victorian shelter was installed concurrently with the opening of the Aquarium in 1904. Interestingly, the owners of the Honolulu Rapid Transit Company also owned the Aquarium. The site for the shelter was chosen in the hopes of luring more passengers to this end of Waikīkī.

The trolley stop was restored in 1975 and affectionately renamed “Jogger’s Rest.” Fortunately, there is a water fountain here, a welcome site indeed for anyone (you?) jogging or walking in the hot sun.

Diamond Head-Makai of the tennis courts, amid a grove of Monkey Pod trees, is a 1968 plaque stating that Lē‘ahi has been designated a Registered National Natural Landmark. (You didn’t know there was such a thing, did you? Now you do.) the Ko‘olau Range Pali is the only other Registered Natural Landmark on O‘ahu.
Stroll away from the beach, diagonally across the park toward the Waikīkī Shell, taking pleasure watching the picnickers, athletes, and strollers as they enjoy the park with you!

The entrance, which is closed when there are no concerts, to the Waikīkī Shell amphitheater is on Monsarrat Avenue. This outdoor theater, built in 1956, and seating 8,000, really looks like a shell, especially from the back as you walk toward it. It has been used for diverse events, ranging from University of Hawai‘i commencement ceremonies to Hawaiian music concerts by local entertainers and the Hawai‘i Symphony Orchestra’s summer series.
The Waikīkī Shell is named the Tom Moffatt Waikīkī Shell in honor and memory of the first rock D. J. and concert promoter known as “Uncle Tom.”

If you can peek though the fence, you’ll see a bust of Gabby Pahinui (1921-1980), one of the greatest Hawaiian musicians. A full-sized statute of Gabby is on Lewers Street and Helumoa Avenue on “Beach Walk.”
The plaque reads:
*spirit.

“A legend in his own time, Gabby with his mastery of slack key guitar and falsetto singing style, sparked a musical renaissance throughout Hawai‘i. His mana* continues to inspire those who love Hawaiian music.”
Gabby “pops” Pahinui, one of Hawai‘i’s great musicians.
In fact, this IS the largest and best zoo, with over 1200 mammals, birds, and reptiles, for 2300 miles around!

If a concert is scheduled, do attend. You’ll never forget the event under the stars. The best and least expensive seats are on the lawn! Come early, bring a blanket and friends, and picnic on the grass before the event begins.

The Kodak Hula Show was held in a smaller area makai of “The Shell.” Established in 1937 at the Sans Souci Beach, the show advertised itself as being the longest continuous operating hula show in Hawai‘i (and probably the world!). The hula show moved to this location in the late 1960s, but the show ended years ago.
Authentic hula shows are often held at the Bishop Museum in Kalihi, a neighborhood mauka of downtown Honolulu.
Walk around the back of the Waikīkī Shell to see a remnant of the streams that once flowed through Waikīkī. Then walk ‘Ewa on Paki Avenue to the garden on the corner at Monsarrat Avenue.

On the mauka-‘Ewa corner of Paki and Monsarrat avenues is a quiet, undisturbed garden, which was founded by the Outdoor Circle in 1926 as Kapi‘olani Nursery. An enormous debt of gratitude is owed that organization for getting billboards banned in Hawai‘i.

During World War II, the nursery was used as a victory garden. In the 1960s it was known as the Kapi‘olani Hibiscus Garden. Then in 1971, the garden became part of Kapi‘olani Park and was officially dedicated as the Queen Kapi‘olani Garden.
Local lore relates that the large boulders at the Diamond Head end of the garden are the guardian stones of the garden, offering spiritual healing to the Hawaiian people.
Walk makai along Monsarrat Avenue to the Honolulu Zoo where Kapahulu, Kalākaua, and Monsarrat avenues come together, as you listen to the wild screeching of the gibbons in the zoo!
For the past 70+ years, Hawai‘i artists have displayed and sold their art and photos every Saturday and Sunday from 9 to 3 outside the zoo on the fence along Monsarrat Avenue.

The main entrance, built in 2011, to the Honolulu Zoo is on Kalākaua Avenue between Kapahulu and Monsarrat avenues, just mauka of the Banyan and Monkey Pod trees. The zoo extends over 40 acres. Be sure to follow the zoo map to get the best experience.

The original renovated entrance, makai of today’s entrance, was designed by Alfred Preis (1911–1994) in 1962, who also designed the Arizona Memorial. Mr. Preis, although he was Austrian, was interned for a while during World War II. Under his leadership at the Hawai‘i State Foundation for Culture and the Arts, Hawai‘i became the first state to set aside 1% of construction budget for public projects to be earmarked for public art. In the 1940s, he designed 14 houses in the hills of Mānoa.
The Honolulu Zoo participates in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (ICUN) Red List of Threatened Species, which keeps track of the conservation status of biological species.
Notice the posted red “dots” as you walk around, from “least concern” to “extinct in the wild.”
One of the largest and most beautiful Banyan trees is outside near the old entrance to the zoo. See if you can find the trunk among all those arial roots!

Once you enter the zoo, find the HONOLULU ZOO sign that proclaims, “This is the best Zoo to be found for 2300 miles in any direction,” and lists the zoos and directions of many other zoos! Is your zoo listed? The sign is near two other huge Banyan trees in the zoo.

The Honolulu Zoo is the only zoo in the US that originated from a Royal Land Grant from the king to his people. The zoo was initially park of Queen Kapi‘olani Park, which included King Kalākaua’s exotic birds as the zoo’s original residents. The birds were soon joined by peacocks and flora from Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. Princess Ka‘iulani’s peacocks were donated to the zoo at that time creating the collection of Hawaiian Monarchy’s birds. The statue of Princess Ka‘iulani on Kūhiō and Ka‘iulani avenues has her posed with a peacock. At the peafowl exhibit, the information placard states that the peafowls “are not part of the Honolulu Zoo’s collection of species,” and roam free. Perhaps you might be lucky to see their magnificent open display of train feathers.

The first park superintendent, Ben Hollinger, brought in the first monkey, bear, lion cubs, and imported birds. Two years later, in 1916, the zoo’s character was changed drastically by the introduction of an African elephant, Daisy, who lived until 1933. How all of Honolulu loved Daisy! She particularly enjoyed carrying around children on her back. Mari and Vaigai, Indian elephants who have replaced Daisy, were presented to the zoo from the children of India. In 1982, Mari, who was born in 1975 in India, came to the zoo. Ten year later, Vaigai, another female, but 10 years younger, was introduced to Mari. Visit The Chief ’s Hut for more information.
No need to go to the Galapagos Islands: we have Galapagos Tortoises here!

During the years of the Depression and World War II, the zoo fell into disrepair. Only the bird collection prospered during that period, due to the efforts of E.H. Lewis, an ornithologist from California. For a while, the zoo was understandably known as Kapi‘olani Bird Park.
In 1947-1948, when the Honolulu Zoo received its present name, it was revitalized with many new animals being added, including a camel, elephants, chimpanzees, and deer.
In 1992 the zoo was again redesigned to its present character, emphasizing the African Savannah, Tropical Forest, Islands of the Pacific, and Children’s Zoo.

In 1928, the Honolulu Zoo received tortoises from the Galapagos. Some of those tortoises are still here today! In 1954, the Honolulu Zoo had the earliest effective Galapagos Tortoise propagation program in captivity.
Be sure to see our native Pueo (‘owl’) who sleeps at night so that he can greet you during the day!
There are several not-to-miss sections:

• Children’s Discovery Forest with native and canoe (Polynesian introduced) plants • Bird Watching in Hawai‘i • Native Plants • Hawai‘i’s Plants and Animals • White Tern feeding area And, of course, • Like Nowhere Else on Earth Walk VII, Kapua, begins at Kalākaua and Kapahulu avenues, just outside the Zoo entrance. The walk proceeds along the eastern section of Kalākaua Avenue, then up Diamond Head Road (not all around Lē‘ahi – do that on your own!)
No matter where you go, our native Pueo turns his head to find you!
