title: Kapua
theme: Diamond Head greets all visitors to Waikīkī!

intro.text: Lē‘ahi greets all visitors to Waikīkī!
The walk meanders along the Diamond Head end of Waikīkī past the Waikīkī Aquarium up to the beach parks on the slope of Lē‘ahi (Diamond Head), at which point, you have 3 alternatives:

1. Turn around and come down Diamond Head Road 2. Continue all the way around Lē‘ahi until it becomes Monsarrat Avenue, and then walk along Monsarrat Avenue to Kapahulu Avenue 3. Take the bus back This walk goes through the historic district or ‘ili, of Kapua, ‘the flower,’ along the oceanfront at the foot of Lē‘ahi. Kapua Channel is visible offshore, Diamond Head of the Natatorium. In 1902 the Commercial Pacific Cable was set in the channel linking San Francisco and Honolulu.
The first part of the walk parallels the area once known as Kāneloa, which today includes Kapi‘olani Park and the Honolulu Zoo, Walk VI, Kāneloa.
In 1823, Kamehameha II presented Kapua as a tribute to a member of his court, Chief Iona Pehu, konohiki (overseer) for all the lands in Honolulu. More history of Kapua is related later.

After the Mahele of 1848 when royal land was divided up, more and more beaches and homes in this area came to be owned by European and American haoles. (Today haole refers to Caucasians but originally, and actually, means any ‘foreigner.’) From Kapahulu Avenue continuing Diamond Head, landowners recorded on an 1895 map of the area were: Magoon Brothers, E. S. Cunha, C.H. Brown, H.M. von Holt, McInerny, F.M. Hatch, A. Herbert, Westervelt, W. G. Irwin, G.W. Macfarlane, and several Castle names.

Some of these landowners never developed their property, but others, such as the Magoon, McInerny, and J.B. Castle families, built beachfront homes. Visible remnants of the Castle mansion still exist at the foot of Lē‘ahi.
Today all beaches in Hawai‘i are public property and completely accessible, except for those at military reservations.

The walk begins on the makai side of Kalākaua Avenue where it meets Kapahulu Avenue. Be sure to be suitably outfitted for this walk: plenty of water, comfortable shoes, a hat, and sunblock. It can get very hot, so be prepared so that you can enjoy the walk

Lē‘ahi is the correct name for Diamond Head crater and will be used in this walk when referring to the crater. However, Diamond Head will be used as a directional and in the street (Diamond Head Road) name.

info: Useful websites: Waikīkī aquarium www.waikikiaquarium.org Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator. Walking times: 2 miles one way; 1.5 hours; 7,000 steps Parking lots: Corner of Kapahulu and Kalākaua avenues at the Honolulu Zoo Corner of Monsarrat and Paki avenues Anywhere along Paki Avenue

stops.title: Kapahulu Avenue, Kapahulu Pier and The Wall

blocks.text: Kapahulu ‘the worn-out soil’ Avenue forms the Diamond Head boundary of Waikīkī beach proper.

Extending into the water from the end of Kapahulu Avenue is Kapahulu Pier, recently renamed more picturesquely, Queen’s Promenade. A walk to the end of the pier, to the gazebo, is absolutely lovely. Do go!
Perpendicular to the pier is “slippery wall,” obviously named: It can be dangerously slick. Don’t go! It was originally built to keep the beach from eroding; unfortunately, it has not helped enough.

If the walkway along the beach is clear (no high tide waves and/or no construction), walk along the oceanfront until you reach the aquarium, then come back to Kalākaua Avenue for the entrance to the Waikīkī Aquarium.

Kuekaunahi Stream originally flowed down from the mountains through Pālolo Valley and emptied into the ocean ‘Ewa of Kapahulu Pier. However, in the 1920s, Kuekaunahi Stream was diverted away from Waikīkī, into the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal (Not a very picturesque name, is it?!) and via the Ala Wai Canal out to the Pacific Ocean.
Lē‘ahi from Pūowaina (Diamond Head to Punchbowl) (Hawai‘i State Archives)
Today, the only reminder of Kuekaunahi Stream in Waikīkī is a break in the coral reef offshore. Kuekaunahi most likely means ‘to remove scales from fish.’

The Ironwood trees lining Kalākaua Avenue were planted by Archibald Cleghorn in 1890. Cleghorn, the first commissioner of parks and a governor of Hawai‘i, was the husband of Princess Likelike and father of of Princess Ka‘iulani. Near the Diamond Head end of Kalākaua Avenue are Shower trees that bloom pink and white in the spring. The Rainbow Shower tree is Honolulu’s official tree, a hybrid developed in Hawai‘i.
Check out Art on the Zoo Fence on Monsarrat Avenue – Saturdays and Sundays, 9am to 3pm. www.artonthezoofencehi.com Art has been on display here since 1953.
Kupalaha Heiau

Queen’s Beach is named in honor of Queen Kapi‘olani (1836-1899), of nearby Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park, the wife of King David Kalākaua. (For more information about the park, follow the Kāneloa Walk VI.)

One of the first non-royal residences here belonged to the Charles Deering family, and then, in the 1930s, to Christopher Holmes. During World War II, the Deering-Holmes Estate, as it was later known, served as a conference center for President Roosevelt.

In 1946 the mansion was converted into the Queen’s Surf Restaurant. Its entertainment area, known as the Barefoot Bar, was a popular center of Hawaiian music and dance. Although the City and County of Honolulu obtained the land in 1953, the restaurant was allowed to continue operations. In 1961 the Spencecliff Corporation leased the restaurant for ten years, and the Queen’s Surf became known for its beach lū‘au. When the Spencecliff lease expired, the mansion-turned-restaurant was demolished in 1971 to create more open space along the beach.
Kupalaha Heiau was a religious structure located at Queen’s Surf Beach. It is thought that it operated in conjunction with Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau on the slope of Lē‘ahi.

Heiau refers to a religious outdoor structure to which access for commoners was strictly limited. There were different types of heiau, the two main ones were agricultural and sacrificial. The agricultural heiau was used for economic needs or husbandry, to ensure the livelihood of the people. The sacrificial heiau usually had a warlike function. Most heiau were damaged after 1819 when the Hawaiian religion and kapu, ‘taboo,’ systems were challenged by Kamehameha II.

Soon after the death of Kamehameha I in 1819, two of his wives and his son, Kamehameha II, set about to abolish The beauty and breezes of the ocean from Kapahulu Pier are unsurpassed. the ways of their traditional religion. This did not come about overnight: Ka‘ahumanu, Kamehameha I’s favorite wife, and Keōpūolani, Kamehameha I’s sacred wife, had already challenged and, thereby, had broken the kapu not only of eating with men, but also eating specific foods including a certain type of banana, lele, which was forbidden to women since it was used for “love magic” – its essence was thought to soar (lele) to the deities. This change opened the way for the Christian religion that was brought to Hawai‘i by the missionaries the following year, 1820.
The Kapi‘olani Park Beach Center houses the public baths, dressing rooms, and refreshment stand.

The history of public baths at this location reflects the city’s attempt to make available to the public all of Waikīkī ’s beaches. In the 1880s the beaches began to be encumbered by houses built along the shore. Access to the beaches gradually became limited to property owners. In 1908 the City and County of Honolulu obtained the land. A public bath facility was constructed, complete with showers, dressing rooms, lounging rooms, and a dance pavilion.
The surfing area offshore is known as Publics, in continuing honor of the public beaches in Hawai‘i!

The district where the park and zoo are now located was known as Kāneloa, meaning ‘tall man.’ The area in Kāneloa is Walk VI. Kāne is also the name of one of the most important Hawaiian deities; he is known as the deity of light, the sun, creation, life, but most importantly with relation to Waikīkī, the deity of freshwater, ‘wai.’
At this point along the shore, walk mauka across the grassy area to Kalākaua Avenue for the entrance to the Waikīkī Aquarium.
The aquarium’s original location was across from today’s “Trolley Stop/ Jogger’s Rest.” (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Waikīkī Aquarium is the second oldest public aquarium in the United States and the oldest in the Pacific Basin. Waikīkī Aquarium was established in 1904 by James B. Castle, Charles M. Cook, and Lorrin Thurston, all local businessmen who were descendants of missionaries, and built on land bequeathed by Castle, whose home was close by.

Coincidentally (and interestingly!), Messieurs Castle, Cook, and Thurston were board members of the Honolulu Rapid Transit Company that had recently established a new electric trolley line from downtown Honolulu to Waikīkī. By locating the aquarium so far Diamond Head, the board members hoped to lure more passengers to ride to the terminus of the trolley line.

Since 1919, the aquarium has been an integral part of the University of Hawai‘i, collaborating on research and information. The aquarium was originally located in Kapi‘olani Beach Park, just ‘Ewa of its present location. In 1955 the aquarium moved to its present building of locally hewn sandstone, built on a living reef.
Ocean water is pumped into the aquarium from a well and pipe that were drilled into the seawall.

The aquarium, which is open every day except Christmas Day, holds over 2,500 organisms and over 420 species of aquatic plant and life forms. The exhibit highlight is that of the endangered Hawaiian Monk Seal, Hō‘ailona, ‘omen or sign,’ as in ‘a sign from the sea.’ In 2021-2023 Hō‘ailona lived in California as scientists studied the monk’s underwater hearing. Check the aquarium’s website for exact opening times and dates www.waikikiaquarium.org There is more information about the Hawaiian Monk Seal when you reach Sans Souci Beach (Stop 7 ).
Notice the lovely flora around the entrance to the aquarium building: red and green Ti and the small bush of ‘akia, native to Hawai‘i and nowhere else.
A Kou tree greets visitors at the center of the “Tropical Sounds” sculptures. The hardy orange blossoms can be made into a lei – all you need is a needle and thread!

Walk diagonally through the “Exceptional” Banyan tree toward the beach. Is it really just one tree? Yes, those are aerial roots that find their way into the ground. An “Exceptional Tree” is one that is deemed culturally or historically significant.
Kapua Kapua Heiau

The War Memorial, as is carved overhead on the Beaux-Arts arch, is known locally as the Natatorium, which is simply Latin for The almost 100-year-old Natatorium looks good from here, but up close its deteriorating condition is clearly noticeable.

“swimming place.” It was inaugurated on August 24, 1927, with a spectacular dive by Duke Kahanamoku on his birthday! The swimming pool at the University of Hawai‘i is formally the Duke Kahanamoku Aquatic Complex.

The War Memorial was dedicated to the local soldiers and British who fought in World War I. Across from the entry archway is a large lava boulder with 101 names of those who died in the Great War. The names are inscribed on a bronze Roll of Honor plaque, bordered with the egg and dart motif, signifying life and death. How appropriate.

Land for the War Memorial project was obtained by the city from the William G. Irwin Estate, whose home was built in 1899 and razed in the 1920s. The architect of the Irwin home, Charles W. Dickey, was also the architect of the only remaining Halekūlani building. He is still well-known for the design of the breeze-catching sloped roof, the “Dickey roof.”

The Natatorium structure was designed by architect Louis P. Hobart, who also designed San Francisco’s Grace Cathedral and the various structures in Golden Gate Park. Notice the graceful carvings and moldings surrounding the Natatorium entrance: garlands, eagles, urns, and the Hawaiian standard and motto. As you stand under the arch, look down to view the geometric design in the drain grate.

The pool itself measures 100 meters by 40 meters, and the structure provided seating for 6,000 spectators. It is in this very pool where Duke Kahanamoku, who went on to win Olympic gold and silver medals in swimming, swam! To this day the Natatorium remains the largest saltwater pool in the United States. Due to its deteriorating condition, the pool portion of the Natatorium was condemned as unfit for use in 1979. It is a National Treasure and will someday be renovated and restored.

Notice the Hau trees growing on a trellis: In one day, the flowers open yellow, turn This is a view of the seating area for the swim meets that once took place at the natatorium. orange, and drop to the ground a brownish red color.
Over 50 graceful coconut trees beautify the area Diamond Head of the Natatorium – a perfect area for picnics and parties!
Continue Diamond Head along the beach.
As mentioned in the introduction to this walk, this entire area was once known as Kapua, ‘the flower.’
During the 1853 smallpox epidemic, which killed thousands of Hawaiians, Kapua was used as a quarantine station for newly arrived visitors.

The protected shore and channel of Kapua formed an important harbor for this part of O‘ahu. Kapua was also the favorite surfing area of one of Kamehameha I’s wives, Ka‘ahumanu. Legend relates that Ka‘ahumanu surfed and lamented in Kapua after she and her lover were discovered. Her lover was slain on a sacrificial heiau at Lē‘ahi at Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau (Stop 21 ).

At least seven heiau, or open-air religious structures, were said to be located in the Waikīkī beach area. This one, Kapua Heiau, was a heiau po‘o kanaka or luakini-type, a place where human sacrifices were offered. Conflicting reports tell of varying sizes. According to J. Gilbert McAllister’s 1933 Archaeology of O‘ahu, this heiau was small, only 240 square feet. According to George S. Kanahele’s Waikīkī 100 B.C. to 1900 A.D: An Untold Story, it was very large, measuring 240 by 240 feet! (You choose which size.) This heiau, along with most other heiau, was destroyed soon after during the struggle between traditional Hawaiian religion and the missionaries’ Christian tenets. A heiau is a sacred stone structure to which access for commoners was strictly limited. There were different types of heiau but the best known were agricultural heiau, for economic needs or husbandry, to ensure the livelihood of the people, and sacrificial heiau, usually as war places of worship.
Kapua is also remembered as the place where Kaolahaka, a chief from the Big Island of Hawai‘i, was sacrificed on suspicion of being as spy. Kapua was wellknown as a place of bone-breaking wrestling.

A heiau in Mānoa Valley has been completely rebuilt as the only intact, restored heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. Be sure to visit the Mānoa Heritage Center to see the noble heiau when you take the Mānoa Valley Walk X.

The beach and ocean area between the Natatorium and the Lighthouse is the Waikīkī Marine Life Conservation District. This means that during every odd-numbered year nothing may be taken from the beach or within 500 yards of the ocean: no sand, no rocks, no coral, no marine animals.

The beach, also part of Kapua, in front of the Kaimana Hotel and neighboring Sans Souci Apartments, is known as Sans Souci Beach, named for the Sans Souci Hotel that once stood here. Sans Souci (French for ‘carefree’) is named for Frederick II (Frederick the Great)’s palace, built in the mid-18th century in Potsdam, Germany.

In 1884 Allen Herbert from Sweden turned his home into a hotel. In 1893, George Lycurgus a Greek immigrant, leased the hotel and ran a successful hostelry as the Sans Souci Hotel. However, Mr. Lycurgus is best known for his counter-revolutionary ideals in the mid1890s. In January 1895, 2 years after the overthrow of Queen Lili‘uokalani by sons of the missionaries, Lycurgus and other Royalists, met and plotted a restoration of the monarchy at the Sans Souci. Henry Bertelmann, whose residence was further along the beach at the foot of Lē‘ahi, was instrumental in concealing ammunition in the sand in front of his home. These counter revolutionists were out-maneuvered and outnumbered, resulting in the arrests and imprisonment of all involved. Lycurgus, in particular, was charged with treason and spent 2 days in jail. Mr. Lycurgus moved to Hawai‘i Island where he developed the Volcano House and died at the age of 101 in 1970!

This area was extremely popular during the 1890s, and the Sans Souci Hotel, which consisted of small bungalows with thatched roofs, became one of Waikīkī’s leading inns, arguably, Waikīkī ’s first famous hotel.
During World War I the hotel was purchased by Mr. and Mrs. Charles Hartwell who replaced the original building, retaining only the original foundation.

The spreading Hau tree, which has been in this spot for over 100 years, lends its name to the Hau Tree Restaurant at the Kaimana Hotel. Hau belongs to the Malvaeceae Mallow family, which includes the Hibiscus. In the course of its life (one day!), the hau blossom displays three different colors: yellow upon opening, then bright orange, finally red-brown when it drops. The Hau tree has many traditional uses: its rough but lightweight wood is used for making canoe outriggers, its fiber is made into rope, and its sap and flowers are used medicinally. It is quite possible that Robert Louis Stevenson, who was a frequent guest to this area, wrote while sitting under this tree! In 1893 he penned:

“If anyone desires such old fashioned things as lovely scenery, quiet, pure air, Sans Souci Beach is not just for humans: the shiny black Hawaiian Monk Seal is the newborn; mom is on the right, a duller grey. clear sea water, good food, and heavenly sunsets hung out before his eyes over the Pacific and the distant hills of Wai‘anae, I recommend him cordially to the Sans Souci.”

The endangered Hawaiian Monk Seals also recommend this beach: In the spring of 2021, under the auspices of NOAA, Kaiwi (‘the bone’), one of our resident seals, gave birth to a boy pup, Lōli‘i (‘carefree’ from the French ‘sans souci’ – the name of the beach, remember?) and in the summer of 2022, the first resident seal (dating to 2017), Rocky, gave birth to another boy pup, Koalani on this beach. Kaiwi returned in the spring of 2023 to give birth to yet another pup!

Portions of this beach and the neighboring beach at the Colony Surf/Outrigger Canoe Club are cordoned off to protect the pups and their mommies. Perhaps you will be lucky enough to have a Hawaiian Monk Seal visit you on the beach; if so, keep your distance -they are very territorial. Mom and pup stay around for about 6 weeks before heading out to the open ocean.
Kaimana (obviously named after the beach where she was born), who was born in 2017 is famously documented in the children’s book, Rocky and Kaimana: Waikīkī’s Hawaiian Monk Seals by Erika Engle.

There is a male Hawaiian Monk Seal at the Waikīkī Aquarium, one of only two native Hawaiian mammals; the other, the hoary bat. The Hawaiian name for the seal, Hawai‘i’s state mammal, is‘Īlio holo i ka uaua’-,‘īlio ‘quadruped,’ holo ‘running,’i ka ‘in the,’ uaua ‘rough’ (seas). Why “monk” seal, you ask? Well, in the late 18th century naturalist, J. Hermann thought their smooth heads reminded him of a monk’s head covered with a hood! However, he was most likely describing the Hawaiian Monk Seals’ cousins, the Mediterranean Monk Seals in Europe.
Enjoy the newly installed beach showers!

Kaimana, although it looks like a Hawaiian word, it is not; rather, it is from the Hawaiianized English word ‘diamond,’ which is what early sailors thought they found in the crater, and therefore, named the crater Diamond Head (Stop 13 for more information).

The McInerny estate was located here in the early part of the 20th century. McInerny was a retail merchant who established his first store on the corner of Merchant and Fort streets in downtown Honolulu.
Do not attempt to cross through the water to the next stop. Please go back to Kalākaua Avenue and pass in front of the Outrigger Canoe Club and Elks Lodge on your way toward Lē‘ahi.
There is a right-of-way to the beach just before the Colony Surf Condominium. If you’d like to sit on the sand for a while, walk through the Colony Surf parking lot to reach the beach.

The Outrigger Canoe Club, at its original location where the Outrigger Hotel stands today, was organized in 1908 to revive the ancient Hawaiian sport of surfing. Its most outstanding member was Alexander Hume Ford. Mr. Ford is often referred to as a visionary because of his foresight in reestablishing the dying, but vital, sport of surfing. He was also the founder of the magazine Mid-Pacific and the still-active Hawaiian Trail and Mountain Club.

Leasing the land from the Elks Lodge (next stop), The Outrigger Canoe Club moved to its present location in 1964. Part of the beach fronting the club was created with sand removed during excavation of the building’s foundation.
Kalehuawehe

Colonel George W. Macfarlane, who was Chamberlain and Secretary to King Kalākaua, called this site home; however, he soon converted his home into the Park Beach Hotel – considered to be the first beachside hotel in Waikīkī.

In 1890, part of Mcfarlane’s property was sold to the Castle family headed by Samuel N. Castle. S. N. Castle came to Hawai‘i as a missionary in 1836. He and Cook founded the Castle & Cooke Corporation in 1851. His son, James Bicknell Castle, built a four-story mansion here in 1899 and called it Kainalu ‘billowy sea.’ It is said that it was the most grandiose home on the islands. Kainalu was designed by Oliver G. Traphagen, the same architect who would later design the Moana Hotel. The Castle home displayed magnificent features: Tiffany stained-glass windows, lānai on each of the levels, a 360° view roof garden, and a salt-water swimming pool!

In 1920 the Honolulu Elks Lodge No. 616 acquired the building and property, establishing their lodge here. Although the original building was completely replaced in 1959, its old pilings and foundation can be seen in the water in front of the lodge.
The Honolulu Elks Lodge was first established in 1901, in the extant lava block Progress Building at Fort and Beretania streets, downtown Honolulu.

Hawaiians, especially the royalty of old, have traditionally enjoyed the fine surf of Waikīkī . Kalehuawehe ‘the removed or untied lehua lei,’ was a favorite surfing course that extended from Kālia through the foot of Lē‘ahi.
The Castle mansion was so large that it presented an astonishing sight offshore. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
There are two Hawaiian mo‘olelo (legend) associated with the name Kalehuawehe:

According to one mo‘olelo, the name originated when a young chief from Mānoa removed his lehua lei and gave it to the daughter of Chief Kākuhihewa. Until then, only the princess has been permitted to surf there, but the kapu, or taboo, was broken by her accepting the lei.

The other mo‘olelo tells us that Pīkoi, the rat killer, went to Waikīkī wearing a lehua lei. He asked a surfing princess if he could borrow her surfboard, which, of course, she refused as the board was kapu. The legend does a flip-flop, however, and they surfed anyway after Pīkoi gave the princess his lei!
Continue walking Diamond Head along Kalākaua Avenue

The graceful fountain in the center of Kalākaua Avenue was dedicated in 1967 to Louise Gaylord Dillingham, wife of the enterprising Honolulu businessman, Walter Dillingham. The Dillinghams lived nearby on the slope of Lē‘ahi (Stop 21 ). The plaque reads that this fountain is dedicated to her in appreciation of her services as a member of the Board of Parks and Recreation.

The fountain’s predecessor was the Phoenix Fountain, erected by the Japanese of Hawai‘i in 1919. At the time, it represented the joining together of East and West; however, because of the tensions during World War II, it was razed on December 14, 1942, in reaction to an outcry of anti-Japanese sentiment.
Depending on the direction of the wind and where you are standing, you might get a nice cooling off!
In the grassy area Diamond Head of the fountain, take a moment to notice this “only-in Hawai‘i”: Hibiscus bushes concealing the fountain’s mechanical pump!
Near the Diamond Head end of this street are several Shower Trees that bloom pink and white. The Rainbow Shower tree, a hybrid developed in Hawai‘i, is Honolulu’s official tree.

There are at least a dozen high-rises here, not noticeable from photos of Lē‘ahi since they are usually cut out of the photographs and postcards, but here they are. A peaceful setting in which to live, away from the crowds.
The Diamond Head Beach Hotel and Residences at 2947 Kalākaua Avenue is interesting for its pyramidal shape: look up at the top floors.

The 14-story Diamond Head Ambassador apartments at 2957 Kalākaua Avenue was The foundation and pilings of the Castle Estate can be seen. The Elks Lodge is at this location today. designed by Vladimir Ossipoff (1907-98) who, although born in Russia, was known as “the master of Hawai‘i modern architecture.” The 1956-Japanese style buildings were not only the first cooperative apartment structures built, but were also the earliest multi-story buildings to use pre-stressed concrete I-beams in the country, an innovation by the engineer Alfred Alphonse Yee (1925-2017). Yee’s work was so wide-spread and influential that the University of Hawai‘i Mānoa College of Engineering has established the endowed Dr. Alfred A. Yee Chair of Sustainability and Resilience.
The first condominium building, a 12-story structure at 3019 Kalākaua Avenue, went up in 1961.

If you have an interest in the architecture and architects of Hawai‘i, continue along Kalākaua Avenue into a surprising enclave of small and lovely houses. Many of the homes have historic status with informational Historic Residence plaques. One of the most noteworthy houses is C.W. Dickey’s 1926 home at 3030 Kalākaua Avenue, which he built and lived in. Dickey (1871-1942) was the creator of the Hawaiian-style double-pitched roof – the roof line is angled to align with the breezes and sun light. His more elaborate home is across from Mākālei Park, which you will walk past on Diamond Head Road.
You can meander in and out of these streets. There is a tour map and guide to these historic homes by the Historic Hawai‘i Foundation: www.historicHawaii.org

A right-of-way to the ocean (“Tonggs Beach,” but no beach, is named for Ruddy Fah Tongg, 1905-1988, an island businessman who had a home here) can be accessed between 3027, the set of Tudor-French-Norman cottages, and 3037 Kalākaua Avenue.
Please do not walk along the seawall – it is illegal and dangerous. But do enjoy the expansive ocean view.
However, you may take the right-of-way across Kalākaua Avenue between 3026 and 3030 Kalākaua Avenue to walk 2 blocks to Diamond Head Road, and then up along the side of Lē‘ahi.
Take the right-of-way or continue along Kalākaua Avenue, turning mauka at Coconut Avenue to walk up Diamond Head Road. One of the streets you will pass is Kiele, ‘gardenia’ Avenue.
As you walk along Diamond Head Road, gaze up at mighty Lē‘ahi. Various government structures were once located on the floor of Lē‘ahi Crater.
Notice the slope of the crater walls: perfect for sledding, which is exactly what the Hawaiians did on a hōlua, ‘sled’. Before Diamond Head had a road named after it, the slope was a direct slide.
This photo of the right-of-way to Diamond Head Road captures not only Lē‘ahi in the background, but also the home of the architect C.W. Dickey.
This walk will not take you inside Lē‘ahi Crater; however, it will afford a good, closeup view.

At a later date, if you are interested in walking into Lē‘ahi Crater, the entrance is on the opposite side and is best reached by car. You can walk around inside the crater and progress up to the top of Lē‘ahi for a spectacular view.
The name Diamond Head dates from the 18th century and refers to the glistening calcite crystals found in the crater by early sailors who mistook the crystals for diamonds.

The crater has also been referred to as Diamond Hill and Kaimana Hill (as in the Kaimana Hotel). The crater’s Hawaiian name is Lē‘ahi, ‘forehead/brow of the yellowfin tuna’ due to its profile resembling the brow or forehead of the ‘ahi (tuna) fish.
The name Lē‘ahi survives as the name of a street on the other side of Lē‘ahi and as the name of a hospital in Kaimukī.

The crater’s highest point, Lē‘ahi peak, is approximately 760 feet (233 meters) above sea level. The most common vegetation inside the gate is non-native; however, there is one special plant found only in Hawai‘i and nowhere else in the world: Kokolau or Bidens cuneata, which is a composite-type flower related to the daisy and sunflower.

Lē‘ahi, the now extinct crater that was formed 300,000 years ago, was the home of Pele, the volcano deity. After traveling the islands, Pele now resides in Halema‘uma‘u Caldera of Kīlauea Crater in Hawai‘i Volcanoes National Park on Hawai‘i Island. Pele still rises up at Halema‘uma‘u – be sure to visit her!
As expected, there are several extraordinary houses along Diamond Head Road, many on the historic register, which can be accessed at historichawaii.org.

C.W. Dickey, the well-known local architect, built another home in 1932: a spectacular house high up on the corner of Diamond Head Road and Mākālei Place, with the palm frond motif prominently displayed.
If you have time, stroll into Mākālei Beach and Mākālei Park, a pocket-beach park. Enjoy the peace and quiet, away from the hustle and bustle of the main Waikīkī Beaches.
Mākālei, ‘fish trap,’ may have been the name of a fishing heiau (an open air religious structure) located on the slopes of Lē‘ahi.

In 1930, this location was first the site of Lanihau, then in 1937 the site of Haumalu, both homes of the Alexander family. Part of each name is hau, referring to the Hau tree close to the ocean: Lanihau means ‘heavenly hau”; Haumalu ‘means the shade of a hau tree.’ The Ficus with the gnarled truck is also original to the Alexander property.
The Alexander family home, with William DeWitt Alexander (1833-1913) as titular head, was on Punahou Street.
Enjoy the beach, especially at low tide, but please do not walk along the seawall.

Lē‘ahi Beach Park was the former residence of Harold G. Dillingham (1881-1971). The Dillingham family was instrumental in the crucial changes to not only to Waikīkī, but also to Hawai‘i. Traces of the dwelling include the seawall, coconut trees, and possibly the patio with the Hau trellis – a respite from the heat of the sun.
Benjamin (Frank) Franklin Dillingham (1844-1918), Harold’s father, lived on Punahou Street in a modest home with a dairy farm, makai and ‘Ewa of the Alexander home.

Beach Road, as its name implies, leads straight down to the beach. It’s an easy walk down, but not so easy up! There are beautiful homes on the waterfront, as well as great swimming and snorkeling in the coral reef.

Diamond Head Lighthouse, at 55 feet, located along Diamond Head Road, has been in continuous use since 1899, but was rebuilt in 1917. The lighthouse is under the jurisdiction of the Coast Guard. The address is 3399 Diamond Head Road. The Lighthouse Keeper’s house dates to 1921.

You can continue on to Kuilei ‘lei stringing’ Cliffs Beach Park, which leads to Kuilei Beach. Here you can walk on a paved walkway along with the surfers to the edge of the beach and watch them surf. Or, if you brought your surfboard to this point, go surfing!
Notice the windblown Kiawe trees and the lovely half-flowers of the Naupaka bushes growing out of the coral cliffs.

A major restoration progress in underway at Kuilei Cliffs by replacing invasive plants such as Kiawe and Koa haole with native plants and trees including Milo, Kou, Naupaka and ‘Ilima. For more information: www.kuileicliffs.org
The marker points out that Amelia Earhart (1897 – disappeared in 1937) was the first person to fly alone from Hawai‘i to North America. This amazing feat took place at 4:40 a.m. on January 11, 1935.
This is the endpoint of this part of the walk. There is one more lookout and then houses. It is recommended that you turn around and return to Waikīkī the way you came, continuing to enjoy the views.

You might question, why walk back the same way? Because although the views up Diamond Head Road were spectacular, The plaque with a model of her airplane and a huge wave below reads: AMELIA EARHART First person to fly alone from Hawai‘i to North America. January 11, 1935. they are even more so in the reverse direction. Enjoy! Think off all the exercise you are getting from walking!
As you return toward Waikīkī along Diamond Head Road, walk Diamond Head on Poni Mō‘i Street up to La Pietra Circle on the grounds of La Pietra Hawai‘i School for Girls.

Poni Mō‘i Road is a mauka-Diamond Head extension of Kalākaua Avenue. Poni Mō‘i has two interpretations, depending on the word split: as one word, ponimō‘i, is the Hawaiian name for the Carnation flower. Although the Carnation is not native to Hawai‘i, it is popular, grows well in Hawai‘i, and is used in making lei. However, as two words, Poni Mō‘i, means ‘royal coronation.’

stops.title: La Pietra Hawai‘i School for Girls

blocks.text: Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau
Follow the purple line to the entrance of La Pietra Hawai‘i School for Girls. Since La Pietra is private property, you may prefer to look in quickly and continue reading outside the grounds.

La Pietra, Italian for ‘the rock’ or ‘the gem,’ is the name of the residence built here in the 1930s by Walter Dillingham. The mansion was built in Mediterranean Revival style, combining characteristics of the original villa in Florence, Italy where the Dillinghams had been married in 1921, with various innovations of Chicago architect David Adler. Construction is of locally quarried bluestone lava, pink stucco, and red roof tiles.

In 1968, when the home was up for sale by Punahou School, to which it was bequeathed by Dillingham, the Hawai‘i School for Girls bought it for one million dollars and welcomed its students in 1969 to the new campus. Unlike other mansions of the time in Waikīkī, this mansion has survived. What a lovely setting for a school!
Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau

Until 1856 there was a sacrificial heiau, ‘place of worship,’ on the lower level of this site, known as Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau. Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau was probably built later than any other Waikīkī heiau, and more is known of this heiau than of the others in Waikīkī . Papa‘ena‘ena means ‘forbidding, glowing, red-hot.’

Kahekili, chief of Maui, may have built Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau in the late 1780s to commemorate his victory over Kahahana, King of O‘ahu, thereby avenging the sacrifice of Kahekili’s ancestor Kauhiakama at ‘Āpuakēhau Heiau. And it is recorded that Kamehameha I rebuilt the heiau and considered it his heiau.

There are at least six descriptions of this heiau as it existed before its final demolition, and all the accounts differ! But all agree that Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau was extremely large, measuring perhaps 130 feet by 75 feet; its lava wall 6 to 8 feet tall, ranging from 8 feet think at its base to 4 feet thick at the top. The side facing the sea would have been open.

Several other well-known Hawaiians were sacrificed here. Among them was Kanihonui, a nephew of King Kamehameha I, who had been caught in compromising circumstances with King Kamehameha I’s favorite wife, Ka‘ahumanu. Also sacrificed here was Ka‘iana, a Hawaiian chief, who not only defected but was also defeated in the infamous Battle of Nu‘uanu in May of 1795 by Kamehameha I. Ka‘iana’s skull, along with those of the other defeated warriors, was impaled atop the walls of this heiau.
You never know who you might meet as you walk up Diamond Head Road.

Understandably, ghost stories abound regarding this area. The most frequently related story is the procession of lights on moonless nights: the famed Night Marchers, ghostly fallen Hawaiian warriors making their way to the heiau for a nightly ritual.

However, Papa‘ena‘ena Heiau was also considered to be a nalu heiau (surfing)where surfers offered sacrifices to facilitate their acquiring mana (‘spiritual / divine power’) and ‘ike (‘knowledge’) of the surf from the foot of Lē‘ahi to Kālia. That course was known as Kalehuawehe.

As mentioned earlier about Kapua Heiau, most heiau were destroyed or damaged in 1819 or soon after when the Hawaiian religion and kapu (taboo), systems were challenged by Kamehameha II and his mothers, Ka‘ahumanu and Keōpūolani.

As you return to Waikīkī, you can go back on Paki Ave, where there are several buses or walk up Monsarrat Avenue to two local carry-out restaurants: South Shore Grill (call in your order) and Diamond Head Market & Grill.
Diamond Head Road now becomes Paki Avenue.

Paki Avenue is named for High Chief Abner Paki, a friend of Kamehameha II and a descendant of Maui chiefs. He and his wives had no biological children of their own; however, Bernice Pauahi and Lydia Paki were their hānai (adopted daughters). Bernice Pauahi became Bernice Pauahi Bishop of the Bishop Estates and Lydia Paki became Queen Lili‘uokalani! Both royal women married haole (foreign-born) men.
Monsarrat Avenue is named either for Marcus Cumming Monsarrat an Irishman who came to Hawai‘i in 1850 or his son, Judge James Melville Monsarrat, advisor to the monarchy.
You are not far from where you started at Kapahulu Avenue and the beachfront. Walk makai-‘Ewa from either Paki or Monsarrat avenues to get back to your starting point.
Or who might inspire you to start running along Diamond Head Road!
See complete Walk viii map on page 114 At this sign, walk up the hill to one of the most magnificent views on this side of the island.
Walk up Kapahulu Avenue through the neighborhood of Kaimukī and its Art Deco buildings into a crater and to the hill (pu‘u) of the crater.
This walk, up Kapahulu Avenue, goes through the neighborhood of Kapahulu, mainly on the Lē‘ahi side (Koko Head direction) of Kapahulu Avenue to the neighborhood of Kaimukī.

The mo‘olelo (legend) is that early Polynesians cooked kī (Ti) roots in the oven here in Kaimukī. Kaimukī means ‘the Ti (kī in Hawaiian) oven’ or ‘oven for cooking the Ti root.’ Kī is an indigenous (local) plant of the Lily family and has been used for roofing, food wrapping, hula skirts, and sandals. The kī root was cooked and used for food and distilling liquor. Today the kī plant is widely used in ornamental plantings around the islands, occurring in many varieties. The kī leaf is still used in present-day Hawaiian cooking: the leaf is wrapped around meat when it is cooked and served in its wrapper. Be sure to try real Hawaiian food: Haili’s Hawaiian or Da Ono on Kapahulu Avenue.
In the twentieth century, the area was known for carnation farms.

Historically, there were several heiau (an open-air religious structure) in Kaimukī: one on the Waikīkī side of Pu‘u o Kaimuki; another on the other side of Ocean View Drive, and a possible third at the parking lot for Lē‘ahi Hospital. Nothing remains of those sacred places. However, an intact restored heiau can be visited in Mānoa Valley at the Mānoa Heritage Center (Mānoa, Walk X).

Suggestion: Walk either early in the morning before the heat of the day or late afternoon, after the heat of the day has subsided. Enjoy the ubiquitous Monkey Pod trees that provide the well-need shade. And don’t forget your hat, water, and good walking shoes.
On this walk, Koko Head is used as a directional interchangeable with Diamond Head (Lē‘ahi) since the perspective varies, depending on where you are along the walk.

title: Kaimukī
theme: Walk into a crater and the pu‘u

intro.text: ROUTE A ROUTE B ROUTE C 13 14 Honolulu Zoo
Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal Kukaunahi Stream Walk VIII Map Key C 19 20 26 28 22A Koko Mauka Makai ʻEwa Head

If you are interested in Art Deco buildings follow the red line through the neighborhood of Kaimukī. This walk can begin anywhere along. Kapahulu Avenue, depending on your interest: choose from among Routes A, B or C.
Route A: The quickest route, best walked in the cool of the afternoon, begins at Stop 1 . (Follow the light green line )

From Waikīkī, the quickest way up to the pu‘u and crater is via Monsarrat Avenue, which is similar to the route you will take back from the crater if you decide to follow the long walk through Kaimukī to explore the Art Deco buildings. Monsarrat is named either for Marcus Cumming Monsarrat, a customs collector, or his son, Judge James Melville Monsarrat, who was advisor to the monarchy.

Monsarrat Avenue, which begins at Kalākaua Avenue between Queen Kapi‘olani Park and the Zoo, turns into Diamond Head Road after about a mile. You will be walking on the mauka side of Lē‘ahi crater. At Diamond Head Road and Makapu‘u Avenue, turn mauka to follow the walk in reverse, starting at Stop 32 .
Route B: Campbell Avenue, another more direct route, begins at Stop 4 . You may park on Date Street, which is free, anytime except no parking M-F 3:30-6:30. (Follow the light blue line )
Campbell Avenue is named after James Campbell of James Campbell Estate. This road led to his family’s summer home.

Campbell Avenue displays the only house on the Historic Register in this area: the 1898 Martin House at 3528 Campbell Avenue. This was the house of Charles Martin, a builder in the area, who also named the next street after his family: Mākini Street, a Hawaiianized word for Martin.
Caption: Across the plains to Kaimukī. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
From Campbell Avenue, continue to Monsarrat Ave/Diamond Head Road and follow this walk in reverse from Stop 32 . The pu‘u is at Stop 24 .
Route C is via Kaimukī Avenue directly into the crater at Crater Drive and begins after Stop 11 (with more detail) and continues at Stop 23 . (Follow the purple line )

info: Ala Wai Canal Ala Wai Golf Course

blocks.text: Kapahulu means ‘the worn-out soil,’ perhaps from the overuse of the land for growing kalo (taro).
If you are walking along Kapahulu Avenue from the beach, you will pass the ‘Ewa side of the Honolulu Zoo and Queen Kapi‘olani Regional Park. (Walk VI, Kāneloa)

On the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue, is the local school, Thomas Jefferson Elementary. If you have a few minutes, admire the ceramic tile wall by the students and the sculpture, E Pluribus Unum, by Eli Marozzi. In Marozzi’s words, this sculpture of intertwined faces and arms symbolizes that “we are many, but we can attain oneness in harmony.” Marozzi also sculpted the images in Old Stadium Park in the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili (Walk IX).
The original intent of the configuration of the Ala Wai Canal was to have another exit to the ocean at this end, but (thankfully) the developers ran out of money.
As you cross Paki Avenue, notice the over-arching Monkey pod trees. Paki is named for Abner Paki, a descendent of Maui chiefs.

Its sleek, clean lines make this building appear quite modern, but it was constructed in 1927. The firehouse was designed by architects Davis and Fishbourne and is surely one of the loveliest firehouses, especially its Hawaiian style roof line, to be found anywhere. Davis and Fishbourne were the original architects for McKinley High School.

The library is one of Waikīkī’s architectural gems. Its exterior walls are made of locally hewn sandstone blocks. The ceiling is of imported cedar wood; the interior doors, the reading bench, and children’s tables are of native koa wood. The cathedral windows provide natural reading light. The first Waikīkī library was in a wooden cottage on the grounds of Thomas Jefferson School. In 1952 the new library, designed by Lemmon and Freeth, opened its doors to the public. In the entryway, view the cement Waikīkī’s Fire Station No. 7 is always ready This outrigger canoe is on the high seas, not on the Ala Wai Canal. sculpture of an outrigger canoe. Lemmon and Freeth were also the architects for the Occidental Building on Pi‘ikoi Street as well as one of the firms for the state capitol.
Behind Waikīkī-Kapahulu Library is another library – the Hawai‘i State Library for the Blind and the Physically Handicapped, which is why the walk signal beeps.
The street mauka-‘Ewa of the libraries leads to the Clubhouse of the Ala Wai GolfCourse.
First Hawaiian Bank, on the Diamond Head (Lē‘ahi) side of Kapahulu Avenue, is architecturally interesting with its sandstone blocks.

Notice the sign “Lei of Parks,” which begins after the Ala Wai Golf Course sign on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu. The intent of these green Lei of Parks signs is for people to (one day) walk from park to park around the island, like a lei.

The neighborhood of Kapahulu, on the Lē‘ahi side of Kapahulu Avenue, is an interesting neighborhood replete with small homes and gardens on the slope of the crater, with lovely views of Waikīkī and Kapi‘olani Park. The side streets also lead up to the crater at Kaimukī Hill with fantastic views of the surrounding area.
Kana‘ina Avenue is named after Charles Kana‘ina, father of King Lunalilo, the 6th Monarch of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i. His name means ‘the conquering.’
Castle Street is named for businessman James Bickness Castle. His home, Kainalu, was a magnificent mansion on the water in Waikīkī (Walk VII).
Herbert and Williams streets are named
for the realtor, Earl Herbert Williams, who launched and built up this area.
Campbell Avenue is named after James Campbell of James Campbell Estate. This road led to his family’s summer home.
Ho‘olulu Street (‘to lie in sheltered waters’), is possibly named after the area on Hawai‘i Island where King Kamehameha I’s bones were allegedly hidden).
Good Guys Music and Sound is on the Diamond Head (Lē‘ahi) side of Kapahulu Avenue, half-way between Ho‘olulu Street and Mo‘oheau Avenue. Be sure to try playing a ‘ukulele ‘jumping flees.’

Date Street, ‘Ewa, leads to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili. On the Diamond Head (Lē‘ahi) side of Kapahulu Avenue, Date Street becomes Mo‘oheau Avenue. Mo‘oheau is the name of the chief who purportedly hid King Kamehameha I’s bones.
Williams Street (see Herbert Street)
There are several well-known local Hawaiian eateries along Kapahulu Avenue.
side of Kapahulu, 1/2 block past Date Street. ‘Ono means ‘good, delicious’; da is local pidgin (Hawaiian English Creole) for ‘the.’

stops.title: Haili’s Hawaiian food is located at

blocks.text: the ‘Ewa intersection of Kapahulu, Winam, and Palani avenues. Palani is the Hawaiianized form of Frank, a developer in this area.
Pāliuli Street. Paliuli means ‘green cliff ’ and is considered to be a paradise of plenty.
Winam Avenue
As you approach Winam Avenue, turn around to see if you can discover the split mural of Lē‘ahi. Ching Winam, a Chinese merchant, owned property here.

stops.title: Waiola (‘Water of Life’) Shave Ice store Mokihana Street

blocks.text: Turn Diamond Head onto Mokihana (a section of Kaua‘i, as well as a tree and its flowers in Kaua‘i) Street for a gustatory delight. That small blue building on the makai side of the street is a 1999 off-shoot of the original store on Waiola Street in Mō‘ili‘ili.
the ‘Ewa side, might be the only shopping center with a 7-foot telescope on its roof. Check for moon-gazing dates:
kapahulushoppingcenter.com
As you walk mauka, enjoy the majestic Ko‘olau Mountains before you.
‘Olu Street. ‘Olu means ‘cool’ – a word found in many Hawaiian mele (songs).

stops.title: Leonard’s Bakery
stops.subtitle: Route C to Pu‘u (hill) o Kaimukī via Kaimukī Avenue

blocks.text: Local, but not necessarily Hawaiian in origin, is Leonard’s Bakery, just past Charles Street. They bake heavenly malasadas, Portuguese (filled) donuts, which - by the way - is spelled malassada in Portuguese, meaning ‘badly baked!’ Try one or two or more malasadas … there’s a great variety…if you don’t mind waiting in an extremely long line for your treat!
Charles Street may have been named after Charles Kana‘ina (Kana‘ina Avenue); Charles Martin, a local builder; or Charles, the son of Miriam Auhea Crowningburg, a developer in the area.

If you are not interested in the downtown area of Kaimukī, but only in the crater and the hill, turn Diamond Head/Koko Head direction along Kaimukī Avenue, which is two blocks before the pillars of the freeway. (If you miss the turn onto Kaimukī Aven ue, Harding Avenue will also take you to the hill).

Continue about a mile up Kaimukī Avenue to 12th Avenue. Stop to admire the lovely one story older Hawaiian style homes between 6th and 8th avenues. After 8th Avenue, the houses seem bigger and newer. At 10th and Kaimukī avenues notice the natural lava outcrop on the corner with the lava wall built on top.
Enjoy the shade of the lovely Shower trees as you walk along the red colored sidewalks; the red is from the iron oxide in the lava dirt here.
The last block from 11th to 12th avenues is the hardest stretch. You’re almost there!

At 12th Avenue, jog mauka a little (Koko Head direction) on Koko Head Avenue unStop in for a treat at Waiola Shave Ice til you come to Pu‘u o Kaimukī Mini Park (Stop 24 ), the Fire Station and the vent for the crater (Stop 23 ) and climb the hill for a breathtaking view!

OR To go directly into the crater, cross 12th Avenue to Crater Road. After the first street, you can see the old reservoir, an abandoned round structure. Notice the “lava house” across from the reservoir made entirely of lava! Then come back to the hill via Koko Head Avenue.
You can return the way you came or go to Stop 25 to walk behind Lē‘ahi to Waikīkī.

Continue to follow the red line to walk through the downtown area of Kaimukī. Walk mauka on Kapahulu Avenue under the pillars for the freeway. Cross Harding Avenue and turn toward Koko Head onto Wai‘alae Avenue to enter the neighborhood of Kaimukī.
Harding Avenue is named after Warren Gamaliel Harding (1865 – 1923) who was president (1921-23) during the time that this street was developed in Kaimukī.

The downtown Honolulu portion of the H-1 freeway was known as Mauka Arterial in 1953, when it was first built. After Hawai‘i became a state in 1959, it became part of the Interstate system. Several extensions, including this one, were added over the years.
Turn Koko Head on Wai‘alae Avenue through downtown Kaimukī to Koko Head Avenue, which is between 12th and
13th avenues. Most blocks have something interesting to observe. Follow the street
names as they move up numerically in the direction of Koko Head.
Kaimukī is the only place that has numbered avenues as street names

Wai‘alae (‘mudhen water’ - named for a spring) Avenue, was the first paved street through Kaimukī, and continues to be its main thoroughfare. Makai of this major street, Harding Avenue and the freeway parallel Wai‘alae Avenue.
A half block up St. Louis Drive is Pālolo Stream of Mānoa Pālolo Drainage Canal fame. Pālolo Stream meets up with Mānoa Stream a few blocks makai of this corner.

Take a minute to admire the locally themed painted traffic signal boxes all along Wai‘alae Avenue. On a spectacular weekend in September 2018, artists from around the area beautified the signal boxes in Kaimukī. The boxes were painted by artists who either lived, worked, or went to school in the Kaimukī-Pālolo area or artists from Kaka‘ako’s POW WOW group known as “Street Art Hawai‘i.”

You can continue to walk another .5 mile to Koko Head Avenue, which will take you to the pu‘u and crater, or you can hop on a bus and get off at Koko Head Avenue and continue the rest of the way on foot.
Buses 1, 9, and 14 run along Wai‘alae Avenue.
Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator.
City Mill, the local hardware store, is located on the mauka-Koko Head corner of St. Louis Drive and Wai‘alae Avenue, next to Pālolo Stream.

City Mill was founded by Chung Kun Ai in 1899 and continues to be managed by his grandchildren. Chung Kun Ai, who was born in China and came to Hawai‘i at the age of 14, received the “Order of the Splintered Paddle,” a prestigious award for his outstanding service. The Law of the Splintered Paddle is a human rights decree that is believed to have originated with Kamehameha I. The Order of the Splintered Paddle is prominently displayed on the badges of our local police officers. Chung Kun Ai had formed a fast friendship with Dr. Sun Yat-Sen, the founder of the Republic of China, resulting in deep discussions about the basic principles of the Chinese Republic.
As you walk on the mauka side of Wai‘alae Avenue to the next stop, notice the 10 foot lava wall and the lone (unused?) lava boulder.
Kalaepōhaku
The Spanish Mission-designed Chaminade University and St. Louis High School, both Catholic supported institutions, are located off 3rd Avenue.

Chaminade University of Honolulu, which began as St. Louis Junior College, was named after Father William Joseph Chaminade (1761-1850), a French Catholic priest who was persecuted during the French Revolution and established the Society of Mary (known as the Marianists). A statue of Father Chaminade was erected at the entrance to the campus on the 250th anniversary of his birth. A plaque honoring the arrival of the first Marianist brothers is located next to the statue. In 1922, the Marianists acquired the ‘ili of Kalaepōhaku ‘the stone protrusion,’ from the Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop Estate.

A United States flag and a State of Hawai‘i flag are proudly flown on the campus. The flag of the State of Hawai‘i, which was officially adopted in 1845, incorporates the Union Jack of the British flag, commemorating the historic relationship with the British empire dating back to Kamehameha I. The 8 horizontal stripes allude to the 8 major islands of the state. The Hawaiian flag was designed by George Charles Beckley (1787-1826), who came to Hawai‘i from England in 1801 and lived in the area now part of the mauka section of the University of Hawai‘i campus. (University of Hawai‘i Campus Walk, XI)

Pālolo Stream runs through the lower part of Chaminade/St. Louis campus, then meets up with Mānoa Stream makai-‘Ewa on Wai‘alae Avenue, where they are, collectively, known as the Mānoa-Pālolo Drain Here are a few lines from the original 1797 Law of the Splintered Paddle (Kānāwai Māmalahoe) and a translation:
A e mālama ho‘i ke kanaka nui a me kanaka iki; E hele ka ‘elemakule, ka luahine, a me ke kama A moe i ke ala ‘A‘ohe mea nāna e ho‘opilikia.
Respect alike the rights of great men and humble men.

May everyone, from the old men and women to the children Be free to go forth and lie in the road Without fear of harm. age Canal. Lovely name… Pālolo Stream parallels Wai‘alae Avenue, crossing under Pālolo Avenue mauka of Pukele ‘muddy’ Avenue Park.

Kaimukī Shopping Center, the battleship beige and grey building, on the makai side of Wai‘alae Avenue between 4th and 5th avenues, houses our local supermarket, drug store, and various community stores.

Ironically, this now commercial space was once (1916-1978) occupied by the King’s Daughters Home for aged and infirm “Anglo-Saxon ladies” who took care of each other. King refers to Christ, as this was a Protestant retreat.
Pālolo Avenue, on the mauka side across from 5th Avenue, leads into the neighborhood of Pālolo Valley.
Relax in the shade of the Ficus and Palm trees at Pālolo Triangle Park or continue along the makai side of Wai‘alae Avenue.

stops.title: Sacred Hearts Academy and St. Patrick Catholic Church

blocks.text: On the makai side of Wai‘alae Avenue between 5th and 7th avenues are the Sacred Hearts Academy and stately St. Patrick Catholic Church. Notice the lava wall topped by Bougainvillea flowers and the symbolic Olive trees on the church lawn. The church, built in 1929, is in the style of a Romanesque cruciform.

St. Patrick Catholic Church is arguably the best-known building designed by architect Ralph Fishbourne (1884–1936), who was also the architect for McKinley High School and (unfortunately overlooked) May’s Shopping Center on the corner of S. Beretania and Pensacola streets. He was also one of the partners who designed the Waikīkī Fire Station. The buildings reflect Romanesque architectural features in the arches. Sacred Hearts Academy was founded in 1909 as a boarding school for Catholic girls living in Hawai‘i. If possible, stand on the lānai of Sacred Hearts Academy for a great view of Pālolo Valley. St. Patrick Church educates boys.
Enjoy the mountain vistas, especially at 7th Avenue, as you walk along and look for rainbows.

Art Deco was a style of architecture popular in the 1920s and 1930s, recognized by the stylized geometric design forms. You will pass many lovely (and some run down, and, therefore, not so lovely) Art Deco buildings. One handsome building, in particular, is on the mauka–Koko Head corner at 8th Avenue. Notice the widow coverings that can be moved to deflect the harsh rays of the sun.

The Y. F. Zane Art Deco building on In this 1930 photo of the Castle mansion in Waikīkī, the buildings of Chaminade / St. Louis School are clearly visible in the hills behind Waikīkī. (Hawai‘i State Archives) the makai-Koko Head corner of 9th and Wai‘alae avenues has been especially wellmaintained.
The playground at Kaimukī Community Park between 10th Avenue and 11th Avenue/Sierra Drive is very inviting!
Victorian-style lampposts extend from here (Sierra Drive) to Koko Head Avenue – an added aesthetic attraction.
On the mauka-Koko Head corner of Sierra Drive and Wai‘alae Avenue you can admire another Art Deco building.
The row of stores and stepped rooftops between Sierra Drive and 12th Avenue are best viewed from the mauka side of Wai‘alae Avenue. Notice the decorative pots above the overhang.

The once beautiful golden-age Queen Theater - with optimistic renovation plans afoot - is located on the mauka side of the avenue on the corner of one of the place-named streets, Center Street, between 10th and 13th avenues. The theater opened in 1936 but fell into disuse in the late 1980s.
Even the Palm trees on Center Street have seen better days! If you have a few minutes, take in the view of Honolulu and the Wai‘anae range from the parking lot.
row. Stop in for a locally baked goodie, then return to Wai‘alae Avenue to continue one more block before turning makai at Koko Head Avenue to the crater.
A plaque next to the sidewalk on the makai-‘Ewa side of 12th Avenue and the alleyway commemorates Kaimukī.
At 3613-3617 Wai‘alae Avenue look down to see a 1938 thank you note from Tuck Yee Yap who was able to rebuild his burntout supermarket thanks to Mayor C.S. Crane.
A 1943 photo of Queen Theater and patrons waiting patiently in the shade. (Lowell Angell Collection)

As you turn makai on Koko Head Avenue, notice the school across the way: this is Queen Lydia Lili‘uokalani Elementary School, which was dedicated by Queen Lili‘uokalani on April 12, 1912 (she passed away in 1917). If you are able (or interested in) going on the grounds, check out the larger-than-life ceramic mural of Queen Lili‘uokalani. Notice the lovely cutout of leaves on the fence. This leaf was a typical pattern that the Queen used on her quilting, a design still used by quilters today.
There was once a zoo here that housed a zebra as its star, only it wasn’t a zebra. It was a donkey painted black and white! Did the zoo owners think it would never rain?
22A A quick, but surprising detour, takes you a block past Koko Head Avenue:

Continue one more block, past the school to Wilhelmina Rise and look mauka: the street goes straight up for a mile and a half, almost vertically! Stop for a minute to take in the view. There will be more views to come at Pu‘u o Kaimukī.

The building on the corner of Wilhelmina Rise and Wai‘alae Avenue is built in a modern Hawaiian style of architecture. One hundred years ago, this was the site of Kaimukī Playhouse – renamed Kaimukī Theater and demolished in 1982.
Come back to Koko Head Avenue and continue makai across the freeway toward Kaimukī Fire Station.

As you cross the freeway, the views get better (but not as great as at the hill), including the view Wai‘anae Range (‘Ewa) – the other mountain range on O‘ahu. The mountain range behind you is the Ko‘olau Range. The bridge, labeled “Koko Head Avenue Separation,” was built in 1964, soon after the freeway was dug out.
Kaimukī Library is a welcome stop to relax and read.
To get to the top of the pu‘u, cross Pāhoa (‘a short dagger’) Avenue, then cross Koko Head Avenue to Kaimukī Fire Station 5.
Queen Lili‘uokalani presided at the opening of her namesake school 5 years before she died - in 1917. The ceramic tile mosaic portraying the queen was hand painted by the children and staff.
“A Dream Come True,” a thanks to Mayor Crane, was carved into this sidewalk entrance when the shop opened

The orange tiled roofed Kaimukī Fire Station 5, built in 1924 with extensive renovations in the 1990s, is nestled into the base of the crater’s outer wall. The building is listed on the National Historic Registry. The vent for the lava cone that built up the area and Kaimukī Hill is clearly visible behind the fire station on the Koko Head side.
Notice the drain spouts on the tower; are they really gargoyles in disguise? Gargoyle, from gargouille, simply means ‘drain spout’ in French.
Kaimukī reservoir

At the sign, PU‘U O KAIMUKĪ MINI PARK, a footpath has been worn into the hill on the ‘Ewa side of the fire station. Follow it up to the steps (go right or left), which are surrounded by many native plants, especially Crown flower and the native ground cover ‘Ilima, in the local Kaimukī red soil. The ‘Ilima is a lovely quarter-sized yellow-orange flower that is made into a special lei – special because it takes hundreds of flowers to make one lei! Notice all the pollinators.
The cactus is not native – there is no native cactus in Hawai‘i.

King Kamehameha I positioned sentries at Pu‘u o Kaimukī to locate his enemy, Kalanikūpule and Kalanikūpule’s troops, Kaimukī: Up Koko Head Avenue to the Fire Station and to Pu‘u o Kaimukī, then into the crater! (Hawai‘i State Archives)
At this sign, walk up the hill to one of the most magnificent views on this side of the island. as they arrived by sea at Waikīkī in his battle for O‘ahu.

From Kaimukī Hill, almost 300 feet high, it is possible to see the Wai‘anae Mountain Range ‘Ewa of here, but facing the other way past Koko Head, to several other Hawaiian Islands, including Moloka‘i and Lāna‘i. The crater below at Kaimukī is still evident, even with all those houses.
Pu‘u o Kaimukī or Kaimukī Hill (pu‘u means ‘hill’) has been referred to by many names:
• Observatory Hill (an early observation telescope)
• Bunker Hill • Christmas Tree Park – At Christmastime, the metal Christmas tree is lit up – atop the hill for all to see!
• Telegraph Hill: In 1857 large moveable arms were used as semaphore. On November 13, 1900, the first Marconi telegraph system between O‘ahu and Moloka‘i was mounted here.

Pu‘u o Kaimukī is the center of a series of secondary eruptions in a row, known as the Kaimukī Rift (cracks) mauka from Ka‘au Crater, Mau‘umae Cone, Kaimukī Lava Cone (the only pit dome on O‘ahu) to Lē‘ahi cone. Secondary means that they were formed after the main formation of the Ko‘olau Range, which erupted 3 to 1.5 million years ago. The Kaimukī series formed 500,000 to 200,000 years ago.

Walk ‘Ewa-makai to the edge and stand in the shade of the trees, then look down into the crater where you will see the wall of the former Kaimukī reservoir (affectionately called “The Bowl,”) built in 1898 with lava stones on the exterior and concrete interior walls. Water from two artesian wells were tapped and stored here. By 1910, other water sources were found, so an entryway was created, and Boy Scout Troop 10 called it home for 79 years! Notice the lava stone house directly across from the reservoir.

If you would like to walk into the crater, go back down to Koko Head Avenue, turn ‘Ewa-makai, follow it around to 12th Avenue, then an immediate turn onto Crater Road. Take Crater Road into the crater where you will see the former Kaimukī Reservoir, which is discussed above.

Depending on your walking stamina, you can continue or take a bus back on Wai‘alae Avenue. Alternatively, if you‘d like to walk back to Kapahulu where you started, when you reach 12th Avenue, look for Kaimukī Avenue, going ‘Ewa, and take it straight down to Kapahulu Avenue.
If you’d like to stay with this adventure and walk around the back of Lē‘ahi to Waikīkī, walk down the ramp on the Koko Head side of the crater to Ocean View Drive.
The sidewalks are stained reddish from the great amount of iron oxide in the lava here.

It is suggested that you walk on the Koko Head side to best admire the houses. As you walk along Ocean View Drive notice the great variety in the architecture of the homes, especially the ones made from locally hewn lava from Kaimukī Crater that are perched on the rim of the crater. Also observe the lava stone walls, retaining walls, steps, and garages.

Shortly after crossing Maunaloa Avenue is a 1936 house listed on the Historic Register, as an excellent example of Hawaiian Planation style architecture. Considering how interesting and unusual the houses are on this street, it is surprising that there are not more homes on the historic registry.
There was once a heiau (an open-air religious structure) in the area toward Kahala.

Ocean View Drive ends at Kīlauea (squirt, numerous, or rise up, as of a volcano) Avenue where you will see Kapi‘olani Community College straight ahead and Lē‘ahi Hospital on the makai -‘Ewa corner of Kīlauea and Makapu‘u avenues.
Cross over to the college side for one short block ‘Ewa on Kīlauea Avenue.

• The number 9 bus runs along Kīlauea Avenue • The number 2 bus runs along Makapu‘u Avenue • There is also a bus stop for buses 2,3,9,23, and 24 on Diamond Head Road. Call 808-848-5555 (option 2 for a live operator).
At Makapu‘u (‘hill beginning’) Avenue – between Kapi‘olani Community College and Lē‘ahi Hospital – walk makai-‘Ewa
a few blocks to Diamond Head Road. Or walk through the campus in the shade of the Monkey Pod trees to Diamond Head Road.
Enjoy the spectacular views of Lē‘ahi, Kapi‘olani Park, and even the Wai‘anae Range.

Lē‘ahi Hospital, which began in 1903 as Victoria Hospital in Kaka‘ako, today is part of Hawai‘i Health Systems Corporation, a public benefit corporation. The hospital, originally with open air pavilions for tuberculosis treatments, is not open for emergency services; rather, it provides traditional long-term care, short-term rehabilitation, and adult day health care.
There most likely was a heiau on this property, which is not surprising, considering the commanding view.
A secure parking space: lava garages along Ocean View Avenue.

Kapi‘olani Community College is part of the University of Hawai‘i system. The community college was originally located at Pensacola Street and Kapi‘olani Boulevard, then moved to the Fort Ruger area in 1974, first repurposing the original Fort Ruger buildings, then developing its own natural landscape and fitting low-rise buildings that are prevalent today. All campus buildings have lovely Hawaiian names of trees and plants. The outdoor areas makai-Koko Head feature sculptures and a cactus garden for relaxation.
Just before you come to Diamond Head Road, you will pass our local theater, Diamond Head Theater on the corner, then turn ‘Ewa onto Diamond Head Road. The

original 1933 theatre was built by the Armyas the Fort Ruger USO movie theater, only to be replaced next door in 2022 with a new theater. The remaining building is the rear portion of the original building.

Fort Ruger, which was established in 1906, was the first permanent military reservation in the Territory of Hawai‘i and was part of O‘ahu’s coastal defense system. From 1906 The “gates” at the entryway to Ft. Ruger.

This 1934 photo of Diamond Head Theater displays the building’s clean, modern lines. (Lowell Angell Collection) to 1911, Fort Ruger was initially established within the crater and on the outer slopes. It was named in honor and memory of Thomas Howard Ruger, who was the superintendent of the U.S. Military Academy at West Point from 1871 to 1876.
The makai walkway parallel to Diamond Head Road is dotted with informational historical signage about Fort Ruger.
The circular planter mauka on Diamond Head Road is one of the few remnants of the earlier defense posts. Two gun barrels were mounted on the sides. But what is under those hillocks?
There is a bus stop here for buses 2,3,9,23, and 24. Call 808-848-5555 (option 2 for a live operator).

Notice all the chickens running around amidst the lovely Naupaka bushes and flowering Shower trees. The Shower tree is a hybrid that was developed in Hawai‘i and has become Honolulu’s city tree. Kiawe and Palm trees line the Lē‘ahi side of the street.
The street below leads to the 1952 Board of Water Supply Fort Ruger Tunnel.
The lava pillars where Diamond Head Road becomes Monsarrat Avenue were part of the original gatepost entryway to Fort Ruger. Fort Ruger pathway runs from Monsarrat Avenue to 22nd Avenue.
The Culinary Institute of the Pacific, nestled into the side of Lē‘ahi, is part of Kapi‘olani Community College.
Makapu‘u Avenue ends at Diamond Head Road. Turn ‘Ewa as the street name changes to Monsarrat and takes you back to Waikīkī Beach, near your starting point.

Diamond Head Road becomes Monsarrat Avenue after a few blocks. Monsarrat is named either for Marcus Cumming Monsarrat, a customs’ collector, or his son, Judge James Melville Monsarrat, who was advisor to the monarchy.
Trousseau Street/Avenue is named

for Georges/George Phillipe Trousseau (1833-1894), court physician to both King Lunalilo and King Kalākaua. Dr. Trousseau was not only Knight Companion of the Royal Order of Kamehameha I, but also a Knight Companion of the Royal Order of Kalākaua. Dr. Trousseau purchased this land from King Lunalilo with the intention of opening an ostrich farm to produce ostrich feathers for fancy ladies’ hats made in Europe. Descendants of those ostriches may roam the grounds of the Honolulu Zoo today!
The houses along Monsarrat Avenue are on the slope of Lē‘ahi; they are entered from street level, but then step down a floor or two.
There are two interesting eateries on Monsarrat Avenue: Diamond Head Market, after you cross Campbell Avenue, and South Shore Grill (order ono tacos), at the end of the block.
Monsarrat Avenue will take you to Kapi‘olani Park - Walk VI, Kāneloa.
(Lē’ahi)
