title: Mō‘ili‘ili
theme: Watch out for the mo‘o, the giant lizard!

intro.text: Watch out for the mo‘o – a giant lizard!

Walk mauka on Kapahulu Avenue to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili. This walk, up the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue, goes through the neighborhood of Kapahulu, along Date Street, to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili.
Suggestion: Enjoy walking under the ubiquitous Monkey Pod trees that provide the well-needed shade. And don’t forget your hat, good walking shoes, and water.

In the time before asphalt streets and buildings, Mō‘ili‘ili was an aquacultural and agricultural area, mainly of kalo (taro) fields. The only remnants are the lo‘i kalo (taro fields) at the University of Hawai‘i. (Visit the lo‘i on the University of Hawai‘i’s Lower Campus, Walk XI).

According to the most authoritative book on Mō‘ili‘ili, Mō‘ili‘ili-The Life of a Community published in 2019, this area was first known as Waikīkī Waena or Middle Waikīkī since it was in the middle of the ahupua‘a ( section of the island that extends from the mountains to the ocean) of Waikīkī.

The mo‘olelo (legend) about Mō‘ili‘ili, ‘pebbled lizard,’ is that Hi‘iaka, Pele’s sister, destroyed the mo‘o ‘lizard,’ then cut him up into pieces and threw the pieces onto a hill, resulting in the highest hill in Mō‘ili‘ili, where the Hawaiian Humane Society is located on Wai‘alae Avenue and S. King Street.

A less colorful origin of the name Mō‘ili‘ili is that it is a contraction of Ka moku ‘ili‘ili, ‘the moku, or land section, of small stones.’ The stones came down from the eruption on Tantalus, the smaller mountain range ‘Ewa of this area.

Mō‘ili‘ili is riddled with underground caverns, none accessible today, but there are mo‘olelo and stories of cave-ins and sink holes occurring as recently as 1989! There were, and probably still are, blind fish there. A pond, once fed by fresh water springs, can be found at the former Willows Restaurant on Hausten Street.
The mo‘olelo attributes the formation of the cave, caverns, and underground streams to Kamapua‘a, the mischievous pig deity.
For an interesting neighborhood stroll, walk to the Diamond Head end of the Ala Wai Canal and proceed mauka along the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili.

info: 2.5 miles; 2 hours; 6,000 steps Buses along Kapahulu Avenue to Mō`ili`ili: Bus routes and times www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator. Parking: Parking lot at the Honolulu Zoo If you would like to drive part way and then park your car, on-street parking can be found along Date Street –free, except no parking 3:30 to 6:30 Monday through Friday.

blocks.text: Kapahulu means ‘the worn-out soil,’ perhaps from the overuse of the land for growing kalo (taro).
If you are walking along Kapahulu Avenue from the beach, you will pass on the ‘Ewa side of the Honolulu Zoo (Walk VI, Kāneloa).

On the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue is one of the two local public schools, Thomas Jefferson Elementary. (The other one, Waikīkī Elementary is a few blocks mauka, off Monsarrat Avenue.) If you have a few minutes, admire the ceramic tile wall by the students as well as the sculpture, E Pluribus Unum, by Eli Marozzi. In Marozzi’s words, this sculpture of intertwined faces and arms symbolizes that “we are many, but we can attain oneness in harmony.” Marozzi also has sculptures in Old Stadium Park in Mō‘ili‘ili, which you will soon visit.
The original intent of the configuration of the Ala Wai Canal was to have another exit to the ocean at this end, but (fortunately) the developers ran out of money.
A little history about the Ala Wai Canal: (For more history and an informative walk, go on the Ala Wai Canal Walk I, which circumnavigates the canal.)

The Ala Wai Canal was built between 1921 and 1928, drastically altering not only the topography, lifestyle, and fate of the beach area known as Waikīkī, but also the lives of the Hawaiian people. Ala Wai means ‘freshwater way,’ referring to the freshwater streams that empty into it from the mountains and valleys.
The flatlands of Mō‘ili‘ili. Low white building is Kamō‘ili‘ili Church (Hawai‘i State Archives)

The Ala Wai Canal is carved out of natural solid coral. Original topography of the area included three streams running down from the mountains into the valleys and through Waikīkī, each emptying directly into the Pacific Ocean. Waikolu Way, a small street between Royal Hawaiian and Seaside avenues, is reminiscent of those three streams: Waikolu means ‘three waters.’
As you cross Ala Wai Boulevard, notice the leafy Monkey pod trees shading Pākī Avenue. The street is named after Abner Pākī, a descendent of Maui chiefs.

The library is one of Waikīkī’s architectural gems. Its exterior walls are made of locally hewn sandstone blocks. The ceiling is of imported cedar wood; the interior doors, the reading bench, and children’s tables are of native Koa wood. The cathedral windows provide natural reading light. The first Waikīkī library was in a wooden cottage on the grounds of Thomas Jefferson School. In 1952, the new library designed by Lemmon and Freeth, opened its doors to the public. In the entryway, view the cement sculpture of an outrigger canoe. Lemmon and Freeth were also the architects for the Occidental Building on Pi‘ikoi Street as well as one of the firms for the state capitol.
Behind Waikīkī-Kapahulu Library is another library – the Hawai‘i State Library for the Blind and the Physically Handicapped, which is why the walk signal across Kapahulu Avenue beeps.
Cross Kapahulu Avenue here to walk on the ‘Ewa side.
The street mauka-‘Ewa of the libraries leads to the Clubhouse of the Ala Wai Golf Course.

Its sleek, clean lines make this building appear quite modern, but it was constructed in 1927. The firehouse was designed by architects Davis and Fishbourne and is surely one of the loveliest firehouses, especially its Hawaiian style roof line, to be found anywhere. Davis and Fishbourne were the original architects for McKinley High School.

stops.title: First Hawaiian Bank also on the

blocks.text: Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue, is architecturally unusual with its sandstone blocks.

You can continue mauka on Kapahulu Avenue or, alternatively, take the shadier “Lei of Parks,” which begins after the Ala Wai Golf Course sign on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue and follows the golf Look at the detail in these tiles: surfers, birds, tree, fish, even an elephant! course around to Date Street.
The intent of these green Lei of Parks signs is for people to walk from park to park around the island, like a lei. Enjoy the shade of the trees as you walk along.

The neighborhood of Kapahulu is on the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue: an interesting neighborhood replete with homes and gardens on the slope of the crater, with lovely views of Waikīkī and Kapi‘olani Park. The side streets also lead up to the crater at Kaimukī Hill with fantastic views of the surrounding area.

stops.title: Date Street/ Mo‘oheau Avenue
stops.subtitle: WALK TO MŌ‘ILI‘ILI AFTER KAPAHULU AVENUE

blocks.text: Date Street leads to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili; on the other side of Kapahulu Avenue, Mo‘oheau Avenue leads to the neighborhood of Kaimukī. Mo‘oheau is the name of the chief who purportedly hid King Kamehameha I’s bones.

Good Guys Music and Sound, on the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue, is half-way between Mo‘oheau Avenue and Ho‘olulu Street ‘to lie in sheltered waters,’ possibly named after the area on Hawai‘i Island where Kamehameha I’s bones were allegedly hidden). Be sure to drop in and check out the ‘ukulele ‘jumping fleas’ for yourself at Good Guys.
At Date Street and Kapahulu Avenue, turn ‘Ewa to continue around the golf course toward Mō‘ili‘ili.

stops.title: The Ala Wai Golf Course, a 146-acre

blocks.text: municipal course, extends from Kapahulu Avenue to the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal, which you will come to soon. The golf course is laced with remnants of earlier streams.

The original nine-hole golf course opened on September 13, 1931, as the first municipal course in Hawai‘i. The course was built on the site of the Territorial Fairgrounds. The second nine holes were opened on July 10, 1937, with one of the structures at the fair serving as its clubhouse. During World War II, the golf course was set up as an emergency landing air stip.

Local lore relates that the origin of the golf course dates to the early 1920s when two men sank a can where hole number 6 is now located for their on-thespot golf course! However, another story recounts that local caretakers of the Territorial Fairgrounds set up their own course, charging 25 cents a hole. At one time, this golf course was reputed to have been the busiest golf course in the United States!
Many First Hawaiian Banks are built with architectural aesthetics.

Along Date Street, on the mauka side, you will pass some unusual street names because even though they look Hawaiian, they are not. Frank L. James developed this area in 1926 and named these streets after members of his family. All except the last one are Hawaiianized English names… • Kamuela Avenue - ‘Samuel,’ family member • Palani Avenue - ‘Frank,’ his son • Makaleka Avenue - ‘Margaret,’ his daughter • Ekela Avenue – ‘Ethel,’ family member • Lukepane Avenue - ‘Lucy Frances,’ his wife • Olokele Avenue - ‘honeycreeper bird’
Date Street is the only extension of the plant and tree-named streets from Sheridan Tract and McCully area.

Just before you cross the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal on a 1937 WPA bridge you might notice ditches on both sides of Date Street. These are most likely remnants of the two separate rivers of the Mānoa and the Pālolo that came together here before the 1920s Ala Wai Canal was built and diverted these two streams. The two rivers now meet a half mile mauka. Notice the houses and their “lawns” on the canal.

At Lā‘au (‘wood’) Street, the Lei of Parks walkway continues around the golf course toward the Ala Wai Canal. The Ala Wai Walk I circumnavigates the canal. However, this walk crosses Date Street to continue to Mō‘ili‘ili.

‘Iolani School, one of the largest private schools in Hawai‘i, is located on the other side of the drainage canal. Dr. Sun YatSen, the first president of the Republic of China, graduated from ‘Iolani in 1882.
A side trip to 520 Kamoku Street (one more block ‘Ewa along Date Street, then makai on Kamoku) will take you to the center for the 100th Infantry Battalion Veterans Club.

stops.title: Walk from Date Street into Mō‘ili‘ili
stops.subtitle: Mahi‘ai Street

blocks.text: Cross Date Street at Lā‘au Street. On the
mauka side of Date Street, find the signal box, then look down: native poppy, Pua Kala, is growing here! It is easily overlooked as if it were a weed growing wild at the base of the traffic pole!
Cross Menehune Lane – the Menehune were either the original peoples of the Hawaiian Islands or legendary small people to whom walls and ditches are sometimes attributed.
At the next street, Mahi‘ai Street, turn mauka to the end, crossing Nāhaku Place.
If you are not comfortable walking in the street, go back to Date Street, where, in one more block, you will come to Kapi‘olani Boulevard. Turn the corner, walk mauka and you will see the footbridge.
And if there is construction in the area, continue along Date Street, cross Kapi‘olani Boulevard at the light to Kalo fields across McCully to Mō‘ili‘ili (Hawai‘i State Archives)
University Avenue, where you can turn mauka to S. King Street and backtrack the walk to Stops 11 through 15 .
Mahi‘ai means ‘farmer,’ but was named for the Chiefess Keali‘imahi‘ai.
Nāhaku Place
Nāhaku, which is shortened from Nāhaku‘eluapua of Mō‘ili‘ili ‘the weaving of two flowers,’ was the mother of Chiefess Keali‘imahi‘ai.
Mahi‘ai Street will take you to a footbridge, which is accessed at Kapi‘olani Boulevard.
A footbridge across Kapi‘olani Boulevard takes you to an interesting cemetery in Mō‘ili‘ili.
If you see a tall building looming in the near distance, it is The Contessa, and you are headed in the right direction.
Turn around for a great view of Lē‘ahi from the bridge across Kapi‘olani Boulevard.

The footbridge will take you ‘Ewa to the well-tended and cared for 1908 Mō‘ili‘ili Japanese Cemetery on Kuilei ‘stringing lei’ Street. The memorial at the entrance, dediAs you walk along farmer (Mahi‘ai) Street, imagine taro fields and farmers that were once here.

This Japanese cemetery honors the first 1868 Japanese migrant workers. Please visit with reverence. cated in 1968, commemorates the 100th year arrival anniversary of the first official group of Japanese immigrants who were called the Gannenmono, meaning the ‘people of the first year’ (of the Meiji period).

The first contract laborers, Imin ‘immigrants,’ came in 1885 to work the sugar cane and pineapple plantations. The statue of King Kalākaua in Waikīkī commemorates the 1885 immigration. (The Kalākaua Avenue Walk IV)
The grounds are open to the public; feel comfortable walking around, respecting the memorials of the Japanese families.

After walking around the cemetery, come back to Kuilei Street and the community gardens on the makai side. Then walk mauka on the next street, Kahoaloha – ‘the friend’ - Lane to S. King Street, the main business district of Mō‘ili‘ili. King Street was originally known as Carriage Road. King Street is divided into North and South King streets (as are North and South Beretania streets) at Nu‘uanu Avenue, the dividing street between the downtown district and Chinatown.
As you walk along Kahoaloha Lane, observe the huge Mango trees with the posted warning, DO NOT PICK!

stops.title: The grounds of Kamō‘ili‘ili Church and Cemetery

blocks.text: As you turn the corner Diamond Head onto S. King Street, you will come face to face with the looming skyscraper of Mō‘ili‘ili, the Contessa, built on the grounds of Kamō‘ili‘ili Church and Cemetery, the second highest point in Mō‘ili‘ili. Yes, the ghost stories abound: the elevator stops mysteriously on every floor, sometimes transporting 3 people with no feet; there are eerie sounds; a dog roams the floors… The highest hill in Mō‘ili‘ili is across the way at the Hawaiian Humane Society. This hill was created when Hi‘iaka tossed the chopped up pieces of the mo’o (lizard) here. (See Stop 26 for more information.)
Kamō‘ili‘ili Church was built in 1846 as an ‘āpana (“branch”) of the downtown main church, Kawaiaha‘o. The graves and the bell As you walk along Kahoaloha ‘the friend’ Lane, do not pick the mangoes!

Kamō‘ili‘ili Church, 1898 (Hawai‘i State Archives) tower of Kamō‘ili‘ili Church and Cemetery were lovingly moved to the burial ground at Kawaiaha‘o Church in downtown Honolulu. A reminder that a church once flourished here is Church Lane on the Diamond Head side of the Contessa.
If school is not in session and you have a few minutes, walk around the grounds of Prince Jonah Kūhiō Elementary School to admire the murals and the sculpted mo‘o.

The three terraced lava walls displaying lovely colorful Bougainvillea on S. King Street, which fronted the old Kūhiō Elementary school, now create a buffer between the busy street and the single level elementary school. Prince Kūhiō served as a delegate to the United States Congress from 1902 until his death in 1922 at the age of 50. He was instrumental in enacting the 1920 Hawaiian Homes Commission Act, which granted 200,000 acres of land to Native Hawaiians.

After imagining what was here, turn around to walk ‘Ewa along S. King Street to the business district of Mō‘ili‘ili and the Japanese shrine at the intersection of S. King Street, S. Beretania Street, and University Avenue.
A few blocks along S. King Street you’ll find Kahuna (literally, ‘the hidden one,’ perhaps referring to a Kahuna, a religious person of authority) Lane.
Kahuna Lane most likely was the path to Mauoki Heiau, a Hawaiian place of worship. The street continues as Kalo (‘taro’) Lane behind the 7-11 (the site of Kūhiō Grill).

A heiau is an open-air religious structure to which access for commoners was strictly limited. There were different types of heiau: the two main ones were agricultural heiau, for economic needs or husbandry, to ensure the livelihood of the people, and sacrificial heiau, often as war shrines. Most heiau were damaged or destroyed in 1819 or soon after when the Hawaiian religion and kapu ‘taboo,’ systems were challenged by Kamehameha II. After the death of Kamehameha I in 1819, his wives and son, Kamehameha II, set about to abolish the ways of their traditional religion. This did not come about overnight: Ka‘ahumanu, Kamehameha I’s favorite wife, and Keōpūolani, Kamehameha I’s sacred wife, had already challenged and, thereby, had broken the kapu (taboo) not only of eating with men, but also of eating certain food, including a type of banana, lele, which was forbidden to women since it was used for “love magic” – its essence was thought to soar (lele) to the deities. This change opened the way for the Christian religion that The bell that was once atop Kamō‘ili‘ili church is now lovingly cared for at the cemetery at Kawaiaha‘o Church downtown. was brought to Hawai‘i by the missionaries the following year, 1820.

Mauoki Heiau would have been in the vicinity between the music building at the University of Hawai‘i and the slope to the Quarry. Two large loko, ‘pond,’ were located directly makai. For more information about the quarry, the university’s lower campus, and athletic fields, follow the Lower Campus Walk XII.
To continue through Mō‘ili‘ili, cross University Avenue, staying on the makai side of S. King Street.

In recent history, there were many flower shops on both sides of S. King Street. This is the main intersection of Mō‘ili‘ili: University Avenue and S. King Street, where there are restaurants that change names on a yearly basis, but then again stores that remain true to the neighborhood, such as Nijiya and Longs.
Kapa‘akea

At the next corner, take a side trip makai along Kapa‘akea Lane - the most interestingly named street in the area because it sounds like the Hawaiian word kapakahi, ‘crooked,’ which is exactly what this street is! Kapa‘akea means ‘coral or limestone surface.’ (There is a Kapakahi Stream that crosses Wai‘alae Avenue in Kāhala -a type of fishon the other side of Lē‘ahi.)

Kapa‘akea Lane is named after Caesar Kaluaiku Kamaka‘ehukai Kahana Keola Kapa‘akea (1815-1866), a Hawaiian chief in the Kalākaua line, who was father to both King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani, and owned land in this area. On the ‘Ewa side of Kapa‘akea Lane is a red wooden building, the original Mō‘ili‘ili Community Center.

Kapa‘akea Lane parallels a little stream,Ala Naio, which runs between Hausten and Coolidge streets all the way to the Ala WaiCanal. (Naio can have several meanings:‘left over taro,’ ‘a type of seaweed,’false Sandalwood, and ‘the Hawks ’ - na‘io).
Dole Street, which separates the upper and lower campuses of the University of Hawai‘i was formerly known as Kapa‘akea.

Once you’ve walked along Kapa‘akea Lane past a few picturesque houses and imagined that houses like this were abundant before the world of apartment buildings and hotels, turn around and walk out Diamond Head on Kuilei Street* back to University Avenue. *(No street sign, as of this writing.)
Continue makai along University Avenue to the makai-Diamond Head corner of Date Street and University Avenue to the Fire Station.
A plaque and artwork that commemorate The Battle of Mō‘ili‘ili can be found at the entrance plaza to the McCully-Mō‘ili‘ili fire station on Date Street and University Avenue.
A once flourishing floral market area, this is one of the remaining florists on N. King Street.
The encounters then took place on the ridge near Pālolo, later onto the valley and mountains of Mānoa.
*Royalists were a mixed bag of the Queen’s supporters; mainly Hawaiian, but many haoles, including George Lycurgus of Sans Souci fame, were allied with the Queen.
** possibly on the shores at George Lycurgus’ Sans Souci at the foot of Lē‘ahi in Waikīkī.
The plaque accompanies an interesting artwork interpretation of the battle by Laura Ruby, who also created the book about Mō‘ili‘ili, Mō‘ili‘ili - The Life of a Community.
For more information about the 1895 battle, take a stroll in Mānoa, Walk X to Stop 43 .
Turn around and come back to Date Street, walking ‘Ewa to Hausten Street where you will turn mauka to walk past the (former) Willows Restaurant back to S. King Street.

On the ‘Ewa side of Hausten Street, you will cross Ala Naio, a vestige of a stream that once flowed through this area. This little fresh water stream continues makai next to the S-shaped Marco Polo condominium, through Ala Wai Community Park, to the Ala Wai Canal. Before the canal was built, this stream provided fresh water for the local aquaculture.
Hausten Street is named after the owner of the former Willows Restaurant, which you might be able to visit if the gates are open. Or at least peek through the gates to glance at the lush gardens.

One of many ponds, Kamulae Pond, was fed from near-by Kānewai Spring.These waters were part of the Mānoa Stream system that still flows through the area - Ala Naio and underground waterways. This pond served as a perfect site for the summer cottage of Victoria Kamāmalu, a descendant of King Kamehameha I.

The land was inherited by Caesar Kapa‘akea, father to King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani. Kapa‘akea is the Robert Wilcox was a multi-faceted man; no matter what he did, he did it with gusto. This statue stands proud on Fort Street Mall, downtown.
 ‘Ena Rd.
The plaque reads:
“The battle of Mō‘ili‘ili was one of several skirmishes in 1895 between the Republic of Hawai‘i forces and royalists* attempting to restore Queen Lili‘uokanlani to the throne of Hawai‘i.

On January 7, two royalist groups, led by Robert Wilcox and Samuel Nowlein, met near Diamond Head** to march on Honolulu. As the royalists advanced along Mō‘ili‘ili Road (Old Wai‘alae Road), they engaged Republic forces sent to counter them.” former name of this area.
Continue mauka on Hausten Street.

Cross S. King Street at Hausten Street and walk up to Triangle Park where you will see a replica of a Japanese Torii. This Torii, a symbol of the Shinto religion, was a gift from Honolulu’s sister city, Hiroshima, presented in 2001 and is a half-size replica of the Miyajima Island Torii gate, just south of Hiroshima. The original Torii was built in the 12th century. In Japan, at low tide, the sea recedes, allowing people to walk under the gate.
The plaque states:
HIROSHIMATO HONOLULU HAWAI‘I FRIENDSHIP TORII It was presented “On the occasion of the 100th anniversary of the establishment of the Honolulu Japanese Chamber of Commerce.”
On August 6, 2020, another plaque in front of a lava boulder was added: “In Commemoration 75th Anniversary Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima.” In both English and Japanese:“Peace and Remembrance”
There are two smaller plaques under the trees, placed in 1994, that honor the original Japanese residents who built up this area:
The ‘Ewa plaque was dedicated to “Kihachi and Shika Kashiwabara, The first Japanese immigrants to settle in Mō‘ili‘ili, 1893.”
The other plaque was dedicated to “Harry G. Yoshimura, in honor of his Mō‘ili‘ili roots (1905) and his far reaching effects on this community.”
If you have time, stop in at the Japanese Cultural Center on the mauka side of S. Beretania Street.
Walk makai-‘Ewa on S. King Street, passing Coolidge Street, the president (1923-29) at the time when this street was cut through.
The Torii stands proud in a neighborhood founded by Japanese families.

stops.title: Isenberg Street is the home of the

blocks.text: Mō‘ili‘ili Community Garden. The garden is across from the former Bowl-O-Drome, which, after 50 years, closed in 2004.

Isenberg Street was named after Daniel Isenberg (1866 -1919), who was president of the Mō‘ili‘ili Baseball league. The Isenberg family was part of a small group of Germans who settled in Hawai‘i and lived in the Punahou-Makiki area.

At the intersection of Isenberg and S. King streets look down at the street art of taro leaves, fish, and streams - in recognition of the streams that once flowed through this area and the taro and fish that populated the waterways. (Remember, street art is ephemeral.)

The stately First Hawaiian Bank building sits on the footprint of the Spreckles mansion, which, in 1913, was moved minus its two lower floors (yes, it was that regal – 4 floors plus a lofty tower!) from its original location on Punahou Street. Adolph Claus Spreckles, an ardent supporter of the monarchy, was best known as the “Sugar King” due to his sugar company, Spreckels Sugar Company. The house, repurposed as a clubhouse, burned to the ground in 1954.

As you admire the architecturally outstanding First Hawaiian Bank, look up to see the etched baseball diamonds in the upper windows. Even the door handles form a baseball diamond! If the bank is open, stop in to see the memorabilia collection with photos of the stadium in the time of its glory and the baseball Cartwright Cup. The trophy is named in honor of Alexander Joy Cartwright Jr. (1820-1892), who is best known as the “Father of Modern Baseball,” and was inducted into Cooperstown’s Baseball Hall of Fame. Cartwright established baseball’s first organized association, the New York Knickerbocker Base Ball Club and contributed to the creation of the rules and regulations of nine players and nine innings. Cartwright Field in Makiki is named in his honor. Cartwright Road in Waikīkī, is also named after him. His son, Bruce Cartwright Sr., was one of the subdividers of Waikīkī.

21A Follow the purple line for the a different experience. Walk mauka on Isenberg Street to cross over the freeway on the footbridge (and then come back to continue your Mō‘ili‘ili walk)! Or not. If you do, hold on to your hat – it gets very windy up there. Then come back to continue the Mō‘ili‘ili Walk. It’s worth the trip over the freeway to see the “HAWAIIAN” mural!

The area of the former Honolulu Stadium (1926-1976) extended from Isenberg Street to Makahiki Way. The stadium site is now the 9-acre “Old Stadium Park,” which For an image of the stadium and a little of its history, read the plaque on the corner of Isenberg and S. King streets. houses a playground, chess/checker tables, a comfort station, and a People’s Open Market (POM), a local farmers’ market on Wednesday mornings from 8:15 to 9:15.

Honolulu Stadium was home to the Islanders who played their last game on September 8, 1975. Hawaiians were honored with the likes of Babe Ruth (his first time here was in 1933) and Joe DiMaggio (1944) - both played here!

If you have heard about shave ice, but have not yet tried it, this is the time to do so! Walk to Waiola (‘water of life’) Shave Ice store at the corner of Waiola and Pā‘ani (‘play, sport’– due to the proximity of the sports stadium) streets. Trust me, this shave ice is worth the detour.

To arrive at Waiola Shave Ice, walk diagonally across Old Stadium Park between the play structure and pavilion, then through the parking lot toward Makahiki Way. Makahiki celebrates the Hawaiian New Year during the winter season.
Before venturing across the park, stop to admire the art works in the park:

• I ka wā mamua, ka wā mahope, ‘The future is in the past.’ The collage-style mural art by artist Luke DeKneef on the ‘Ewa side went up in the spring of 2021. The mural reflects the community over the years, especially incorporating the history of the stadium.
• As You Like It The low white sculptures dispersed around the park are by Eli Marozzi (1913–1999).
As you leave the parking lot, you will see a bright blue two-story building with a painted rainbow: WAIOLA STORE open every day 12-6. Chances are that there will be a long line for the shave ice.
You can go back to Old Stadium Park and sit on the benches under a Kukui tree near the pavilion while you enjoy your shave ice and play a game of chess or checkers…or continue walking as you slurp.

Walk mauka on Wiliwili Street (the street after Pā‘ani Street), which is named for the native Wiliwili tree that produces lovely red seeds used as beads and necklaces. The streets along McCully Street are names of plants and trees.

A map and photo of the World War II battles fought by the soldiers of the 100th/422 regiment are proudly displayed at 933 Wiliwili Street. The regiment’s motto, GO FOR BROKE, meant that they were “all in till the end.” True heroes. There is another, larger and more accessible memorial in Waikīkī on Kalākaua Avenue. (Kalākaua Avenue Walk IV).
You can view the two buildings of faith from the mauka side of S. King Street; no need to cross, then continue around the corner to McCully Street.
On the mauka side of S. King Street are two faith structures:
• St. Mary’s Episcopal Church with its requisite Olive trees (but no olives), which was founded as a mission in 1917. The church building dates to 1958.

• Hawai‘i Ishizuchi Jinja Shrine (1913), which served the local Japanese who worked in the nearby Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, reflected in the meaning of its name, ‘Rockhammer.’ (Joel Bradshaw “Midtown Places of Worship”)

Continue ‘Ewa on S. King Street to McCully Street, where you will walk makai to Waikīkī. It is recommended that you walk on the shady side of the street: Diamond Head in the morning; ‘Ewa in the afternoon.

McCully is named for Lawrence McCully (1831 - 1892), a Justice of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i Supreme Court under Kalākaua. He was also involved in the development of the Punahou area, which you can walk through if you take the Mānoa Walk.

On the Diamond Head-Makai corner of S. King and McCully streets is the James M. Chrones Building, a lovely Art Deco building that now houses a barbershop and other locally owned shops. The Chrones Building – in its former life - was home to McCully Chop Sui (1948-2006). The University of Hawai‘i Federal Credit Union Building with its Anthurium flower motif wraps around this 1948 building.
Continue makai along McCully Street, noticing and admiring the houses and
This fence tells it all: Mō‘ili‘ili is great!
local atmosphere.
At the corner of McCully and Algaroba streets, as of this writing, a large wooden fence is decorated with geckos (in the style of M.C. Escher) and a history of Mō‘ili‘ili.
Even if the mural is no longer up, what was posted is still of great interest.

Algaroba, also known as Kiawe and Mesquite, is a large tree, native to South America; however, the first Algaroba tree was brought to Hawai‘i from Paris by a Catholic priest! The original tree was planted in downtown Honolulu on the mauka end of Fort Street at the Catholic church: the stump still exists with a plaque attesting to its origin.
Despite its name, there do not appear to be any Kiawe trees on this street.
If you missed the shave ice place, turn Diamond Head on Waiola Street at the next corner.
Only 5 more blocks to Kapi‘olani Boulevard, the Ala Wai Canal, and Waikīkī. The street name continue with names of trees and plants: Citron, Date, Fern, and Lime.

The major intersection just before the canal is Kapi‘olani Boulevard, a major west-east thoroughfare. Queen Kapi‘olani ruled with King Kalākaua from 1874 to 1891; King Kalākaua died of a stroke while traveling in California. Queen Kapi‘olani lived another 8 years but did not rule; Queen Lili‘uokanlani, King Kalākaua’s sister, became the monarch until the overthrown of the Hawaiian kingdom in 1893. Interestingly, Queen Kapi‘olani did not speak English and needed an interpreter at political functions.
Notice the overarching Monkey Pod trees along Kapi‘olani Boulevard, which give us never-ending shade!
From here, you can cross the McCully Bridge into the ‘Ewa end of Waikīkī.
Bus routes and times www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator.
For more information and to circumnavigate the Ala Wai Canal, take the Ala Wai Canal Walk I.
 The plaque reads:
The mural is a tribute to much loved Mō‘ili‘ili – the area between ‘Mānoa & Waikīkī’.
The region’s history dates back to ancient times with a legendary battle between Pele’s sister, Hi‘iaka, and a lizard mo‘o whom she tured into pebbles ‘ili‘ili.
The area is best known for its underground caverns, kalo cultivation, strong Japanese culture, and once being the center of local sports at Honolulu Stadium.
Thank you FOR YOUR KŌKUA IN KEEPING MŌ‘ILI‘ILI Beautiful.
Wa‘ahila Ridge – the Kanaka (commoners) side of Mānoa Valley
Home to the first coffee, sugar cane, and pineapple in Hawai‘i!

Walk up McCully Street, around Punahou School to the neighborhood of Mānoa Valley and Mānoa Heritage Center to the only restored, intact heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. And then continue beyond, to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery, Mānoa Falls, and Lyon Arboretum!
In the morning, it is recommended that you walk on the Diamond Head side or the mauka side of the street.
In the afternoon, it is recommended that you walk on the ‘Ewa side or the makai side of the street.

Mānoa is part of the much larger ahupua‘a (land division) of Waikīkī, which extends from Ke‘eaumoku (Queen Ka‘ahumanu ’s father) Street on the west to Kuli‘ou‘ou (a type of knee drum) in the east, and from the ocean shore to the top of the Ko‘olau mountain range.

Coffee, sugar cane, and pineapple were first grown in Mānoa Valley, not on Hawai‘i Island! Chief Boki, who lived on the Diamond Head side of the valley, brought in these agricultural products with the intent of fostering a great agricultural growth. (More about Boki and his wife, Liliha, on the University of Hawai‘i campus walk, XI.)

Mānoa is part of the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī – the breadbasket of Waikīkī. While Waikīkī oceanfront was the aquacultural provider, Mānoa Valley was the agricultural provider. Waikīkī offered seafood; Mānoa, the ‘breadbasket,’ offered sustenance in the form of kalo (taro), which is the staple food of Hawai‘i - even today - and sweet potato.
This route will take you into the beautifully lush valley of Mānoa, where you will find rainbows.

Further along, are Mānoa Falls and Lyon Arboretum and, on the other side of the valley, is the Chinese Cemetery, Mānoa is generally translated as ‘vast,’ which this valley is. However, the word noa translates as ‘free from kapu (taboo),’ perhaps this is why (or because) Queen Ka‘ahumanu chose Mānoa Valley as her special home. Please read more about Ka‘ahumanu at Stop 39 . The word ‘ma,’ without the kahakō (long mark over the vowel) can mean ‘in, on, or at.’

This walk begins at McCully Street and Kalākaua Avenue, around the Ala Wai Canal. However, it can start at any convenient place along the way, depending on the walker’s interests and location. For example, for a walk around Punahou School, you could start at Stop 7 or 8 . Or if the walker is interested solely in Mānoa Valley, Stop 27 is a great starting point.
