blocks.text: McCully Street is named for Lawrence McCully, a Justice of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i Supreme Court under King Kalākaua. He was also involved in the development of the Punahou area, which you will walk through after you cross over the freeway.

Cross the canal on the Diamond Head side and you might catch a crew in their outrigger canoes. If not, at least admire the sleek canoes and the attached outriggers. This area is the home of the Ala Wai Community Park.

The first intersection after the canal is Kapi‘olani Boulevard, a major westeast thoroughfare, named for Queen Nāpelakapuokākae Kapi‘olani. She ruled with King Kalākaua from 1874 to 1891. King Kalākaua died of a stroke while traveling in California. After his death, Lili‘uokalani became the monarch.
Mānoa Valley in 1924, including Kūali‘i, the Cooke house. (Hawai‘i State Archives)

Notice the lovely Monkey Pod trees as you cross Kapi‘olani Boulevard to Judd Park, which is supported by Frank Case Judd’s (1915-1976) friends and family, going back to an early missionary in Hawai‘i .
Continue along McCully Street, observing and admiring the small garden apartment buildings, houses, and local atmosphere.
Lime Street is the first of many streets in the area named after trees and plants.
Fern Street, although it is a plant, is said to be named after George Fern, the brother of Honolulu’s first mayor, Joseph Fern.
Notice the beautifully carved aluminum fence of leaves, outrigger canoes, dolphins, and even Lē‘ahi on the Diamond Head side of McCully between Fern and Date streets.
Date Street continues Diamond Head to Kapahulu Avenue.
Citron Street. Citron means ‘lemon’ in French.

You will be passing though the neighborhoods of McCully (‘Ewa side) and Mō‘ili‘ili (Diamond Head side). In the time before there were asphalt streets and buildings, Mō‘ili‘ili, ‘pebbled lizard,’ was an agricultural area mainly of taro fields. The only remnant is the reincarnated lo‘i at the University of Hawai‘i (Lower Campus Walk XII ).

According to the most authoritative book on Mō‘ili‘ili, Mō‘ili‘ili-The Life of a Community, this area was first known as Waikīkī Waena or Middle Waikīkī since it was in the middle of the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. Mō‘ili‘ili is riddled with underground caverns, none accessible today, but filled with stories of cave-ins and sink holes as recently as 1989! There were, and probably still are, blind fish there. A pond, once fed by fresh water springs, can be found at the Willows (formerly) Restaurant on Hausten Street. (Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX)
Waiola Shave Ice

If you’d like to take a little detour for our local shave ice, turn Diamond Head at Waiola Street to Waiola Shave Ice store at the corner of Pa‘ani Street. You won’t be sorry. Waiola means ‘water of life’… well, shave ice is made from water… Look for a bright blue building with a long line waiting to order shave ice. Don’t worry; it’s worth it!
At the corner of McCully and Algaroba streets a large wooden fence is decorated with geckos and a history of Mō‘ili‘ili.

Algaroba, also known as Kiawe and Mesquite is a large tree, native to South America; the first Algaroba tree was brought to Hawai‘i from Paris by a Catholic priest! The original tree was planted in downtown Honolulu on Fort Street. However, there are no Kiawe trees on this street.
Treat yourself to the ‘water of life!’
Even if the mural is no longer up, what was posted is still of great interest:

It’s one more block to S. King and S. Beretania streets, after which you will go over the freeway into the neighborhood of Punahou. You will cross these two major east-west streets: S. King Street, one way heading east, and S. Beretania Street, one way west.

Across S. Beretania Street at McCulley Street, notice the (often politically incorrect) sign above Hawaiian Rent-All. Cross over to the other side of the freeway on the 1956 McCully Overpass. The downtown portion of the H1 freeway was known as Mauka Arterial in 1953, when it was built. After Hawai‘i became a state in 1959, it became part of the Interstate system. Several extensions were added over the years.
Hawaiian Rent-All never has a dull sign!
This sign is a landmark.
 ‘Ena Rd.
The mural sign states:
The mural is a tribute to much loved Mō‘ili‘ili – the area between ‘Mānoa & Waikīkī’
The region’s history dates back to ancient times with a legendary battle between Pele’s sister Hi‘iaka, and a lizard mo‘o whom she turned into pebbles ‘ili‘ili.
The area is best known for its underground caverns, kalo cultivation, strong Japanese culture, and once being the center of local sports at Honolulu Stadium.
Thank you FOR YOUR KŌKUA IN KEEPING Mō‘ili‘ili Beautiful.

As you cross the McCully bridge, look up to the left/‘Ewa to see the green roofs of the internationally known Punahou School, alma mater to President Obama. These are the school buildings for the Case Middle School at Punahou. Steve Case, of AOL fame, who graduated from Punahou in 1976, gave money to his alma mater in honor of his parents.
‘Ili of Kapa‘akea ‘Ili of Punahou
After crossing the freeway, at the foot of the bridge, you will cross Dole Street. Continue one more block mauka, turn ‘Ewa onto Wilder Avenue.

Dole Street is not named for the territorial governor and major player in the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893; rather for Reverend Daniel Dole, the first teacher and administrator at Punahou School. However, on earlier maps, this street is labeled Kapa‘akea, who was father to both King Kalakaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani. There is a small street by that name in Mō‘ili‘ili. Kapa‘akea can refer to a coral or limestone surface.
As you walk along Dole Street, notice the sweet perfume smell of the ‘Alani (Mock Orange) flower in the bushes.

After Dole Street, McCully Street becomes Metcalf Street. Theophilus Metcalf was the first experienced surveyor for the 1848 Mahele. The Metcalf family owned property from here past the University of Hawai‘i campus. Theophilus Metcalf was the father of Emma Nakuina, the first female judge in Hawai‘i .

Dole and Metcalf streets are routes to the University of Hawai‘i . Dole Street, after a few blocks, divides the university into the lower (makai) and upper (mauka) campuses. If you are interested in a tour of the University of Hawai‘i Mānoa campus, follow Walk XI of the Upper (main) Campus and/or the Walk of the Lower Campus XII (mainly the athletic fields).
The area around here is the ‘ili (land division) of Kapa‘akea; however, after you turn ‘Ewa you will be in the ‘ili of Punahou.

As mentioned in the introduction, you are walking in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. An ahupua‘a is divided into smaller divisions, ‘ili. You will be walking in one of the largest ‘ili in Mānoa, the ‘ili of Punahou. Attributed to the abundance of springs - puna ‘spring’ and hou ‘new’ - this ‘ili was known as Punahou. The mo‘olelo (legend) relates that the deity, Kāne, plunged his staff into the ground here and brought up water, the spring.

Punahou land extended as far as to today’s University Avenue. Originally crown land, it passed through the hands of governors Boki and Liliha, whose uncensored and licentious behavior Queen Ka‘ahumanu could not curtail, to the waiting arms of Hiram Bingham, the missionary.
As you walk across McCully Bridge, notice the green roofed building on the ‘Ewa side of the hills before you. This is Punahou’s middle school.

To walk around the campus of Punahou School and, ultimately, deep into Mānoa Valley, continue two blocks mauka on McCully/Metcalf Street, where you will turn ‘Ewa to walk along Wilder Avenue. Cross McCully/Metcalf Street after the huge Monkey Pod tree. It is recommended that you walk on the mauka side in the morning and makai side in the afternoon to avoid the harsh rays of the sun.
7-11s are everywhere, but this one on the corner is particularly aesthetic with a Hawaiian style roof and pretty glass windows of local plants and flowers.
9 Wilder Avenue is named for Samuel Wilder (1831-1888), entrepreneur and Minister of the Interior under King Kalākaua.
There are several interestingly named streets on the makai side of Wilder Avenue, as well as a fascinating bit of history on the mauka side. The streets and places of interest along Wilder Avenue:

Avenue) was named for Father Clement Evrand, who founded Sacred Heart Catholic Church, which was first located here. Father Clement said mass for the people of Marquesville, the local Portuguese population.

(makai side) are both named in honor of Dr. Auguste Marquès’ wife, Evelyn Oliver Marquès, who helped her husband educate the local Portuguese community. The house at 1519 Oliver Street is a Historic Residence. Built in 1926, it is an example of the type of houses - Craftsman Style Bungalow – that abounded all around at that time.

Across from Evelyn Lane, on the mauka side of Wilder Avenue, is a plaque embedded in a lava boulder regarding the first Artesian well in Honolulu brought to this place in 1880 for Dr. Auguste Marquès (18411929). This was part of the spring system in the Punahou area. The well was sealed in 1938. In the early 20th century, this area was known as Marquesville, obviously after Dr. Marquès and ‘ville’ (city) due to the large Portuguese community here with whom the Marquèses were involved. Dr. Marquès, who received his doctorate in science from the University of Lisbon, served in the legislature under King Kalākaua.
The campus of Punahou School begins along here at the low lava stone wall topped by the Night-Blooming Cereus. Notice the palm frond motif on the light fixtures and buildings.

Portions of the lower wall were built by Queen Ka‘ahumanu to keep her cattle on her property. After Queen Ka‘ahumanu gave a portion of her land to Hiram Bingham, he became the founder of Punahou School. Bingham’s home is indicated on campus with a plaque.
13 Artesian Way is named for the well dug in this area. The first artesian well on the island, down to 240 feet, at Fort Weaver Road near ‘Ewa Beach was opened in September 1879 and sealed in 1939.

stops.title: Alexander Street is named for the

blocks.text: missionary, William Patterson Alexander, who lived nearby. Alexander Field on the Punahou campus is named for his son Samuel T. Alexander. A plaque about the Alexander family is mounted near the playing field on Mānoa Road. William DeWitt Alexander was a supporter of the Provisional Government that overthrew the monarchy headed by Queen Lili‘uokalani.

On the mauka side of Wilder Avenue, across from Alexander Street is the ubiquitous Lunalilo Freeway H-1 West sign. King William Lunalilo (1835-18974), the first elected monarch and the 6th king of Hawai‘i , ruled only the last year of his life, succumbing to tuberculosis.
Enjoy the shade of the Monkey Pod trees as you continue along Wilder Avenue.

dedicated in 1914, is an significant place as attested by the pillars. Sacred Heart was the first Catholic church in Mānoa Valley, first built as a white wooden chapel across the way at Clement Street and Wilder Avenue.

Bachelot Memorial Hall is named for Father Alexis Bachelot (1796-1837), who was not only the first Catholic priest in Hawai‘i as part of the Catholic missionary group, but was also responsible for bringing the Kiawe tree to Hawai‘i (Recall Algaroba Street on your way up McCully Street.) Due to the religious conflicts following the changes from the Hawaiian religion to Christianity, he served for only 4 years (1827-1831) when he was banished. Despite his exile, he attempted to return, but died en route to Hawai‘i .
The church and adjacent buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places.
either to the school next door or to Punahou, across the street.

stops.title: Spreckels Street was named for Claus

blocks.text: Spreckels, a controversial sugar magnate and supporter of the monarchy, who lived nearby.

The Mānoa Trolley Transfer Point shelter stands proud diagonally across from the entrance to Punahou School at the corner of Punahou Street and Wilder Avenue. The Mānoa Valley Electric Trolley ran from this intersection to O‘ahu Avenue and ‘Anuenue Street from 1901 to 1933 – a 3.4 mile round trip.
There are enormous Monkey Pod trees on 3 of the corners at this intersection!

A quick side trip will take you to the intersection of two Makiki Streams: Kanahā and Makiki streams that, as one stream historically, became the Pi‘inaio and flowed into the ocean near today’s ‘Ilikai Hotel. The former Pi‘inaio / presentday Makiki Stream flows into the 1920s Ala Wai Canal. If you are interested in waterways, cross Punahou Street on the mauka side, walk two short blocks to a small bridge at 1614 Anapuni where you will see the two streams come together: Kanahā Stream, from the ‘Ewa side of Makiki, comes through the opening on the left; Makiki Stream, from the Diamond Head side of Makiki, comes in on the right.
Return to Punahou Street / Mānoa Road to learn about Punahou School and continue your journey to Mānoa Valley.
This covered shelter serviced the 1.7 mile open-air trolley ride to the terminus in Mānoa Valley.

As you walk around the campus from Wilder Avenue to Punahou Street/Mānoa Road, notice the seal that displays a Hala tree with its root spread out and two taro leaves on the sides. Two-Night Blooming Cereus flowers and Honolulu, Hawai‘i were added to the seal in 1940. Notice the Hala (walking trees) on the gates.
Spread over 76 acres, Punahou School, which is home to a diverse population of over 3,000 students, originated as a school for the first missionary children of Hawai‘i in 1841.

At the entryway to Punahou School, on the corner of Mānoa Road and Wilder Avenue stands a large upright lichen-encrusted lava boulder, Pōhakuloa, ‘the long rock’ with the plaque “Punahou School Founded 1841.” A mo‘olelo (legend) relates that in the 1830s Queen Ka‘ahumanu had two large pōhaku (stones) at the entryway to the wall from Punchbowl to Punahou to keep cattle out and to mark her property. Another mo‘olelo tells us that Pōhakuloa was held sacred, bringing wisdom and strength to the children of the women who venerated Pōhakuloa. Pōhakuloa communicates with another upright stone on campus, Keapopo.

The double row of stately Royal Palm trees, which line Palm Drive, were a gift from the Class of 1894, as stated on the plaque inside the gate. Dr. Gerrit Judd, one of the third wave of missionaries who was a founder of Punahou School and became a trusted advisor to King Kamehameha III, supplied the Palm tree seeds.
The road into Punahou School is Chamberlain Drive, named after a trustee’s grandson.
The school is named for Punahou spring, which still flows around Thurston Memorial Chapel as the Lily Pond.

A few years after the founding of the school, the ubiquitous Night Blooming Cereus that continues to bloom in the summer months, was brought to Hawai‘i from Mexico and planted by Mrs. Bingham. The Night Blooming Cereus (panini o kapunahou), piled jungle-like on the lava walls, Punahou “new spring” School’s seal incorporates the ubiquitous Hala tree in the center and Taro leaves in the outer circle. blooms in the heat of the summer nights, then closes in the cool of the morning. So come early morning (as the sun rises over Pu‘u o Mānoa - Rocky Hill) to take photos but be wary of the swarming bees!
The walk around Punahou campus that started along Wilder Avenue, continues mauka up Mānoa Road into Mānoa Valley.
As you walk, continue to admire the campus, including the buildings and flora, especially the large, old Monkey Pod trees.

The first building on Punahou Street /Mānoa Road, a white stucco structure, is Montague Hall, built in 1937 and donated by the Atherton family (More about the Athertons at Stop 27 ) in honor of the Montague women who were involved with Punahou School in the mid-19th century. Notice the Hawaiian motif on the overhang and the unusually styled Spanish-tiled roof.

21 Pauahi Hall, the next building, completed in 1896, is most noticeable along Punahou Street/Mānoa Road with its lava rock walls, topped with a dome, painted buff (the color of sand) and blue (the ocean). If you stand on the corner of Dominis and Pauahi streets, you will be able to see the red and gold topped dome of the once rival, Roosevelt High School. They are now in different leagues.

Pauahi Hall, which continues to serve the campus as office spaces and classrooms, was named in honor of Princess Bernice Pauahi (1831-1884), a great-granddaughter of King Kamehameha the Great. Pauahi Hall was designed by Ripley and Dickey, in the the Richardsonian Romanesque style. Richardson Romanesque incorporated (believe it or not) 11th and 12th century southern French, Spanish, and Italian Romanesque styles.

The oldest building on campus, not visible from the street, is aptly named Old School Hall and was constructed out of stone blasted from the nearby hill in 1851. The names of the first students in this building are recorded on a plaque.

22 Bingham Hall, the original one built in 1883, was replaced by this one in 1959. It was named for Hiram Bingham (1789-1869) the leader of the first group of the 1820 missionaries. His son, Hiram Bingham II, was also a missionary to the Kingdom of Hawai‘i. His grandson Hiram Bingham III explored Machu Picchu. His great-grandson Hiram Bingham IV rescued people of Jewish ancestry during the Holocaust. Quite an illustrious family line!
23 Cross Nehoa (‘strong’) Street where Punahou Street becomes Mānoa Road.
Soon after the lava wall and cereus plants end at the entrance to Alexander Field, you will see Lē‘ahi peeking out through the trees and the President’s House just mauka.
You are walking around Pu‘u o Mānoa – the hill of Mānoa, a cinder cone. Up on the hill you can see the blue “tank.”
Across from the entrance to Alexander Field, notice the huge in situ lava wall on the ‘Ewa side of Mānoa Road with the local lava rock wall built around it!
Along Mānoa Road just past the tennis courts and before the tall lava wall begins anew, a sign points to “Chapel”; however, the chapel is not visible from the street.

Thurston Memorial Chapel was designed by Vladimir Ossipoff in 1966, who was the architect of the Daniel Inouye Honolulu International Airport Terminal, as well as many beautiful homes around Honolulu (You will pass a home by Ossipoff on the walk to the Mānoa Heritage Center.) The entrance doors, designed by Jean Charlot, who lived in Hawai‘i from 1949 until his death in 1979, are made from local koa wood and executed in copper. The chapel is named in memory of Robert Shipman Thurston Jr, class of 1941 who was lost on a military plane in the Pacific at the end of World War II. The chapel is in the center of the campus.
Piper’s Pali Street, which runs mauka through campus was named after Leo Piper, a maintenance engineer for Punahou School – an exceptionally good one, it is hoped! Pali means ‘cliff.’
Notice the twisted-bark Kiawe tree trunks.

‘Ewa and mauka is Sugar Loaf – Hawaiian, Pu‘u Kākea (the name of a stormy Mānoa wind) - which produced lava approximately 70,000 years ago that flowed down into the valley resulting in the floor of Mānoa Valley. The lava flow pushed Mānoa Stream to the Diamond Head side of the valley over to the other side of the University of Hawai‘i. The lower edge of the flow created the beautiful lava that was dug out at the Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, now the lower campus. The 50-foot-high wall, separating the lower campus from the upper campus is visible from the parking structure. (Lower Campus Walk XI)
Alternatively, you can take bus number 5 on Mānoa Road directly to Mānoa Heritage Center and all the way back into Mānoa Valley to Lyon Arboretum and Mānoa Falls.
Come back to Punahou School in February for their awesome Punahou Carnival!

At the first street and signal light, Diamond Head side, cross Lanihuli (turning royal chief) Drive with a huge Hala, aka walking tree, across the way. Continue walking mauka along Mānoa Road (which after a few blocks will split into Mānoa Road and E. Mānoa road); however, after 2 blocks, turn Diamond Head to Kamehameha Avenue, a broad street with wider grassy sidewalks.

On your way, you’ll cross Linohau (‘beautifully decorated’) Way. The former home of the Mānoa Tennis Club was located on the makai-Diamond Head corner. Kamehameha Avenue is the junction where the Mānoa streetcar/trolley turned off from Mānoa Road to go back into the valley.
Follow the purple line on the map to a “Secret” right of way.
25A “Secret” right of way

An alternative side route, if you have lots of time (or come back another day for this hike), cross Mānoa Road ‘Ewa at the light at Lanihuli Way, walk mauka past Judd Hillside Road, to a “secret” right of way just past Kamehameha Avenue (It’s actually an easement.) between the low lava wall with bushes on the makai side of Mānoa Road and a high lava wall with glass light globes on the mauka side up to Ferdinand Avenue - the street up the hill that parallels Mānoa Road. As you exit the secret passageway, notice the exquisite 1925 house on the mauka-Diamond Head side of the street by architect Hart Wood.

For the more adventuresome among you, after you exit this “secret” passage and look at the beautiful homes around you, walk mauka to the end of the street, turn ‘Ewa up Ventura Street, then walk either way on Sonoma Street, which dead ends on both ends. Look for the houses with tramways up to the front door. (Hint: both houses are on the mauka side of Sonoma). Comeback down the hill to cross (carefully) both Mānoa Road and E. Mānoa Road to Kamehameha Avenue.

Walking along Kamehameha Avenue, notice the “Exceptional” Earpod Tree on the mauka side, just past the turn off E. Mānoa Road. You’ll cross McKinley (under whose presidency Hawai‘i passed from Hawaiian to American hands) Street and Beckwith (Rev. Beckwith was a past president of Punahou School) Street. After 2 blocks, Kamehameha Avenue veers makai for one block. Just before the turn, notice 9 stately Palm trees on the mauka side signifying an important and impressive house. Continue to the University of Hawai‘i ’s President’s House up on the hill.

This area also part of Punahou, now known as College Hill Tract, was first developed by the enterprising real estate developer, Percy Marty Pond beginning in 1900. Pond was also involved in the Kālia district of Waikīkī. (Kālia Walk II)
Follow Kamehameha Avenue around to the 2.6-acre University of Hawai‘i ’s President’s House at College Hills, with its magnificent trees, especially on the Diamond Head side.

College Hills, the first suburban development in the valley, is named after O‘ahu College (now Punahou School), not the University of Hawai‘i. Frank and Eleanor Atherton lived in this stately house from 1902 and donated it to the University of Hawai‘i in 1964. Mr. Atherton was an astute businessman whose vocations included corporate secretary for the Bank of Hawai‘i, president of Castle and Cooke, and president of Honolulu Star-Bulletin newspaper (now the Star-Advertiser). He was involved in many philanthropic associations, especially the (former) YMCA, a few blocks makai of here on University Avenue, which he financed Formerly the home of the Atherton family, now the “president’s house” of the University of Hawai‘i, it is used mainly for academic gatherings. for low-income University of Hawai‘i students. Mr. Atherton was also an avid gardener – one of his orchid houses is still on the property.
Today, this magnificent house is used to entertain faculty, visiting scholars, and guests.
Follow purple line on map along

Hunnewell Street. A side stroll, a few blocks makai of the President’s House is the historic 1919 Mānoa Valley Inn at 2001 Vancouver Drive (corner of Hunnewell Street), which still accommodates guests. It is listed on the National and Hawaiian Register of Historic Places.

Walk makai on Hunnewell – businessman and a founder of Brewer and Co (17941869) – Street. After the curve Diamond Head, notice the native Cotton, ma‘o, tree on the mauka side. You will pass these interestingly named streets:

• Hā‘ena –‘red hot’ – Drive • Halulu – a legendary man-eating bird!– Way • Damon - Reverend of Seamen’s Bethel and founder of anti-royalist newspaper, The Friend (1815-1885) – Street • Atherton – of the President’s House – Road • Hyde – Reverend and principal at a missionary school (1832-1899) -Street When you reach Mānoa Valley Inn, notice the Inn’s setback and porte-cochère. Each of the 7 rooms has individualized special décor.
After admiring this over 100-year-old building, retrace your steps along Hunnewell Street to continue your journey into the Valley.
Seaview Tract
Seaview Tract, the streets makai of the Inn to Metcalf Street, which was the first development in Mānoa Valley, opened in 1886. No traces of those early homes exist.

stops.title: At the glorious Monkey Pod tree

blocks.text: At the glorious Monkey Pod tree, follow Kamehameha Avenue in the direction of Diamond Head around on the sidewalk (one of the few places where you will find a sidewalk in this section of Mānoa), then mauka to O‘ahu Avenue, into the beautiful valley.

As you walk on the makai side of the presidential mansion, be sure to notice the Loulu Palm tree – the only native Palm –as well as other local trees, such as Kukui with its broad leaves and the gnarly Kiawe.

Kamehameha and O‘ahu avenues are the routes where the Mānoa electric streetcar/ trolley ran (from 1901 to 1933), resulting in wider than usual Mānoa streets. It’s easiest to walk along on the ‘Ewa side of O‘ahu Avenue (which parallels University Avenue when you walk out of the valley) where the grassy sidewalks are wider; however, beware of the tricky tree roots – don’t let them trip you up!
Across from the president’s house on the O‘ahu Avenue side is the site of an early synagogue: paradoxically, where the Honolulu Christian Church sits today.
After you turn the corner mauka to O‘ahu Avenue, look up and enjoy the view of the majestic Ko‘olau mountains!

A stroll along O‘ahu Avenue, after a mile, will take you to Mānoa Heritage Center (Stop 36 ). If you would like to visit, you should make reservations for a 1-hour tour of the property and the only restored heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. Call or email before you go: manoaheritagecenter.org or 808-988-1287

The first street, Ka‘ala Way/Street is named after the tallest mountain on O‘ahu in the Wai‘anae range on the ‘Ewa side of the island, at a little over 4,000 feet. The mountain straight ahead, Kōnāhuanui - the tallest in the Ko‘olau range (this mountain range) - peaks at 3,100 feet.

Ka‘ala Street is the entryway to Mid-Pacific Institute, K to 12 private school established in 1908, which borders the University of Hawai‘i campus. If you look Diamond Head down the street, you can see the entry gates. (More about Mid-Pac, its local name, as you walk out of the valley on University Avenue.)

On O‘ahu Avenue just after Ka‘ala Way/ Street, are several interesting homes with Historic Residence plaques, some by well-known architects, such as Thomas Gill, Vladimir Ossipoff, and Hart Wood. Please do stop to admire the exteriors of these lovingly cared-for homes. Some homeowners with equally beautiful homes have chosen not to list their homes on the registry.

stops.title: On the Diamond Head side of O‘ahu Avenue

blocks.text: On the Diamond Head side of O‘ahu Avenue is the “Chalet,” a blue-roofed 1902 house on the hill that was an early home of the Cooke family, whose second (and present) home you will visit at the Mānoa Heritage Center. Notice the lava wall up high. The Cookes moved to their home, Kūali‘i in 1911, but this house remained in the family for several years.

Mauka of the “Chalet” is home to a gorgeous Exceptional - the official term for its cultural significance - Tree at the former residence of Harold St. John, a University of Hawai‘i botanist who was responsible for much of the bounteous plantings on campus. He, quite obviously, took great care with this garden, interspacing the plants with handsome lava boulders. There is a Historic Register plaque at this 1912 house. Notice the cut at the base of the trunk of the Sandbox tree for the driveway next door. By the way, do not hug the tree – look closely at the trunk and you’ll see why!

There are two magnificent houses on Armstrong Street, which you will walk past on your way out of the valley. Armstrong Street is named after the reverend who replaced Hiram Bingham, of the first missionary group.
As you walk along O‘ahu avenue, look up to take in the glory of the Ko‘olau mountains. Kōnāhuanui – straight ahead – at 3,100 is the highest point.

graces the ‘Ewa side of the intersection of O‘ahu and University avenues. Notice the lovely plantings and Palm trees partially hidden by the high wall. Wan-Tsick Buddhist Temple, a female temple, traces its roots to Wan-Tsick Temple in Hong Kong. Wan-Tsick means ‘Illusory Traces.’ The Foo Dogs (actually lions) guard the temple and its people.
Cross E. Mānoa Road on the ‘Ewa side, where University Avenue ends, to continue mauka on O‘ahu Avenue.
Ghost golf course

After 6 houses, between 2 lava walls, you will see 5 broad lava steps to an asphalt paved walkway up to more steps hewn out of lava - as are many street curbs, in case you haven’t noticed. Most likely, all this lava came from the Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry just below the main campus of the University of Hawai‘i , now known as its lower campus. The UH campus Walk XI visits the quarry.

If you have time, and are able, climb the 2 sets of steps all the way up (to Hillside Avenue and then to Terrace Drive) for a magnificent view of the valley, Lē‘ahi, and out to the Pacific Ocean! There are several homes on the Historic Register along Hillside Avenue and Terrace Drive.
This area from Terrace Drive to Mānoa Road (the next block ‘Ewa) was home to a short lived 9-hole golf course - from 1904 to 1906.
Turn around and come back down the steps to continue mauka on O‘ahu Avenue to the Mānoa Heritage Center (Stop 36 ) as you enjoy the fantastic view of the valley and its mountains.

33A A side stroll at Terrace Drive: walk mauka, ‘Ewa to Mānoa Road, then turn Diamond Head on Cooper Road, which will take you back to O‘ahu Avenue and then a ½ block mauka to the Mānoa Heritage Center.
If you do take this route, notice the coral block wall on the makai-‘Ewa corner at Cooper Road and Hillside Avenue.
The street across from Cooper Road, Halelena - yellow house – Place, carries the name of the ‘ili (division within the ahupua‘a) in this area.

The turn-around point for the Mānoa streetcar, which ran along O‘ahu Avenue from 1901 to 1933, was between Cooper Road and Ānuenue Street. Turn-around was simply reversing the seats and heading makai!
On the makai-Diamond Head corner of Ānuenue (‘rainbow’) Street and O‘ahu Avenue are two magnificent Exceptional Trees, both Earpod trees.
After your tour at the Mānoa Heritage Center, you might want to come back to this street to walk a few blocks Diamond Head to the local Mānoa Marketplace (directions below at Stop 36A ).
O‘ahu avenue with all its Historic Residences rivals Kāhala Avenue for its beauty.

As you walk along O‘ahu Avenue, you will understand why this is referred to as the Kāhala Avenue of Mānoa, except with more hills. The houses may not be as grandiose as the Kāhala homes, but certainly beautiful. Particularly notable is a 1939 house by the architect Vladimir Ossipoff (1907-1998), who also designed the Thurston Memorial Chapel on the Punahou campus and the lānai-style concourses at the Daniel Inouye Honolulu International Airport, as well as many homes in Kāhala. The Ossipoff house is ‘Ewa, across from ‘Ānuenue Street. In summer, the NightBlooming Cereus (atop the lava wall) put on a glorious display.

After Cooper Road, follow the lava wall to the Mānoa Heritage Center. This interesting lichen-encrusted lava wall, which extends up and around to Mānoa Road, at one time surrounded only the 1911 house and the heiau at the Mānoa Heritage Center.

stops.title: Mānoa Heritage Center at 2856 O‘ahu Avenue

blocks.text: Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau

You have arrived at a Wahi Pana, a sacred place, certainly one of the most important places in Mānoa Valley: the Mānoa Heritage Center, where you will be able to visit the only restored heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī.
Please make reservations for a tour in advance (open some Saturdays; closed Sundays) manoaheritagecenter.org or call 808-988-1287.
If you are taking the 5 bus here, there are two bus stops for Mānoa Heritage Center One bus stop at Ānuenue Street; another, just past the center. Ask the bus driver.

Two buses take you out of the valley: the 5 and 6. The 5 runs along O‘ahu Avenue, then out makai on Mānoa Road. The 6 runs along E. Mānoa Road, a few blocks Diamond Head, which you can catch after a side trip to Mānoa Marketplace (Stop 36A ).
Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau is the only intact reconstructed heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī.

Mānoa Heritage Center, opened in 1996, is the gem of Mānoa: the center contains the only reconstructed intact heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī, Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau, which can be translated several ways, depending on the spelling variations with the ‘okina (glottal stop) and kahakō (macron indicating a long vowel):
Kūka‘ō‘ō – Kū (Hawaiian deity) of the digging stick (ka ‘ō‘ō)
– the digging stick (ka ‘ō‘ō) stands upright (kū)
Kūkao‘o – Kū (Hawaiian deity) of mature growth (ka o‘o)
– attainment of maturity Regardless of the actual meaning, the importance of the name is that it involves agricultural concepts, as this was a heiau dedicated to rain, fertility, and agriculture.

Pu‘u Kākea, which towers above the Center, produced lava approximately 70,000 years ago that flowed down into the valley resulting in the floor of Mānoa Valley. The lava flow pushed Mānoa Stream to the Diamond Head side of the valley over to the other side of the University of Hawai‘i. The lower edge of the flow created the beautiful lava that was dug out at the Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, now the lower campus. The 50-foot-high wall, separating the lower campus from the upper campus is visible from the parking structure (Lower Campus Walk XII).

There are several other heiau in Mānoa Valley, but none as accessible or recognizable; in some places only centuries-old lava boulders strewn about stand testimony to heiau of the past. A former heiau, still visible, but not rebuilt or reconstructed, is located at Kamānele Park (Stop 51 ), which you will walk past on your way out of the valley.

The Cooke house, Kūali‘i, designed by Emory and Webb, was built in 1911 with on-site lava stones. The heiau, Kūka‘ō‘ō,was built hundreds of years before, but lovingly restored by Billy Fields in 1994 with the dry-stack method – no mortar among the stones!
Charles M. Cooke Sr. and Anna Rice Cooke presented this property to their son, Charles Montague “Monte” Cooke Jr. and his wife, Lila Lefferts Cooke, as a wedding present in 1901.

Although a member of the founding family for Castle and Cooke, Monte, did not follow in the footsteps of his father and most of his siblings. As a well-known Malacologist, he was a curator at the Bishop Museum. Monte passed away in 1948 and Lila lived at Kūali‘i until her death in 1970.
Sam (1937-2015) and Mary Cooke (19362022), the last residents, lovingly restored the area with the intention of presenting the house as a historic house museum as part of Mānoa Heritage Center.
Follow the purple line on the map to Mānoa marketplace, if you are interested.
At the end of the lava wall, on the mauka side of Mānoa Heritage Center is a Ronald McDonald House.

If, after visiting Mānoa Heritage Center, you would like to return to your starting place, consider a side trip to our local shopping center, Mānoa Marketplace (next stop), and then take a bus out of the Valley. If not, continue to the Chinese Cemetery (Stops 37-41 ) or Mānoa Falls (Stops 37-39, then 42 )/ Lyon Arboretum (Stops 37-39, then 43 ).
This intersection was the turnaround point for the Mānoa streetcar/trolley, which ran until 1933.
Another Exceptional Tree - on Ānuenue Street – is an Olive tree, this time. The lawn also proudly supports a “Certified Wildlife Habitat” garden (nwf.org).

From Ānuenue Street, walk mauka on Kahawai (‘stream, ditch’) Street –where there are great views of the valley mountains – then turn Diamond Head on Huapala (‘ornamental vine; sweetheart; pretty’) Street, directly to Mānoa Marketplace on E. Mānoa Road with loads of stores and restaurants.
36A Mānoa Marketplace “The Village”

On the mauka -‘Ewa corner of E. Mānoa Road and Huapala Street you will pass a lovely 1930s building that is often featured in Japanese magazines; hence, the frequent photo ops by our visitors from Japan.

Across E. Mānoa Road, you’ll see the Safeway façade of sandstone blocks. The Bottle Brush and Monkey Pod trees provide welcomed shade. At one point the fate of these gorgeous Monkey Pod trees was in balance: the owners of the marketplace wanted to cut down the Monkey Pod trees because of the roots popping up in the parking areas and the shedding of the flowers and leaves; however, thanks to neighborhood outcry, the trees survived! Here’s to Neighborhood Power!

Check out the website and you’ll see the great variety of stores: manoamarketplacehawaii.com/ Once, just a few stores and known as “The Village,” the shopping area has mushroomed into several dozen stores and services, including a pre-school, doctors, and banks. Mānoa Marketplace opened to Mānoa Valley residents and community in 1961.

Follow the purple line on the map for a side trip. Walk makai-‘Ewa on E. Mānoa Road to a few interesting places. This area was once owned by Queen Lili‘uokanlani! Today we see a theater, banks, stores, and schools.
36B Hawaiian Cemetery Mānoa Valley Theater

Mānoa Valley Theater is a half block makai of Mānoa Marketplace on E. Mānoa Road. Mānoa Church was established here – as evidenced by the tombstones, many engraved in Hawaiian –only to be replaced by a theater in 1987. Dating back to 1823, there are only 37 headstones in the cemetery; however, there are over 100 burial plots, some marked with natural features known only to the family. Descendants of the Woolsey family (of Woolsey Poi Factory fame), a local This often-photographed corner is our local gathering place.
Hawaiian family, are buried on the makai side of the entrance walkway. The original sign to the factory is still visible on O‘ahu Avenue (Stop 37 ).
Reminders of the church include not only the graveyard, but also the lava wall, pillars at the entryway, and the lava rock belfry, which is rung to alert theatergoers.
Ceramic Mural
Just past the theater, the ceramic mural outside Bank of Hawai‘i is interesting: does it depict Mānoa Falls or a giraffe, which is how some children interpret this artwork!
Toyo’s Superette

The row of stores, mainly restaurants, on the corner of Keama Place, was the home – for 80 years – of our local market: Toyo’s, from 1918 to 1998. Keama translates as ‘the outrigger float.’ Theh street is named for two kalo famers, Noah and James Keama.
Japanese Language School building

Across the way, the long grey building is the Japanese Language School, which is established in one of the former Mānoa Elementary School buildings when the elementary school moved near Mānoa Valley District Park in 1952.
From this point, you can take the 6 bus back into town or skip to Stop 44 or 45 and walk out of the Valley.
Or to go to the Chinese Cemetery, Mānoa Falls, and Lyon Arboretum, continue with Stop 37 .
Kawapopo Heiau Woolsey Poi Factory Ka‘aipū Dairy
Across from Mānoa Heritage Center is Koganji Temple, in honor of the Jizo Bodhissattva. It was dedicated in 1981 after expanding to the street below.
Kawapopo Heiau reigned supreme on this hillock. Remnants of those sacred stones are lovingly, but inaccessibly, protected under a shed behind the temple.
This gate was the entryway to the Woolsey Poi Factory.
Pass Ka‘aipū Avenue (see Stop 39 for an interesting rendition of the street name.)
Stop here for a few moments and look at the beauty and majesty of the Ko‘olau mountains around you.
Just after Ka‘aipū Avenue, on the Diamond Head side of O‘ahu Avenue, a tall hedge of slender Palm trees partially covers the sign:

WOOL E This was the entrance to the Woolsey Poi Factory that was destroyed by a storm in the spring of 1923. Water, rocks, and mud came flying and tumbling down the mountainside, destroying the Woolseys’ kalo fields and factory.
Up in the hills, was the residence of the Montano family, the proprietors of Ka‘aipū Dairy.
The intersection of O’ahu Avenue, E. Mānoa Road, and Lowrey Avenue

At the ‘Ewa corner of O‘ahu Avenue and Mānoa Road are two interesting small structures long abandoned by a utility company, but recently lovingly restored as housing. These two streets also intersect with Lowrey Avenue, named for Frederick Dwight Lowrey (1885-1970), a local businessman, Director of the Bank of Hawai‘i , Trustee at Punahou School, and Territorial Representative. However, more importantly, this is the area that had an abundance of lo‘i kalo (taro fields).

In this area, approximately 70,000 years ago, lava from the mountains on the ‘Ewa side, pushed Mānoa Stream to the other side of the valley! That is why the stream that begins on the west side of the valley is now on the east side of the valley, behind the University of Hawai‘i .
Puka‘ōma‘o Ka‘aipū

If you would like to take a break from walking along O‘ahu Avenue, you can drop in at the Wai‘oli (‘joyful water’) Kitchen and Bake Shop (affectionately known as Wai‘oli Tea Room) , mauka-‘Ewa of the intersection at O’ahu Avenue and Mānoa Road.
Open Tuesday through Saturday 8 to 1. www.waiolikitchen.com or call 808-744-1619.
Wai‘oli Tea Room was opened in 1922 as part of the Salvation Army as vocational Wai‘oli Kitchen and Bake Shop is lovingly known as Wai‘oli Tea Room to locals.

1898 photo - Mānoa residence of the Montano family, owners of Ka‘aipū Dairy. (Hawai‘i State Archives) training for orphaned girls. Today they “hire individuals who have successfully completed post-incarceration treatment programs.” Wai‘oli is a haven for them.
Kamehameha III’s country home was nestled here among the greenery. Kamehameha III, often considered the most influential leader after Kamehameha the Great, ruled from 1825 to 1854.

Somewhere in the mountains above the Wai‘oli Kitchen and Bake shop was the valley residence of Queen Ka‘ahumanu, King Kamehameha I‘s favorite wife. Queen Ka‘ahumanu was kuhina nui (co-regent) with King Kamehameha II and Kamehameha III, after King Kamehameha I died in 1819. Queen Ka‘ahumanu, along with Kamehameha II and Keōpūolani (King Kamehameha I’s sacred wife), broke the ‘ai kapu – the eating prohibitions of forbidden foods and improper gender mingling while eating.
You are in the ‘ili of Ka‘aipū, which translates as ‘the eating together,’.

Ka‘aipū Avenue (Stop 37 ), is a reminder of the ‘ai noa, the ‘free eating’ associated with Queen Ka‘ahumanu. Furthermore, Manoa (without the kahakō on the first ‘a’) could be translated as ‘freed of taboo, released from restrictions’ (trussel2.com) and ‘ma’ as location, ‘in, on, at.’

Puka‘ōma‘oma‘o is the name of the ‘ili (district) here. Queen Ka‘ahumanu’s house, Puka‘ōma‘o / Puka‘ōma‘oma‘o ‘green opening’ (puka also means ‘hole’) had green shutters. The house was located on Pu‘uluahine ‘hill of the old woman’ who moved here with her two sons who were turned into stones; she was turned into the hill. Queen Ka‘ahumanu’s bathing place, Kuwaiho‘olana (‘the water causes one to float’) was where she floated in a spring of fresh water. Huelani, a street mauka of the Wai‘oli Kitchen and Bake Shop, translates as ‘royal gourd’ that referred to the well used by Queen Ka‘ahumanu. This is the place Ka‘ahumanu came to die on June 5, 1832.
Queen Ka‘ahumanu came back to her home in the hills of Mānoa to die. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
Mānoa Valley, across the plains to the Ko‘olau mountains, veiled in the fine rain of Ua Tuahine. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
The name Ka‘aipū has a strong historic significance in the lives of the Hawaiians.
There are two areas of Mānoa Valley: the west side, known as the ali‘i (chief) part and the east side, for the or kanaka (commoners).
MĀNOA RAINS
The most incredible aspect of Mānoa Valley is its rain: the Ua Tuahine, found nowhere else.

I have, personally, seen and felt this rain: on my frequent walks in the valley, I would often see this phenomenon: Ua Tuahine coming across the valley floor with the rain from the ali‘i or ‘Ewa side on only one of my arms as the rain starts to drift to the kanaka or Diamond Head side.

Tuahine alternates with Kuahine in the mo‘olelo (legend) about Kahalaopuna - Mo‘olelo o Kahalaopuna - who was repeatedly killed by her jealous husband, Kauhi. In the mo‘olelo, Tuahine/Kuahine is either Kahalaopuna’s mother or sister who turn into the Ua (‘rain’) Tuahine mist rain found only in Mānoa. The male counterpart became the wind Kahaukāne, pushing Ua Tuahine. Kahalaopuna is manifested as the Mānoa rainbows. Kahalaopuna is also known as ‘the beauty of Mānoa.’ There are many mo‘olelo about Kahalaopuna and Kauhi.

In the depression of the easterly ridge is a grove (12) of magnificent Mexican Cohune Nut Palms planted by Dr. George F. Straub, who started Straub (“Straub Clinic”) Medical Center in 1921. They are listed as Exceptional Trees, trees that are culturally and historically significant.

Another mo‘olelo emphasizes other Mānoa mountain features. The Beauty of Mānoa, Kahalaopuna was born to Kahaukani (variant spellings), the wind of Mānoa and Kauakuahine (also Tuahine), the rain of Mānoa. Kahaukani and Kauakuahine were brother and sister, born to ‘Akāka (clearness), the projecting spur of the Mānoa mountain range, and Nālehua‘akāka, ‘the Lehua flowers on the brow of the Mānoa ridge.’
A variant Kahalaopuna mo‘olelo is written up at the Mānoa Heritage Center.
Other Kahalaopuna mo‘olelo are displayed at our two local elementary schools, Mānoa and Noelani.

From O‘ahu Avenue, cross (carefully!) Lowrey Avenue to Mānoa Road. Notice that there are sidewalks here, thanks to a 1965 rewidening and straightening of the street. Local legend claims that the rewidening was in anticipation of a tunnel through the Ko‘olau to the other side!
Continue walking along Mānoa Road until you come to the park, when you need to decide where you want to go to next: Chinese Cemetery (Stops 40-41 ) Mānoa Falls (Stop 42 ) Lyon Arboretum (Stop 43 )
If you would like to visit Mānoa Falls or Lyon Arboretum (you need a reservation for the Arboretum 808-988-0456 or go to Eventbrite), continue past Mānoa Val-
According to a modern mo‘olelo, the mountains in the eastern side of the Ko‘olau Mountains form a profile of a face. Notice the Palm tree grove under the dip between the hills.
ley District Park and Mānoa Elementary School for another mile to the entrance for both Lyon Arboretum and Mānoa Falls. Then continue with Stops 42 and 43 , below.
Or take a bus at the sheltered bus stop in front of the school (and the steps).

If you would like to go directly to the Chinese Cemetery follow the orange dotted line., continue on the Diamond Head side of Mānoa Road, past Mānoa Valley District Park, past the sign to the park, the parking lot, and the bus shelter with the steps to the school.

At Olopua -a native hardwood tree – Street and the welcome sign to the school, turn Diamond Head at the street behind Mānoa Elementary School (Home of the Tigers – their mascot. The only non-human tigers in Hawai‘i are at the zoo.).

Enjoy the Rainbow Shower trees, which were crossbred in Hawai‘i. Mānoa Elementary School was established in 1854 originally on E. Mānoa Road near the fire station. It was one of the first English speaking schools in Hawai‘i.

Follow the street Diamond Head, snaking behind the school, toward the ballfields to the small parking lot lined with Monkey Pod trees. Continue in the shade of the trees, past the lovingly tended Mānoa Community Garden.
Mānoa Gardens, next to the community gardens, are the charming 2-story pastelcolored buildings that serve as senior citizen residential housing units near Mānoa Stream.
What a great, unobstructed view of the mountains!
Notice the miniature amphitheater on the ‘Ewa side of Mānoa Stream before crossing over to E. Mānoa Road. Sit for a while, relax, enjoy the peace of this place under the Monkey Pod and Hala trees.
There are so many place to visit at the Chinese Cemetary.
Cross Mānoa Stream at the 1954 bridge

at Kahaloa Drive. Kahaloa, which means ‘long or eternal breath,’ is the name of the ‘ili (district within the ahupua‘a). However, there are two other important possibilities: one, is the name of a chief ’s wife who lived here; the other, named for Hāloa, the first Hawaiian man who, because of his birth, was responsible for the kalo plant. This last explanation is most likely since this is the place where kalo grew abundantly. Kahaloa is also the name of one of the 4 Kāhuna in Waikīkī –be sure to take the Waikīkī Walk III in Helumoa for more information.
Walk to the traffic lights, turn mauka. It’s less than a half-mile along E. Mānoa Road to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery.

Over 10 acres with 10,000 burials, The Mānoa Chinese Cemetery, formally, Lin Yee Chung Cemetery, which means ‘united in righteousness,’ was established in 1852. It is the largest and oldest Chinese cemetery in Hawai‘i.

At the entrance you will be greeted by 2 sets of lions: one pair of granite; the other of marble. The lions are placed there specifically to guard the spirits of the ancestors in the cemetery. Many other lions roam the grounds (inanimate ones). Visitors leave tokens of coins, small meaningful objects, and even candy!

These guardian lions share the entrance with a statue of Qin Shihuangdi (aka Qin Shi Huang), China’s first emperor of the third century BCE, who after unifying China, initiated the building of the Great Wall of China and his tomb of terra cotta army. This is a traditional Chinese cemetery in that the headstones are upright stones in rows facing a body of water. The oldest part of the cemetery is mauka and ‘Ewa, with many headstones falling down or even crumbling.

A plaque next to the statue of the emperor commemorates (or perhaps memorializes, since this is a cemetery) the Sandalwood trade from China to Hawai‘i , hence the former moniker for Hawai‘i , “Sandalwood Mountains” or “Tahn Heong Sahn,” in Chinese. Sadly, Sandalwood, ‘iliahi, was sorely depleted by the 1840s, but now is being reintroduced on Hawai‘i Island.

Interestingly, in 1826, a sandalwood tax was the kingdom’s first written law: every man was obliged to deliver a minimum amount of sandalwood to his district governor or pay a certain amount of equivalent money! Queen Ka‘ahumanu , a devout Christian, fined Chief Boki 80 piculs of sandalwood for adultery and drunkenness! A picul, used as a measurement of weight by the Chinese, corresponds to 133 pounds.
Up on the hill, a white, green, and red Chinese monument is encircled with white marble zodiac animals and other fantastic animals including dragon horses. Take a photo next to your sign.
Be sure to locate the Boddhisatva sculpture at the top of the cemetery hill and the Grand Ancestor’s Tomb.
To leave the Valley from the Chinese Cemetery, walk makai the way you came, but continue along E. Mānoa Road and cross Lowrey Avenue.
OR take a bus (6) out of the valley! Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 (option 2 for a live operator)

After crossing Lowrey Avenue, you will go across Mānoa Stream at the 1950 bridge. Approximately 70,000 years ago, lava flowed down from the ‘Ewa side of the valley and pushed the stream from the west side to the east to form this stream course. After the bridge, continue makai to Mānoa Marketplace (Stops 36A and 44 ).

If you would like to visit Mānoa Falls or Lyon Arboretum (you need a reservation for the Arboretum: 808-988-0456 or go to Eventbrite), continue past Mānoa Valley District Park and Mānoa Elementary School for another mile to the street en trance for both Lyon Arboretum and Mānoa Falls.

Alternatively, hop on the bus (number 5) at the sheltered bus stop just before Mānoa Elementary School for a quick 2 minute ride to the street entrance of the Falls/ Arboretum Both places are quintessential Hawaiian places: way back on the ali‘i side of the valley in the forest of Mānoa Valley. Feel the mountains embracing you as you walk further and further back into the valley!

Some of the houses are newer; interestingly, the houses on the Diamond Head side of Mānoa Road are lower – the ground slopes to Mānoa Stream. Most houses date to the 1920s and 30s. Some of the older houses are listed on the Historic Register. Look for the plaque.
As you continue back into the valley, you will cross these interestingly named streets:

• Olopua - a native hardwood tree – Street • Halelani – heavenly house – Drive • Pāwaina – vineyard – Street • Poelua – 2 nights or fighting people – Street Just mauka-Diamond Head you can see Mānoa Chinese Cemetery.
• Peneku – longtime resident – Place • O‘ahu/Pāwaina – these two streets form a broken oval; Pāwaina, in the direction of Diamond Head leads to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery.
• Nipo– desire; drowsy – Street A group of men planning their next hike in Mānoa Valley. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
• Kumuone – sandstone, sandbank – Street This is the bus stop for the 5 bus to Ala Moana Center and the bus route makai to Ala Moana Center.

• Wa‘akaua –war canoe or army formation – Street. This street leads to a gated community. (Wa‘akaua Street crosses Waihī Stream one block Diamond Head, which then joins Lua‘alaea Stream to form Mānoa Stream, all on private property.)

On the road into Lyon Arboretum/Mānoa Falls, you will pass the 76-acre Paradise Park (1968-1994), a former botanical and zoological garden on private conservation land. There was even a charter school for a few years. Treetops Restaurant, which was lovingly run by Martin Lee for 18 years, was a nature-gustatory treat tucked away in this forest.

Paradise Park, carefully tended to by Napualani and Warren Wong is a welcome resting place to buy some gifts (nā makana), snacks, find the restrooms, and enjoy the paintings, and historic photos on the walls.
Mānoa Falls

Interestingly, Mānoa Falls is not on Mānoa Stream, but rather on Waihī (‘trickling water’) Stream, which flows into Mānoa Stream after it leaves the forest. ‘Aihualama Stream, which flows through Lyon Arboretum, unites with Waihī Stream, which then joins Lua‘alaea (‘pit of red earth’) Stream, to form Mānoa Stream. Mānoa Stream meets up with Pālolo Stream about 3 miles from here. Together they become the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal (not a very picturesque name) to the Ala Wai Canal, then to the ocean at the Ala Wai Harbor, near Ala Moana Center.

Mānoa Falls Trail, which leads to its 150foot waterfall, is sometimes too wet and hazardous to hike, so the trail is occasionally closed. Due to possible infection by the bacteria, Leptospira, which causes leptospirosis, swimming is not allowed. However, the walk is beautiful and should be cherished.
The arboretum is in the ‘ili of Haukulu ‘dipping dew’ and was originally the property of Kana‘ina, the father of King Lunalilo.

Lyon Arboretum, ‘Ewa of Mānoa Falls Trail, is open by appointment to walk and hike to their waterfall, ‘Aihualama Falls, which is on ‘Aihualama Stream. Lyon Arboretum is a 193-acre public botanic garden affiliated with the University of Hawai‘i .

It was first established by the Hawaiian Sugar Planters Association as Mānoa Arboretum in 1918. The area was transferred to the University of Hawai‘i in 1953 when it was named for its first director Dr. Harold One of many waterfalls in Mānoa Valley – only 5 miles from Waikīkī Beach! (Hawai‘i State Archives)

L. Lyon, a plant pathologist who understood and encouraged the importance of history and conservation. The scientists who work there today continue his interests and work to save rare and endangered plants. The average annual rainfall back in this part of the valley is 165 inches – bring a rain poncho!
The Lyon Arboretum Trail guide welcomes visitors with the description:

“The Lyon Arboretum will be the destination for all those seeking an intimate understanding and appreciation of tropical systems, knowledge of the traditional uses of the land, and a celebration of the intersection of biological and cultural diversity.”
Ask for the activity book for children to learn more about plants and birds of the arboretum. The booklet also contains various scavenger hunts.
Once you leave the forest, walk back on Mānoa Road or look for the number 5 bus near Wa‘akaua (‘war canoe’ or ‘army formation’) Street.
The Pen

In January of 1895, 2 years after the overthrow of Queen Lili‘uokalani’s realm, several supporters of the Queen headed by Lot Lane, Samuel Nowlein, and Robert Wilcox known as the Royalists, attempted to restore her to the throne. The conflict began at the foot of Lē‘ahi at today’s Sans Souci Beach, came up into Mō‘ili‘ili but as thing got worse, moved into the Mānoa mountains in an area known as The Pen. The Pen was beyond today’s Lyon Arboretum near ‘Aihualama Stream. Nothing remains of this rebellion.
A statue of the Garibaldi-inspired Robert Wilcox is erected at the foot of Fort Street Mall in downtown Honolulu. (The Mo’ili‘ili Walk, Stop 18 refers to this event.)
43A Alternate walk to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery and to Mānoa Marketplace from Mānoa Falls or Lyon Arboretum Follow the purple line on the map for an alternate walk to Manoa Chinese Cemetery
Revolution of 1895 in the hills of Mānoa. (Hawai‘i State Archives)
to walk out of the valley from Mānoa Falls or Lyon Arboretum, walk makai on Mānoa Road to Pāwaina Street, where you will
turn Diamond Head. This is also the route both to Mānoa Marketplace as well as the back route to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery.
OR take bus #5 from the stop on Mānoa Road at Kumuone Street.
Bus routes and time: www.thebus.org Or call 808-848-5555 (option 2 for a live operator)
To walk to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery from Mānoa Falls or Lyon Arboretum, turn Diamond Head on Pāwaina – vineyard - Street (the street across from O’ahu Avenue) crossing the 1961 bridge at Mānoa Stream.
You will pass Pinao – dragonfly - Street.
Notice that the houses are newer here (1960s).
Continue on Pāwaina Street as it curves makai-Diamond Head around to Pakanu ‘garden, planting field’ Street, the street that leads to Mānoa Chinese Cemetery and E. Mānoa Road.
After visiting the cemetery (Stop 41 ), you can walk out on E. Mānoa Road:
Along E. Mānoa road you will pass streets associated with the kalo fields that once were abundant here. Also notice the long driveway on the ‘Ewa side leading down to Mānoa Stream.
• Pakanu – garden, planting field – Street (borders the cemetery)

• Kolomona – native shrub – Place • Kinohou –new body, beginning, first – Place • Ka‘amali‘o Drive is miswritten: it should be Kāma’alio, “horseshoe,” as in the shape of the street and, therefore, crosses the stream twice!

• Napua‘a –the pigs - Place • Mānoa Stream Ditch with a 1938 bridge • Kahāloa Drive (On the Diamond Head side, steps lead up to Alani and Paty Drives; on the ‘Ewa side, the road leads to Mānoa Valley District Park). Hāloa is the ancestor of the Hawaiian people that established the connection of kalo to the Hawaiian people. In the mo‘olelo of the Hawaiian people, Hāloa is considered to be the firstborn who when planted became the kalo plant.
• Lo‘i Street (named for the many kalo fields in the area.) Kalo‘aluiki (a deity of the lo‘i) Street is a block mauka.

• Kahewai –flowing water – Place • Lowrey –Frederick Lowrey was a representative to the Territory of Hawai‘i in the 1920s – Avenue • Ono Road (ono is a type of fish as well as the number 6; ‘ono means ‘tasty, delicious’)
of Hawai‘i
(Check out Stop 36A for more information about Mānoa Marketplace and the area along E. Mānoa Road.)
Take a break at our newly renovated Mānoa Marketplace on E. Mānoa Road where you will find stores and restaurants, and a new keiki play structure! Look for our two anchor stores: Longs and Safeway.
Come to our Farmers’ Market of local produce on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays from 8 to 2.
During the 15 years after World War Two, this area, as well as Noelani Elementary School’s location, was the base for 1,000 families in the community of Mānoa War Homes.
Enjoy the marketplace, then continue on a delightful walk out of the valley along Woodlawn Drive and Kolowalu Street.

Informally known as the Mauka Campus, the University of Hawai‘i has several buildings spread out on both sides of the street. The Mānoa Innovation Center (on the mauka side of Mānoa Stream), the newest of the building, houses several university research offices.
The University of Hawai‘i’s Department of Tropical Plant and Soil Sciences across the way is a research center for its Tropical Green Roof and Living Wall.

Along the ‘Ewa-mauka side of Woodlawn Drive you will pass the 2012 Energy Efficient LEED Certified Mānoa Library – stop in and browse through their Hawaiiana section. Enjoy the planting in front: Palm, Hala, and Kou trees, and lots of Hibiscus flowers. Breathe in the scent of the White Hibiscus – if it has a sweet fragrance, it is native. Enjoy!

The University of Hawai‘i Institute for Astronomy is based here, but a great deal of data gathering for research takes place on Hawai‘i Island and at Haleakalā on Maui. If the courtyard is open, enjoy the play of light and rainbows from the prisms (over 150!) on the mauka wall, representing the star field of the Pleiades/Subaru (in Japanese)/ the Seven Sisters/ Makali‘i in Hawaiian, which (in October or November) signals the beginning of winter and the Makahiki season of peace and new year.

Outside, in front, there is a unique tree, a Koa tree - found only in Hawai‘i and nowhere else. Here is it a small tree (smaller than the surrounding flowering trees) with crescent shaped leaves; in the mountains, it grows tall and straight.
Continue makai-‘Ewa along Woodlawn Drive, which changes to Kolowalu Street after Noelani (‘mist of heaven’) Elementary

School. The school is part of the State system, not the university. Notice the geckos - the school mascot - all over the buildings and signs. See if you can find a gecko – real or artwork. If it is not a school day, read an alternate Kahalaopuna story outside the main office building. It is a variation on the mo‘olelo you read earlier.
At the end of this street, on the makai side, two ‘ili meet: Kolowalu and Pamoa.

Kolowalu, the name of the ‘ili (district) in this area, signifies an ancient Hawaiian law Noelani Elementary School greets its students each day with a welcome: E Komo Mai! The children enjoy the ‘mist of heaven.’
Over 150 prisms can create over 150 rainbows on this wall! that obliged farmers and fishermen to feed the hungry in their district.
And Pāmoa (‘chicken enclosure’) Road; there still are a lot of chickens running around here - I guess the enclosure didn’t work!

As you round the corner of Kolowalu Street toward E. Mānoa Road you will pass the University of Hawai‘i Press, which publishes first class academic books and journals. Its motto is “Bringing the world books on Asia, Hawai‘i , and the Pacific.”
Cross Pāmoa Road, then turn makai on E. Mānoa Road past a home with a Historic

Residence plaque. There is another Historic Residence on University Avenue. Pāmoa Road takes you to a back (fire) entrance for the University of Hawai‘i , to the Energy House of the 1970s as well as to the campus of the (former) St. Francis School, which closed in 2019. (Upper Campus Walk XI) This is the site of another heiau – Hipawai (‘water foolishness!’) –that has been converted to a wall.

Up the hill, where E. Mānoa Road curves, across from a 10-foot lava block wall, notice an unusual house with a metal Westeel wheel, in its former life a gear at a sugar mill now a garden decoration, and former lava curbstones installed in the driveway.

At the intersection of E. Manoa Road and O‘ahu Avenue, at the over-arching Monkey Pod tree, turn makai-Diamond Head for one block. Cross Alaula (‘early dawn light’) Way – very carefully – to University Avenue. (Do you recognize this corner? Across the way, you walked mauka on O‘ahu Avenue into the Valley.)
Continue along University Avenue on the grassy sidewalk, which leads to the University of Hawai‘i, leaving the glorious mountains behind you.
Originally known as Vancouver Drive on early maps, University Avenue runs from the Ala Wai Canal to this intersection.

After Alaula Way is Armstrong Street, the back entrance to Mid-Pacific Institute. The house closest to the school is the Guard residence erected in 1939 for the Guard family but is known as the Armstrong Manor.

The lava basalt building inside the fence, Kawaiaha‘o Hall built in 1908 –the year the school was established from in-situ lava stone –is one of the oldest school buildings in Hawai‘i in continuous use.

There are some lovely homes on University Avenue. The 1902 home at 2375 University Avenue is particularly interesting with its name “Ho‘oluana” on the lintel, meaning ‘to live in comfort and ease.’ The home of Janet Taylor MacIntyre, a businesswoman of the 1920s, was one of the first homes in the development of College Hills. “ College” referred to Punahou, which was then known as O‘ahu College, not to the University of Hawai‘i.
You will pass Halele‘a – ‘happy house’ – Place!

At the corner of Ka‘ala Street and University Avenue is Kamānele Park, where President Barack Obama played. Well, I’m not positive about that, but he lived across the street when he was a little boy while his mother attended the University of Hawai‘i. Kamānele Park was dedicated in 1915 with Queen Lili‘uokalani, who passed away 2 years later, in attendance. It was named in honor of chiefess Mele Kamānele, the daughter of John Adams Kuakini, advisor to King Kamehameha the Great. Mele, who lived nearby and was betrothed to King Kamehameha III, died at the age of 20. A local mo‘olelo relates that Kahalaopuna of rainbow fame resided here.
Kamānele Park is most interesting archeologically: a heiau entwined with the Banyan tree has recently been revealed. It is lovingly cared for by Mālama Mānoa, Outdoor Circle, OASES, and friends.
Continue makai along University Avenue.

Mid-Pacific Institute, a pre-K through high school private school, is located next to Kamānele Park. Of interest on campus is Wailele Spring, a natural spring thanks to the mountain streams. Wailele is the name of this ‘ili (district).

The next street, Maile (a type of vine that flourishes in the mountains) Way, is the mauka extent of the University of Hawai‘i . Maile Way may have been named after another heiau in the area, Kauwalomaile.
Follow the University of Hawai‘i Campus Walk XI, if you are interested.
Or hop on the bus – 13 or 6. Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 (option 2)
Bus stops: • Number 13 bus stop: makai-Diamond Head on Maile Way • Number 6 bus stop: makai-‘Ewa on University Avenue Mānoa Valley 1890 (Hawai‘i State Archives)
