The University of Hawai‘i, nestled in the beauty of Mānoa Valley, is home to approximately 20,000 students, from every island in Hawai‘i, every state in the union, and over 100 countries.

The University of Hawai‘i is in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. Within the ahupua‘a, the university is located across several ‘ili (smaller land sections), Pa‘akea, Kānewai, Puahia, Wailele, Kauwala‘a, but especially in the largest, Pilipili, where we begin.
Early morning is the best time to take this walk. Please be sure to take along a hat and water.

Mānoa Stream runs along the back (Diamond Head side) of the campus; you may not even know that the stream is there. Unfortunately, there’s no good viewing point from campus. However, you can get up close on the lower campus walk (XII) at the Center for Hawaiian Studies on Dole Street.
This is a combination art, botanical, and history walking tour of the University of Hawai‘i campus.

From Waikīkī there are several ways to walk to the University of Hawai‘i campus: up Kapahulu Avenue on the east, then up University Avenue from Kapi‘olani Boulevard or S. King Street; or up McCully on the west side of Waikīkī. This walk to the campus of the University of Hawai‘i takes you mauka on McCully Street, Diamond Head on Dole Street, then mauka on University Avenue to the center of campus.
The walk starts at McCully Street and the Ala Wai Canal but can be begun at Dole Street and University Avenue at Stop 7 .

title: University of Hawai‘i

intro.text: Mall at the University of Hawai‘i Street is named for Lawrence McCully, a Justice of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i Supreme Court under King Kalākaua. He was also involved in the development of the Punahou area, which you will walk past in a mile after you cross over the freeway.

info: B a c k t o c o l l e g e ! Parking: Street parking on Date Street – free except for afternoons Monday through Friday Parking lot across from the Hale Koa Hotel on Kālia Road. Street parking on Dole Street on the weekends Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 – for a live operator. There are several buses that will take you directly to the UH campus A, 4, 13, 6, 18. Get off at Sinclair Circle, a sheltered bus stop.

blocks.text: For an interesting stroll on the lower/makai campus of the University of Hawai‘i, walk to the Diamond Head end of the Ala Wai Canal, and proceed mauka along Kapahulu Avenue.

2 hours; 3 miles; 5,000 steps Street parking along Date Street – free, but no parking 3:30-6:30 Monday through Friday. Parking lot at the Zoo or at Monsarrat and Paki avenues. Street parking along Dole Street Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 - option 2 for a live operator.

Cross over the canal on the Diamond Head side and you might catch a crew in their outrigger canoes. If not, at least admire the sleek canoes and their attached outriggers. This area is the home of the Ala Wai Community Park. If this area interests you, take a walk around the Ala Wai Canal, Walk I.

The first intersection after the canal is Kapi‘olani Boulevard, a major west-east thoroughfare. Queen Kapi‘olani ruled with King Kalākaua from 1874 to 1891; King Kalākaua died of a stroke while traveling in California. Lili‘uokalani became queen upon his death.
Across Kapi‘olani Boulevard is Judd Park, provided by the Judd family.

Continue along McCully Street, noticing and admiring the small garden apartment buildings, houses, and local atmosphere. You will be passing though the neighborhoods of McCully (‘Ewa side) and Mō‘ili‘ili (Diamond Head side). Lime Street is the first of many streets in the area named after trees and plants; Fern, although it is a plant, is said to be named after George Fern, the brother of Honolulu’s first mayor, Joseph Fern.
At the corner of McCully and Algaroba streets a large wooden fence is decorated with geckos and a history of Mō‘ili‘ili. (For more information, read Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX).

Caption: The College of Hawai‘i, as it was known in 1917, 5 years after moving to Mānoa. Notice all the surrounding agricultural fields and the University Farm, fittingly since the school was founded as an agricultural college. Facing ‘Ewa, Hawai‘i Hall, built in 1912, is without steps! (University Archives)
Judge Lawrence McCully (1831 - 1892) meets Queen Kapi‘olani (1834 – 1899)!

Algaroba, also known as Kiawe and Mesquite, is a tree that is native to South America; the first Algaroba tree was brought to Hawai‘i from Paris by Father Alexis Bachelot (1796-1837), who was not only the first Catholic priest in Hawai‘i as part of the Catholic missionary group, but is also responsible for bringing the Kiawe tree to Hawai‘i. The original tree was planted in downtown Honolulu on Fort Street. However, there are no Kiawe trees on this street.
Even if the mural is no longer up, what was posted is still of great interest:
The mural sign states:
The mural is a tribute to much loved Mō‘ili‘ili – the area between ‘Mānoa & Waikīkī’
The region’s history dates back to ancient times with a legendary battle between Pele’s sister Hi‘iaka, and a lizard mo‘o whom she turned into pebbles ‘ili‘ili.
The area is best known for its underground caverns, kalo cultivation, strong Japanese culture, and once being the center of local sports at Honolulu Stadium.
Thank you FOR YOUR KŌKUA IN KEEPING MŌ‘ILI‘ILI Beautiful.

stops.title: S. King and S. Beretania streets

blocks.text: It’s one more block to S. King and S. Beretania streets -the 2 main east-west thoroughfares – after which you will walk over the freeway. After S. Beretania Street, as you cross over to the other side of the freeway, notice the often politically incorrect sign at Hawaiian Rent-All.

The downtown Honolulu portion of the H1 freeway was known as Mauka Arterial in 1953, when it was first built. After Hawai‘i became a state in 1959, it became part of the Interstate system. Several extensions were added over the years.
After walking across the freeway on the
McCully Bridge, turn Diamond Head to walk to the University of Hawai‘i along Dole Street, which parallels the freeway. Notice
the older homes that still exist despite the destruction of many houses in order to build the freeway.
Welcome to Mō‘ili‘ili !
Sometimes inappropriate, but always funny!
On old maps, Kapa‘akea is the original name for Dole Street.

Dole Street is not named for the territorial governor, Sanford Dole; rather for Reverend Daniel Dole, the first teacher and administrator at Punahou School. However, on earlier maps, this street is labeled Kapa‘akea, who was father to King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani. There is a small street by that name in Mō‘ili‘ili. Kapa‘akea can refer to a coral or limestone surface.

At the intersection with Wilder Avenue, cross Dole Street, then Wilder Avenue at the crosswalk (carefully - because the cars are coming fast off the freeway). Continue up Dole Street, cross Ho‘onanea – ‘relax’ – Street, and go past the University of Hawai‘i Children’s Center.

If Dole Street and/or Wilder Avenue are under construction, go back to Metcalf Street and walk mauka-Diamond Head to the university via Metcalf Street on the makai side of the street where there is some semblance of a sidewalk.

The University of Hawai‘i was initially established in 1907 under the Morrill Act as The College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts of the Territory of Hawai‘i. In 1912, when the school moved to Mānoa, it shortened its name to the College of Hawai‘i. In 1920, it was formally recognized as the University of Hawai‘i.
The University of Hawai‘i had its origins downtown, at the makai-Diamond Head corner of Thomas Square (S. Beretania and Victoria streets).

At the corners of University Avenue and Dole Street, you will come to Founders’ Gate - two arches and benches on either side of University Avenue. These two entry arches signify the melding of the two campuses: The University of Hawai‘i and the Normal (Teachers’ College) School in 1931, hence the intertwined UH at the top of the archways.
1923 photo with the mountains of Mānoa in the background. Hawai‘i Hall is dead center. (University Archives)
 The plaque on that site reads:

UNIVERSITY OF HAWAI‘I FOUNDING SITE In 1907, The College of Hawai‘i was founded on a portion of this site to provide advanced educational opportunities to the people of this state. Later moved to Mānoa Valley, the college in 1920 became the University of Hawai‘i, now a statewide system extending the reach of higher education throughout the Hawaiian Islands The bench is inscribed on the Diamond Head side in Hawaiian:
MALUNA A‘E O NĀ LĀHUI APAU KE OLA KE KANAKA The bench on the ‘Ewa side is in English:

ABOVE ALL NATIONS IS HUMANITY This maxim is attributed to Godwin Smith, an Oxford humanities scholar who chaired the English Department at Cornell University. The inscription was originally inscribed on a bench at Cornell University. Why the Cornell connection, you ask. Most of the founders of the University of Hawai‘i, including the university president and professors, were from Cornell University, also a land-grant college, better known as the federally funded 1862 Morrill Act.

The architect of Founders’ Gate, Ralph Fishbourne (1884-1936) also designed Andrews Amphitheater (Stop 37 ), St. Patrick’s Cathedral in Kaimukī (Kaimukī Walk VIII), and McKinley High School in downtown Honolulu.

At Dole Street and University Avenue, search for the Hawaii block at the base of the Diamond Head archway. Interesting story: There were more blocks, one for each state originally slated to line University Avenue, one at each Monkey Pod tree. However, the blocks were so big that they interfered with the underground utilities. As you walk around the campus, you will notice that there are no above ground utilities. 16 blocks mark the side entrances to Hemenway Hall (Stop 42 ).
As you walk mauka on University Avenue, enjoy the shade of the stately Monkey Pod trees.

The College of Education property, which includes a pre-school and the charter University Laboratory School, covers the entire block from Dole Street to Metcalf Street on the ‘Ewa side of University Avenue. The school includes a full academic curriculum from kindergarten through high school. There are several memorable buildings:
“Above all nations is humanity” - the translation - is inscribed on the bench across University Avenue.

• Castle Memorial Hall, near Dole Street, was designed by Mark Potter in 1941, who also planned Bilger Hall, the chemistry building on campus, as well as many homes in the area. Castle Memorial is part of the secured pre-school and is not visitable.

• Wist Hall is the only campus building by C.W. Dickey (1871-1942), the creator of the Hawaiian style double pitched roof – the roof line is angled to align with the breezes and sunlight. Dickey’s home, which he designed in 1926 and lived in, is in Waikīkī. In 1932 he built a more spectacular house on Diamond Head Road. (Both houses can be seen on the Kapua Walk VII)
Benjamin Wist (1889-1951) was the first Dean of Education when the Teachers’ College merged with the university.
• Everly Hall is named after Hubert Everly, Dean of Education from 1956 to 1980.

Both Wist and Everly halls are easily viewed from the Diamond Head side of University Avenue, off Metcalf Street. Many native trees and plants – including Kalo and ‘Ilima plants; Kukui, Kou, and Palm trees – grow on the College of Education campus.
The Tamarind tree on the corner at RISE continues to stand tall thanks to the loving care from the Outdoor Circle.

RISE rises on the mauka-‘Ewa corner of Metcalf Street and University Avenue. RISE – Residences for Innovative Student Entrepreneurs – is “the University of Hawai‘i’s only Live-Learn-Work Community.” RISE, one of the first-of-itskind in America is a University of Hawai‘i center created to foster creative enterprises and innovations among UH students. It houses not only residences, but also classrooms, labs, coworking spaces, and a café! RISE incorporates the former Charles Atherton House. The Atherton House was originally the local YMCA – the pink 1932 building – that housed University of Hawai‘i students of moderate income. The Athertons were long-time residents of Hawai‘i who lived a few blocks mauka on Kamehameha Avenue at what is now the University of Hawai‘i’s President’s House. (Mānoa Valley Walk X)
As you walk Diamond Head from University Avenue, you are entering the ‘ili of Pilipili, perhaps named after a kind of grass that grew here.
1932 photo. Originally Teachers’ College Building (left center, the dark building). It was renamed Wist Hall after Wist’s death. (University Archives)
Atherton House in 1932 – former YMCA, the precursor to RISE. (University Archives)
Turn Diamond Head after Sinclair Student Success Center (former Sinclair Library), the pink brick sandstone building, which might be undergoing renovations. The walk-

way parallels Campus Drive, an extension of Metcalf Street. Theophilus Metcalf was the first professional surveyor for the 1848 Mahele, which divided the land of the ali‘i, ‘royalty.’ Metcalf ’s land extended from here in Pilipili to Kauwala‘a, the area around the Biomedical Sciences Building. Metcalf was father to the fabulous Emma Metcalf Beckley Nakuina, about whom you will learn more when we get to that section of campus (Stop 22 ).
Notice the “Exceptional Trees” - an official destination for trees that are deemed important due to their historic or cultural value - on campus.
The campus plant signs are highly informative. At a glance you can tell if it is native or not:
• The green signs are placed at native to Hawai‘i-only plants and trees.
• The blue signs indicate “canoe” plants and trees, referring to plants and trees that came in canoes with the early Polynesians.
• The brown signs reference trees and plants from elsewhere in the world.
You will see these color-coded signs all over campus.

Although bird watching is not often an urban activity, it is on campus. Aside from the Egret, the large awkwardly walking white birds, be sure not to miss the native White Terns – Manu o Kū (“bird of the deity, Kū”) - the official bird of the City and County of Honolulu. The trees in which they nest are quite noticeable because the trunks are encircled by a blue plastic ribbon “TRIM WITH CAUTION - NESTING WHITE TERNS.” Sure enough, look up, and you will see a Tern sitting on a branch tending to an egg or its chick. These seabirds do not make nests. And when they fly, they are exceptionally graceful. Just wait and watch; they usually fly in 2s and 3s.
Check out www.whiteterns.org

To walk to the “quad,” the original campus buildings, turn mauka after the Rubber tree, walk to the first building, the Architecture Building, into the “quad” area where there are 6 neo-classical style academic buildings.

The Architecture Building is obviously the newest building (1993) since it is the only one without tall stately Palm trees; it has several small ones that were planted shortly after it was built. These lovely neo-classical buildings, however, due to their western design, do not capture the beauty of the Mānoa breezes.
Continue walking diagonally across the quad in the open grassy area lined with Kamani trees.

Kamani wood is used in wood carving, such as for food vessels and boat building. The oil The “quad” in 1926 with the original Cooke Field. Today this is location of Sinclair Library, Hemenway Hall, and the Campus Center. (University Archives) that can be extracted from Kamani tree is useful: it burns well and can stimulate the treatment of skin wounds.

As the original campus, the quad houses some of the oldest buildings, with Hawai‘i Hall as the oldest permanent building on campus, completed as “Main Hall” in 1912. This building contains artistic gems by Jean Charlot’s students and colleagues. Charlot lived in Hawai‘i from 1949 until his death in 1979. When the building was renovated in 2003, including the walls, the frescoes by his students were cut out of the canac walls (a by-product of sugar cane), repurposed into canvas format, and remounted as individual works of art. If the building is open, climb up the stairs for a look at these treasures. There are 2 huge murals by Charlot in Bachman Hall, which you can visit on your way off campus.
Hawai‘i Hall is located where the Metcalf Plantation House would have been.
The Palm Garden on the makai-Diamond Head side of Hawai‘i Hall is particularly restful with the birds flitting and chirping.
Follow the purple line on the map to visit Shidler College of Business. Mauka

of the quad is Shidler College of Business, built in 1971, on the makai-Diamond Head corner of Maile Way and University Avenue. Shidler College is named after the benefactor Jay H. Shidler, who graduated from the University’s School of Business Administration in 1968.
1843 photo of undergrads posing at the bomb shelter near Hawai‘i Hall (University Archives)(University Archives)
In the Shidler courtyard, can you find the State of Hawai‘i on the wall map?

Walk into the lower level courtyard of Shidler. If you know your alphabet – at least A through G – you might notice that there is no F Tower. F Tower was deemed so poorly built that it was more cost effective to tear it down rather than repair it! While you are there, try to find the Hawaiian Islands on the reverse (blue = land; beige = water!) colored map on the Diamond Head wall of the courtyard.

Walk diagonally across the quad toward the ubiquitous (in Hawai‘i, not on campus) Kiawe-Mesquite tree in the mauka-Diamond Head section of the lawn, then mauka of Hawai‘i Hall to the newer Saunders Hall with its lovely open atrium as a study space.

Saunders, the social sciences building, has an interesting history, having first been named after Stanley Porteus in 1974, when it was built. A year later, university faculty and students pointed out the racist and sexist references in his academic work; however, it was not until 1998 that that building was renamed– with much fanfare – in honor of Allan Saunders and Marion Saunders, both political science professors. Thanks to Allan Saunders, aloha shirts are the preferred sartorial dress by UH faculty: in 1953, after the governor prohibited aloha shirts worn by territorial employees, Saunders proclaimed “Faculty Wearers of Aloha Shirts, Tails Out,” rejecting neckties, Aloha Shirts prevailed!
Not to ignore the aesthetic side, Saunders Hall has an unusual and magnificent ceramic mural by Jean Charlot, entitled “Night Hula.”

Walk makai-Diamond Head back to Campus Road toward Varney Circle Fountain, with the ki‘i (tiki) motif. Varney Circle (1932) was named in honor of Ada Susan Varney of the Territorial Normal and Training School (now College of Education).

The 4 story building on the mauka side of the circle is one of the newest on campus. The Queen Lili‘uokalani Center for Student Services is named for the last reigning monarch of Hawai‘i (1838-1917). The building has a lovely courtyard and skillfully placed lānai, facing the ocean with glorious views of Lē‘ahi.
The Crown flowers on the ‘Ewa side of the entrance steps make a lovely lei.

The ahu at Queen Lili‘uokalani Center for Student Services –Ke Ahu ‘o Kamaka‘eha –on the Diamond Head portion of the garden is sacred and is named for HRM Queen Lydia Lili‘uokalani Kamaka‘eha. It was built on September 5, 2000, to celebrate the 162nd birthday of Hawai‘i’s last monarch. Onipa‘a! Stand firm! An ahu This sacred ahu commemorates Kamaka‘eha - Queen Lili‘uokalani. is a shrine established to mark a ceremonial or spiritual event or purpose. There are two ahu at Bachman Hall.
The center is festooned in purple during the week of Queen Lili‘uokalani’s birthday, September 2.
The one-mile Health and Wellness Walking path begins on the mall. See if you can find the yellow mile markers, and after your leisurely tour through the campus, come back for a one-mile power walk!

As you leave Campus Drive and Varney Circle, you will embark on the “Mall,” originally McCarthy Road. McCarthy Mall was named in 1962 after Charles McCarthy, governor of the Territory of Hawai‘i from 1918 to 1921. Enjoy the shade of the fabulous flowering Monkey Pod/Rain trees (Albizia saman), native to Central and South America.

Webster Hall, named for Ernest Charles Webster (1883-1956), professor of mathematics and engineering, is the building on the mauka side after the circle. The mosaic on the ground is engraved with the university seal and the legendary words of Kamehameha III:
UA MAU KE EA O KA ‘ĀINA I KA PONO “The life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness”.

The University’s seal is composed of a Roman torch of learning with the word, Mālamalama, meaning ‘light of knowledge or enlightenment.’ Many University of Hawai‘i seals also have the Pacific Ocean etched as background. The Kukui trees surrounding the seal are symbolic of enlightenment, such as the learning through higher studies.

On the makai side after the circle is the Art Building, with its interesting walkways, especially the Bamboo forest walkway in the center of the courtyard with impressions of human forms, such as noses, lips and tongue, hands, even the profile of a face. While you are in the courtyard, listen to the music of the rustling Bamboo.
Local lore relates that the stylistic X on the building, as support beams, was envisioned by two chopsticks crossing on a bowl of rice!
This marker in front of the Queen Lili‘uokalani Center is the second sign of 30 for the mile fitness walk on campus. The first marker is on the mall – try find it!
Are you able to find this sculpture in the atrium of the art building. You might also find sculpted ears and mouths!

A sculpture, “Fourth Sign” by Tony Smith, graces the mauka side of the Art Building. The fourth sign of the zodiac is Cancer the Crab – this is a stylized form of the crab. Smith, a visiting scholar, created the work and sent the illustrations to be constructed locally.

On the ‘Ewa side of the Art Building, is a Baobab tree, an “Exceptional Tree.” This is the very tree that The Little Prince cares for. On early campus maps it was referred to as the “dead rat tree” – oh my! Follow the snake-like roots. Notice how the building crenellates around the tree, thanks to a studio room that was given up in order to save the tree!
The ground floor art galleries are usually open for student exhibits. Drop in to see the latest in the art world.
‘Ili of Pilipili

Next to the Art Building is Bilger Hall, the chemistry building, planned in 1951 by the local architect, Mark Potter. He also designed Castle Memorial Hall on the College of Education campus across University Avenue. The building has no inner hallways, thereby taking advantage of the cooling Hawaiian breezes –lanai style. Step inside – you’ll see. Pause a moment at the entryway to read the chiseled names of chemists and their achievements (Except for John Ruskin who was an art critic!).
Bilger Hall is named for two chemists who taught (from 1925 to the 1960s) at the university: Leonora Bilger and Earl Bilger.

There are frescoes on the subject of the 4 elements in the exterior corridors: “Water” by David Asherman, “Earth” by Sueko Kimura, “Fire” by Richard Lucier, and “Air” by Juliette May Fraser (1887-1983) – arguably the best known artist of the 4.

The “Exceptional” Hutu tree, native to the south Pacific islands, stands boldly before Bilger Hall, beckoning children to come climb. The Loulu palm tree in front of Bilger is representative of the only native Hawaiian palm tree. There are no native coconut trees.
The signage and nearby medallion with a QR code will give you information about the site.
Turn mauka here and walk up the steps.

Hamilton Library sits atop a short flight of steps. Thomas Hale Hamilton was the 7th president of the university from 1963-68. If the library is open to the public, please admire the artwork, Nana i ke Kumu (Look to the Source) at the entrance by Yvonne Cheng (who also has a large piece at the Kālia tower in the Hilton Hawaiian Village.)

Immediately inside the library lobby is a noteworthy display about local Hawai‘iborn William Kwai Fong Yap who Do these two crossed beams look like chopsticks?!? petitioned the college –and succeeded –to expand the college to a university. Why? He had 11 children and was, obviously, concerned about how he would be able to afford to pay for their high education expenses.

The library addition houses an informative exhibit and portrait of Alice Ball who found a cure for leprosy. There is also a plaque in her honor at the Chaulmoogra tree near Bachman Hall, which you will visit at the end of this campus tour.
Walk mauka toward Maile Way, the mauka border of the main part of the campus.
Paradise Palms, if open, awaits you not only with international foods and cold drinks, but also with photos of old Hawai‘i.

On the Maile Way side of Hamilton Library are native-to-Hawai‘i-only Hibiscus flowers: Koki‘o Ke‘oke‘o, the Hawaiian White Hibiscus, a fragrant hibiscus. The petals are a longer oval than most hibiscus flowers. The flower buds and leaves can be used as a soothing healing for newborns and their mothers. The fibers are used for ropes and the wood for charcoal.

The tree in the center of the walkway as you walk toward Maile Way is a Kou tree, native to Hawai‘i and to other Pacific Island, a “canoe plant.” The small bright orange flowers can be strung into a lei. All you need is a needle and some heavy thread. Try it.

Do admire the variety of Shower Trees. The Rainbow Shower tree, the official tree of Honolulu and conceived in Hawai‘i, is a cross between the Golden Shower tree from India and the Pink and White Shower trees from Indonesia.
You are now entering the ‘ili of Wailele – one of the many smaller land divisions in Mānoa.

Wailele Spring is located on the campus of Mid-Pacific Institute, which you can pass on the way to the Energy House (Stop 22A ). Wailele Spring is one of 3 Mānoa Valley springs around which mo‘olelo (legends) spin. The other two are Punahou Spring, on the Punahou School campus, and Kānewai, located near the lo‘i at Kānewai.

The ‘ili of Wailele (waterfall, jumping water), was government land owned by Chief Boki (c. 1785-c.1829), the governor of O‘ahu and his wife Chiefess Liliha (c. 1802– 1839). Boki brought coffee, pineapple and sugar to Mānoa – the first in Hawai‘i!

One of the tenants on Boki’s land was Captain George Charles Beckley who designed the flag of Hawai‘i. He was First Advisor to Kamehameha I, then became the first commander of Honolulu Fort (downtown). His grandson Frederick William Kahapula Beckley Sr. (1845-1881) married Emma Kaili Metcalf (18871929) who lived near here on her father’s (Theophilus Metcalf) land, in the ‘ili of Kauwala‘a. Emma Kailikapuolono Metcalf Beckley Nakuina (she remarried after Beckley died) was the first female judge and a water rights legal expert. Their son Frederick William Kahapula Beckley Jr. (18741943) was the first Hawaiian language instructor at the University of Hawai‘i.

Hipawai Heiau, ‘water foolishness’! was located mauka of this area near Mānoa Stream, on the former St. Francis campus, in the ‘ili of Kauwla‘a. A heiau is an open air religious structure. The lava building stones of the heiau are still there, repurposed as walls. Another campus heiau was most likely located where the Music buildings are, near University Avenue and Dole Street (For more information follow the Lower Campus Walk XII)

Follow the purple line Energy House. Beyond Maile Way is a section of the University campus that you might want to return to another day: the Energy House, designed by architect Jim Pearson and constructed by the University of Hawai‘i School of Architecture in 1976. Pearson and his family lived in the home for a while, demonstrating its energy-saving aspects. Notice especially the tank collecting rainwater for reuse, skylights admitting natural light, sliding shoji-like walls to capture cross breezes, and a lānai around the house.

In 2010, the Energy House was lovingly restored by Professor Mary Martini and friends. It is not a straight path to the reach the Energy House, but it is worth it – perhaps for another trip back here.
When you arrive, you will see why it is called the Energy House: a “green” house, off the grid with an urban plant garden.
Continue across Maile Way between the one-story Agricultural Engineering building (‘Ewa) and the 6-story Harold St.

John Plant Science Laboratory building (Diamond Head). Then continue straight ahead to the pathway shrubs of ‘akia (‘Ewa) and pohinahina (Diamond Head) on the walkway between the ditch and fence on the Mid-Pacific Institute property, and the
UH Dance Studio. Mid-Pacific Institute, a college preparatory K-through 12 private school, was established in 1908.
Follow the pathway to the Diamond Head side of the small building in front of you where you will see a sign “To Biomed Building.” Go through to the Biomed Building parking lot.
Walk mauka through for the Biomedical Science Building. Continue, snaking past several older parking lot single story frame structures until you reach the reddish-colored Energy House.
Please don’t pick any of the vegetation.
To return to the main walk, take the road Diamond Head of the Energy House and just before the gardens to the intersection of Maile Way and East-West Road.
Follow the sidewalk pathway around to the front of the Biomed Science Building, reading about it. Then continue on EastWest Road to complete the campus tour.

Continue mauka, past Paradise Palms, turn Diamond Head on Maile Way (Maile is a native vine that grows in the forests of Hawai‘i), then mauka on East-West Road toward the tall pagoda-looking structure, the Biomedical Science Building. The ‘Ewa

courtyard is home to Honolulu’s bird, the White Tern. Look up in the Kukui trees – You’ll be sure to see the lovely white seabird. White Terns do not build nests: they find a branch or a scar on a tree on which to perch.
Can you find the legendary Energy House behind all that greenery?

This building housed the medical school until 2005, when it moved to Kaka‘ako to a new, larger space. The architect, Edward Durell Stone (1902-1978), is best known for his work on the mainland: Radio City Music Hall and Museum of Modern Art in New York City; John F. Kennedy Center and National Geographic in Washington, DC; and Scrips Research Institute and Stanford Medical Center in California, among many other structures.
The low building in front, C-MORE: Center for Microbial Oceanography Research and Education, unfortunately, hides the beauty of Stone’s architecture.

In the midst of the interestingly landscaped front lawn of C-MORE is Bumpei Akaji’s (1921-2002) copper and brass sculpture “Maka‘ā e ‘Ike Aku i ke Awāwa Uluwehi i nā Kuahiwi o Mānoa” (Glowing Eyes Looking at the Lush Valley in the Mountains of Mānoa, 1979). Akaji, who was born on Kaua‘i, served with the 100th Battalion of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team in Italy.
The pebbled walkway is aesthetically delightful. Rest a while on the lava benches amidst the plants and trees.

stops.title: Plant courtyard of G. Donald
stops.subtitle: Sherman and Harold St. John Plant Science Laboratories

blocks.text: Returning makai to East-West Road, but before crossing Maile Way, walk into the courtyard between G. Donald Sherman Laboratory and Harold St. John Plant Science Laboratory to view several native-to-Hawai‘i-only plants. G. Donald Sherman was a professor and chairman of Department of Agronomy and Soil Science. Dr. Harold St. John taught from 1929 to 1958, often serving as the chair of the Botany Department. The lava rock garden at his former home, nearby on O‘ahu Avenue, is a testament to his talents.
On the corner, as you walk into the courtyard, is an interesting, but not native, tree: the Mindanao Gum tree with its striped variegated bark is particularly stunning.
Continuing makai along East-West Road you will pass Moore Hall, which houses the language and linguistics departments.
Notice the copious native plants -if you are interested -in the small gardens scattered around the interior courtyard.
A Bo tree, in memory of Gregg M. Sinclair, the 4th university president, is the type of tree under which Buddha was believed to have received enlightenment.
This fluffy baby White Tern is waiting patiently for a parent to bring back food from the ocean. They do not eat worms!
This building is a tribute to the architectural talent of Edward Durell Stone.
The great variety of Shower trees in the medians at Maile Way and East-West Road are particularly magnificent in the spring and summer months.

On the ‘Ewa side of East-West Road is one of the newest buildings on campus, Isabella Aiona Abbott Life Sciences Building, with the sign ‘ili of Kauwala‘a. Nearby there is a medallion with a QR code that will give you information about the site.
The surroundings have been carefully landscaped with local plants: ground cover Pohinahina and tall white Hibiscus flowering shrubs.
‘Ili of Puahia

East-West Road is home to the East-West Center and cuts through the ‘ili of Puahia, with two meanings: ‘swift,’ as in the neighboring swift moving Mānoa Stream and ‘hazy, gray,’ as in the Mānoa rains.

The East-West Center was a 1960s brainstorm of bringing together the cultures of the east and the west for mutual understanding and research, with an AsianPacific focus. I. M. Pei, renowned for his buildings around the world (Just to name a few: the Glass Pyramids at the Louvre, Paris; the East Wing of the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC; Bank of China, Hong Kong; Javits Convention Center, New York) was selected as the architect for the 5 original buildings, including Kennedy Theater.

The main East-West Center building is Thomas Jefferson Hall, which houses the Hawai‘i Imin International Conference Center. The huge wooden doors are very impressive! The guardian stone Fu Dogs (really lions) were a gift from Taiwan.

John Burns Hall is named after Hawai‘i Governor John Burns (1909-75; governor 1962-74), one of the founders of the EastWest Center. It is the most makai EastWest Center building (just before Dole Street) and houses the East-West Center Gallery. Stop in for interesting pacific exhibitions.
27 On the Diamond Head side of Maile Way, you will pass several Asian structures:
Korean Center, Thai Pavilion, and Japanese Garden and Tea House.

• Center for Korean Studies, which was dedicated in 1980, consists of the building and pavilion, replicas of the original Kyŏngbok Palace, which was built in the 1390s in Seoul, the most important royal palace of the Joseon dynasty. The building is faced with Korean granite and green glazed roof tiles from Korea. The main brownishred and green colors are traditional palace colors. There is much more detail about these building on the back of the Korean Center sign.
• The granite boulders on the makai side of the pavilion mark the centennial in 1982 of US-Korean Relations.

• The gilded and magnificent Royal Sala, the Thai pavilion, was a gift in 1967 from King Bhumibol Adulyadej of Thailand to the East-West Center. Yes, you may sit in it and enjoy the view of the campus and surrounding mountains.

• Japanese Garden, which is hidden in clear sight behind the Conference Center, was designed by landscape architect Kenzo Ogata in 1963. The garden stream follows the symbolic life cycle, from the mountains to the sea.
• The Plumeria Grove, on the way to the Japanese Garden, was dedicated by Mrs. Lyndon Baines Johnson in 1966 with the words “Beauty – a Language of Mankind.”
• The Tea House, Chashitsu Jakuan, ‘Cottage of Tranquility,’ and Tea Garden, Seien, were presented to the University of Hawai‘i by a XVth-generation grand tea master.

Mānoa Stream runs behind all these structures. Please tread carefully as you seek a view of this magnificent stream. A closer and eye-level view of the stream can be seen at the lo‘i on the Lower Campus Walk XII.

Pu‘u Kākea (the name of a stormy Mānoa wind), informally known as Sugar Loaf, which produced lava approximately 70,000 years ago flowed down into the valley resulting in the floor of Mānoa Valley. The lava flow pushed Mānoa Stream from the ‘Ewa side to the Diamond Head side of the valley and behind the University of Hawai‘i. The lower edge of the flow created the beautiful basalt lava found in Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, now the lower campus. This basalt lava is the basic building block for many houses and buildings in Honolulu. The 50-foot-high wall, separating the lower campus from the upper campus is visible from the parking structure.

John F. Kennedy Theater, also designed by I. M. Pei in 1963, was named for President Kennedy a month after his assassination. The theater has a full Kabuki stage, one of the few locations outside of Japan with a stage built to accommodate Kabuki, a traditional form of Japanese theater dating to the 17th century. Kennedy Theater opened with a Kabuki play, “Benten the Thief,” followed by “Hamlet.” Considering JFK’s untimely death, fitting plays.

On the grassy area makai of Kennedy Theater and on the way to Correa Road (named after the Territorial senator during whose time Hawai‘i College became the University of Hawai‘i) stands a Hawai‘i Peace Memorial commemorating the thousands of Japanese immigrants beginning in 1868 who came to Hawai‘i. Notice the 5 elements in Japanese and in English – on both structures.
Another memorial to the Japanese workers is located at the Japanese Cemetery in Mō‘ili‘ili. (Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX).
Have a snack while you sit in the glorious Thai Pavilion presiding over the campus.
The Japanese Garden behind the Imin Center is tranquility personified.

On Correa Road in front of Watanabe Hall, after the University Health Sciences (the clinic), is a sculpture titled “Krypton,” by Bruce Hopper - a monolith based on the one in the novel 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Follow the makai path just past Watanabe Hall to the courtyard of the Hawai‘i Institute of Geophysics and School of Ocean and Earth Science and Technology. In the

courtyard is a plaque about the Tragedy of the Holoholo, a University of Hawai‘i research vessel that in December 1978 never reached its destination. The 7 scientists and 3 crew members were proclaimed “lost at sea.”
Walk back to Correa Road, Diamond Head to East-West Road, and then makai.

On the way to Dole Street, you will pass the most understated, minimalist campus sculpture ever seen: “Divers” by Robert Stackhouse. It is a brass sculpture in the shape of a boat’s framework, level with the ground.
As you turn the corner, ‘Ewa at Dole Street, orient yourself on campus:
• Diamond Head of here is the campus gem, the lo‘i – taro fields – in the ‘ili of Kānewai, ‘the waters of the deity Kāne.’
• Makai is the lower campus with the athletics departments and fields.
(Both Kānewai and the athletics departments are on the Lower (makai) Campus Walk XII.)
• ‘Ewa is University Avenue; however, you will be walking diagonally mauka through the campus to reach University Avenue.

The huge campus building on the corner of Dole Street and East-West Road is Wilfred J. Holmes Hall, the engineering building with a remarkable sculpture (yes, the opposite of “Divers”) -- that huge redorange steel sculpture titled “Gate of Hope” by Alexander Liberman (1912-1990). The plaque reads:
“This sculpture alludes to man’s ability to build complex structures through the understanding of engineering principles.”
Holmes (1900-1986) served in various capacities from faculty to Vice President of the university, but mainly as Dean of Engineering.

A June 2021 plaque about an IEEE milestone is located on the makai side of the engineering building – at this Diamond Head bay. The plaque states that the ALOHA packet radio led to the development of Ethernet and today’s wireless technologies.
As you continue along Dole Street, walk in the splendid shade of the Monkey Pod trees.

The low building, ‘Ewa on Dole Street, is Krauss Hall; more interesting, however, is its earlier incarnation name, Pineapple Research Institute, hence the PRI above the mauka doors and gates. Krauss Hall is named for Frederick Krauss who contributed a great deal to local agricultural research. Walk through the building and enjoy this oasis of peace. The Water Garden -- designed by Lorraine Kuck and Richard C. Tongg in 1948 -- provides a well-needed haven.
Exit Krauss Hall on the makai -‘Ewa side but walk mauka back toward the center of campus.
Across Dole Street are the law school buildings and the stairs to the parking garage and the lower/makai campus (Lower Campus Walk XII)

However, what stand out is the bronze sculpture by George Segal entitled “Chance Meeting,” with the requisite local directionals. If only these models were dressed for Hawaiian weather in T-shirts, shorts, and slippahs (our local word for the ubiquitous flip-flops)! Students often decorate the figures with lei, especially on Lei Day/ May Day, May 1st, and graduation.

Walk ‘Ewa-mauka through Legacy Walk, installed in 2003, with inscribed bricks surrounded by pillars and benches, then mauka in the walkway between the trees, including Hala, Ulu (breadfruit), Kiawe/ Mesquite, and Ficus.

On the ‘Ewa side of the walkway is the underutilize, but lovely, Andrews Outdoor Theater, which was built in 1935 by the same architect, Ralph Fishbourne, who designed Founders’ Gate, the entry archways to the University of Hawai‘i at the intersection of University Avenue and Dole Street. If you hear of an event taking place at Andrews, do attend for a special experience.

On the Diamond Head side of the walkway is the John Young Museum of Art (founded in 1999) with changing art exhibits, mainly photographic. If it’s open, do drop in – the air conditioning is set extremely high! John Young (1909-1997), an Abstract Expressionist artist, was a philanthropist who helped establish this museum on campus for the general community.
Notice the interlaced aerial roots of the Hala trees lined up against the building. The huge tree in the circle on the Diamond Head side is a Weeping Fig.
You are back in the ‘ili of Pilipili.

The Campus Center, ‘Ewa of here, has a terrific multi-international gustatory food court and multi-cultural bookstore. Starbucks holds an interesting surprise: The bottom portion of the counter is from the Ficus that once grew where the Rec Center stands today! (Read the artwork in the store).

The immense 2-sided mural at the top of the steps reflects life in the valley of Mānoa through the ages: Hawai‘i Ka‘u Kumu, ‘Hawai‘i, My Teacher.’ A huge Monkey Pod tree in the middle of the courtyard shades the students who are either studying or eating, or both.
A pool was once on this site. The presentday pool is on the lower campus – Walk XII.
Notice the logo on the buildings: triple Cs (for Campus Center Complex) as a rainbow and back-to-back Cs as a stylized Hala tree.
A “Chance Meeting” is often festooned with lei.
Former Engineering Buildings
The gym, Warrior Recreation Center, which opened in 2014 bathes its athletes in natural light.

The architects ingeniously incorporated one of the early campus buildings, repurposing it into a weight room. The one-story attached building on the Diamond Head side of the building was one of 5 1920sengineering buildings that formed Young Engineering Quadrangle. This one building was fortunate enough to have been saved. The engineering department is now in Holmes Hall with the giant red-orange sculpture that you passed on Dole Street.
As you work your way back to University Avenue, climb up the stairs between the campus center and the gym to greet HINA O NA LANI – ‘Hina (the deity) of the heavens.’
Walk makai on the path between Hemenway Hall and Sinclair.

Hemenway Hall is named for Charles Reed Hemenway (1875-1947) who chaired the Board of Regents for 20 years. Hemenway was instrumental in the FBI’s decision not to intern the local Hawaiian Japanese population during World War II. He was able to persuade the FBI director of the Japanese Americans’ loyalty to the United States.
Hemenway Hall was the first student union building. The 16 state blocks mentioned earlier in the walk are on the ‘Ewa side of Hemenway.

The building on the ‘Ewa side of the path is Sinclair (former) Library, built of local Wai‘anae sandstone in 1956, and was named for Gregg M. Sinclair, the 4th university president. Sinclair, now the Student Success Center, was the undergraduate library from 1956 to 2019.
Continue to follow the path behind Bachman Hall to come out on Dole Street.

The last building as you leave the campus is Bachman Hall, the Administrative Building, named after Paul Bachman (1901-1957), the fifth president of the university. The architect, Vladimir Ossipoff, who was influenced by Frank Lloyd Wright’s style, not only designed many homes in Mānoa and other residential areas, but also designed the open-air lānai style terminal at the Daniel Inouye International Honolulu Airport. Ossipoff was born in Russia, but came to love and live in Hawai‘i. Bachman Hall has several interesting architectural features, such as the large glass windows and doors, and the inviting open lānai facing University Avenue.
Bachman Hall underwent an extensive renovation in the early 2020s.

Jean Charlot has two outstanding frescoes in this building: one on each floor. The first floor fresco, “The Relation of Man and Nature in Old Hawai‘i,” is clearly visible through the glass wall; “Commencement,” a second floor mural. Jean Charlot lived in Hawai‘i from 1949 until his death in 1979.

On the mauka side of Backman Hall is a plaque indicating the Chaulmoogra tree and a tribute to the African American woman, Alice Augusta Ball whose research with the oil from the seed of this tree resulted in the first treatment for leprosy in 1916. Unfortunately, Alice Ball passed away at the age of 24 due to contamination in her lab and was never given the praise she deserved – because she was a woman? An African American woman? Or just being young? Her discovery was used until 1941 when sulfone drugs were introduced. Hamilton Library has a lovely portrait of her. Alice Ball Day is celebrated on February 28.
On the Diamond Head side of Bachman is a native-to-Hawai‘i-only Koa tree. It is small here but grows quite large in the mountains and forest. Koa also means ‘warrior.’

There are 2 ahu at Bachman Hall. An ahu is a Hawaiian shrine used for ceremonies and spiritual reasons. The ahu in the Bachman courtyard signifies the responsibility of the university to its students and its larger community. The ahu at Wise Field was established to protect Mauna Kea on Hawai‘i Island. Activists protested the Ten Meter Telescope, set up this ahu and began a vigil in this field. Bachman was also home to antiwar protests in the 1970s. The ahu are surround by red and green kī (ti) plants, representing the royal kāhili or standard.
Polynesians make a raincoat by layering the leaves of the ki plant. Dried, the ki leaves can be woven, notably, into sandals.

Two flags fly at Bachman Hall: the US flag and the flag of the State of Hawai‘i, which has an interesting history. The flag of the State of Hawai‘i, which was officially adopted in 1845, incorporates the Union Jack of the British flag, commemorating the historic relationship with the British empire dating back to Kamehameha I. The 8 horizontal stripes allude to the 8 major islands of the state. The Hawaiian flag was designed by George Charles Beckley (1787-1826), who came to Hawai‘i from England in 1801, whom we “met” in the ‘ili of Wailele on campus.
Across from Bachman Hall are the Music Building and Law School, both are discussed on the Lower Campus Walk XII. Mauoki Heiau – an open air religious structure – was most likely in this area.
You are back to where you started: University Avenue and Dole Street.
If you want to travel makai, a sheltered bus stop is across the way at University Avenue and Metcalf Street. Bus routes and times: www.thebus.org or call 808-848-5555 (option 2 for a live operator)
Continue Walk X into Mānoa Valley .

1929 photo. The original engineering buildings – Young Engineering Quadrangle – is the H-shaped complex in the center. That facility was replaced by the Campus Center and the Rec Center, with one of the 5 engineering buildings attached to the gym. The University Farms have been replaced by Webster Hall, Art Building, and Kuykendall Hall. (University Archives)

Walk up Kapahulu Avenue to the Hawaiian Center in Kānewai, named for the water given by the deity Kāne. Then walk down to the athletic center into the former quarry.
There are two major stops on this walk:
• The Hawaiian Center, the gem of the University of Hawai‘i campus: Kamakakūokalani (‘Upright eye of heaven’) Center for Hawaiian Knowledge and the lo‘i, the university’s kalo (taro) fields.

• Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, which was worked for 60 years. The lower campus, the athletic center, is carved out of the basalt quarry that furnished the building blocks for many Honolulu houses and buildings, and even curbstones.

You are walking in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī within the moku (larger land division) of Kona on the island of O‘ahu. An ahupua‘a is divided into ‘ili, ‘districts.’ The names of the various ‘ili will be mentioned as you walk along.

While Waikīkī oceanfront was the aquacultural provider, Mānoa was the agricultural provider. Waikīkī offered seafood; Mānoa, the ‘breadbasket,’ offered sustenance in the form of kalo (taro) and u‘ala (sweet potato). You will walk in a lo’i (kalo field) in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī alongside Mānoa Stream.
Early morning is the best time to talk this walk. Please be sure to take along a hat, water, and wear sturdy shoes.
This walk begins at the Diamond Head end of the Ala Wai Canal at Kapahulu Avenue

title: Lower Campus
theme: The Hawaiian center at Kānewai and the old quarry

intro.text: Hale at the Center for Hawaiian Studies Kapahulu means ‘the worn-out soil,’ perhaps from the overuse of the land for growing kalo (taro).

blocks.text: If you are walking along Kapahulu Avenue from the beach, you will pass the ‘Ewa side of the Honolulu Zoo. (You can visit in Kāneloa, Walk VI.)
The original intent of the configuration of the Ala Wai Canal was to have another exit to the ocean at this end, but (thankfully) the developers ran out of money.

On the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue, is the local school, Thomas Jefferson Elementary. If you have a few minutes, admire the ceramic tile wall by the students and the sculpture, E Pluribus Unum, ‘one from many,’ by Eli Marozzi. In Marozzi’s words, this sculpture of intertwined faces and arms symbolizes that “we are many, but we can attain oneness in harmony.” Marozzi also has sculptures in Old Stadium Park in Mō‘ili‘ili, Walk IX. In 1776 Thomas Jefferson was one of the proponents for including the motto for the Great Seal of the United States.

Its sleek, clean lines make this building appear quite modern, but it was constructed in 1927. The firehouse was designed by architects Davis and Fishbourne and is surely one of the loveliest firehouses, especially its Hawaiian style sloped-roof line, to be found anywhere.
Davis and Fishbourne were the original architects for McKinley High School.
1939 photo. Quarry excavation (1889 to 1949) is evident in the background (upper left); this will be developed as the University’s lower campus. (University Archives)
E Pluribus Unum - ‘one from many’

The library on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue is one of Waikīkī’s architectural gems. Its exterior walls are made of locally hewn sandstone blocks. The ceiling is of imported cedar wood; the interior doors, the reading bench, and children’s tables are of native Koa wood. The cathedral windows provide natural reading light. The first Waikīkī library was in a wooden cottage on the grounds of Thomas Jefferson School. In 1952 the new library, designed by Lemmon and Freeth, opened its doors to the public. In the entryway, view the cement sculpture of an outrigger canoe. Lemmon and Freeth were also the architects for the Occidental Building on Pi‘ikoi Street as well as one of the firms for the state capitol.
Behind Waikīkī-Kapahulu Library is another library – the Hawai‘i State Library for the Blind and the Physically Handicapped, which is why the walk signal beeps.
The street mauka-‘Ewa of the libraries leads to the clubhouse of the Ala Wai Golf Course.
ally outstanding for a bank. If the bank is open, step inside to gaze at the huge old photographs of Waikīkī.

Notice the sign “Lei of Parks,” which begins after the Ala Wai Golf Course sign on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu. The intent of these green Lei of Parks signs is for people to walk from park to park around the island, like a lei.

The neighborhood of Kapahulu, on the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue, is an interesting community with homes and gardens on the slope of the crater and great vistas of Waikīkī, including Kapi‘olani Park. The side streets also lead up to the crater at Kaimukī Hill with fantastic views of the surrounding area. (If walking into a crater intrigues you, follow the Kaimukī Walk VIII into a crater.)
Kana‘ina Avenue is named after Charles Kana‘ina, father of King Lunalilo, the 6th Monarch of the Kingdom of Hawai‘i. His name means “the conquering.”
Castle Street is named for businessman James Bickness Castle. His home, Kainalu, was a magnificent mansion on the water in Waikīkī (Walk VII).
Herbert and Williams street are named
for the realtor, Earl Herbert Williams, who launched and built up this area.
Campbell Avenue is named after James Campbell of James Campbell Estate. This road led to his family’s summer home.
Ho‘olulu Street (‘to lie in sheltered waters’), is possibly named after the area on Hawai‘i Island where King Kamehameha I’s bones were allegedly hidden).
An architecturally stunning fire station with Lē‘ahi in the background!
Good Guys Music and Sound is on the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue, half-way between Ho‘olulu Street and Mo‘oheau Avenue. Be sure to try out the ‘ukulele ‘jumping fleas.’

Date Street ‘Ewa of Kapahulu Avenue, leads to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili; Mo‘oheau Avenue, on the Diamond Head side, goes to Kaimukī. Mo‘oheau is the name of the chief who purportedly hid King Kamehameha I’s bones.
Da ‘Ono Hawaiian food is on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue, 1/2 block past Date Street. ‘Ono means ‘good, delicious’; da is local pidgin (Hawaiian English Creole) for ‘the.’
Hunter Street – Unknown source; perhaps part of the makai alphabetically-named streets
As you approach Winam Avenue, turn around to see if you can discover the split mural of Lē‘ahi. Ching Winam, a Chinese merchant, owned property here.

stops.title: Haili’s Hawaiian food is at the ‘Ewa

blocks.text: intersection of Kapahulu, Winam, and Palani avenues.. Palani is the transliteration of Frank, a developer in this area.
Pāliuli Street. Paliuli means ‘green cliff ’ and is considered to be a paradise of plenty.

Kapahulu Shopping Center, a little further up on the ‘Ewa side of Kapahulu Avenue, might be the only shopping center with a 7-foot telescope on its roof. Check dates for https://kapahulushoppingcenter.com/
As you walk mauka, enjoy the majestic Ko‘olau Mountains before you.

If you would like to try one of the best shave ice in town, turn Diamond Head onto Mokihana (a section of Kaua‘i, as well as a flower found on the trees of Kaua‘i) Street. It’s a small blue building on the makai side of the street. Stop in for a real treat! The original store is off McCully Street, which you can visit for more ‘ono shave ice when you take Mānoa Walk X or Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX.
‘Olu Street. ‘olu means ‘cool’ – a word found in many Hawaiian mele (songs).
Local, but not necessarily Hawaiian, is Leonard’s Bakery, just past Charles Street on the Diamond Head side of Kapahulu Avenue. Leonard’s bakes heavenly malasadas, Portuguese (filled) donuts.
Leonard’s Malasadas – try one, try them all. You won’t be sorry!
Malassadas (correctly, with 2 S’s) were introduced by Portuguese plantation workers in 1878. Try them…there’s a great variety…if you don’t mind waiting in a very long line!
Charles Street may have been named after Charles Kana‘ina (Kana‘ina Stret); Charles Martin, a local builder; or Charles, the son of Miriam Auhea Crowningburg, a developer in the area.
Kaimukī Avenue -‘the Ti (kī in Hawaiian)
oven’ or ‘oven for cooking the Ki root.

Lincoln Avenue may have been named for Abraham Lincoln Harding Avenue is named after Warren Gamaliel Harding (1865 – 1923) who was president (1921-23) during the time that this street was developed in Kaimukī.

Continue mauka along Kapahulu Avenue until you come to Wai‘alae (mud hen water - named for a spring) Avenue, which is right after the freeway overpass. The downtown Honolulu portion of the H1 freeway was known as Mauka Arterial in 1953 when it was first built. After Hawai‘i became a state in 1959, it became part of the Interstate system. Several extensions were added over the years.
Cross Wai‘alae Avenue in the direction of Diamond Head at St. Louis Drive.

On your way to the lower campus, you will pass by City Mill (on the maukaKoko Head corner of St. Louis Drive and Wai‘alae Avenue), our local hardware store. Its founder, Chung Kun Ai was a classmate of Sun Yat-Sen, the founder of the Republic of China at ‘Iolani School.

Chung Kun Ai, who was born in China and came to Hawai‘i at the age of 14, received the “Order of the Splintered Paddle,” a prestigious award for his outstanding service. The Order of the Splintered Paddle is a human rights decree that originated with Kamehameha I. The Order of the Splintered Paddle is prominently displayed on the badges of our local police officers.

Continue mauka on St. Louis Drive, then at the first intersection, turn ‘Ewa on Dole Street toward the University of Hawai‘i campus. Dole Street divides the University of Hawai‘i into the upper (most of the buildings and academics) on the
 ‘Ena Rd.
Kānāwai Māmalahoe (original 1797 law):
E nā kānaka, E mālama ‘oukou i ke akua A e mālama ho‘i ke kanaka nui a me kanaka iki; E hele ka ‘elemakule, ka luahine, a me ke kama A moe i ke ala ‘A‘ohe mea nāna e ho‘opilikia.
Hewa nō, make.
English translation Law of the Splintered Paddle:

Oh people, Honor the god; respect alike the rights of great men and humble men ; May everyone, from the old men and women to the children Be free to go forth and lie in the road (i.e., by the roadside or pathway)
Without fear of harm. Break this law and die.
mauka side and lower campus (mainly athletics) on the makai side.

On St. Louis Drive you will cross Pālolo (‘clay’) Stream, which comes down from the mountains on the Diamond Head side and meets up with Mānoa Stream a few blocks away to form the Mānoa-Pālolo Drainage Canal. The combined stream then flows into the Ala Wai Canal near the Ala Wai Golf Course.

Before the Ala Wai Canal was built in the 1920s, these streams emptied directly into the ocean at Waikīkī. You will be walking to the shores of Mānoa Stream at the lo‘i kalo (‘taro field’). Mānoa Stream was known as ‘Āpuakehau Stream as it flowed into the ocean at today’s Outrigger Hotel (and still does, into its garage!).
As you turn ‘Ewa onto Dole / Kapa‘akea Street, notice the remarkable intact lava walls on the mauka-Diamond Head corner as well as along Dole Street.
‘Ili of Kapa‘akea

Dole Street is not named for the territorial governor and major player in the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893; rather for Reverend Daniel Dole, the first teacher and administrator at Punahou School. However, on earlier maps, this street is labeled Kapa‘akea, who was father to both King Kalākaua and Queen Lili‘uokalani. There is a small street by that name in Mō‘ili‘ili. Kapa‘akea can refer to a coral or limestone surface.
The area around here and ‘Ewa is the ‘ili (land division) of Kapa‘akea.
The walk to the lower/makai campus starts at the Hawaiian Center, then down to the lower campus and the athletic fields.

You are now entering the ‘ili of Kānewai. This walk to the University’s Hawaiian Center and later to the lower campus will take you past Kānewai Street, which leads to the local elementary school, Hokulani ‘Star of Heaven,’ the neighborhood and ‘ili of Kānewai, and Kānewai Community Park, all named for the water given by the deity Kāne.
Ka Papa Lo‘i ‘O Kānewai

You will know that you have reached the Hawaiian Center when you see 4 Hawaiian style roofs that look like Hawaiian thatched hale (houses). This is the gem of the University of Hawai‘i campus: Kamakakūokalani (Upright Eye of Heaven) Center for Hawaiian Knowledge and lo‘i, The rooftops of Kamakakūokalani Center for Hawaiian Studies resemble Hawaiian Hale the university’s kalo (taro) fields. The round buildings behind the center are university dormitories on the other side of Mānoa Stream.

This center is part of the University of Hawai‘i. The University of Hawai‘i began as a land grant college under the land grant Morrill Act of 1890, first established in 1907 on Thomas Square close to downtown on S. Beretania Street, then moved to its present location in Mānoa Valley in 1912. As an original land grant college, it is fitting that a kalo (taro) field is part of the university system.

Kamakakūokalani Center for Hawaiian Studies is named after Gladys Kamakakūokalani ‘Ainoa Brandt (19062003). Better known as Aunty Gladys, she was instrumental in the establishment of the University of Hawai‘i’s Center for Hawaiian Studies and served on the university’s board of regents. Aunty Gladys was not only the first woman public school principal in Hawai‘i, but was also the first woman superintendent of schools and served on the board of regents for the University of Hawai‘i.

Aunty Gladys is honored by the water sculpture on the lower level courtyard lovingly created by Ipō Dowson Nihipali, a native Hawaiian woman artist. The piko (‘center, bellybutton’) section reaches upright to the heavens, signifying the height of knowledge. Ho‘opulapula (to procreate) creates the essence of life as depicted in the flowing wai (waters). The spirals on the floor are stylized ferns, which are representative of new life, the first growth after a lava flow.
The main entryway sculpture, also by Ipō Dowson Nihipali is the artist’s interpretation of Kumulipo, the Hawaiian creation story as the “origin, genesis, source of life”
- the evolution of life forms.

Both sculptures were reinforced with lava stones by Fields Masonry, which also recreated the only restored heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī, Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau. That authentic heiau can be visited at the Mānoa Heritage Center, on the Mānoa Walk X.

Although the University of Hawai‘i was established in 1907, the first course in Hawaiian language wasn’t until 1919. The main office of the Hawai‘inuiākea School of Hawaiian Knowledge is located in the Queen Lili‘uokalani Student Center on the upper campus (between the “mall” and the “quad”), which you can visit on the Upper Campus Walk XI.

Hawaiian Studies was initially established in 1970; the Center for Hawaiian Studies was established in 1987, with the Center for Hawaiian Studies building on 5-acres opening in 1997. Hawai‘inuiākea School of Hawaiian Knowledge, encompassing this center, the Kawaihuelani Center for Hawaiian Language, Ka Papa Lo‘i ‘O Kānewai Cultural Garden, and the Native Hawaiian Student Services, was established in 2007.
Professor Haunani-Kay Trask, who passed away in 2021, was one of the founders of the Center for Hawaiian Studies at the University of Hawai‘i.

This building and lānai are named in honor of the first University of Hawai‘i students who, in 1980, re-discovered and restored the Hawaiian aquaculture and agriculture in this area long-known as Kānewai, ‘water of (the deity) Kāne.’ Kalo was the kino lau, the body form of Kāne, the deity of creation and the ancestor of chiefs and commoners, alike.
The lānai, or open porch, is named • Ho‘okahewai Ho‘oūlu ‘Āina Lānai:

• Ho‘okahewai – causing the water to flow • Ho‘oūlu ‘Āina -increased productivity of the land Notice the open – literally –classroom on the lower level: open on 3 sides! Since the floor is carpeted, students leave their “slippahs” outside and sit barefoot in class!

Kānewai was well-known for its highly productive lo‘i – a terrace for kalo (taro) growing –even in the years before Kamehameha I united the islands. The students, with the help and guidance of local kūpuna (elders), restored the area by rebuilding the ‘auwai (irrigation ditch) that runs off Mānoa Stream, reestablishing the kalo patches, and building a hālau (thatched pavilion).

There are many varieties of kalo, wet and dry. These lo’i were planted with the wet variety, as were the lo’i in lower Waikīkī. In the Hawaiian creation myth, kalo plays a pivotal role as Hāloa, the common ancestor of the Hawaiian people. Poi, the staple of the native Hawaiian diet, is made from the of the kalo (taro) plant. Hawaiians believed that the essence of Hāloa, their fabled ancestor, was among them when a container of poi was at the meal; consequently, all disagreements were put on hold.

Taro, or kalo in Hawaiian (The letter and sound “t” does not exist in standard Hawaiian.), is a starchy vegetable similar to the potato. Generally, all parts of this vital plant are eaten: the leaves are cooked as greens, similar to spinach; the fleshy stems and roots are eaten baked, boiled, or steamed with water to make poi, the staple Hawaiian food. Parts of the kalo, however, if eaten raw can be a dangerous irritant or even toxic. It must be well-cooked before eaten. My own grandson mistook the kalo stem for a green bean, and much to his dismay, he felt like something was stinging his mouth!
Ka Papa Lo‘i ‘O Kānewai Kalo (taro) once grew abundantly in Hawai‘i. Today, this lo‘i is a model for the resurgence of kalo lo‘i (taro fields).
Mānoa Stream runs ‘Ewa and makai of the lo’i, with the ‘auwai (drainage canal) parallel and above it on the Diamond Head side of the stream. This is the water that feeds the lo’i.

When you leave, as you walk up the steps behind the workhouse to Dole Street, enjoy the Kou trees with the orange flowers that can be strung into lei. Walk ‘Ewa toward the campus to continue into the lower campus.

Across Dole Street is UH faculty housing as well as the entryway to Wa‘ahila (the name of a soothing Mānoa rain) Ridge, native plant gardens. At last glance, it was too overgrown to form a trail into the garden.

On your way to the lower campus, walking along Dole Street – just before crossing the Mānoa Stream bridge (dated June 1953) –notice the lava flow of pāhoehoe on the mauka side of the road, above and below the ‘a‘ā (chucks of lava) that are in between.

Directly across and makai from East West Road, the main street into the upper campus is the stairwell down to the lower campus. The stairwell is between and behind Gateway House and Johnson Hall B. The stairs will take you to the front of the practice field and the quarry pond, which is filled with algae, migratory ducks, koi (large goldfish), and an occasional tilapia swimming around waiting for someone to fish it out.
As you walk down the 87 steps, after gazing at the majesty of Lē‘ahi in the distance, notice the lava walls left behind in the quarry.
The lower campus walk will take you around and through the athletic fields and buildings. At the end, you will walk out toward Dole Street near University Avenue.

This walk will take you to the lower campus, formerly Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, which was worked from 1889 to 1949, with its The lower campus is carved out of the basalt quarry that furnished the building blocks for many Honolulu houses and buildings, and even curbstones. Central Union Church, on S. Beretania and As you walk down the steps, look around; you are walking down the face of the excavated quarry, as in the lower right corner of this photo. (University Archives)
Just past the dormitory, Gateway House, are the mathematical steps to the lower campus/ former quarry: 12 steps times 7 sets = ?. And what a view from the top!
Punahou streets purports to be the first building to have received the first stones from the quarry.
The University of Hawai‘i bought the land in 1953, with Klum Gym (Stop 26 ) as its first building in 1957.

Sugar Loaf – Hawaiian, Pu‘u Kākea (the name of a stormy Mānoa wind) – in the back of the valley, produced lava approximately 70,000 years ago that flowed down into the valley resulting in the floor of Mānoa Valley. The lava flow pushed Mānoa Stream to the Diamond Head side of the valley over to the other side and behind the University of Hawai‘i. The lower edge of the flow created the beautiful basalt lava that was dug out at the Mō‘ili‘ili Quarry, now the lower campus. The 50-foot-high wall, separating the lower campus from the upper campus is visible as you walk down the stairs and from the parking structure.
Birds

Observe the elegant White Terns, a seabird, in the Kukui tree. The Terns do not make nests; rather, the egg is hatched on the Y branch of a tree, often a Kukui tree, such as this one. The White Terns are the official bird of Honolulu. The blue ribbon at the base of the tree alerts us to the presence of these magical birds.
The larger white birds strolling and strutting around are Egrets.
From the ‘ili of Kānewai, where the lo‘i is located, you are now entering the ‘ili of Piliamo‘o.
This quarry pond is ground water that seeps up from the underground waters in the area, reminiscent of the springs and streams in this area.
The White Terns, since they are seabirds, feed on fish, not worms. Mama bird flies out to the ocean, scoops up small fish and feeds her chick.

With the practice fields, known as Cooke Field, on the Diamond Head side of the walkway and the tennis courts on the ‘Ewa side, continue makai around the Rainbow Wahine Softball Stadium. Turn ‘Ewa after the Softball Stadium, walking on the mauka side of the football field toward the dome of Stan Sheriff Center.

Listen and look for a 3 X 3 grate in the middle of the road to hear the rushing water! This is an underground stream – from the mountains on its way to the ocean. Imagine the streams that were once here!
21A ROTC buildings

Follow the purple line on the map to the ROTC headquarters. The ROTC (Reserve Officers’ Training Corps) Headquarters are on the makai-Diamond Head section of this lower campus. If you would like to visit (and see a wooden Warrior statue), walk out Diamond Head along Kalele (‘the flight’) Road in the shade of the Rainbow Shower trees. The road comes out on Lower Campus Road by turning Diamond Head a little, then makai-‘Ewa to the ROTC buildings on the Diamond Head side of the road.

There are also memorials to the University of Hawai‘i Warriors who perished in World War II, Vietnam War, and Iraq/Afghanistan Wars. Do sit for a while in the shade of the Plumeria trees to contemplate the warriors’ sacrifice and heroism. But then come back to the original pathway.
Kalele Road leads to the Diamond Head roadway for the lower campus.
There are also several university departments here in the (former) quarry, including Speech Pathology and Audiology, and Center on Disability Studies.
Les Murakami Stadium is named after the legendary baseball Hawai‘i Rainbow Warriors’ coach who won 1,079 games.
Enjoy a leisurely walk around the Asian-styled garden on the lower level of the Athletic Center.
‘Ili of Pa‘akea
You are now entering the ‘ili of Pa‘akea, ‘coral bed, limestone’
Continue walking around (mauka-‘Ewa) the Clarence T. C. Ching Athletics Complex, with the palm frond motif. Clarence Ching
was a businessman and philanthropist. This athletic complex was built in 2015 and includes space for Hawai‘i beach volleyball, cross country, women’s soccer, track and field, and the football field.
Previously, the area was known as Cooke Field, but Cooke Field now refers to the grass football and soccer practice fields.
As of the 2021-2022 season, the University of Hawai‘i football team began playing on this renovated field as their home turf. Come watch the Warriors! Lē‘ahi reigns supreme in the background!
Continue on the pathway at the Ching Field between the football field and the parking garage toward the Hawai‘i Athletics building and the dome of Stan
Sherriff Center. The low building with the brown roof is Klum Gym (Stop 26 ).

Walk around on the ground floor at the Stan Sheriff Center where it’s nice and cool – out of the Hawaiian sun –and enjoy the peaceful and contemplative Asian style rock gardens and stone lanterns. The center is named after a well-loved University of Hawai‘i athletic director (from 1983 until his death in 1993).

Continue to walk around and through the ground floor to Lower Campus Road. But before exiting the building, go up the flight of stairs to SimpliFi Arena to see some interesting works of art, especially the sculptures:

• Rainbow spirit by Babs Miyano-Young – on the makai-Diamond Head side • Hula by Mataumu Toelupe Alisa – a ceramic tile mural on the upper floor outdoor hallway • Rainbows by Shige Yamada –on the mauka-‘Ewa side
Then come back down the stairs to the aquatic complex.

On the Diamond Head side of the Stan Sheriff Center is the pool: Duke Kahanamoku Aquatic Complex, named after Hawai‘i’s local golden boy. Duke Paoa Kahanamoku (1890-1968) was a fullblooded Hawaiian, who was raised in Waikīkī. He was well-loved in Hawai‘i, not only for winning Olympic silver and gold Are you able to figure out why this set of sculptures is called “Rainbows”? The artist, Shige Yamada, created “Storyteller” in Waikīkī as well as “Maui” at the Kahului, Maui airport. medals in swimming, but also as a surfer, hero, movie actor, and Honolulu sheriff. Local lore relates that in 1917 the Duke rode the longest wave ever: a mile and a quarter on a 35-foot wave!
25A Mō‘ili‘ili Gateway

The purple line leads to Mō‘ili‘ili Gateway. The toll booth across the way is Mō‘ili‘ili Gateway, the roadway to the neighborhood of Mō‘ili‘ili, graced by Loulu, the native Palm tree; Kou trees with their orange blossoms; and the half-flowers on the Naupaka bushes.

If you would like to walk out of the lower campus this way, walk to Varsity Place straight ahead, under the freeway to Kalo Place then to S. King Street or ‘Ewa on Varsity Place to University Avenue. (You can continue with the business district Mō‘ili‘ili Walk IX.)
Walk ‘Ewa-mauka along Lower Campus Road up to Dole Street.

As you walk out of the quarry past the parking structure, notice the face of the quarry. In some places the lava is covered with a coating of cement; in other places, by a net to avoid the falling boulders on students and cars.
If you missed the sculptures on the second level of Stan Sheriff Center, walk up the steps on the Diamond Head side of the walkway to see them now.

Down below in the quarry between the arena and the parking garage is the original gym, Klum gym, with the brown roof. The gym, built in 1957, is named after the legendary athletic director and football coach from 1921 to 1940, Otto “Proc” Klum (1875-1944). He was the first University of Hawai‘i coach to take his team to the mainland: they traveled by steamer. The team was called the “Rainbows” because in a 1922-23 season game when a rainbow appeared, the team scored. However, more recently the football team’s name was changed to the Warriors/Rainbow Warriors.

stops.title: William S. Richardson School of Law

blocks.text: The low-rise buildings on the makaiDiamond Head side of Lower Campus Road and Dole Street are the University of Hawai‘i’s law school buildings. The law school was first established in temporary buildings in 1973.
The wood of the elegant bench is from a 100-year-old Mango tree.

Look for the wooden bench outside the nearby building, just past the parking lot. After your trek through lower campus, relax on this 100-year-old Mango wood from the ahupua‘a of Kamananui, O‘ahu (near Waialua). Enjoy the array of local plants: Ti, ground-cover Pohinahina, Plumeria, and Kou trees.

William S. Richardson School of Law, established in 1973, is named for former Hawai‘i State Supreme Court Chief Justice William S. Richardson (1919 – 2010). Richardson was the first Lieutenant Governor of Hawaiian heritage. As a child he was harassed while playing on at-the -time private beaches. One of his rulings was to ensure public access to all beach areas. Thanks to Chief Justice Richardson there are no private beaches in Hawai‘i.
Mauoki Heiau

The music buildings, on the ‘Ewa side of Lower Campus Road, were built in stages: first 1958 (the main building), then 1962 (Orvis Auditorium), and in 1972 more studios. The music department had the foresight to be the first (1993) to honor a Kanaka ‘Ōiwi, a native Hawaiian, on an academic building: Dorothy M. Kahananui.
Mauoki Heiau

You are on or near the area of Mauoki Heiau. A heiau is a sanctuary or a place of worship constructed of lava boulders. Mauoki Heiau was one of many heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī. This heiau would have been in the vicinity between the Music Building at the University of Hawai‘i and the top of the quarry. Two large loko, ‘pond,’ were located directly makai.
The only restored and intact heiau in the ahupua‘a of Waikīkī is in Mānoa Valley, which you can visit on Mānoa Walk X. Kūka‘ō‘ō Heiau has been completely reconstructed at the Mānoa Heritage Center.

Although there is no longer a heiau in this area, there are 3 ahu on the upper campus that harken back to the days of old. The ahu is an altar honoring a person or place. One ahu is on Wise Field, the lawn fronting University Avenue; another, in the courtyard at Bachman Hall. Ke Ahu o Wise (the altar on Wise lawn) was set up to protest the telescope that was planned for Mauna Kea on Hawai‘i Island. A third ahu on campus is at the Queen Lili‘uokalani Student Services building.

Now that you are out of the quarry, you can orient yourself by looking around: on the ‘Ewa side is University Avenue. You can continue with the Upper Campus Walk XI that begins at the corner of University Avenue and Dole Street.
The Kahananui building is the first academic building on campus to be named after a Hawaiian.
WALK: 1
HAWAIIAN GLOSSARY

ahi fire ‘ahi yellow-fin tuna ahupua‘a a large, historic-based land division that extends from the mountain crest to the ocean. The boundaries are often marked by a pile of stones (ahu) topped with the head or an image of a pig (pua‘a).

‘ai food, to eat ‘āina land akamai smart akua deity (god) ala way ali‘i chief, royalty aloha love, affection, compassion ‘alohi to shine, bright ‘āpua fish trap, handle ‘au‘au to bathe ‘aumakua spirit ‘Ewa in a westerly direction; away from Diamond Head, toward the plantation town of ‘Ewa (past Pearl Harbor) hale house hali‘a remembrance Hāloa the common ancestor of the Hawaiian people. hau native Hibiscus; dew heiau religious structure hewa not correct, mistake; hua fruit hula native dance i to (marks the object ) ihe spear ‘ike knowledge ‘ili small land section within the ahupua‘a ‘ili‘ili pebble ‘ilima small yellow-orange native flower/ shrub ‘io hawk ‘iu heights iwi bone ka (and ke) the kaha to soar kahi place kahakai seaside kahakō macron, the long mark over a vowel to indicate lengthening the sound kahuna (kāhuna, plural) a professional specialist in religion, education, or medicine Hawaiian words are followed by English translations. For more detailed translations, please refer to the Hawaiian Dictionary by Mary Kawena Pukui and Samuel H. Elbert.
